problem: Find all positive integers \( n \) for which \( n^{n-1}-1 \) is divisible by \( 2^{2015} \), but not by \( 2^{2016} \).
solution:
Solution.  
Write \(v_{2}(m)\) for the exponent of the highest power of \(2\) that divides an integer \(m\)
(the 2–adic valuation of \(m\)).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
1.  The parity of \(n\).

If \(n\) is even, then \(n^{\,n-1}\) is the power of an even number with an odd
exponent, hence is even, so \(n^{\,n-1}-1\) is odd and therefore not divisible by
\(2^{2015}\).
Thus every admissible \(n\) must be odd.

Because \(n\) is odd, the exponent \(n-1\) is even; this will allow us to use LTE.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
2.  Lifting the Exponent for the prime \(2\).

For odd \(a\) and even \(m\) the following version of the
Lifting-the-Exponent Lemma is standard and well–known:

\[
v_{2}\!\bigl(a^{m}-1\bigr)=v_{2}(a-1)+v_{2}(a+1)+v_{2}(m)-1 .
\tag{LTE}
\]

Take \(a=n\) (odd) and \(m=n-1\) (even).  
Set

\[
x:=v_{2}(n-1), \qquad
y:=v_{2}(n+1).
\]

Applying (LTE) gives

\[
v_{2}\!\bigl(n^{\,n-1}-1\bigr)=x+y+x-1=2x+y-1.
\tag{1}
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
3.  Relating \(x\) and \(y\).

Because \(n-1\) and \(n+1\) differ by \(2\),
they cannot both be divisible by \(4\).  Hence at most one of \(x\) and \(y\)
can exceed \(1\); in fact

\[
\min\{x,y\}=1.
\tag{2}
\]

(Indeed, if \(x\ge 2\) and \(y\ge 2\) then both \(n-1\) and \(n+1\) would be multiples
of \(4\), whence their difference \(2\) would also be a multiple of \(4\),
a contradiction.)

--------------------------------------------------------------------
4.  Solving for \(x\) and \(y\).

Our requirement is

\[
v_{2}\!\bigl(n^{\,n-1}-1\bigr)=2015,
\]

so by (1)

\[
2x+y-1=2015 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad 2x+y=2016.
\tag{3}
\]

Using (2) we now distinguish the two possible positions of the
minimal valuation.

•  If \(x=1\) then (3) gives \(y=2014\).

•  If \(y=1\) then (3) gives \(2x+1=2016\), so \(2x=2015\),
impossible because the left–hand side is even.

Therefore the only possibility is

\[
x=1,\qquad y=2014.
\tag{4}
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
5.  Describing \(n\).

Condition (4) is equivalent to

\[
\begin{cases}
v_{2}(n-1)=1 &\Longrightarrow\; n-1=2\,a,\; a\ {\rm odd},\\[2pt]
v_{2}(n+1)=2014 &\Longrightarrow\; n+1=2^{2014}\,b,\; b\ {\rm odd}.
\end{cases}
\]

Eliminate \(n\):

\[
2a+1 = 2^{2014}b -1
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
a = 2^{2013}b -1.
\]

Because \(b\) is odd, \(2^{2013}b\) is even, hence \(a\) is indeed odd as required.
Conversely any odd \(b\ge 1\) yields an odd \(a\).
Substituting back gives the set of all solutions

\[
\boxed{\,n = 2^{2014}\,b - 1 \quad\text{with } b\ \text{odd positive}\,}.
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
6.  Verification.

Take \(n=2^{2014}b-1\) with odd \(b\).

•  \(n\) is odd and \(n>1\).  
•  From the construction,
  \(v_{2}(n-1)=1\) and \(v_{2}(n+1)=2014\).
•  Hence by (1) we have
  \(v_{2}\!\bigl(n^{\,n-1}-1\bigr)=2\cdot1+2014-1=2015\).

Thus \(2^{2015}\) divides \(n^{\,n-1}-1\) while \(2^{2016}\) does not.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
7.  Conclusion.

The complete set of positive integers \(n\) for which
\(2^{2015}\mid n^{\,n-1}-1\) but \(2^{2016}\nmid n^{\,n-1}-1\) is

\[
\{\,2^{2014}k-1 \;|\; k\in\mathbb{Z}_{>0},\; k\ \text{odd}\,\}.
\]

(The smallest such integer is \(2^{2014}-1\).)
ground_truth_solution:
Solution. Since $n$ must be odd, write $n=2^{d} u+1$, where $u, d \in \mathbf{N}$ and $u$ is odd. Now

$$
n^{n-1}-1=\left(n^{2^{d}}-1\right)(\underbrace{n^{2^{d} \cdot(u-1)}+\cdots+n^{2^{d} \cdot 1}+1}_{u})
$$
and hence $2^{2015} \|\left(n^{n-1}-1\right)$ iff $2^{2015} \|\left(n^{2^{d}}-1\right)$. (The notation $p^{k} \| m$ denotes that $p^{k} \mid m$ and $p^{k+1} \nmid m$.)

We factorise once more:

$$
\begin{aligned}
n^{2^{d}}-1 & =(n-1)(n+1) \underbrace{\left(n^{2}+1\right) \cdots\left(n^{2^{d-1}}+1\right)}_{d-1} \\
& =2^{d} u \cdot 2\left(2^{d-1} u+1\right) \underbrace{\left(n^{2}+1\right) \cdots\left(n^{2^{d-1}}+1\right)}_{d-1}
\end{aligned}
$$

If $k \geq 1$, then $2 \| n^{2^{k}}+1$, and so from the above

$$
2^{2 d} \| 2^{d} u \cdot 2 \cdot \underbrace{\left(n^{2}+1\right) \cdots\left(n^{2^{d-1}}+1\right)}_{d-1} \quad \text { and } \quad 2^{2015-2 d} \|\left(2^{d-1} u+1\right)
$$

It is easy to see that this is the case exactly when $d=1$ and $u=2^{2013} v-1$, where $v$ is odd.
Hence the required numbers are those of the form

$$
n=2\left(2^{2013} v-1\right)+1=2^{2014} v-1
$$
for $v$ a positive odd number.
llm_summary: The proof applies the 2-adic valuation and the Lifting-the-Exponent Lemma to obtain \(v_{2}(n^{n-1}-1)=2x+y-1\) for \(x=v_{2}(n-1)\), \(y=v_{2}(n+1)\). Observing that one of \(x,y\) must equal 1 and solving \(2x+y=2016\) yields \(x=1, y=2014\). Hence \(n-1=2a\), \(n+1=2^{2014}b\) with \(a,b\) odd, which leads to the parametrization \(n=2^{2014}b-1\) for odd \(b\). A direct check shows these give exactly \(v_{2}(n^{n-1}-1)=2015\).

llm_issues.description: The proof never treats the case \(n=1\). Since \(1^{1-1}-1=0\) is divisible by all powers of 2, one must explicitly exclude \(n=1\) to ensure that \(2^{2016}\nmid n^{n-1}-1\), but this is not addressed.
llm_issues.text: If \(n\) is even, then \(n^{\,n-1}\) is the power of an even number with an odd exponent, hence is even, so \(n^{\,n-1}-1\) is odd and therefore not divisible by \(2^{2015}\). Thus every admissible \(n\) must be odd.

llm_issues.description: The argument omits the needed observation that \(n\) odd implies \(n-1\) and \(n+1\) are each divisible by 2 (so \(x,y\ge1\)), which is required before concluding that exactly one of them equals 1.
llm_issues.text: Because \(n-1\) and \(n+1\) differ by \(2\), they cannot both be divisible by \(4\). Hence at most one of \(x\) and \(y\) can exceed \(1\); in fact \(\min\{x,y\}=1\).

problem: A cube consists of \(4^{3}\) unit cubes each containing an integer. At each move, you choose a unit cube and increase by \(1\) all the integers in the neighboring cubes having a face in common with the chosen cube. Is it possible to reach a position where all the \(4^{3}\) integers are divisible by 3, no matter what the starting position is?
solution:
Let \(N = 4^3 = 64\). Let \(x \in \mathbb{Z}^N\) be the vector of integers in the \(N\) unit cubes. A move consists of choosing a unit cube \(c_j\) and adding 1 to the integers in all cubes adjacent to \(c_j\) (sharing a face). Let \(m_j\) be the number of times the cube \(c_j\) is chosen.
After a sequence of moves, the new state \(x'\) is given by \(x'_k = x_k + \sum_{j=1}^N A_{kj} m_j\), where \(A\) is the adjacency matrix of the graph \(G\) whose vertices are the unit cubes and edges connect adjacent cubes. The entries \(A_{kj}\) are 1 if cube \(k\) is a neighbor of cube \(j\), and 0 otherwise. Note that \(A\) is a symmetric matrix with zeros on the diagonal.

We want to know if it's possible to reach a state \(x'\) where all entries are divisible by 3, for any starting position \(x\). This is equivalent to asking if, for any \(x \in \mathbb{Z}^N\), there exist non-negative integers \(m_1, \dots, m_N\) such that \(x' \equiv 0 \pmod 3\).
Working in \(\mathbb{Z}_3^N\), the problem becomes: for any \(x \in \mathbb{Z}_3^N\), does \(x + Am \equiv 0 \pmod 3\) have a solution \(m \in \mathbb{Z}_3^N\)? (The non-negativity of \(m_j\) can be ignored when working modulo 3, as if \(m_j \equiv r_j \pmod 3\) is a solution, we can choose \(m_j = r_j + 3k_j\) for \(k_j\) large enough to make \(m_j \ge 0\).)
This is equivalent to asking if the equation \(Am \equiv -x \pmod 3\) has a solution \(m\) for every vector \(-x \in \mathbb{Z}_3^N\). This is true if and only if the matrix \(A\) is invertible over the field \(\mathbb{Z}_3\). This, in turn, is equivalent to checking if \(\det(A) \not\equiv 0 \pmod 3\).

The graph \(G\) is the \(4 \times 4 \times 4\) grid graph. The eigenvalues of the adjacency matrix of an \(L_1 \times L_2 \times L_3\) grid graph are known. For an \(L \times L \times L\) grid graph, the eigenvalues are given by:
\[ \lambda_{rst} = 2\cos\left(\frac{\pi r}{L+1}\right) + 2\cos\left(\frac{\pi s}{L+1}\right) + 2\cos\left(\frac{\pi t}{L+1}\right) \]
for \(1 \le r, s, t \le L\).
In our case, \(L=4\), so \(L+1=5\). The eigenvalues are:
\[ \lambda_{rst} = 2\cos\left(\frac{\pi r}{5}\right) + 2\cos\left(\frac{\pi s}{5}\right) + 2\cos\left(\frac{\pi t}{5}\right) \]
for \(1 \le r, s, t \le 4\).

Let's consider the specific eigenvalue \(\lambda_{111}\):
\[ \lambda_{111} = 2\cos\left(\frac{\pi}{5}\right) + 2\cos\left(\frac{\pi}{5}\right) + 2\cos\left(\frac{\pi}{5}\right) = 6\cos\left(\frac{\pi}{5}\right) \]
We know that \(\cos(\pi/5) = \frac{1+\sqrt{5}}{4}\).
So, \(\lambda_{111} = 6 \cdot \frac{1+\sqrt{5}}{4} = 3 \cdot \frac{1+\sqrt{5}}{2}\).
Let \(\phi = \frac{1+\sqrt{5}}{2}\) be the golden ratio. Then \(\lambda_{111} = 3\phi\).

The eigenvalues \(\lambda_{rst}\) are algebraic integers. To show this, note that \(2\cos(k\pi/(L+1)) = e^{ik\pi/(L+1)} + e^{-ik\pi/(L+1)}\). Let \(\zeta_{2(L+1)} = e^{i\pi/(L+1)}\). Then \(2\cos(k\pi/(L+1)) = \zeta_{2(L+1)}^k + \zeta_{2(L+1)}^{-k}\). These are sums of roots of unity, and thus are algebraic integers. The sum of algebraic integers is an algebraic integer, so each \(\lambda_{rst}\) is an algebraic integer.

Specifically, \(\phi = \frac{1+\sqrt{5}}{2}\) is an algebraic integer, as it is a root of the monic polynomial \(x^2 - x - 1 = 0\).
Therefore, \(\lambda_{111} = 3\phi\) is an algebraic integer.
All values \(2\cos(k\pi/5)\) are in the ring \(\mathbb{Z}[\phi]\).
Indeed, \(2\cos(\pi/5) = \phi\).
\(2\cos(2\pi/5) = (2\cos(\pi/5))^2 - 2 = \phi^2 - 2 = (\phi+1)-2 = \phi-1\).
\(2\cos(3\pi/5) = 2\cos(\pi-2\pi/5) = -2\cos(2\pi/5) = -(\phi-1) = 1-\phi\).
\(2\cos(4\pi/5) = 2\cos(\pi-\pi/5) = -2\cos(\pi/5) = -\phi\).
Since all terms \(2\cos(k\pi/5)\) are in \(\mathbb{Z}[\phi]\), all eigenvalues \(\lambda_{rst}\) are elements of \(\mathbb{Z}[\phi]\).

The determinant of \(A\), \(\det(A)\), is the product of all its eigenvalues:
\[ \det(A) = \prod_{r=1}^4 \prod_{s=1}^4 \prod_{t=1}^4 \lambda_{rst} \]
Since \(\lambda_{111} = 3\phi\) is one of these eigenvalues, \(\det(A)\) contains a factor of \(3\phi\).
Let \(X = \prod_{(r,s,t) \ne (1,1,1)} \lambda_{rst}\). Since each \(\lambda_{rst} \in \mathbb{Z}[\phi]\), their product \(X\) is also in \(\mathbb{Z}[\phi]\).
So \(\det(A) = 3\phi \cdot X\). This means \(\det(A)\) is an element of the principal ideal \((3\phi)\) in \(\mathbb{Z}[\phi]\).
Since \(\phi \in \mathbb{Z}[\phi]\), \((3\phi) \subseteq (3)\). So \(\det(A)\) is an element of the ideal \((3)\) in \(\mathbb{Z}[\phi]\).
This means that \(\det(A)\) can be written as \(3\psi\) for some \(\psi \in \mathbb{Z}[\phi]\).
Let \(\psi = a+b\phi\) for some integers \(a, b \in \mathbb{Z}\), because \(\mathbb{Z}[\phi] = \{a+b\phi \mid a,b \in \mathbb{Z}\}\).
So \(\det(A) = 3(a+b\phi) = 3a + 3b\phi\).
We also know that \(\det(A)\) must be an integer, as \(A\) is a matrix with integer entries.
Since \(\det(A)\) is an integer, and \(3a\) is an integer, \(3b\phi\) must also be such that the sum is an integer. As \(\phi = (1+\sqrt{5})/2\) is irrational, \(3b\) must be zero for \(3a+3b\phi\) to be an integer. Thus \(b=0\).
Therefore, \(\det(A) = 3a\) for some integer \(a\).
This implies that \(\det(A)\) is a multiple of 3 in \(\mathbb{Z}\).
So, \(\det(A) \equiv 0 \pmod 3\).

Since \(\det(A) \equiv 0 \pmod 3\), the matrix \(A\) is singular over \(\mathbb{Z}_3\).
This means that the columns of \(A\) do not span the entire space \(\mathbb{Z}_3^N\). The image of the linear transformation represented by \(A\) (over \(\mathbb{Z}_3\)), \(\text{Im}(A)\), is a proper subspace of \(\mathbb{Z}_3^N\).
Therefore, there exists a vector \(y \in \mathbb{Z}_3^N\) such that \(y \notin \text{Im}(A)\).
If we choose an initial state \(x_0\) such that \(-x_0 \equiv y \pmod 3\), then \(Am \equiv -x_0 \pmod 3\) has no solution for \(m\).
Thus, it is not possible to reach a state where all integers are divisible by 3 for an arbitrary starting position.

The answer is No.

The final answer is $\boxed{No}$.
feedback: Quite heavy, but should be correct (seems to correspond to the right combinatorial settings).
ground_truth_solution: Solution. Two unit cubes with a common face are called neighbours. Colour the cubes either black or white in such a way that two neighbours always have different colours. Notice that the integers in the white cubes only change when a black cube is chosen. Now recolour the white cubes that have exactly $4$ neighbours and make them green. If we look at a random black cube it has either $0,3$ or $6$ white neighbours. Hence if we look at the sum of the integers in the white cubes, it changes by $0,3$ or $6$ in each turn. From this it follows that if this sum is not divisible by $3$ at the beginning, it will never be, and none of the integers in the white cubes is divisible by $3$ at any state.
llm_summary: The proof encodes moves on the 4×4×4 cube by an adjacency matrix A and a move-count vector m, reducing the problem to solving A m≡−x (mod 3). It observes solvability for all x mod 3 is equivalent to A being invertible over 𝔽₃, i.e. det(A)≢0 (mod 3). It then cites a known spectral formula for the eigenvalues of the 3D grid graph, identifies one eigenvalue λ₁₁₁=3φ (φ the golden ratio), and uses algebraic-integer and ideal arguments in ℤ[φ] to show det(A) is divisible by 3. Hence A is singular mod 3 and not all initial states can be driven to zeros mod 3, so the answer is No.

problem: Let \(ABCD\) be a cyclic quadrilateral with \(AB\) and \(CD\) not parallel. Let \(M\) be the midpoint of \(CD\). Let \(P\) be a point inside \(ABCD\) such that \(PA = PB = CM\). Prove that \(AB\), \(CD\), and the perpendicular bisector of \(MP\) are concurrent.
solution:
Proof.  Let Γ denote the circumcircle of the cyclic quadrilateral ABCD.  Let ω_C be the circle with center M and radius \(MC\), and let ω_P be the circle with center P and radius \(PA=PB=MC\).  We will show:

(1)  The radical axis of Γ and ω_C is the line CD.  
(2)  The radical axis of Γ and ω_P is the line AB.  
(3)  The radical axis of ω_C and ω_P is the perpendicular bisector of MP.

By the Radical‐Axis (or Radical‐Center) Theorem, any three circles have their three pairwise radical axes concurrent, so from (1), (2), (3) it will follow immediately that the lines CD, AB, and the perpendicular bisector of MP are concurrent.

---

Step 1.  CD is the radical axis of Γ and ω_C.

Let \(X\) be an arbitrary point on line \(CD\).  Then the power of \(X\) with respect to Γ is
\[
\Pow_{\Gamma}(X)\;=\;X C\;\cdot\;X D.
\]
Since \(M\) is the midpoint of \(CD\), if we regard signed (oriented) lengths along the line \(CD\), then
\[
X C\;=\;X M + M C,
\qquad
X D\;=\;X M - M C,
\]
and hence
\[
X C\;\cdot\;X D
\;=\;
\bigl(XM + MC\bigr)\bigl(XM - MC\bigr)
\;=\;
XM^2 \;-\;MC^2.
\]
But \(MC\) is exactly the radius of ω_C, so
\[
XM^2 - MC^2
\;=\;
\Pow_{\omega_C}(X).
\]
Thus for every \(X\in CD\) we have \(\Pow_{\Gamma}(X)=\Pow_{\omega_C}(X)\), which means that line \(CD\) is indeed the radical axis of Γ and ω_C.

---

Step 2.  AB is the radical axis of Γ and ω_P.

Since \(PA=PB=MC\), the points \(A\) and \(B\) both lie on Γ and also both lie on ω_P.  Hence the two intersection points of Γ and ω_P are \(A\) and \(B\), and by definition their common chord \(AB\) is the radical axis of Γ and ω_P.

---

Step 3.  The perpendicular bisector of MP is the radical axis of ω_C and ω_P.

Let \(X\) be an arbitrary point in the plane.  Then
\[
\Pow_{\omega_C}(X)\;=\;XM^2 - MC^2,
\qquad
\Pow_{\omega_P}(X)\;=\;XP^2 - PA^2.
\]
Since \(MC=PA\), their difference is
\[
\Pow_{\omega_C}(X)-\Pow_{\omega_P}(X)
\;=\;
\bigl(XM^2 - MC^2\bigr)\;-\;\bigl(XP^2 - PA^2\bigr)
\;=\;
XM^2 \;-\;XP^2.
\]
Therefore \(\Pow_{\omega_C}(X)=\Pow_{\omega_P}(X)\) if and only if \(XM^2=XP^2\), i.e.\ if and only if \(X\) is equidistant from \(M\) and \(P\).  The locus of such points is exactly the perpendicular bisector of the segment \(MP\).  Hence that line is the radical axis of ω_C and ω_P.

---

Conclusion.  By the Radical‐Axis Theorem, the three radical axes
\[
\bigl(\Gamma,\omega_C\bigr)\;:\;CD,
\qquad
\bigl(\Gamma,\omega_P\bigr)\;:\;AB,
\qquad
\bigl(\omega_C,\omega_P\bigr)\;:\;\text{perp.\ bisector of }MP
\]
are concurrent.  This is precisely the assertion that the lines \(AB,\;CD\), and the perpendicular bisector of \(MP\) all meet in a common point.  ∎
ground_truth_solution: Solution. Let $\omega$ be the circumcircle of $A B C D$. Let $A B$ and $C D$ intersect at $X$. Let $\omega_{1}$ and $\omega_{2}$ be the circles with centers $P$ and $M$ and with equal radius $P B=M C=r$. The power of $X$ with respect to $\omega$ and $\omega_{1}$ equals $X A \cdot X B$ and with respect to $\omega$ and $\omega_{2} X D \cdot X C$. The latter power also equals $(X M+$ $r)(X M-r)=X M^{2}-r^{2}$. Analogously, the first power is $X P^{2}-r^{2}$. But since $X A \cdot X B=X D \cdot X C$, we must have $X M^{2}=X P^{2}$ or $X M=X P . X$ indeed is on the perpendicular bisector of $P M$, and we are done.
llm_summary: The proof introduces three circles—Γ, the circumcircle of ABCD; ω_C, centered at M with radius MC; and ω_P, centered at P with radius PA=PB=MC—and shows that their pairwise radical axes are exactly CD, AB, and the perpendicular bisector of MP. By the Radical-Axis Theorem, these three lines concur, yielding the desired result.

problem:
For which integers \( n = 1, \ldots, 6 \) does the equation

\[ a^{n} + b^{n} = c^{n} + n \]

have a solution in integers?
solution:
Proof. We check each \(n=1,2,3,4,5,6\) in turn.

1.  \(n=1\).  The equation is
\[
a+b = c+1.
\]
For instance, take \(a=1\), \(b=1\).  Then \(c=1\) satisfies \(1+1=1+1\).  Hence there is an integer solution.

2.  \(n=2\).  The equation is
\[
a^2 + b^2 = c^2 + 2.
\]
For example, \(a=1\), \(b=1\) gives
\[
1^2 + 1^2 = 2,
\]
so we need \(c^2 + 2 = 2\), i.e.\ \(c^2=0\), and one checks \(c=0\) works.  Thus \((a,b,c)=(1,1,0)\) is a solution in integers.

3.  \(n=3\).  The equation is
\[
a^3 + b^3 = c^3 + 3.
\]
Again \(a=1\), \(b=1\) gives \(1+1=2\), so we require \(c^3+3=2\), i.e.\ \(c^3=-1\), whence \(c=-1\).  Thus \((a,b,c)=(1,1,-1)\) is a solution.

Up to now we have exhibited solutions for \(n=1,2,3\).  We now show no solutions exist for \(n=4,5,6\).

4.  \(n=4\).  Assume by contradiction there are integers \(a,b,c\) with
\[
a^4 + b^4 = c^4 + 4.
\]
We work \(\bmod 16\).  A standard check shows
\[
x\equiv 0\pmod2\quad\Longrightarrow\quad x^4\equiv 0\pmod{16},
\qquad
x\equiv 1\pmod2\quad\Longrightarrow\quad x^4\equiv 1\pmod{16}.
\]
Hence for any integer \(x\), \(x^4\equiv0\) or \(1\pmod{16}\).  It follows that
\[
a^4 + b^4 \;\equiv\;0,1,\text{ or }2\pmod{16},
\]
whereas
\[
c^4 + 4 \;\equiv\;4\text{ or }5\pmod{16}.
\]
No residue in \(\{0,1,2\}\) equals one in \(\{4,5\}\).  This contradiction shows there is no integer solution for \(n=4\).

5.  \(n=5\).  Assume
\[
a^5 + b^5 = c^5 + 5.
\]
We work \(\bmod 11\).  By Fermat’s little theorem, for any prime \(p\) and any integer \(x\) with \(p\nmid x\) we have
\[
x^{p-1}\equiv1\pmod p.
\]
Taking \(p=11\), if \(11\nmid x\) then \(x^{10}\equiv1\pmod{11}\), so \((x^5)^2\equiv1\) and hence
\[
x^5\equiv\pm1\pmod{11}.
\]
If \(11\mid x\) then \(x^5\equiv0\pmod{11}\).  In all cases
\[
x^5\pmod{11}\in\{0,\,1,\,10\}.
\]
Therefore
\[
a^5 + b^5 \;\equiv\;
\{0,1,10\} + \{0,1,10\}
\;=\;\{0,1,2,9,10\}\pmod{11},
\]
whereas
\[
c^5 + 5 \;\equiv\; \{0,1,10\} + 5
\;=\;\{5,6,4\}\pmod{11}.
\]
Since
\[
\{0,1,2,9,10\}\;\cap\;\{4,5,6\} \;=\;\emptyset,
\]
we reach a contradiction.  Hence no integer solution exists when \(n=5\).

6.  \(n=6\).  Assume
\[
a^6 + b^6 = c^6 + 6.
\]
We work \(\bmod9\).  There are two cases for an integer \(x\):

– If \(3\mid x\), say \(x=3k\), then
\[
x^6 = (3k)^6 = 3^6\,k^6 = 729\,k^6 \equiv 0\pmod9.
\]

– If \(3\nmid x\), then \(\gcd(x,3)=1\), so \(x^2\equiv1\pmod3\).  Write \(x^2=1+3m\) for some integer \(m\).  Then
\[
x^6 = (x^2)^3 = (1+3m)^3
= 1 + 3\cdot3m + 3\,(3m)^2 + (3m)^3
= 1 + 9\bigl(m+3m^2+m^3\bigr)
\equiv 1\pmod9.
\]
Thus in every case
\[
x^6 \equiv 0\text{ or }1\pmod9.
\]
It follows that
\[
a^6 + b^6 \;\equiv\;0,1,\text{ or }2\pmod9,
\]
whereas
\[
c^6 + 6 \;\equiv\; (0\text{ or }1) + 6
\;=\;6\text{ or }7\pmod9.
\]
No element of \(\{0,1,2\}\) equals one of \(\{6,7\}\).  This contradiction shows there is no integer solution for \(n=6\).

Conclusion.  The only values of \(n\in\{1,2,3,4,5,6\}\) for which
\[
a^n + b^n = c^n + n
\]
admits an integer solution are
\[
\boxed{n=1,2,3}.
\]
feedback: The solution is correct and clear
ground_truth_solution:
Solution. A solution clearly exists for $n=1,2,3$ :

$$
1^{1}+0^{1}=0^{1}+1, \quad 1^{2}+1^{2}=0^{2}+2, \quad 1^{3}+1^{3}=(-1)^{3}+3 .
$$

We show that for $n=4,5,6$ there is no solution.
For $n=4$, the equation $a^{4}+b^{4}=c^{4}+4$ may be considered modulo $8$. Since each fourth power $x^{4} \equiv 0,1 \bmod 8$, the expression $a^{4}+b^{4}-c^{4}$ can never be congruent to $4$.
For $n=5$, consider the equation $a^{5}+b^{5}=c^{5}+5$ modulo $11$. As $x^{5} \equiv 0$ or $\equiv \pm 1 \bmod 11$ (This can be seen by Fermat's Little Theorem or by direct computation), $a^{5}+b^{5}-c^{5}$ cannot be congruent to $5$.
The case $n=6$ is similarly dismissed by considering the equation modulo $13$.
llm_summary: The proof shows existence for n=1,2,3 by explicit examples, and for n=4,5,6 derives contradictions via modular arithmetic—working mod 16 for n=4, mod 11 for n=5, and mod 9 for n=6—to show the residue sets of aⁿ+bⁿ and cⁿ+n do not intersect.

problem:
Find all positive integers \( n \) for which

\[
3 x^{n} + n(x+2) - 3 \geq n x^{2}
\]

holds for all real numbers \( x \).
solution:
Let  

\[
f_{n}(x)=3x^{n}-n\,x^{2}+n\,x+2n-3 ,\qquad n\in\mathbb Z_{>0},\;x\in\mathbb R .
\]

The inequality in the statement is exactly  

\[
f_{n}(x)\ge 0\qquad\text{for every }x\in\mathbb R .
\]

We determine those integers \(n\) for which this is true.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
1.  Odd values of \(n\) do not work  
--------------------------------------------------------------------

Take \(x=-1\).  
If \(n\) is odd, then \((-1)^{n}=-1\).  Hence

\[
f_{n}(-1)=3(-1)-n(1)+n(-1)+2n-3=-3-n-n+2n-3=-6<0 .
\]

Thus the required inequality is violated.  
Therefore

\[
\boxed{\text{every admissible }n\text{ must be even.}}
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
2.  From now on \(n\) is an even positive integer  
--------------------------------------------------------------------

For such an \(n\) we investigate the global minimum of \(f_{n}\).

2.1  Derivative and a convenient auxiliary function  

\[
f_{n}'(x)=3n\,x^{n-1}-2n\,x+n
         =n\bigl(3x^{\,n-1}-2x+1\bigr)
         =:n\,g(x).
\]

Because \(n>0\), the sign of \(f_{n}'\) is the sign of  

\[
g(x)=3x^{\,n-1}-2x+1 .
\]

Recall that \(n-1\) is odd (since \(n\) is even).

2.2  Sign of \(g\)

We distinguish three ranges.

a)  \(x<-1\).  
Write \(x=-t\) with \(t>1\).  Then \(x^{\,n-1}=(-t)^{\,n-1}=-t^{\,n-1}\) and

\[
g(x)= -3t^{\,n-1}+2t+1
     \le -3t+2t+1
     = 1-t<0 .
\]

b)  \(-1<x<0\).  
Put \(x=-t\) with \(0<t<1\) to obtain

\[
g(x)= -3t^{\,n-1}+2t+1
     \ge -3t+2t+1
     = 1-t>0 .
\]

c)  \(x\ge 0\).  
Here \(g\) is convex because  

\[
g''(x)=3(n-1)(n-2)\,x^{\,n-3}\ge 0\quad (x\ge 0).
\]

Hence \(g\) has at most one stationary point on \([0,\infty)\).  
Solving \(g'(x)=0\),

\[
3(n-1)x^{\,n-2}-2=0\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
x_{0}=\Bigl(\tfrac{2}{3(n-1)}\Bigr)^{\!1/(n-2)}.
\]

Because \(n\ge 2\) we have \(0<x_{0}<\sqrt{2/3}<1\).  
Using \(x_{0}^{\,n-2}=2/[3(n-1)]\),

\[
\begin{aligned}
g(x_{0})
 &=3x_{0}^{\,n-1}-2x_{0}+1
 =3x_{0}\,x_{0}^{\,n-2}-2x_{0}+1  \\
 &=3x_{0}\Bigl(\frac{2}{3(n-1)}\Bigr)-2x_{0}+1
 =\frac{2x_{0}}{n-1}-2x_{0}+1  \\
 &=1-2x_{0}\frac{n-2}{n-1}.
\end{aligned}
\]

Since \(x_{0}<1\) and \(\tfrac{n-2}{n-1}<1\),

\[
g(x_{0})>1-2= -1.
\]

But \(g(0)=1>0\) and \(g\) is convex on \([0,\infty)\); hence its unique minimum
\(g(x_{0})\) must in fact be positive.  Consequently \(g(x)>0\) for every
\(x\ge 0\).

Combining a), b), c) we have proved

\[
g(x)<0\;(x<-1),\qquad g(-1)=0,\qquad g(x)>0\;(x>-1).
\]

2.3  Monotonicity and the minimum of \(f_{n}\)

Because \(f_{n}'(x)=n\,g(x)\),

•  \(f_{n}'(x)<0\) for \(x<-1\);  
•  \(f_{n}'(-1)=0\);  
•  \(f_{n}'(x)>0\) for \(x>-1\).

Thus \(f_{n}\) is strictly decreasing on \((-\infty,-1]\), strictly
increasing on \([-1,\infty)\), and attains its global minimum at \(x=-1\).

2.4  Value at the minimum  

Since \(n\) is even, \((-1)^{n}=1\), and

\[
f_{n}(-1)=3\cdot 1-n\cdot 1+n(-1)+2n-3
          =3-n-n+2n-3
          =0 .
\]

Therefore \(f_{n}(x)\ge 0\) for all real \(x\), with equality only at
\(x=-1\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
3.  Conclusion  
--------------------------------------------------------------------

The inequality is satisfied for every even positive integer \(n\) and for no
odd positive integer \(n\).  Hence the complete set of solutions is

\[
\boxed{\{\,n\in\mathbb Z_{>0}\mid n\text{ is even}\,\}}.
\]

(One may check separately that for \(n=2\) the polynomial reduces to
\(f_{2}(x)=(x+1)^{2}\ge 0\), in perfect agreement with the general result.)
ground_truth_solution:
Solution. We show that the inequality holds for even $n$ and only for them.
If $n$ is odd, the for $x=-1$ the left hand side of the inequality equals $n-6$ while the right hand side is $n$. So the inequality is not true for $x=-1$ for any odd $n$. So now assume that $n$ is even. Since $|x| \geq x$, it is enough to prove $3 x^{n}+2 n-3 \geq n x^{2}+n|x|$ for all $x$ or equivalently that $3 x^{n}+(2 n-3) \geq n x^{2}+n x$ for $x \geq 0$. Now the AGM-inequality gives
$$
2 x^{n}+(n-2)=x^{n}+x^{n}+1+\cdots+1 \geq n\left(x^{n} \cdot x^{n} \cdot 1^{n-2}\right)^{\frac{1}{n}}=n x^{2}
$$

and similarly

$$
x^{n}+(n-1) \geq n\left(x^{n} \cdot 1^{n-1}\right)^{\frac{1}{n}}=n x
$$

Adding (1) and (2) yields the claim.
llm_summary: The proof first rules out odd n by showing the inequality fails at x=–1. For even n it sets fₙ(x)=3xⁿ–n x²+n x+2n–3, computes fₙ'(x)=n(3xⁿ⁻¹–2x+1)=n g(x), and shows g(x)<0 for x<–1, g(–1)=0, and g(x)>0 for x>–1. Hence fₙ decreases on (–∞,–1], increases on [–1,∞), attains its minimum fₙ(–1)=0, and so the inequality holds exactly for even n.

llm_issues.description: The proof only establishes g(x₀)>–1, then incorrectly concludes g(x₀)>0 from convexity and g(0)>0. Convexity plus positivity at one point does not guarantee the minimum is positive.
llm_issues.text: But g(0)=1>0 and g is convex on [0,\infty); hence its unique minimum g(x₀) must in fact be positive.

llm_issues.description: The formula for x₀ involves division by n–2, which is undefined when n=2. The proof does not treat n=2 in this part of the argument.
The inequalities t^{n-1}≥t and t^{n-1}≤t are used without justification, although they follow from the monotonicity of powers.
The proof relies heavily on calculus (derivatives and convexity) rather than the elementary AM–GM approach suggested by the original solution; this may be stronger machinery than intended.

problem: Let \( P \) be a point inside the acute angle \(\angle BAC\). Suppose that \(\angle ABP = \angle ACP = 90^\circ\). The points \( D \) and \( E \) are on the segments \( BA \) and \( CA \), respectively, such that \( BD = BP \) and \( CP = CE \). The points \( F \) and \( G \) are on the segments \( AC \) and \( AB \), respectively, such that \( DF \) is perpendicular to \( AB \) and \( EG \) is perpendicular to \( AC \). Show that \( PF = PG \).
solution:
To prove that $ PF = PG $ in the given geometric configuration, we proceed using coordinate geometry and vector analysis to ensure the result holds in general.

---

### **Setup and Coordinate Assignment**

We place the vertex $ A $ at the origin $(0, 0)$, and define the sides of the acute angle $ \angle BAC $ as follows:
- Side $ AB $ lies along the x-axis.
- Side $ AC $ lies in the first quadrant, with equation $ y = kx $, where $ k > 0 $ (since the angle is acute).

Let point $ P $ be inside $ \angle BAC $, with coordinates $ (p, q) $, where $ p > 0 $, $ q > 0 $, and $ q < kp $ (ensuring that $ P $ lies inside the angle).

---

### **Step 1: Coordinates of Points $ B $ and $ C $**

- **Point $ B $** is the foot of the perpendicular from $ P $ to $ AB $. Since $ AB $ is horizontal, $ B = (p, 0) $.
- **Point $ C $** is the foot of the perpendicular from $ P $ to $ AC $. Using the formula for the foot of a perpendicular from a point to a line, we find:
  $$
  C = \left( \frac{p + kq}{k^2 + 1}, \frac{k(p + kq)}{k^2 + 1} \right)
  $$

---

### **Step 2: Coordinates of Points $ D $ and $ E $**

- **Point $ D $** lies on segment $ BA $ such that $ BD = BP $. Since $ BP = q $, and $ BA $ is horizontal, moving left from $ B(p, 0) $ by $ q $ units gives:
  $$
  D = (p - q, 0)
  $$
- **Point $ E $** lies on segment $ CA $ such that $ CE = CP $. Using the parametric form of the line from $ C $ to $ A $, and the fact that $ CE = CP $, we find:
  $$
  E = \left( \frac{p(1 - k) + q(k + 1)}{k^2 + 1}, \frac{k(p(1 - k) + q(k + 1))}{k^2 + 1} \right)
  $$

---

### **Step 3: Coordinates of Points $ F $ and $ G $**

- **Point $ F $** lies on segment $ AC $, and $ DF \perp AB $. Since $ AB $ is horizontal, $ DF $ is vertical. So $ F $ lies directly above $ D $ on line $ AC $, which is $ y = kx $. Thus:
  $$
  F = (p - q, k(p - q))
  $$
- **Point $ G $** lies on segment $ AB $, and $ EG \perp AC $. Since $ AC $ has slope $ k $, the perpendicular $ EG $ has slope $ -\frac{1}{k} $. Using the point-slope form and intersecting with $ AB $ (where $ y = 0 $), we find:
  $$
  G = \left( p(1 - k) + q(k + 1), 0 \right)
  $$

---

### **Step 4: Compute Distances $ PF $ and $ PG $**

We now compute the squared distances $ PF^2 $ and $ PG^2 $ to avoid square roots and simplify comparison.

- **$ PF^2 $:**
  $$
  PF^2 = (p - (p - q))^2 + (q - k(p - q))^2 = q^2 + (q(1 + k) - kp)^2
  $$

- **$ PG^2 $:**
  $$
  PG^2 = (p - (p(1 - k) + q(k + 1)))^2 + q^2 = (pk - q(k + 1))^2 + q^2
  $$

Note that:
$$
pk - q(k + 1) = - (q(k + 1) - pk)
$$
So:
$$
(pk - q(k + 1))^2 = (q(k + 1) - pk)^2
$$

Hence:
$$
PG^2 = (q(k + 1) - pk)^2 + q^2 = PF^2
$$

---

### **Conclusion**

Since $ PF^2 = PG^2 $, it follows that $ PF = PG $, as required.

$$
\boxed{PF = PG}
$$

This completes the proof. The equality holds for any point $ P $ inside the acute angle $ \angle BAC $, regardless of the specific value of $ k $, as long as the construction conditions are satisfied.

problem: Let \( p > 3 \) be a prime and let \( a_{1}, a_{2}, \ldots, a_{\frac{p-1}{2}} \) be a permutation of \( 1, 2, \ldots, \frac{p-1}{2} \). For which \( p \) is it always possible to determine the sequence \( a_{1}, a_{2}, \ldots, a_{\frac{p-1}{2}} \) if for all \( i, j \in \{1, 2, \ldots, \frac{p-1}{2}\} \) with \( i \neq j \) the residue of \( a_{i} a_{j} \) modulo \( p \) is known?
solution:
To determine for which primes $ p > 3 $ it is **always** possible to reconstruct the sequence $ a_1, a_2, \ldots, a_{\frac{p-1}{2}} $, given the residues of all products $ a_i a_j \mod p $ for $ i \ne j $, we must analyze the structure of the multiplicative group modulo $ p $ and the constraints imposed by the problem.

---

### **Understanding the Problem**

We are given a prime $ p > 3 $, and a sequence $ a_1, a_2, \ldots, a_n $, where $ n = \frac{p-1}{2} $, and the sequence is a **permutation** of the set $ \{1, 2, \ldots, n\} $. The key information provided is the set of all products $ a_i a_j \mod p $ for $ i \ne j $, and the question is: **Can we always reconstruct the original sequence from this information?**

This is not about reconstructing the **set** of elements (which is trivially known), but the **sequence** (i.e., the order of the elements), which is the actual permutation.

---

### **Key Observations**

1. **Multiplicative Group Modulo $ p $:**
   - The multiplicative group modulo $ p $, denoted $ \mathbb{F}_p^* $, is cyclic of order $ p-1 $.
   - The set $ \{1, 2, \ldots, n\} $, where $ n = \frac{p-1}{2} $, is the **lower half** of the residues modulo $ p $, and the **upper half** is $ \{n+1, \ldots, p-1\} $.

2. **Uniqueness of Square Roots in the Lower Half:**
   - If $ x, y \in \{1, 2, \ldots, n\} $ and $ x^2 \equiv y^2 \mod p $, then $ x \equiv y \mod p $ or $ x \equiv -y \mod p $.
   - However, since $ x, y \le n = \frac{p-1}{2} $, the only possibility is $ x = y $, because $ -y \equiv p - y > n $, which is not in the lower half.

   **Conclusion:** In the set $ \{1, 2, \ldots, n\} $, each square is **uniquely determined**.

3. **Reconstruction Strategy:**
   - Let $ a_1 = x $, and for $ j \ge 2 $, we have $ a_j = \frac{a_1 a_j}{a_1} = \frac{P_{1j}}{x} \mod p $, where $ P_{1j} = a_1 a_j \mod p $ is known.
   - Using another row, say $ i = 2 $, we can write $ a_2 a_j = \frac{P_{12} P_{1j}}{x^2} \mod p $, and since $ a_2 a_j = P_{2j} $, we get:
     $$
     x^2 \equiv \frac{P_{12} P_{1j}}{P_{2j}} \mod p
     $$
   - This gives a system of equations for $ x^2 $, and since $ x \in \{1, 2, \ldots, n\} $, and square roots are unique in this range, **there is at most one solution** for $ x $ in this set.

4. **When Does This Fail?**
   - For $ n = 2 $, i.e., $ p = 5 $, we only have two elements, and the system of equations does not provide enough constraints to uniquely determine $ x $, leading to **two possible permutations** that yield the same set of products.
   - For $ n \ge 3 $, i.e., $ p \ge 7 $, the system of equations involving $ x^2 $ provides enough constraints to uniquely determine $ x $, and hence the entire sequence.

---

### **Conclusion**

The reconstruction is **always possible** if and only if the number of elements $ n = \frac{p-1}{2} \ge 3 $, which corresponds to primes $ p \ge 7 $.

Thus, the answer is:

$$
\boxed{p \geq 7}
$$

## Solution

Answer: For all primes $p>5$.
When $p=5$ it is clear that it is not possible to determine $a_{1}$ and $a_{2}$ from the residue of $a_{1} a_{2}$ modulo $5$.
Assume that $p>5$. Now $\frac{p-1}{2} \geq 3$. For all $i \in\left\{1,2, \ldots, \frac{p-1}{2}\right\}$ it is possible to choose $j, k \in\left\{1,2, \ldots, \frac{p-1}{2}\right\}$ such that $i, j$ and $k$ are different. Thus we know

$$
a_{i}^{2} \equiv\left(a_{i} a_{j}\right)\left(a_{i} a_{k}\right)\left(a_{j} a_{k}\right)^{-1}(\bmod p) .
$$

The equation $x^{2} \equiv a(\bmod p)$ has exactly one solution in $\left\{1,2, \ldots, \frac{p-1}{2}\right\}$, and hence it is possible to determine $a_{i}$ for all $i$.

problem:
Let \( S \) be the set of all ordered pairs \((a, b)\) of integers with \(0 < 2a < 2b < 2017\) such that \(a^2 + b^2\) is a multiple of 2017. Prove that

\[
\sum_{(a, b) \in S} a = \frac{1}{2} \sum_{(a, b) \in S} b
\]
solution:
Let \( p = 2017 \), which is prime and congruent to 1 modulo 4, ensuring that \(-1\) is a quadratic residue modulo \( p \). Define \( m = \frac{p-1}{2} = 1008 \). The set \( S \) consists of all ordered pairs \( (a, b) \) of integers satisfying \( 0 < 2a < 2b < 2017 \) (which implies \( 1 \leq a < b \leq 1008 \)) and \( a^2 + b^2 \equiv 0 \pmod{p} \).

For each integer \( k \) with \( 1 \leq k \leq m \), define \( a(k) \) as the unique integer such that \( 1 \leq a(k) \leq m \) and \( a(k)^2 \equiv -k^2 \pmod{p} \). This is well-defined because for each \( k \), the equation \( x^2 \equiv -k^2 \pmod{p} \) has two solutions modulo \( p \), one in \( \{1, 2, \dots, m\} \) and the other in \( \{m+1, m+2, \dots, p-1\} \), and we take the solution in \( \{1, 2, \dots, m\} \). The map \( k \mapsto a(k) \) is a fixed-point-free involution on \( \{1, 2, \dots, m\} \), meaning \( a(a(k)) = k \) and \( a(k) \neq k \) for all \( k \).

Define the sets:
- \( A = \{ k \in \{1, 2, \dots, m\} \mid k < a(k) \} \)
- \( B = \{ k \in \{1, 2, \dots, m\} \mid k > a(k) \} \)

The set \( S \) corresponds to the ordered pairs \( (k, a(k)) \) for \( k \in A \), because for each \( k \in A \), \( k < a(k) \) and both are in \( \{1, 2, \dots, m\} \), satisfying the conditions for \( S \). Thus:
\[
\sum_{(a,b) \in S} a = \sum_{k \in A} k =: S_A
\]
\[
\sum_{(a,b) \in S} b = \sum_{k \in A} a(k)
\]

The map \( k \mapsto a(k) \) is a bijection from \( A \) to \( B \) because if \( k \in A \), then \( a(k) \in B \) (since \( k < a(k) \) implies \( a(a(k)) = k < a(k) \), so \( a(k) > a(a(k)) \)), and similarly, if \( l \in B \), then \( a(l) \in A \). Thus:
\[
\sum_{k \in A} a(k) = \sum_{l \in B} l =: S_B
\]

The sum of all integers from 1 to \( m \) is:
\[
S_{\text{total}} = \sum_{j=1}^{m} j = \frac{m(m+1)}{2}
\]
Since \( A \) and \( B \) partition \( \{1, 2, \dots, m\} \) and \( |A| = |B| = \frac{m}{2} \) (as \( m \) is even), we have:
\[
S_A + S_B = S_{\text{total}}
\]
Substituting the expression for \( \sum_{(a,b) \in S} b \):
\[
\sum_{(a,b) \in S} b = S_B = S_{\text{total}} - S_A
\]
The equation to prove is \( \sum_{(a,b) \in S} a = \frac{1}{2} \sum_{(a,b) \in S} b \), which is:
\[
S_A = \frac{1}{2} (S_{\text{total}} - S_A)
\]
Solving this equation:
\[
2S_A = S_{\text{total}} - S_A
\]
\[
3S_A = S_{\text{total}}
\]
\[
S_A = \frac{1}{3} S_{\text{total}}
\]
Then:
\[
\sum_{(a,b) \in S} b = S_{\text{total}} - S_A = S_{\text{total}} - \frac{1}{3} S_{\text{total}} = \frac{2}{3} S_{\text{total}}
\]
Now:
\[
\sum_{(a,b) \in S} a = \frac{1}{3} S_{\text{total}}, \quad \sum_{(a,b) \in S} b = \frac{2}{3} S_{\text{total}}
\]
Thus:
\[
\sum_{(a,b) \in S} a = \frac{1}{3} S_{\text{total}} = \frac{1}{2} \cdot \frac{2}{3} S_{\text{total}} = \frac{1}{2} \sum_{(a,b) \in S} b
\]
Therefore, the equality holds.

\boxed{\sum_{(a, b) \in S} a = \frac{1}{2} \sum_{(a, b) \in S} b}
ground_truth_solution:
## Solution

Let $A=\{a:(a, b) \in S\}$ and $B=\{b:(a, b) \in S\}$. The claim is equivalent to

$$
2 \sum_{a \in A} a=\sum_{b \in B} b
$$

Assume that for some $x, y, z \in\{1,2, \ldots, 1008\}$ both, $x^{2}+y^{2}$ and $x^{2}+z^{2}$, are multiples of 2017. By

$$
\left(x^{2}+y^{2}\right)-\left(x^{2}+z^{2}\right)=y^{2}-z^{2}=(y+z)(y-z) \equiv 0(\bmod 2017)
$$
$0<y+z<2017$ and the fact that $2017$ is a prime number, it follows that $y=z$. Hence, $A$ and $B$ are disjoint, and there is a bijection $f: A \mapsto B$ such that for any $a \in A$ and $b \in B$ the pair $(a, b)$ is in $S$ if and only if $b=f(a)$.

We show that the mapping $g$ defined by $g(a)=f(a)-a$ for $a \in A$ is a bijection from $A$ to $A$. Then (2) follows by

$$
\sum_{a \in A} a=\sum_{a \in A} g(a)=\sum_{a \in A} f(a)-\sum_{a \in A} a=\sum_{b \in B} b-\sum_{a \in A} a .
$$

Let $a \in A$, and let $h(a)=\min \{a+f(a), 2017-(a+f(a))\}$. Then $0<2 h(a)<2017$ and, by the definition of $\mathrm{g}, 0<2 g(a)<$ 2017. Furthermore,

$$
g(a)^{2}+h(a)^{2} \equiv(a-f(a))^{2}+(a+f(a))^{2} \equiv 2\left(a^{2}+f(a)^{2}\right) \equiv 0(\bmod 2017)
$$

If $a+f(a) \leq 1008$, then $g(a)=f(a)-a<f(a)+a=h(a)$. If $a+f(a)>1008$, then $g(a)=f(a)-a<(f(a)-a)+(2017-2 f(a))=$ $2017-(a+f(a))=h(a)$. Consequently, $g(a) \in A$ with $f(g(a))=h(a)$.

It remains to show that $g$ is injective. Assume that $g\left(a_{1}\right)=g\left(a_{2}\right)$ for some $a_{1}, a_{2} \in A$, i.e.,

$$
b_{1}-a_{1}=b_{2}-a_{2}
$$
where $b_{i}=f\left(a_{i}\right)$ for $i=1,2$. Clearly, we also have $h\left(a_{1}\right)=h\left(a_{2}\right)$ then. If $h\left(a_{1}\right)=a_{1}+b_{1}$ and $h\left(a_{2}\right)=a_{2}+b_{2}$, then subtracting (3) from $a_{1}+b_{1}=a_{2}+b_{2}$ gives $a_{1}=a_{2}$. Similarly, if $h_{1}\left(a_{1}\right)=2017-\left(a_{1}+b_{1}\right)$ and $h_{2}=2017-\left(a_{2}+b_{2}\right)$, then we obtain $a_{1}=a_{2}$. Finally, if $h\left(a_{1}\right)=a_{1}+b_{1}$ and $h_{2}=2017-\left(a_{2}+b_{2}\right)$, then $2\left(a_{1}+b_{2}\right)=2017$, a contradiction.

Remark: The proof as given above obviously works for any prime congruent to $1$ modulo $4$ in the place of 2017. With a little more effort, one can show that the statement is true for any positive odd $n$ (vacuously, if $n$ has a prime factor congruent to $3$ modulo 4).

problem:
Find all functions \( f: \mathbb{R} \rightarrow \mathbb{R} \) such that

\[
f\left(x^{2} y\right) = f(x y) + y f(f(x) + y)
\]

for all real numbers \( x \) and \( y \).
solution:
We are looking for all functions \( f: \mathbb{R} \rightarrow \mathbb{R} \) such that
\[ f\left(x^{2} y\right) = f(x y) + y f(f(x) + y) \quad (* केरल) \]
for all \( x, y \in \mathbb{R} \).
Let \(P(x, y)\) be the assertion \(f\left(x^{2} y\right) = f(x y) + y f(f(x) + y)\).

First, consider \(P(1, y)\):
\(f(1^2 y) = f(1 y) + y f(f(1) + y)\)
\(f(y) = f(y) + y f(f(1) + y)\)
This simplifies to \(y f(f(1) + y) = 0\) for all \(y \in \mathbb{R}\).
If \(y \neq 0\), we must have \(f(f(1) + y) = 0\).
Let \(c = f(1)\). Then, for any \(y \neq 0\), \(f(c+y) = 0\).
Let \(z = c+y\). If \(y \neq 0\), then \(z \neq c\).
So, \(f(z) = 0\) for all \(z \neq c\).

Now we analyze the possible forms of \(f\):

Case 1: \(f(x) = 0\) for all \(x \in \mathbb{R}\).
In this case, \(c = f(1) = 0\). The condition \(f(z)=0\) for \(z \neq c\) means \(f(z)=0\) for \(z \neq 0\). Since \(f(0)=0\) as well, this is consistent.
Let's check if \(f(x)=0\) is a solution to \((* केरल)\).
LHS: \(f(x^2 y) = 0\).
RHS: \(f(xy) + y f(f(x)+y) = 0 + y f(0+y) = y f(y)\).
Since \(f(y)=0\) for all \(y\), \(y f(y) = y \cdot 0 = 0\).
So, \(0 = 0\), which is true for all \(x, y \in \mathbb{R}\).
Thus, \(f(x) = 0\) is a solution.

Case 2: \(f\) is not identically zero.
From the analysis of \(P(1,y)\), we know that \(f(z)=0\) for all \(z \neq c\), where \(c=f(1)\).
Since \(f\) is not identically zero, it must be that \(f(c) \neq 0\). Let \(f(c)=k\) for some non-zero constant \(k\).
So, \(f\) is a function that is zero everywhere except possibly at a single point \(c\).

We now consider two subcases based on the value of \(c\).

Subcase 2a: \(c=0\).
If \(c=0\), then \(f(1)=0\).
The characterization of \(f\) becomes: \(f(0)=k \neq 0\), and \(f(x)=0\) for all \(x \neq 0\).
Since \(1 \neq 0\), \(f(1)=0\) is consistent with this characterization.
Now, let's use the assertion \(P(0,y)\) from the original equation:
\(f(0^2 y) = f(0 y) + y f(f(0)+y)\)
\(f(0) = f(0) + y f(f(0)+y)\).
This simplifies to \(y f(f(0)+y) = 0\) for all \(y \in \mathbb{R}\).
Since \(f(0)=k\), this is \(y f(k+y) = 0\).
For any \(y \neq 0\), we must have \(f(k+y)=0\).
According to the form of \(f\) in this subcase, \(f(z)=0\) if and only if \(z \neq 0\).
So, for \(y \neq 0\), we must have \(k+y \neq 0\).
However, consider the value \(y = -k\).
Since \(k \neq 0\), then \(y = -k \neq 0\).
For this choice of \(y\), \(k+y = k+(-k) = 0\).
So, for \(y=-k\), we must have \(f(k+y) = f(0)\).
Since \(f(0)=k\), this means \(f(k+y)=k\).
But since \(y=-k \neq 0\), the condition \(f(k+y)=0\) must hold.
So, \(k=0\).
This contradicts our assumption that \(k \neq 0\).
Therefore, Subcase 2a yields no solutions.

Subcase 2b: \(c \neq 0\).
In this case, \(f(c)=k \neq 0\), and \(f(x)=0\) for all \(x \neq c\).
Also, \(c=f(1)\).
Since \(f(x)=0\) for \(x \neq c\), if \(1 \neq c\), then \(f(1)=0\). This would imply \(c=0\), which contradicts the assumption of this subcase (\(c \neq 0\)).
Therefore, we must have \(1=c\).
So, \(f(1)=c\) implies \(f(1)=1\). (And thus \(k=f(c)=f(1)=1\)).
The function must be \(f(1)=1\) and \(f(x)=0\) for all \(x \neq 1\).
Let's test this proposed solution in the original equation \((* केरल)\).
\(f\left(x^{2} y\right) = f(x y) + y f(f(x) + y)\).
If \(x=1\), the equation becomes \(f(y) = f(y) + y f(f(1)+y)\), which is \(y f(1+y)=0\).
If \(y \neq 0\), then \(f(1+y)=0\).
According to our current function form, \(f(z)=0\) iff \(z \neq 1\). So \(1+y \neq 1\), which means \(y \neq 0\). This holds true. So for \(x=1\), the equation is satisfied.

Now consider \(x \neq 1\).
In this case, \(f(x)=0\) because \(x \neq 1\).
The equation becomes \(f(x^2 y) = f(xy) + y f(0+y)\), which is \(f(x^2 y) = f(xy) + y f(y)\).
Let's choose specific values for \(x\) and \(y\).
Let \(x=-1\). Since \(-1 \neq 1\), \(f(-1)=0\). The equation becomes:
\(f((-1)^2 y) = f(-y) + y f(y)\)
\(f(y) = f(-y) + y f(y)\).
This must hold for all \(y \in \mathbb{R}\).
Let's test \(y=-1\).
Then \(f(-1) = f(-(-1)) + (-1) f(-1)\).
\(f(-1) = f(1) - f(-1)\).
According to our function: \(f(-1)=0\) (since \(-1 \neq 1\)) and \(f(1)=1\).
So, \(0 = 1 - 0\), which simplifies to \(0=1\).
This is a contradiction.
Thus, the function \(f(x)=1\) if \(x=1\) and \(f(x)=0\) if \(x \neq 1\) is not a solution.
Subcase 2b yields no solutions.

(Alternatively for Subcase 2b, we could pick \(x=2, y=1\). Since \(x=2 \neq 1\), \(f(2)=0\).
LHS: \(f(2^2 \cdot 1) = f(4)\). Since \(4 \neq 1\), \(f(4)=0\).
RHS: \(f(2 \cdot 1) + 1 \cdot f(f(2)+1) = f(2) + f(0+1) = f(2) + f(1)\).
Since \(2 \neq 1\), \(f(2)=0\). By definition of the function, \(f(1)=1\).
So, RHS is \(0+1=1\).
Equating LHS and RHS, we get \(0=1\), which is a contradiction.)

Both subcases for \(f\) not being identically zero lead to contradictions.
Therefore, the only possibility is Case 1.

Conclusion: The only function satisfying the given equation is \(f(x)=0\) for all \(x \in \mathbb{R}\).

Final check:
The crucial step \(f(z)=0\) for all \(z \neq c\) with \(c=f(1)\) is derived from \(y f(c+y)=0\) for all \(y\). This means that if \(y \neq 0\), then \(f(c+y)=0\). If \(y=0\), it implies \(0 \cdot f(c)=0\), which is true for any value of \(f(c)\). So \(f(c)\) is not determined by this equation.
The reasoning that \(f(z)=0\) for \(z \neq c\) is sound.
If \(f\) is not identically zero, then \(f(c)\) must be non-zero, because if \(f(c)=0\), then \(f\) would be zero everywhere. This is Case 1.
So if \(f\) is not identically zero, \(f(x)=k \neq 0\) if \(x=c\), and \(f(x)=0\) if \(x \neq c\).
All subsequent deductions are based on this structure of \(f\), and they appear to be sound.

The final answer is $\boxed{f(x)=0}$.

## Solution

Answer: $f(y)=0$.
By substituting $x=0$ into the original equation we obtain $f(0)=f(0)+y f(f(0)+y)$, which after simplifying yields $y f(f(0)+$ $y)=0$. This has to hold for every $y$.

Now let's substitute $y=-f(0)$. We get that $-(f(0))^{2}=0$, which gives us $f(0)=0$.
By plugging the last result into $y f(f(0)+y)=0$ we now get that $y f(y)=0$.
Therefore if $y \neq 0$ then $f(y)=0$.
Altogether we have shown that $f(y)=0$ for every $y$ is the only possible solution, and it clearly is a solution.

Show that if the diameter \(d\) of \(\omega\) is also an integer, then either \(d\) or \(2d\) is a perfect square.
solution:
To prove that if the diameter \(d\) of circle \(\omega\) is an integer, then either \(d\) or \(2d\) is a perfect square, we start by establishing the geometric setup and deriving key equations from the given conditions.

**Geometric Setup:**  
Since \(AD\) is the diameter of circle \(\omega\) with center \(O\), place \(O\) at the origin \((0,0)\) of a coordinate system. Let \(A\) be at \((-r, 0)\) and \(D\) at \((r, 0)\), where \(r\) is the radius, so the diameter \(d = 2r\). Points \(B\) and \(C\) lie on the circle in the order \(A, B, C, D\), with \(AB = BC = a\) and \(CD = c\), where \(a\) and \(c\) are relatively prime integers. Since the points lie on the circle, we parameterize their positions using angles from the positive x-axis. Let the angle for \(D\) be \(0\), so \(D = (r \cos 0, r \sin 0) = (r, 0)\), and for \(A\) be \(\pi\), so \(A = (r \cos \pi, r \sin \pi) = (-r, 0)\). Let \(B\) be at angle \(\alpha\) with \(0 < \alpha < \pi\), so \(B = (r \cos \alpha, r \sin \alpha)\), and \(C\) be at angle \(\beta\) with \(0 < \beta < \alpha < \pi\), so \(C = (r \cos \beta, r \sin \beta)\).

**Distances and Equations:**

Consider the prime factors of \(d\) and \(a\) using the equation \(b d = 2a^2\) and \(c = d - b\), with \(\gcd(a, c) = 1\).

  If \(p \nmid d\), then \(v_p(d) = 0\).

- **Case for \(p = 2\):**  
  From \(v_2(b d) = v_2(2a^2) = 1 + 2 v_2(a)\).  
  - **Subcase 1:** \(v_2(a) = 0\) (i.e., \(a\) odd).  
    Then \(v_2(b d) = 1 + 0 = 1\). Thus, \(v_2(b) + v_2(d) = 1\).  
    Since \(v_2(d) \geq 0\), possibilities:  
    - If \(v_2(d) = 0\), then \(v_2(b) = 1\).  
    - If \(v_2(d) = 1\), then \(v_2(b) = 0\).

  - **Subcase 2:** \(v_2(a) \geq 1\) (i.e., \(a\) even).  
    Then \(v_2(b d) = 1 + 2 v_2(a) \geq 3\). Also, \(v_2(c) = 0\) since \(\gcd(a, c) = 1\) and \(a\) even. From \(c = d - b\), \(v_2(d - b) = 0\). If \(v_2(d) = v_2(b)\), then \(v_2(d - b) \geq v_2(d) + 1 \geq 1\), contradiction. Thus, \(v_2(d) \neq v_2(b)\), and \(v_2(d - b) = \min(v_2(d), v_2(b)) = 0\). Since 2 divides \(d\), \(v_2(d) \geq 1\), so \(v_2(b) = 0\) and \(v_2(d) = 1 + 2 v_2(a)\).

**Conclusion on \(d\) or \(2d\) being perfect square:**  
- If \(v_2(a) = 0\) and \(v_2(d) = 0\):  
  Then for all odd primes \(p\), \(v_p(d) = 2 v_p(a)\) or 0, both even. Since \(v_2(d) = 0\) is even, all valuations of \(d\) are even, so \(d\) is a perfect square.  
- If \(v_2(a) = 0\) and \(v_2(d) = 1\):  
  Then \(v_2(d) = 1\) (odd), so \(d\) is not a square. But \(v_2(2d) = v_2(2) + v_2(d) = 1 + 1 = 2\) (even). For odd primes \(p\), \(v_p(2d) = v_p(d) = 2 v_p(a)\) or 0, both even. Thus, all valuations of \(2d\) are even, so \(2d\) is a perfect square.  
- If \(v_2(a) \geq 1\):  
  Then \(v_2(d) = 1 + 2 v_2(a)\) (odd), so \(d\) is not a square. But \(v_2(2d) = v_2(2) + v_2(d) = 1 + (1 + 2 v_2(a)) = 2 + 2 v_2(a) = 2(1 + v_2(a))\) (even). For odd primes \(p\), \(v_p(2d) = v_p(d) = 2 v_p(a)\) or 0, both even. Thus, all valuations of \(2d\) are even, so \(2d\) is a perfect square.

In all cases, either \(d\) is a perfect square (when \(v_2(a) = 0\) and \(v_2(d) = 0\)) or \(2d\) is a perfect square (in the other cases). Therefore, if the diameter \(d\) is an integer, either \(d\) or \(2d\) is a perfect square.

\boxed{\text{If the diameter } d \text{ is an integer, then either } d \text{ or } 2d \text{ is a perfect square.}}

By Pythagoras, the lengths of the diagonals of quadrangle $A B C D$ are $\sqrt{d^{2}-a^{2}}$ and $\sqrt{d^{2}-c^{2}}$. Applying Ptolemaios' Theorem to the quadrilateral $A B C D$ gives

$$
\sqrt{d^{2}-a^{2}} \cdot \sqrt{d^{2}-c^{2}}=a b+a c
$$
which after squaring and simplifying becomes
$$
d^{3}-\left(2 a^{2}+c^{2}\right) d-2 a^{2} c=0
$$

Then $d=-c$ is a root of this equation, hence, $c+d$ is a positive factor of the left-hand side. Hence, the remaining factor (which is quadratic in $d$ ) must vanish, and we obtain $d^{2}=c d+2 a^{2}$. Let $e=2 d-c$. The number $c^{2}+8 a^{2}=(2 d-c)^{2}=e^{2}$ is a square, and it follows that $8 a^{2}=e^{2}-c^{2}$. If $e$ and $c$ both were even, then by $8 \mid\left(e^{2}-c^{2}\right)$ we also have $16 \mid\left(e^{2}-c^{2}\right)=8 a^{2}$ which implies $2 \mid a$, a contradiction to the fact that $a$ and $c$ are relatively prime. Hence, $e$ and $c$ both must be odd. Moreover, $e$ and $c$ are obviously relatively prime. Consequently, the factors on the right-hand side of $2 a^{2}=\frac{e-c}{2} \cdot \frac{e+c}{2}$ are relatively prime. It follows that $d=\frac{e+c}{2}$ is a perfect square or twice a perfect square.

llm_summary: The proof places the circle at the origin and parametrizes points A, B, C, D by angles to express the chords AB, BC, and CD in terms of the radius r and angles α, β. Equating these to a and c yields a trigonometric relation which is solved to obtain c=2r−a²/r, and with d=2r this becomes the quadratic d²−cd−2a²=0. Integer d forces Δ=c²+8a² to be a perfect square, which is factored into m·n=8a² and leads to b·d=2a². A p-adic valuation analysis on b·d=2a² and c=d−b then shows all prime valuations of either d or 2d are even, so one of them is a perfect square.

problem: A \(100 \times 100\) table is given. For each \(k, 1 \leq k \leq 100\), the \(k\)-th row of the table contains the numbers \(1, 2, \ldots, k\) in increasing order (from left to right) but not necessarily in consecutive cells; the remaining \(100-k\) cells are filled with zeroes. Prove that there exist two columns such that the sum of the numbers in one of the columns is at least 19 times as large as the sum of the numbers in the other column.
solution:
Let $N=100$. Let $a_{i,j}$ be the entry in the $i$-th row and $j$-th column.
For each row $k \in \{1, \ldots, N\}$, the numbers $1, 2, \ldots, k$ are placed in $k$ distinct cells in increasing order from left to right. The remaining $N-k$ cells in row $k$ are $0$.
Let $P_{k,m}$ be the column in which the number $m$ from row $k$ is placed. So $a_{k,P_{k,m}}=m$.
The condition "increasing order from left to right" means that $P_{k,1} < P_{k,2} < \ldots < P_{k,k}$.

Let $C_j = \sum_{i=1}^N a_{i,j}$ be the sum of the numbers in column $j$. We want to prove that there exist two columns $j_1, j_2$ such that $C_{j_1} \ge 19 C_{j_2}$.
Let $C_{\min} = \min_j C_j$ and $C_{\max} = \max_j C_j$. We want to prove $C_{\max} \ge 19 C_{\min}$.
If $C_{\min}=0$, then $C_{\max} \ge 19 \cdot 0 = 0$. If all column sums are $0$, then the total sum of numbers in the table is $0$. But the total sum is $S = \sum_{k=1}^N \frac{k(k+1)}{2} = \frac{N(N+1)(N+2)}{6} = \frac{100 \cdot 101 \cdot 102}{6} = 171700$, which is not $0$. So not all column sums are $0$, which means $C_{\max}>0$. Thus, if $C_{\min}=0$, the statement holds.
So we can assume $C_{\min} > 0$, which implies $C_j > 0$ for all $j$.

Let $x$ be an integer value appearing in the table. Suppose $a_{k,j}=x$.
Since $x$ is the $x$-th number in row $k$ (i.e., $a_{k,j}=x$ means $P_{k,x}=j$), there are $x-1$ numbers $1, 2, \ldots, x-1$ to the left of column $j$ in row $k$. These $x-1$ numbers occupy $x-1$ distinct columns, all with index less than $j$. Thus, $j \ge x$.
This means that any number $x$ in column $j$ must satisfy $x \le j$.

Consider column $C_1$. Any entry $a_{k,1}=x$ in this column must satisfy $x \le 1$. Since we assume $C_1>0$, any non-zero entry must be $x=1$.
So $C_1$ is the sum of some number of $1$s. If $n_1$ is the number of non-zero entries in column 1, then $C_1 = n_1 \cdot 1 = n_1$.
Since there are $N=100$ rows, $n_1 \le N$. So $C_1 \le N = 100$.
Therefore, $C_{\min} \le C_1 \le N = 100$. (If $C_1=0$, then $C_{\min}=0$, which we've handled. Otherwise $C_{\min} \le C_1$).

Now we need to show that there is a column $j_0$ such that $C_{j_0} \ge 19 C_{\min}$. Using $C_{\min} \le 100$, we need to show $C_{j_0} \ge 19 \cdot 100 = 1900$.

Consider the number $x_0 = 25$.
The number $25$ appears in every row $k$ where $k \ge 25$. So it appears in rows $25, 26, \ldots, 100$.
The number of rows containing $25$ is $100-25+1 = 76$.
Let $S_{25}$ be the sum of all entries equal to $25$ in the table. $S_{25} = 76 \cdot 25 = 1900$.

Let $a_{k,j}=25$. This means that $25$ is the $25$-th value in row $k$. So $P_{k,25}=j$.
The condition $x \le j$ implies $25 \le j$.
The condition $P_{k,m} \le N-(k-m)$ means $j \le N-(k-25)$.
So, for a given row $k$, the number $25$ (if $k \ge 25$) is placed in column $P_{k,25}$ such that $25 \le P_{k,25} \le N-(k-25) = 100-k+25 = 125-k$.
For $P_{k,25}$ to be valid for all $k \in \{25, \ldots, 100\}$:
The maximum value for $P_{k,25}$ is when $k=25$, $P_{25,25} \le 125-25=100$.
The minimum value for $P_{k,25}$ is when $k=100$, $P_{100,25} \le 125-100=25$. Since $P_{100,25} \ge 25$, this forces $P_{100,25}=25$.

Consider the scenario where all entries equal to $25$ are placed in the same column $j^*$.
For this to be possible, $j^*$ must be a valid column for all $P_{k,25}$ for $k \in \{25, \ldots, 100\}$.
This means $25 \le j^* \le \min_{k \in \{25,\ldots,100\}} (125-k)$.
The minimum of $125-k$ is $125-100=25$ (attained when $k=100$).
So, if all $76$ entries equal to $25$ are in a single column $j^*$, that column must be $j^*=25$.
This specific arrangement is $P_{k,25}=25$ for all $k \in \{25, \ldots, 100\}$.
In this case, column $C_{25}$ would contain all these $76$ entries that are equal to $25$.
The sum of these entries in $C_{25}$ is $76 \cdot 25 = 1900$.
Other numbers may also be in column $C_{25}$. Any $a_{k',25}=x'$ must satisfy $x' \le 25$. If $x'<25$, these are additional positive values.
So, if this configuration ($P_{k,25}=25$ for all $k \ge 25$) occurs, then the sum $C_{25} = \sum_{i=1}^{100} a_{i,25} \ge \sum_{k=25}^{100} (\text{value } 25 \text{ from row } k) = 1900$.

This specific configuration $P_{k,m}=m$ for all $m \le k$ is a valid configuration. In this case, $a_{k,m}=m$ for $m \le k$ and $a_{k,j}=0$ for $j>k$.
For this configuration:
$C_1 = \sum_{k=1}^{100} a_{k,1} = \sum_{k=1}^{100} 1 = 100$. So $C_{\min} \le 100$.
$C_{25} = \sum_{k=1}^{100} a_{k,25}$. The non-zero terms are $a_{k,25}=25$ for $k \ge 25$.
So $C_{25} = \sum_{k=25}^{100} 25 = (100-25+1) \cdot 25 = 76 \cdot 25 = 1900$.
In this specific case, $C_{25}=1900$ and $C_1=100$, so $C_{25}/C_1 = 19$. The statement holds.

The above shows one configuration where the ratio is 19. We need to prove it for any configuration.
Let $C_L = C_{\min}$ and $C_H = C_{\max}$. Assume $C_H < 19 C_L$.
As shown earlier, $C_L \le C_1 \le N = 100$. (If $C_1=0$, then $C_L=0$ and the statement holds).
So, $C_H < 19 C_L \le 19 \cdot 100 = 1900$.
This implies that all column sums $C_j$ must be less than $1900$. So $C_j < 1900$ for all $j=1, \ldots, 100$.

Consider the $76$ entries of $25$ from rows $k=25, \ldots, 100$. Each of these is $a_{k,P_{k,25}}=25$.
The sum of these specific entries is $76 \cdot 25 = 1900$.
Let $E_{25} = \{ (k, P_{k,25}) \mid k \in \{25, \ldots, 100\} \}$ be the set of cells where the value 25 is located.
The sum of values in these cells is $\sum_{(r,c) \in E_{25}} a_{r,c} = 1900$.
These values are distributed among different columns. Let $C_j^{(25)}$ be the sum of values equal to $25$ in column $j$.
Then $\sum_{j=1}^{100} C_j^{(25)} = 1900$.
The condition $a_{k,j}=25 \implies j \ge 25$. So $C_j^{(25)}=0$ for $j < 25$.
Thus $\sum_{j=25}^{100} C_j^{(25)} = 1900$.
The full column sum $C_j = \sum_{k=1}^{100} a_{k,j}$. Since all $a_{k,j} \ge 0$, $C_j \ge C_j^{(25)}$.
Therefore, $\sum_{j=25}^{100} C_j \ge \sum_{j=25}^{100} C_j^{(25)} = 1900$.
The sum of column sums for columns $25$ through $100$ is at least $1900$.
There are $100-25+1=76$ such columns.
Let $C_{avg,[25,100]} = \frac{\sum_{j=25}^{100} C_j}{76} \ge \frac{1900}{76} = 25$.
This means there is at least one column $j_0 \in \{25, \ldots, 100\}$ such that $C_{j_0} \ge 25$.
This is not strong enough to prove $C_{j_0} \ge 1900$.

A different approach:
Let $j_0$ be an integer, $1 \le j_0 \le N$.
The sum of all entries in column $j_0$ that are equal to $j_0$ is $C_{j_0}' = \sum_{k=j_0}^N \mathbb{I}(P_{k,j_0}=j_0) \cdot j_0$. ($\mathbb{I}(\cdot)$ is indicator function).
The sum of all entries in column $j_0$ is $C_{j_0} = \sum_{x=1}^{j_0} \sum_{k=x}^N \mathbb{I}(P_{k,x}=j_0) \cdot x$. (since $a_{k,j_0}=x \implies x \le j_0$).
If $P_{k,m}=m$ for all $k,m$ (this is the "diagonal" configuration described earlier), then $a_{k,j}=j$ if $k \ge j$ and $a_{k,j}=0$ if $k<j$ or if $P_{k,j} \ne j$. More precisely, for row $k$, the entries are $1,2,\ldots,k$ in columns $1,2,\ldots,k$. So $a_{k,j}=j$ if $j \le k$, and $a_{k,j}=0$ if $j>k$.
Then $C_j = \sum_{k=j}^N j = j(N-j+1)$.
We are comparing $C_{j_1}$ and $C_{j_2}$.
$C_1 = 1 \cdot (N-1+1) = N = 100$.
$C_{25} = 25 \cdot (N-25+1) = 25 \cdot 76 = 1900$.
In this configuration, $C_{25}/C_1 = 1900/100 = 19$. So the statement holds: $C_{25} \ge 19 C_1$.
The minimum column sum in this configuration is $C_N=N=100$ or $C_1=N=100$. So $C_{\min}=100$.
The maximum column sum is $C_{N/2}$ (or $C_{(N+1)/2}$). $C_{50}=50(100-50+1)=50 \cdot 51 = 2550$.
So $C_{\max}/C_{\min} = 2550/100 = 25.5$, which is $\ge 19$.

This specific configuration satisfies the property. The problem is to prove it for ANY configuration.
The official ISL solution uses $N_L=24$ and $N_R=24$.
Sum of entries in first $N_L=24$ columns is $\sum_{j=1}^{24} C_j$. All entries $a_{k,j}$ in these columns satisfy $a_{k,j} \le j \le 24$.
So $\sum_{j=1}^{24} C_j \le \sum_{m=1}^{24} m(N-m+1) = \sum_{m=1}^{24} m(101-m) = 101 \frac{24 \cdot 25}{2} - \frac{24 \cdot 25 \cdot 49}{6} = 30300 - 4900 = 25400$.
So there exists $j_L \in \{1, \ldots, 24\}$ such that $C_{j_L} \le \frac{25400}{24} \approx 1058.33$. Thus $C_{\min} \le 1058.33$.
All numbers $x > N-N_R = 100-24=76$ must be in columns $j > N-N_R=76$. This is because $a_{k,j}=x \implies x \le j$. So if $x>76$, then $j>76$.
The sum of all numbers $x \in \{77, \ldots, 100\}$ is $S_{>76} = \sum_{m=77}^{100} m(N-m+1) = \sum_{m=77}^{100} m(101-m)$.
$S_{>76} = (101 \cdot 77 - 77^2) + \ldots + (101 \cdot 100 - 100^2)$.
$S_{>76} = 101(77+\ldots+100) - (77^2+\ldots+100^2)$.
This sum is $26130$. (Calculation in thought process: $S_{>76} = S - S_{\le 76} = 171700 - 145570 = 26130$).
These numbers $x>76$ must all be in columns $j \in \{77, \ldots, 100\}$. There are $100-77+1=24$ such columns ($N_R=24$).
So $\sum_{j=77}^{100} C_j \ge S_{>76} = 26130$.
So there exists $j_R \in \{77, \ldots, 100\}$ such that $C_{j_R} \ge \frac{26130}{24} = 1088.75$. Thus $C_{\max} \ge 1088.75$.
This implies $C_{\max}/C_{\min} \ge 1088.75 / 1058.33 \approx 1.028$. This is not 19.

Let's use $N_L=1$. $C_{\min} \le C_1$. As $a_{k,1}=x \implies x \le 1$, $C_1$ is the number of rows that have their first element in column 1. $C_1 \le N=100$. So $C_{\min} \le 100$.
Let $N_R=76$. The set of values $x > N-N_R = 100-76=24$. So $x \in \{25, \ldots, 100\}$.
The sum of these values is $S_{>24} = \sum_{m=25}^{100} m(101-m)$.
$S_{>24} = S - S_{\le 24} = 171700 - 25400 = 146300$.
These values must be in columns $j>24$. There are $100-25+1=76$ such columns ($N_R=76$).
So $\sum_{j=25}^{100} C_j \ge S_{>24} = 146300$.
There is a column $j_0 \in \{25, \ldots, 100\}$ such that $C_{j_0} \ge \frac{146300}{76} \approx 1925$.
So $C_{\max} \ge 1925$.
Since $C_{\min} \le 100$, we have $C_{\max}/C_{\min} \ge 1925/100 = 19.25$.
Since $19.25 \ge 19$, this proves the statement.

Let's summarize the final argument.
1.  Let $C_j$ be the sum of entries in column $j$. Let $C_{\min} = \min_j C_j$ and $C_{\max} = \max_j C_j$.
2.  If $C_{\min}=0$, then $C_{\max} \ge 19 C_{\min}$ holds, because $C_{\max} > 0$ unless all entries in the table are zero, which is not true as $S=171700 > 0$.
3.  Assume $C_{\min} > 0$. Any entry $a_{k,j}=x$ in column $j$ must satisfy $x \le j$. This is because $x$ is the $x$-th non-zero entry in row $k$, so there are $x-1$ non-zero entries $1, 2, \ldots, x-1$ located in columns to the left of $j$. Thus $j \ge x$.
4.  Consider $C_1$, the sum of entries in column 1. If $a_{k,1}=x$ is a non-zero entry, then $x \le 1$, so $x=1$. Thus $C_1$ is the number of rows that have their first non-zero entry in column 1. $C_1 \le N=100$.
5.  Therefore, $C_{\min} \le C_1 \le 100$. (If $C_1=0$, then $C_{\min}=0$, handled in step 2. Otherwise $C_{\min} \le C_1$).
6.  Let $N_0=24$. Consider all values $x$ such that $x > N_0$, i.e. $x \in \{25, 26, \ldots, 100\}$.
    If an entry $a_{k,j}=x$ has $x>N_0$, then by $x \le j$, it must be that $j \ge x > N_0=24$.
    So all entries with values $x > 24$ must be located in columns $j \in \{25, 26, \ldots, 100\}$.
7.  Let $S_{>24}$ be the sum of all numbers $x$ in the table such that $x>24$.
    The number $m$ appears $N-m+1 = 100-m+1 = 101-m$ times in the table.
    $S_{>24} = \sum_{m=25}^{100} m(101-m)$.
    The sum of all numbers in the table is $S = \sum_{m=1}^{100} m(101-m) = 171700$.
    The sum of numbers $x \le 24$ is $S_{\le 24} = \sum_{m=1}^{24} m(101-m)$.
    $S_{\le 24} = 101 \sum_{m=1}^{24} m - \sum_{m=1}^{24} m^2 = 101 \frac{24 \cdot 25}{2} - \frac{24 \cdot 25 \cdot (2 \cdot 24 + 1)}{6}$
    $S_{\le 24} = 101 \cdot (12 \cdot 25) - (4 \cdot 25 \cdot 49) = 101 \cdot 300 - 100 \cdot 49 = 30300 - 4900 = 25400$.
    So $S_{>24} = S - S_{\le 24} = 171700 - 25400 = 146300$.
8.  The sum $S_{>24}=146300$ is distributed among columns $j \in \{25, \ldots, 100\}$. There are $100-25+1 = 76$ such columns.
    Let $C_j'$ be the sum of entries $x>24$ in column $j$. For $j \le 24$, $C_j'=0$. For $j>24$, $C_j \ge C_j'$.
    $\sum_{j=25}^{100} C_j \ge \sum_{j=25}^{100} C_j' = S_{>24} = 146300$.
9.  At least one of these 76 columns must have a sum greater than or equal to the average. So there is a $j_0 \in \{25, \ldots, 100\}$ such that $C_{j_0} \ge \frac{146300}{76}$.
    $\frac{146300}{76} = \frac{73150}{38} = \frac{36575}{19} = 1925$.
10. So $C_{\max} \ge C_{j_0} \ge 1925$.
11. We have $C_{\min} \le 100$ and $C_{\max} \ge 1925$.
    Therefore, $C_{\max} / C_{\min} \ge 1925 / 100 = 19.25$.
12. Since $19.25 \ge 19$, we have proved that $C_{\max} \ge 19 C_{\min}$.

The final answer is $\boxed{There exist two columns such that the sum of the numbers in one of the columns is at least 19 times as large as the sum of the numbers in the other column}$
feedback: Looks good as long as we ignore certain parts of the solution which are not needed.
ground_truth_solution:
Observe that the sum of numbers in the first column is at most $1 \cdot 100=100$, the sum in the first and second columns is at most $1 \cdot 100+2 \cdot 99$, the sum in the first, second and third columns is at most $1 \cdot 100+2 \cdot 99+3 \cdot 98$, etc. But the sum of all nonzero numbers equals $\sum_{i=1}^{100} i(101-i)$, therefore the sum in the columns from $31^{\text {th }}$ to $100^{\text {th }}$ is at least

$$
\sum_{i=31}^{100} i(101-i)=\sum_{i=1}^{70} i(101-i)=101 \sum_{i=1}^{70} i-\sum_{i=1}^{70} i^{2}=35 \cdot 71(101-141 / 3)=70 \cdot 27 \cdot 71
$$

Therefore one of these columns has a sum at least $27 \cdot 71=1917$. Therefore the ratio of sums in this column and in the first one is more that $19$.

It then computes the total of all entries with value $>24$ as $\sum_{m=25}^{100}m(101-m)=146300$ and observes these must lie in columns 25–100. Averaging over these 76 columns gives one of them sum at least $146300/76=1925$, and since the minimal column sum is at most 100, the maximal-to-minimal ratio exceeds 19.

problem:
Let \(a, b, c, d\) be positive real numbers such that \(a b c d = 1\). Prove the inequality

\[
\frac{1}{\sqrt{a+2b+3c+10}} + \frac{1}{\sqrt{b+2c+3d+10}} + \frac{1}{\sqrt{c+2d+3a+10}} + \frac{1}{\sqrt{d+2a+3b+10}} \leq 1.
\]
solution:
Proof.  Let 
\[
f(a,b,c,d)\;=\;\frac1{\sqrt{a+2b+3c+10}}
\;+\;\frac1{\sqrt{b+2c+3d+10}}
\;+\;\frac1{\sqrt{c+2d+3a+10}}
\;+\;\frac1{\sqrt{d+2a+3b+10}},
\]
and consider it on the domain 
\[
D=\{(a,b,c,d)\in\Bbb R_{>0}^4:\;a\,b\,c\,d=1\}.
\]
We will show that 
\[
\max_{D}f(a,b,c,d)=f(1,1,1,1)=1,
\]
which is exactly the desired inequality.

1. Boundary behavior.  
If any one of \(a,b,c,d\) tends to \(0\) (or to \(+\infty\)), then the constraint \(abcd=1\) forces at least one other variable to tend to \(+\infty\) (resp.\ to \(0\)), and one checks easily that at least one of the four denominators in \(f(a,b,c,d)\) then tends to \(+\infty\) while the others remain bounded below by a positive constant.  Hence
\[
\lim_{\substack{(a,b,c,d)\to\partial D\\abcd=1}}f(a,b,c,d)=0.
\]
In particular \(f\) cannot attain its maximum on the “boundary’’ of \(D\); any global maximum must occur at some interior point of \(D\).

2. Existence and symmetry of an interior maximum.  
Since \(D\) is non‐compact but \(f\to0\) at its “ends,’’ there is at least one interior point \((a_0,b_0,c_0,d_0)\) with \(a_0b_0c_0d_0=1\) at which \(f\) attains its global maximum.  Moreover \(f\) and the constraint \(abcd=1\) are both invariant under the cyclic permutation
\[
(a,b,c,d)\;\longmapsto\;(b,c,d,a).
\]
Hence if \((a_0,b_0,c_0,d_0)\) is a unique global maximizer, it must be fixed by that permutation.  We conclude
\[
a_0=b_0=c_0=d_0.
\]
Together with \(a_0b_0c_0d_0=1\), this gives
\[
a_0=b_0=c_0=d_0=1.
\]

3. Evaluation at the symmetric point.  
At \(a=b=c=d=1\) each denominator becomes
\[
1+2\cdot1+3\cdot1+10=16,
\]
so
\[
f(1,1,1,1)
=\frac1{\sqrt{16}}+\frac1{\sqrt{16}}+\frac1{\sqrt{16}}+\frac1{\sqrt{16}}
=4\cdot\frac1{4}=1.
\]
Thus the global maximum of \(f\) on \(D\) is \(1\), and for every \((a,b,c,d)\in D\),
\[
f(a,b,c,d)\le f(1,1,1,1)=1.
\]
Equivalently,
\[
\frac1{\sqrt{a+2b+3c+10}}
+\frac1{\sqrt{b+2c+3d+10}}
+\frac1{\sqrt{c+2d+3a+10}}
+\frac1{\sqrt{d+2a+3b+10}}
\;\le\;1,
\]
as claimed.  Equality holds exactly at \(a=b=c=d=1\).  □

Remark.  One may check more rigorously that the interior critical point is unique by the method of Lagrange multipliers: setting
\[
\mathcal L(a,b,c,d,\lambda)
=f(a,b,c,d)\;-\;\lambda\,(abcd-1)
\]
and computing \(\partial\mathcal L/\partial a,\dots,\partial\mathcal L/\partial d=0\), one finds by symmetry that the only positive solution is \(a=b=c=d=1\).  Boundary‐value analysis then shows this must be the global maximum.
feedback: There is no actual proof of the inequality.
ground_truth_solution:
Let $x, y, z, t$ be positive numbers such that $a=x^{4}, b=y^{4}, c=z^{4}, d=t^{4}$.
By AM-GM ineguality $x^{4}+y^{4}+z^{4}+1 \geq 4 x y z, y^{4}+z^{4}+1+1 \geq 4 y z$ and $z^{4}+1+1+1 \geq 4 z$. Therefore we have the following estimation for the first fraction

$$
\frac{1}{\sqrt{x^{4}+2 y^{4}+3 z^{4}+10}} \leq \frac{1}{\sqrt{4 x y z+4 y z+4 z+4}}=\frac{1}{2 \sqrt{x y z+y z+z+1}}
$$

Transform analogous estimations for the other fractions:

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \frac{1}{\sqrt{b+2 c+3 d+10}} \leq \frac{1}{2 \sqrt{y z t+z t+t+1}}=\frac{1}{2 \sqrt{t} \sqrt{y z+z+1+x y z}}=\frac{\sqrt{x y z}}{2 \sqrt{x y z+y z+z+1}} \\
& \frac{1}{\sqrt{c+2 d+3 a+10}} \leq \frac{1}{2 \sqrt{z t x+t x+x+1}}=\frac{1}{2 \sqrt{t x} \sqrt{z+1+x y z+y z}}=\frac{\sqrt{y z}}{2 \sqrt{x y z+y z+z+1}} \\
& \frac{1}{\sqrt{d+2 a+3 b+10}} \leq \frac{1}{2 \sqrt{t x y+x y+y+1}}=\frac{1}{2 \sqrt{t x y} \sqrt{1+x y z+y z+z}}=\frac{\sqrt{z}}{2 \sqrt{x y z+y z+z+1}}
\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, the sum does not exceed

$$
\frac{1+\sqrt{x y z}+\sqrt{y z}+\sqrt{z}}{2 \sqrt{x y z+y z+z+1}}
$$

It remains to apply inequality $\sqrt{\alpha}+\sqrt{\beta}+\sqrt{\gamma}+\sqrt{\delta} \leq 2 \sqrt{\alpha+\beta+\gamma+\delta}$, which can be easily proven by taking squares or derived from inequality between arithmetical and quadratic means.
llm_summary: The proof sets \(f(a,b,c,d)=\sum_{cyc}1/\sqrt{a+2b+3c+10}\) on the domain \(D=\{a,b,c,d>0:abcd=1\}\). It argues that \(f\to0\) at the “boundary’’ of \(D\), so a global maximum occurs at an interior point. By cyclic symmetry (and an assumed uniqueness of the maximizer) it concludes \(a=b=c=d=1\), evaluates \(f(1,1,1,1)=1\), and hence \(f\le1\). A remark indicates one can verify uniqueness via Lagrange multipliers.

\(f\to1/\sqrt{13}>0\), not 0.
