problem:
A graph has \(N\) vertices. An invisible hare sits in one of the vertices. A group of hunters tries to kill the hare. In each move, all of them shoot simultaneously: each hunter shoots at a single vertex, and they choose the target vertices cooperatively. If the hare was in one of the target vertices during a shoot, the hunt is finished. Otherwise, the hare can stay in its vertex or jump to one of the neighboring vertices.

The hunters know an algorithm that allows them to kill the hare in at most \(N!\) moves. Prove that there exists an algorithm that allows them to kill the hare in at most \(2^{N}\) moves.
solution:
Let \(G\) be a finite graph with vertex–set  
\[
V=\{v_{1},v_{2},\dots ,v_{N}\},\qquad |V|=N .
\]

Throughout a game the only information the hunters really have is the set of vertices in
which the hare can still be alive.
For every turn we therefore introduce

 • \(S_{t}\subseteq V\) – the set of all vertices in which the hare may be just before the
\(t\)-th shot is fired ( \(S_{0}=V\) );

 • \(H_{t}\subseteq V\) – the set of vertices that the hunters decide to shoot at that turn
(they may use several hunters, but this is irrelevant – only the set \(H_{t}\) matters).

If the hare is hit while the shots of turn \(t\) are fired the game ends; otherwise the
hare is known to be in \(S_{t}\setminus H_{t}\) at that instant and, immediately
afterwards, it may either stay where it is or move to an adjacent vertex.
Hence, at the beginning of the next turn it must be somewhere in  

\[
\operatorname{Nbr}\bigl(S_{t}\setminus H_{t}\bigr):=
\bigl(S_{t}\setminus H_{t}\bigr)\cup
\{u\in V\;|\;\exists w\in S_{t}\setminus H_{t}\ \text{with}\ uw\in E(G)\}.
\]

Consequently the sets \(S_{t}\) obey the deterministic recurrence  

\[
S_{t+1}= \operatorname{Nbr}\bigl(S_{t}\setminus H_{t}\bigr)\qquad
\text{whenever the hare survives turn }t .
\tag{1}
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
1.  A strategy = a function on the \(2^{N}\) possible states
--------------------------------------------------------------------

Because (1) shows that the whole *state of knowledge* of the hunters is
the current subset \(S_{t}\subseteq V\), any *deterministic* strategy is completely
described by a function  

\[
\Phi:\; 2^{V}\longrightarrow 2^{V},\qquad
H_{t}= \Phi(S_{t}) .
\]

In other words, at every turn the hunters look at the present knowledge–set \(S_{t}\)
and fire at the vertex–set \(\Phi(S_{t})\).
There are only \(2^{N}\) different arguments a strategy ever has to consider.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
2.  Loop–free strategies are short
--------------------------------------------------------------------

Assume that a *winning* strategy \(\Phi_{0}\) is known that guarantees a
capture in at most \(N!\) moves, whatever the hare does.
Let the hare play so as to stay alive as long as the strategy allows.
Under this worst–case play we obtain a sequence  

\[
S_{0},S_{1},\dots ,S_{k}\qquad (k\le N!)
\]

of knowledge–sets, where the hare is killed immediately after the
\(k\)-th shot.

If two indices \(0\le i<j\le k\) satisfy \(S_{i}=S_{j}\) we speak of a *loop*.
Observe what the hunters were going to do the second time the
(identical) state \(S_{j}=S_{i}\) occurred:
they would shoot at the set \(H_{j}=\Phi_{0}(S_{j})\) and, from that point on,
\(\Phi_{0}\) would still have guaranteed a capture.
Hence, starting from \(S_{i}\) they could forget everything they did in between
and immediately use the plan beginning with \(H_{j}\).
Removing the whole piece of play lying strictly between
\(S_{i}\) and its repetition \(S_{j}\) therefore shortens the maximal game–length
without destroying the guarantee of success.

Applying the same *loop deletion* step as long as some knowledge–set is
visited twice, we transform the original strategy into another winning
strategy \(\Phi\) with the property

 “No knowledge–set is encountered twice before the hare is hit.”

--------------------------------------------------------------------
3.  The new bound
--------------------------------------------------------------------

Because there are only \(2^{N}\) different subsets of \(V\), a play in which no
state repeats can last at most \(2^{N}-1\) unsuccessful moves.
Consequently the loop–free strategy \(\Phi\) captures the hare after at most  

\[
2^{N}\quad\text{moves}.
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
4.  Conclusion
--------------------------------------------------------------------

Starting from any strategy that guarantees a capture in at most \(N!\) moves
we have constructed a (possibly different) strategy which always succeeds
in at most \(2^{N}\) moves.
Therefore

 “There exists a strategy that kills the hare in at most \(2^{N}\) moves.”  ∎
ground_truth_solution:
Let hunters apply optimal (fastest) algorithm. Let say that a vertex has a smell of a hare, if there exists an initial vertex and a sequence of moves of the hare for which the hare is still alive and now occupies this vertex. After every shoot mark the set of all the vertices that have a smell of a hare. In the beginning all the vertices of the graph have a smell of hare, and after finish of hunting this set is empty. The idea is that in optimal strategy these sets can not repeat!

Indeed, the hunting does not imply feedback, the hunters' shoots do not depend on hare's moves because the hunters try to foresee all possible moves of hare. So if a set of vertices $A$ appears after the k -th shoot and once again after the $m$-th shoot, then then the strategy is not optimal because all shoots form $k$-th to $(m-1)$-th can be omitted with the same result of hunting.

Since it is possible to mark at most $2^{N}$ sets the hunting will finish in at most $2^{N}-1$ shoots.
llm_summary: The proof models the hunters’ knowledge by the set S_t of possible hare positions before the t-th shot and shows that any deterministic strategy is a function Φ from subsets of V to shot–sets. Given a winning strategy with at most N! moves, one removes all loops in the sequence of visited states—skipping from a repeated state directly to its next occurrence—without affecting the guarantee of capture. Since there are only 2^N subsets of V, a loop-free strategy makes at most 2^N moves.

problem:
Let \( a_{0} > 0 \) be a real number, and let

\[
a_{n} = \frac{a_{n-1}}{\sqrt{1+2020 \cdot a_{n-1}^{2}}}, \quad \text{for } n=1,2,\ldots,2020
\]

Show that \( a_{2020} < \frac{1}{2020} \).
solution:
To solve the problem, we are given a recursive sequence defined by:

$$
a_n = \frac{a_{n-1}}{\sqrt{1 + 2020 \cdot a_{n-1}^2}}, \quad \text{for } n = 1, 2, \ldots, 2020
$$

with the initial condition $ a_0 > 0 $. We are to prove that:

$$
a_{2020} < \frac{1}{2020}
$$

---

### Step 1: Transform the Recurrence

Let us define a new sequence $ b_n = \frac{1}{a_n} $. Since $ a_n > 0 $, this is well-defined and $ b_n > 0 $ for all $ n $.

We now express $ b_n $ in terms of $ b_{n-1} $:

$$
a_n = \frac{a_{n-1}}{\sqrt{1 + 2020 a_{n-1}^2}} \Rightarrow \frac{1}{a_n} = \frac{\sqrt{1 + 2020 a_{n-1}^2}}{a_{n-1}} = \sqrt{\frac{1}{a_{n-1}^2} + 2020}
$$

Thus,

$$
b_n = \sqrt{b_{n-1}^2 + 2020}
$$

---

### Step 2: Square Both Sides

Squaring both sides of the recurrence gives:

$$
b_n^2 = b_{n-1}^2 + 2020
$$

This is a linear recurrence relation for $ b_n^2 $, and we can solve it explicitly.

---

### Step 3: Solve the Recurrence

We are given $ b_0 = \frac{1}{a_0} $, so:

$$
b_n^2 = b_0^2 + 2020n
$$

Taking square roots (since $ b_n > 0 $):

$$
b_n = \sqrt{b_0^2 + 2020n}
$$

Therefore, the original sequence $ a_n $ is:

$$
a_n = \frac{1}{b_n} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{b_0^2 + 2020n}} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{\frac{1}{a_0^2} + 2020n}}
$$

---

### Step 4: Evaluate at $ n = 2020 $

We now compute $ a_{2020} $:

$$
a_{2020} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{\frac{1}{a_0^2} + 2020 \cdot 2020}} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{\frac{1}{a_0^2} + 2020^2}}
$$

We want to show that this is less than $ \frac{1}{2020} $, i.e.,

$$
\frac{1}{\sqrt{\frac{1}{a_0^2} + 2020^2}} < \frac{1}{2020}
$$

This is equivalent to:

$$
\sqrt{\frac{1}{a_0^2} + 2020^2} > 2020
$$

Squaring both sides (since both sides are positive):

$$
\frac{1}{a_0^2} + 2020^2 > 2020^2
$$

$$
\frac{1}{a_0^2} > 0
$$

This is always true since $ a_0 > 0 $, so $ \frac{1}{a_0^2} > 0 $.

---

### Final Conclusion

Since the inequality $ \frac{1}{a_0^2} > 0 $ holds for all $ a_0 > 0 $, it follows that:

$$
a_{2020} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{\frac{1}{a_0^2} + 2020^2}} < \frac{1}{2020}
$$

Thus, the desired inequality is proven.

$$
\boxed{a_{2020} < \dfrac{1}{2020}}
$$
llm_summary: The proof sets b_n = 1/a_n and rewrites the given recurrence as b_n = √(b_{n-1}^2 + 2020).  Squaring gives the linear relation b_n^2 = b_{n-1}^2 + 2020, which by telescoping yields b_n^2 = b_0^2 + 2020n.  Hence a_n = 1/√(1/a_0^2 + 2020n), and substituting n = 2020 leads to a_{2020} = 1/√(1/a_0^2 + 2020^2) < 1/2020 since 1/a_0^2 > 0.

llm_issues.description: The proof asserts the closed‐form solution to the recurrence b_n^2 = b_{n-1}^2 + 2020 by telescoping without showing the intermediate induction or telescoping argument.
The final inequality is labelled trivial without explicitly justifying that squaring both sides preserves the inequality direction under the assumption of positivity.
llm_issues.text: This is always true since 1/a_0^2 > 0

llm_issues.description: The derivation of this formula skips the detailed algebraic manipulation of pulling 1/a_{n-1}^2 inside the square root and simplifying the resulting expression.
The proof claims without proof that the sequence a_n remains positive for all n ≥ 1, which is needed to ensure b_n is well-defined and to justify taking square roots.

problem:
Let \( n \geq 1 \) be a positive integer. We say that an integer \( k \) is a fan of \( n \) if \( 0 \leq k \leq n-1 \) and there exist integers \( x, y, z \in \mathbb{Z} \) such that

\[
\begin{aligned}
x^{2}+y^{2}+z^{2} & \equiv 0 \pmod{n}; \\
xyz & \equiv k \pmod{n}.
\end{aligned}
\]

Let \( f(n) \) be the number of fans of \( n \). Determine \( f(2020) \).
solution:
Here is a self‐contained proof that  
\[
f(2020)\;=\;101\,.
\]

**Proof.**  
Write  
\[
2020 \;=\;4 \times 5 \times 101,
\]  
and observe that \(\gcd(4,5)=\gcd(4,101)=\gcd(5,101)=1\).  By the Chinese Remainder Theorem, an integer \(k\) modulo \(2020\) is a fan of \(2020\) if and only if its reductions
\[
k \bmod 4,\quad k \bmod 5,\quad k \bmod 101
\]
are fans of \(4,5,101\) respectively.  Hence
\[
f(2020) \;=\; f(4)\,\times f(5)\,\times f(101)\,.
\]

We now compute each factor in turn.

1.  **Computation of \(f(4)\).**  
    In \(\Bbb Z/4\Bbb Z\), every square is \(0\) or \(1\).  If
    \[
      x^2 + y^2 + z^2 \;\equiv\;0\pmod4,
    \]
    then each summand must be \(0\pmod4\) (since three 1’s sum to \(3\), not \(0\)).  Hence
    \[
      x\equiv y\equiv z\equiv 0\pmod2
      \quad\Longrightarrow\quad
      xyz\equiv 0\pmod4.
    \]
    No other residue of \(xyz\) can occur.  Therefore
    \[
      f(4)\;=\;1,
    \]
    namely only \(k\equiv0\) is a fan mod 4.

2.  **Computation of \(f(5)\).**  
    In \(\Bbb Z/5\Bbb Z\), the set of squares is \(\{0,1,4\}\).  If
    \[
      x^2 + y^2 + z^2 \;\equiv\;0\pmod5,
    \]
    then each of \(x^2,y^2,z^2\) lies in \(\{0,1,4\}\), and one checks by exhaustively listing
    \[
       1+1+1=3,\quad 1+1+4=6\equiv1,\quad1+4+4=9\equiv4,\quad4+4+4=12\equiv2
    \]
    that *no* triple of nonzero squares can sum to 0.  Thus at least one of \(x,y,z\) must be divisible by 5, forcing
    \[
      xyz\equiv0\pmod5.
    \]
    Hence again only \(k\equiv0\) is realized, so
    \[
      f(5)\;=\;1.
    \]

3.  **Computation of \(f(101)\).**  
    We break into two steps:

    (a)  **Existence of one invertible solution.**  
         One checks the identity of ordinary integers
         \[
           6^2 + 4^2 + 7^2
           \;=\;
           36 + 16 + 49
           \;=\;
           101.
         \]
         Reducing modulo 101, this says
         \[
           x^2+y^2+z^2\;\equiv\;0\pmod{101}
         \]
         with
         \(
           (x,y,z)=(6,4,7)
         \)
         and none of \(6,4,7\) is a multiple of 101.  In particular \(x,y,z\in(\Bbb Z/101)^\times\).

    (b)  **Generating *all* nonzero residues via scaling.**  
         The multiplicative group \((\Bbb Z/101)^\times\) is cyclic of order \(100\).  Since
         \(\gcd(3,100)=1\), the map
         \[
           t\;\longmapsto\; t^3
           \quad:\;
           (\Bbb Z/101)^\times\;\to\;(\Bbb Z/101)^\times
         \]
         is bijective.  Let \(k_0\equiv xyz\pmod{101}\) be the product of our example triple.  Then for *every* nonzero residue \(k\in(\Bbb Z/101)^\times\) there is a unique \(t\in(\Bbb Z/101)^\times\) with
         \[
           t^3\;=\;k\,k_0^{-1}.
         \]
         But then
         \(
           (t x,\;t y,\;t z)
         \)
         still satisfies
         \[
           (t x)^2 + (t y)^2 + (t z)^2
           \;=\;
           t^2\,(x^2+y^2+z^2)
           \;\equiv\;0\pmod{101},
         \]
         and its product is
         \[
           (t x)\,(t y)\,(t z)
           \;=\;
           t^3\,(x y z)
           \;\equiv\;
           k_0\;t^3
           \;=\;
           k
           \pmod{101}.
         \]
         Finally, \(k=0\) is also attained (for instance by the triple \((0,1,10)\), since \(0^2+1^2+10^2=101\equiv0\pmod{101}\) and its product is \(0\)).  We conclude that *every* residue class \(k\in\{0,1,2,\dots,100\}\) is a fan mod 101.  Hence
         \[
           f(101)\;=\;101.
         \]

Combining these by the Chinese Remainder Theorem,
\[
  f(2020)
  \;=\;
  f(4)\,\times f(5)\,\times f(101)
  \;=\;
  1\;\times\;1\;\times\;101
  \;=\;
  101.
\]
This completes the proof.  
∎
ground_truth_solution:
Solution.
Answer: $f(2020)=f(4) \cdot f(5) \cdot f(101)=1 \cdot 1 \cdot 101=101$.
To prove our claim we show that $f$ is multiplicative, that is, $f(r s)=f(r) f(s)$ for coprime numbers $r, s \in \mathbb{N}$, and that
(i) $f(4)=1$,
(ii) $f(5)=1$,
(iii) $f(101)=101$.

The multiplicative property follows from the Chinese Remainder Theorem.
(i) Integers $x, y$ and $z$ satisfy $x^{2}+y^{2}+z^{2} \equiv 0 \bmod 4$ if and only if they are all even. In this case $x y z \equiv 0 \bmod 4$. Hence $0$ is the only fan of $4$.
(ii) Integers $x, y$ and $z$ satisfy $x^{2}+y^{2}+z^{2} \equiv 0 \bmod 5$ if and only if at least one of them is divisible by $5$. In this case $x y z \equiv 0 \bmod 5$. Hence $5$ is the only fan of $5$.
(iii) We have $9^{2}+4^{2}+2^{2}=81+16+4=101$. Hence $(9 x)^{2}+(4 x)^{2}+(2 x)^{2}$ is divisible by $101$ for every integer $x$. Hence the residue of $9 x \cdot 4 x \cdot 2 x=72 x^{3}$ upon division by $101$ is a fan of $101$ for every $x \in \mathbb{Z}$. If we substitute $x=t^{67}$, then $x^{3}=t^{201} \equiv t \bmod 101$. Since $72$ is coprime to $101$, the number $72 x^{3} \equiv 72 t$ can take any residue modulo $101$.

Note: In general for $p \not \equiv 1(\bmod 3)$, we have $f(p)=p$ as soon as we have at least one non-zero fan.

It then checks directly that f(4)=1 by examining squares mod 4, that f(5)=1 by listing squares mod 5, and that f(101)=101 by finding one nonzero solution to x²+y²+z²≡0 (mod 101) and using the cyclicity of (ℤ/101)× to scale this solution to realize every residue, finally multiplying to obtain f(2020)=101.

problem: Denote by \(d(n)\) the number of positive divisors of a positive integer \(n\). Prove that there are infinitely many positive integers \(n\) such that \(\lfloor\sqrt{3} \cdot d(n)\rfloor\) divides \(n\).
solution:
Let \(d(n)\) denote the number of positive divisors of the positive integer \(n\).
We shall exhibit an explicit infinite family of integers \(n\) for which
\[
\bigl\lfloor \sqrt 3 \, d(n)\bigr\rfloor \mid n .
\]

1.  A convenient value of \(d(n)\).

   We first look for a positive integer \(m\) such that
   \[
       \Bigl\lfloor\sqrt3\,m\Bigr\rfloor = 20.
   \]
   Because \(20<\sqrt3\,m<21\) implies
   \[
       20^2 < 3m^{2} < 21^{2}\qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad
       400<3m^{2}<441 ,
   \]
   we get \(134 < m^{2} < 147\).  The only positive integer whose square is in
   this interval is \(m=12\).  Hence

   \[
       m=12 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad
       \Bigl\lfloor\sqrt3\,m\Bigr\rfloor = 20 .
   \]

2.  Producing integers with \(d(n)=12\).

   Write \(20 = 2^{2}\cdot 5\).  
   For any prime \(p\) different from \(2\) and \(5\) define
   \[
       n:=20p = 2^{2}\cdot 5\cdot p .
   \]
   Since the prime factorisation of \(n\) is
   \(2^{2}\,5^{1}\,p^{1}\) we have
   \[
        d(n)=(2+1)(1+1)(1+1)=3\cdot2\cdot2=12 .
   \]

3.  Computing \(\lfloor\sqrt3\,d(n)\rfloor\).

   Because \(d(n)=12\),
   \[
       \sqrt3\,d(n)=12\sqrt3 .
   \]
   We already observed that \(20<12\sqrt3<21\); therefore
   \[
       \Bigl\lfloor\sqrt3\,d(n)\Bigr\rfloor = 20 .
   \]

4.  Verifying the divisibility.

   By construction \(20\) is a factor of \(n=20p\), hence
   \[
       20 \mid n .
   \]
   Combining this with the previous step,
   \[
       \Bigl\lfloor\sqrt3\,d(n)\Bigr\rfloor = 20 \mid n .
   \]

5.  Infinitely many such integers.

   There are infinitely many primes \(p\neq2,5\);
   for each of them the associated integer \(n=20p\) satisfies
   \[
       \Bigl\lfloor\sqrt3\,d(n)\Bigr\rfloor \mid n .
   \]
   Consequently there are infinitely many positive integers possessing the
   required property.

Hence we have proved:  
There exist infinitely many positive integers \(n\) such that
\(\bigl\lfloor\sqrt 3 \, d(n)\bigr\rfloor\) divides \(n\).
ground_truth_solution:
Solution $1$.
Note that $|\sqrt{3} \cdot 8|=13$. Therefore all numbers with $8$ divisors that are divisible by $13$ satisfy the condition. There are infinitely many of those, for example, all numbers in the form $13 p^{3}$, where $p$ is a prime different from $13$.

## Solution $2$.

Based on the solution by the Finnish team: Instead of finding infinitely many solutions with $d(n)=2^{3}$, we prove that every power $2^{k}, k \geqslant 0$, has at least one solution with $d(n)=2^{k}$.

Let $k \geqslant 0$ be given, and let $p_{1}, p_{2}, \ldots$ be the sequence of all prime numbers. We then write the prime factorization of $\left\lfloor 2^{k} \sqrt{3}\right\rfloor$ as

$$
\left\lfloor 2^{k} \sqrt{3}\right\rfloor=\prod_{i=1}^{\infty} p_{i}^{b_{i}}
$$
with $b_{i} \geqslant 0$ and only finitely many $b_{i}$ different from $0$.
Since $\sqrt{3}<2$, we have
$$
2^{k+1}>\left\lfloor 2^{k} \sqrt{3}\right\rfloor=\prod_{i=1}^{\infty} p_{i}^{b_{i}} \geqslant \prod_{i=1}^{\infty} 2^{b_{i}}=2^{\sum_{i=1}^{\infty} b_{i}},
$$

and from this we conclude $\sum_{i=1}^{\infty} b_{i} \leqslant k$. We know that $m+1 \leqslant 2^{m}$ for any integer $m \geqslant 0$, and this brings us a further estimate

$$
\sum_{i=1}^{\infty}\left\lceil\log _{2}\left(b_{i}+1\right)\right\rceil \leqslant \sum_{i=1}^{\infty} b_{i} \leqslant k
$$

By increasing values if necessary, we can choose a sequence of non-negative integers $a_{1}, a_{2}, \ldots$ such that $a_{i} \geqslant\left\lceil\log _{2}\left(b_{i}+1\right)\right\rceil$ for all $i$, and $\sum_{i=1}^{\infty} a_{i}=k$. [Editor's note: In fact, unless $\sum_{i=1}^{\infty}\left\lceil\log _{2}\left(b_{i}+1\right)\right\rceil=k$ already, we have an infinite choice of such sequences - each leading to a distinct $n$ with the required properties.] We now define

$$
n=\prod_{i=1}^{\infty} p_{i}^{2^{a_{i}}-1}
$$
which is a valid product since all but finitely many $a_{i}$ are equal to zero. By construction we have $2^{a_{i}}-1 \geqslant b_{i}$ for all $i$, so $\left\lfloor 2^{k} \sqrt{3}\right\rfloor$ divides $n$. Finally, the number of divisors in $n$ can be calculated as
$$
d(n)=\prod_{i=1}^{\infty}\left(\left(2^{a_{i}}-1\right)+1\right)=\prod_{i=1}^{\infty} 2^{a_{i}}=2^{\sum_{i=1}^{\infty} a_{i}}=2^{k}
$$

so $n$ satisfies that $\lfloor d(n) \sqrt{3}\rfloor=\left\lfloor 2^{k} \sqrt{3}\right\rfloor$ divides $n$.
Solution $3$.
Based on the solution by the Norwegian team: In this third solution, instead of letting $d(n)$ be a power of $2$, we prove that there a infinitely many solutions with $n=2^{k}$.

Consider the sequence $a_{i}=\lfloor i \sqrt{3}\rfloor$ for $i \geqslant 1$. If $k \geqslant 3$, then $(k+1) \sqrt{3}<2(k+1) \leqslant 2^{k}$. Consequently, whenever $a_{k+1}=2^{m}$ and $k \geqslant 3$, we get

$$
\left\lfloor d\left(2^{k}\right) \sqrt{3}\right\rfloor=\lfloor(k+1) \sqrt{3}\rfloor=a_{k+1}=2^{m}\left\lfloor 2^{k}\right.
$$
so $n=2^{k}$ satisfies the properties of the problem. It is therefore sufficient to prove that the integer sequence $a_{i}=\lfloor i \sqrt{3}\rfloor$ contains infinitely many powers of $2$. Since $\sqrt{3}>1$, the sequence is strictly increasing, and since $\sqrt{3}<2$, we have
$$
a_{i+1}-a_{i}=\lfloor(i+1) \sqrt{3}\rfloor-\lfloor i \sqrt{3}\rfloor<(i+1) \sqrt{3}-(i \sqrt{3}-1)=\sqrt{3}+1<3 .
$$

Hence the sequence jump by at most $2$ at each step.
Suppose for contradiction that the sequence constains only finitely many powers of two, say the largest is $2^{N}$. Then for every $m>N$ we can find a unique index $k$ such that $a_{k}=2^{m}-1$ and $a_{k+1}=2^{m}+1$.

Define $d_{i}=i \sqrt{3}-a_{i}$ to be the fractional part for each $i$, so that $0 \leqslant d_{i}<1$. For $k$ as above we then have

$$
\begin{aligned}
k \sqrt{3}-\left(2^{m}-1\right) & =d_{k} \geqslant 0 \\
(k+1) \sqrt{3}-\left(2^{m}+1\right) & =d_{k+1} \geqslant 0, \\
\text { and thus }(2 k+1) \sqrt{3}-2^{m+1} & =d_{k}+d_{k+1} \geqslant 0 .
\end{aligned}
$$

If $d_{k}+d_{k+1}<1$, we would have $a_{2 k+1}=2^{m+1}$ contrary to our assumptions, hence $1 \leqslant d_{k}+d_{k+1}<2$ and consequently $a_{2 k+1}=2^{m+1}+1$ and $a_{2 k}=2^{m+1}-1$.

Since $a_{2 k}=2^{m+1}-1$, we have a recursive expression for $d_{2 k}$ as well:

$$
d_{2 k}=2 k \sqrt{3}-\left(2^{m+1}-1\right)=2\left(d_{k}+2^{m}-1\right)-\left(2^{m+1}-1\right)=2 d_{k}-1
$$

We can now repeat the process with $2 k$ and $2 k+1$ in place of $k$ and $k+1$ in order to prove the following statements by induction for all $j \geqslant 0$ :

- $a_{2^{j}}{ }=2^{m+j}-1$ and $a_{2^{j}}{ }_{k+1}=2^{m+j}+1$
- $d_{2^{j} k}=2^{j} d_{k}-\left(2^{j}-1\right)=2^{j}\left(d_{k}-1\right)+1$

Finally, since $d_{k}-1<0$, the second property implies that $d_{2 j}$ tends to $-\infty$ as $j$ tends to $\infty$. This clearly contradicts that $d_{2^{j}} \geqslant 0$ for all $k$ and $j$, hence we conclude that the sequence $a_{i}$ contains infinitely many powers of $2$ as required.
llm_summary: The proof observes that \(\lfloor\sqrt3\,m\rfloor=20\) uniquely when \(m=12\), so one seeks integers \(n\) with \(d(n)=12\). Writing 20=2²·5 and taking any prime \(p\neq2,5\), the integer \(n=20p\) has factorization 2²·5·p and hence \(d(n)=3·2·2=12\). Since \(\lfloor12\sqrt3\rfloor=20\) and 20 divides \(n=20p\), each such \(n\) satisfies the required divisibility, and there are infinitely many choices of \(p\).

solution:
To prove that \(b_1 + b_2 + \cdots + b_{2020} < \frac{2}{3}\), we analyze the sequences \(a_n\) and \(b_n\) as defined. The sequence \(a_n\) starts with \(a_0 = 2\), and for \(n \geq 1\),

\[
a_n = 
\begin{cases} 
a_{n-1}^2 & \text{if } a_{n-1} < \sqrt{3} \\
\frac{a_{n-1}^2}{3} & \text{if } a_{n-1} \geq \sqrt{3}.
\end{cases}
\]

The sequence \(b_n\) for \(n \geq 1\) is defined by

\[
b_n = 
\begin{cases} 
0 & \text{if } a_{n-1} < \sqrt{3} \\
\frac{1}{2^n} & \text{if } a_{n-1} \geq \sqrt{3}.
\end{cases}
\]

We need to bound the sum \(s_N = \sum_{n=1}^N b_n\) for \(N = 2020\).

Consider the behavior of \(a_n\). Note that \(a_0 = 2 > \sqrt{3} \approx 1.732\), and all subsequent terms satisfy \(a_n > 1\) because:
- If \(a_{n-1} < \sqrt{3}\), then \(a_n = a_{n-1}^2\). Since \(a_{n-1} > 1\) (as established inductively, starting from \(a_0 = 2 > 1\)), \(a_n > 1\).
- If \(a_{n-1} \geq \sqrt{3}\), then \(a_n = \frac{a_{n-1}^2}{3}\). Since \(a_{n-1} \geq \sqrt{3}\), \(a_{n-1}^2 \geq 3\), so \(a_n \geq \frac{3}{3} = 1\), and equality holds only if \(a_{n-1} = \sqrt{3}\), but since \(\sqrt{3}\) is irrational and the operations involve squares and division by 3, \(a_n > 1\) strictly.

Define \(x_n = \ln a_n\). The recursion for \(a_n\) translates to:
- If \(a_{n-1} < \sqrt{3}\), then \(x_n = \ln(a_{n-1}^2) = 2x_{n-1}\).
- If \(a_{n-1} \geq \sqrt{3}\), then \(x_n = \ln\left(\frac{a_{n-1}^2}{3}\right) = 2x_{n-1} - \ln 3\).

The condition \(a_{n-1} \geq \sqrt{3}\) is equivalent to \(x_{n-1} \geq \frac{1}{2} \ln 3\), since \(\sqrt{3} = e^{\frac{1}{2} \ln 3}\), and the natural logarithm is strictly increasing.

Set \(\alpha = \ln 3\) and \(y_n = \frac{x_n}{\alpha} = \frac{\ln a_n}{\ln 3}\). Then:
- \(y_{n-1} < \frac{1}{2}\) implies \(x_{n-1} < \frac{1}{2} \ln 3\), so \(a_{n-1} < \sqrt{3}\), and \(x_n = 2x_{n-1}\), thus \(y_n = \frac{2x_{n-1}}{\alpha} = 2y_{n-1}\).
- \(y_{n-1} \geq \frac{1}{2}\) implies \(x_{n-1} \geq \frac{1}{2} \ln 3\), so \(a_{n-1} \geq \sqrt{3}\), and \(x_n = 2x_{n-1} - \ln 3\), thus \(y_n = \frac{2x_{n-1} - \alpha}{\alpha} = 2y_{n-1} - 1\).

So the recurrence for \(y_n\) is:

\[
y_n = 
\begin{cases} 
2y_{n-1} & \text{if } y_{n-1} < \frac{1}{2} \\
2y_{n-1} - 1 & \text{if } y_{n-1} \geq \frac{1}{2}.
\end{cases}
\]

The initial value is \(y_0 = \frac{\ln a_0}{\ln 3} = \frac{\ln 2}{\ln 3}\). Since \(a_n > 1\) for all \(n\), \(x_n > 0\), so \(y_n > 0\). Also, \(y_n < 1\) for all \(n\):
- If \(y_{n-1} < \frac{1}{2}\), then \(y_n = 2y_{n-1} < 1\).
- If \(y_{n-1} \geq \frac{1}{2}\), then \(y_n = 2y_{n-1} - 1 \geq 2 \cdot \frac{1}{2} - 1 = 0\), and since \(y_{n-1} < 1\) (by induction), \(y_n < 2 \cdot 1 - 1 = 1\).

Thus, \(y_n \in [0, 1)\) for all \(n \geq 0\). The recurrence \(y_n = 
\begin{cases} 
2y_{n-1} & \text{if } y_{n-1} < \frac{1}{2} \\
2y_{n-1} - 1 & \text{if } y_{n-1} \geq \frac{1}{2}
\end{cases}
\) is equivalent to \(y_n = \{2y_{n-1}\}\), where \(\{ \cdot \}\) denotes the fractional part, because:
- If \(y_{n-1} < \frac{1}{2}\), then \(2y_{n-1} < 1\), so \(\{2y_{n-1}\} = 2y_{n-1}\).
- If \(y_{n-1} \geq \frac{1}{2}\), then \(2y_{n-1} \geq 1\), so \(\{2y_{n-1}\} = 2y_{n-1} - 1\).

Moreover, \(y_0 = \theta = \frac{\ln 2}{\ln 3}\), and by induction, \(y_n = \{2^n \theta\}\) for all \(n \geq 0\).

The definition of \(b_n\) states that \(b_n = \frac{1}{2^n}\) if \(a_{n-1} \geq \sqrt{3}\), which is equivalent to \(y_{n-1} \geq \frac{1}{2}\), and \(b_n = 0\) otherwise. Thus, \(b_n = \frac{1}{2^n}\) if and only if \(y_{n-1} \geq \frac{1}{2}\).

Consider the binary expansion of \(\theta = \frac{\ln 2}{\ln 3}\). Let \(\theta = \sum_{k=1}^{\infty} d_k 2^{-k}\), where \(d_k \in \{0, 1\}\) is the \(k\)-th binary digit. The digits are generated by the process: set \(z_0 = \theta\), and for \(k \geq 1\), \(d_k = \lfloor 2 z_{k-1} \rfloor\), and \(z_k = \{2 z_{k-1}\}\). Note that \(d_k = 1\) if and only if \(z_{k-1} \geq \frac{1}{2}\).

Since \(z_k = \{2^k \theta\} = y_k\) for all \(k \geq 0\), we have \(d_k = 1\) if and only if \(y_{k-1} \geq \frac{1}{2}\). Therefore, \(b_n = \frac{1}{2^n}\) if and only if \(d_n = 1\), and \(b_n = 0\) otherwise. Thus, \(b_n = d_n \cdot 2^{-n}\).

The sum \(s_N = \sum_{n=1}^N b_n = \sum_{n=1}^N d_n 2^{-n}\). This is the partial sum of the binary expansion of \(\theta\), so \(s_N < \theta\) for all \(N \geq 1\), because \(\theta\) is irrational (as established below) and the tail of the series is positive.

To see that \(\theta = \frac{\ln 2}{\ln 3}\) is irrational, suppose it is rational, say \(\theta = \frac{p}{q}\) for integers \(p, q\) with \(q \neq 0\). Then \(\frac{\ln 2}{\ln 3} = \frac{p}{q}\), so \(q \ln 2 = p \ln 3\), hence \(\ln(2^q) = \ln(3^p)\). Since the natural logarithm is injective, \(2^q = 3^p\). But \(2^q\) is a power of 2, \(3^p\) is a power of 3, and they are equal only if \(p = q = 0\), a contradiction. Thus, \(\theta\) is irrational, and \(s_N < \theta\) for all finite \(N\).

Now, \(\theta = \frac{\ln 2}{\ln 3} < \frac{2}{3}\). To show this, note that \(\frac{\ln 2}{\ln 3} < \frac{2}{3}\) if and only if \(3 \ln 2 < 2 \ln 3\), since \(\ln 3 > 0\). This is equivalent to \(\ln(2^3) < \ln(3^2)\), i.e., \(\ln 8 < \ln 9\). Since the natural logarithm is strictly increasing, \(\ln 8 < \ln 9\) holds because \(8 < 9\). Thus, \(\theta < \frac{2}{3}\).

Therefore, for any \(N \geq 1\), \(s_N < \theta < \frac{2}{3}\). In particular, for \(N = 2020\),

\[
s_{2020} = b_1 + b_2 + \cdots + b_{2020} < \frac{2}{3}.
\]

This completes the proof.

\boxed{\text{proved}}
ground_truth_solution:
The first step is to prove, using induction, the formula

$$
a_{n}=\frac{2^{2^{n}}}{3^{2^{n}\left(b_{1}+b_{2}+\cdots+b_{n}\right)}} .
$$

The base case $n=0$ is trivial. Assume the formula is valid for $a_{n-1}$, that is,

$$
a_{n-1}=\frac{2^{2^{n-1}}}{3^{2^{n-1}\left(b_{1}+b_{2}+\cdots+b_{n-1}\right)}} .
$$

If now $a_{n-1}<\sqrt{3}$, then $b_{n}=0$, and so

$$
a_{n}=a_{n-1}^{2}=\frac{2^{2^{n}}}{3^{2^{n}\left(b_{1}+b_{2}+\cdots+b_{n-1}\right)}}=\frac{2^{2^{n}}}{3^{2^{n}\left(b_{1}+b_{2}+\cdots+b_{n-1}+b_{n}\right)}},
$$
whereas if $a_{n-1} \geqslant \sqrt{3}$, then $b_{n}=\frac{1}{2^{n}}$, and so
$$
a_{n}=\frac{a_{n-1}^{2}}{3}=\frac{2^{2^{n}}}{3^{2^{n}\left(b_{1}+b_{2}+\cdots+b_{n-1}\right)+1}}=\frac{2^{2^{n}}}{3^{2^{n}\left(b_{1}+b_{2}+\cdots+b_{n-1}+b_{n}\right)}} .
$$

This completes the induction.
Next, we inductively establish the inequality $a_{n} \geqslant 1$. The base case $n=0$ is again trivial. Suppose $a_{n-1} \geqslant 1$. If $a_{n-1}<\sqrt{3}$, then

$$
a_{n}=a_{n-1}^{2} \geqslant 1^{2}=1
$$
whereas if $a_{n-1} \geqslant \sqrt{3}$, then
$$
a_{n}=\frac{a_{n-1}^{2}}{3} \geqslant \frac{(\sqrt{3})^{2}}{3}=1
$$

and the induction is complete.
From

$$
1 \leqslant a_{n}=\frac{2^{2^{n}}}{3^{2^{n}\left(b_{1}+b_{2}+\cdots+b_{n}\right)}}=\left(\frac{2}{3^{b_{1}+b_{2}+\cdots+b_{n}}}\right)^{2^{n}}
$$
we may then draw the conclusion
$$
3^{b_{1}+b_{2}+\cdots+b_{n}} \leqslant 2
$$

Since $3^{2 / 3}>2$ (and the function $x \mapsto 3^{x}$ is strictly increasing), we must have

$$
b_{1}+b_{2}+\cdots+b_{n}<\frac{2}{3}
$$
for all $n$, and we are finished.
Remark. Using only slightly more work, it may be proved that
$$
1 \leqslant a_{n}=\frac{2^{2^{n}}}{3^{2^{n}\left(b_{1}+b_{2}+\cdots+b_{n}\right)}}<3
$$

which entails

$$
1^{\frac{1}{2^{n}}} \leqslant \frac{2}{3^{b_{1}+b_{2}+\cdots+b_{n}}}<3^{\frac{1}{2^{n}}}
$$
for all $n$, hence
$$
3^{b_{1}+b_{2}+\cdots}=2
$$

The problem thus provides an algorithm for calculating

$$
b_{1}+b_{2}+\cdots=\log _{3} 2 \approx 0.63
$$
in binary.

problem: Let \( n \) be a given positive integer. A restaurant offers a choice of \( n \) starters, \( n \) main dishes, \( n \) desserts, and \( n \) wines. A group of guests dines at the restaurant, with each guest choosing a starter, a main dish, a dessert, and a wine. No two people place exactly the same order. It turns out that there is no collection of \( n \) guests such that their orders coincide in three of these aspects, but in the fourth one they all differ. What is the maximal number of guests?
solution:
Let $S, M, D, W$ be the sets of starters, main dishes, desserts, and wines, respectively. We are given that $|S|=|M|=|D|=|W|=n$. Let $N$ be the number of guests. Each guest chooses an order $(s,m,d,w)$ where $s \in S, m \in M, d \in D, w \in W$. All guests choose distinct orders. Let $O \subseteq S \times M \times D \times W$ be the set of orders chosen by the guests. Then $N = |O|$.

The crucial condition is: "there is no collection of $n$ guests such that their orders coincide in three of these aspects, but in the fourth one they all differ".
Let's analyze this condition. There are four symmetric ways this condition can apply, based on which three aspects coincide and which one differs.

1.  Consider the case where the orders of $n$ guests coincide in $S, M, D$ and differ in $W$.
    This means there is no subset of $n$ guests, say $K = \{g_1, \ldots, g_n\}$, such that for some fixed $s_0 \in S, m_0 \in M, d_0 \in D$:
    (a) The order for guest $g_i$ is $(s_0, m_0, d_0, w_i)$ for each $g_i \in K$.
    (b) Their choices of wine $w_1, \ldots, w_n$ are all distinct. Since there are $n$ guests and $n$ possible wines, this means $\{w_1, \ldots, w_n\} = W$.
    Let $O_{s_0m_0d_0} = \{w \in W \mid (s_0,m_0,d_0,w) \in O\}$. These are the wines chosen by guests who ordered starter $s_0$, main $m_0$, and dessert $d_0$. Since all orders in $O$ are distinct, the number of such guests is $|O_{s_0m_0d_0}|$.
    The condition implies that there is no $(s_0,m_0,d_0)$ for which $O_{s_0m_0d_0} = W$.
    Thus, for any $(s_0,m_0,d_0) \in S \times M \times D$, $O_{s_0m_0d_0}$ must be a proper subset of $W$.
    This means $|O_{s_0m_0d_0}| \le n-1$.

We can sum the number of guests over all possible choices of $(s,m,d)$:
$N = |O| = \sum_{(s,m,d) \in S \times M \times D} |O_{smd}|$.
Since $|S \times M \times D| = n \cdot n \cdot n = n^3$, and for each $(s,m,d)$, $|O_{smd}| \le n-1$, we have:
$N \le \sum_{(s,m,d) \in S \times M \times D} (n-1) = n^3 (n-1)$.

This gives an upper bound for the number of guests.
The same logic applies if we fix any other combination of three aspects. For example, if we fix $(s_0,m_0,w_0)$, then the set of desserts $O_{s_0m_0w_0} = \{d \in D \mid (s_0,m_0,d,w_0) \in O\}$ must satisfy $|O_{s_0m_0w_0}| \le n-1$. Summing over $(s,m,w)$ also gives $N \le n^3(n-1)$.

To show that $n^3(n-1)$ is the maximal number of guests, we need to construct a set of orders $O$ of this size that satisfies the condition.
Let $S = M = D = W = \{0, 1, \ldots, n-1\}$.
Consider the function $f: S \times M \times D \to W$ defined by $f(s,m,d) = (s+m+d) \pmod n$.
This function has the property that if any two of its arguments are fixed, it is a bijection in the remaining argument. For example, for fixed $m_0, d_0$, the map $s \mapsto (s+m_0+d_0) \pmod n$ is a bijection from $S$ to $W$. This is because if $s_1+m_0+d_0 \equiv s_2+m_0+d_0 \pmod n$, then $s_1 \equiv s_2 \pmod n$. Since $s_1,s_2 \in \{0, \ldots, n-1\}$, $s_1=s_2$. This shows injectivity. Since $S$ and $W$ are finite sets of the same size $n$, this map is also surjective. Similarly, $m \mapsto f(s_0,m,d_0)$ and $d \mapsto f(s_0,m_0,d)$ are bijections. (Such a function is known as a Latin cube).

Let the set of orders be $O = \{ (s,m,d,w) \in S \times M \times D \times W \mid w \neq f(s,m,d) \}$.
That is, $O = \{ (s,m,d,w) \mid w \not\equiv (s+m+d) \pmod n \}$.
The total number of possible orders in $S \times M \times D \times W$ is $n^4$.
The set $O$ is formed by removing all orders $(s,m,d,w)$ where $w = (s+m+d) \pmod n$. For each of the $n^3$ possible choices of $(s,m,d)$, exactly one wine $w$ is excluded. So $n^3$ orders are removed.
Thus, the number of orders in $O$ is $N = n^4 - n^3 = n^3(n-1)$.

Now we must verify that this set $O$ satisfies the condition.
1.  Fix $(s_0,m_0,d_0)$. The set of wines chosen by guests with this combination of starter, main, and dessert is $O_{s_0m_0d_0} = \{w \in W \mid (s_0,m_0,d_0,w) \in O\}$.
    By construction, $(s_0,m_0,d_0,w) \in O$ if and only if $w \not\equiv (s_0+m_0+d_0) \pmod n$.
    So $O_{s_0m_0d_0} = W \setminus \{(s_0+m_0+d_0) \pmod n\}$.
    This set has size $n-1$. Thus, it is not $W$. This part of the condition is satisfied.

2.  Fix $(s_0,m_0,w_0)$. The set of desserts chosen by guests with this combination is $O_{s_0m_0w_0} = \{d \in D \mid (s_0,m_0,d,w_0) \in O\}$.
    By construction, $(s_0,m_0,d,w_0) \in O$ if and only if $w_0 \not\equiv (s_0+m_0+d) \pmod n$.
    This is equivalent to $s_0+m_0+d \not\equiv w_0 \pmod n$, or $d \not\equiv (w_0-s_0-m_0) \pmod n$.
    So $O_{s_0m_0w_0} = D \setminus \{(w_0-s_0-m_0) \pmod n\}$.
    This set has size $n-1$. Thus, it is not $D$. This part of the condition is satisfied.

3.  Fix $(s_0,d_0,w_0)$. The set of main dishes is $O_{s_0d_0w_0} = \{m \in M \mid (s_0,m,d_0,w_0) \in O\}$.
    $(s_0,m,d_0,w_0) \in O \iff w_0 \not\equiv (s_0+m+d_0) \pmod n \iff m \not\equiv (w_0-s_0-d_0) \pmod n$.
    So $O_{s_0d_0w_0} = M \setminus \{(w_0-s_0-d_0) \pmod n\}$.
    This set has size $n-1$. Thus, it is not $M$. This part of the condition is satisfied.

4.  Fix $(m_0,d_0,w_0)$. The set of starters is $O_{m_0d_0w_0} = \{s \in S \mid (s,m_0,d_0,w_0) \in O\}$.
    $(s,m_0,d_0,w_0) \in O \iff w_0 \not\equiv (s+m_0+d_0) \pmod n \iff s \not\equiv (w_0-m_0-d_0) \pmod n$.
    So $O_{m_0d_0w_0} = S \setminus \{(w_0-m_0-d_0) \pmod n\}$.
    This set has size $n-1$. Thus, it is not $S$. This part of the condition is satisfied.

All four symmetric versions of the condition are satisfied. For any choice of three fixed aspects, the number of choices for the fourth aspect is $n-1$. Since $n$ is a positive integer, $n \ge 1$.
If $n=1$, then $n-1=0$. The set of choices for the fourth aspect has size 0. This is not the set of all choices (which has size 1). So the condition is satisfied.
The number of guests for $n=1$ by the formula is $1^3(1-1) = 0$. This is correct, because if there is $n=1$ guest, say with order $(s_1,m_1,d_1,w_1)$, then this guest forms a forbidden collection. For example, fix $(s_1,m_1,d_1)$. Then this guest's wine is $w_1$. The set of wines is $\{w_1\}$. Since $W=\{w_1\}$, this is $W$. This is forbidden. So there must be 0 guests.

The construction provides a set of $N=n^3(n-1)$ orders that satisfy all conditions. Since we have shown that $N \le n^3(n-1)$, this is the maximal possible number of guests.

Final check of the problem statement: "No two people place exactly the same order". This is satisfied because $O$ is defined as a set of distinct tuples. "there is no collection of n guests such that their orders coincide in three of these aspects, but in the fourth one they all differ". This means that for any fixed values for 3 aspects, the set of values for the 4th aspect is not the set of all $n$ possible values. Our construction ensures this set has $n-1$ values. This is not the set of all $n$ values (as long as $n>0$, which it is).

Thus, the maximal number of guests is $n^3(n-1)$.

The final answer is $\boxed{n^3(n-1)}$.
ground_truth_solution:
## Solution.

Answer: The maximal number of guests is $n^{4}-n^{3}$.
The possible menus are represented by quadruples

$$
(a, b, c, d), \quad 1 \leqslant a, b, c, d \leqslant n
$$

Let us count those menus satisfying

$$
a+b+c+d \not \equiv 0 \quad(\bmod n) .
$$

The numbers $a, b, c$ may be chosen arbitrarily ( $n$ choices for each), and then $d$ is required to satisfy only $d \not \equiv-a-b-c$. Hence there are

$$
n^{3}(n-1)=n^{4}-n^{3}
$$
such menus.
If there are $n^{4}-n^{3}$ guests, and they have chosen precisely the $n^{4}-n^{3}$ menus satisfying $a+b+c+d \not \equiv 0(\bmod n)$, we claim that the condition of the problem is fulfilled. So suppose there is a collection of $n$ people whose orders coincide in three aspects, but differ in the fourth. With no loss of generality, we may assume they have ordered exactly the same food, but $n$ different wines. This means they all have the same value of $a, b$ and $c$, but their values of $d$ are distinct. A contradiction arises since, given $a, b$ and $c$, there are only $n-1$ values available for d.

We now show that for $n^{4}-n^{3}+1$ guests (or more), it is impossible to obtain the situation stipulated in the problem. The $n^{3}$ sets

$$
M_{a, b, c}=\{(a, b, c, d) \mid 1 \leqslant d \leqslant n\}, \quad 1 \leqslant a, b, c \leqslant n
$$
form a partition of the set of possible menus, totalling $n^{4}$. When the number of guests is at least $n^{4}-n^{3}+1$, there are at most $n^{3}-1$ unselected menus. Therefore, there exists a set $M_{a, b, c}$ which contains no unselected menus. That is, all the $n$ menus in $M_{a, b, c}$ have been selected, and the condition of the problem is violated.
llm_summary: The proof first shows that for any fixed starter–main–dessert triple there can be at most \(n-1\) wines chosen, so summing over the \(n^3\) triples gives \(N\le n^3(n-1)\). It then constructs the set of orders \,\(O=\{(s,m,d,w):w\not\equiv s+m+d\pmod n\}\,\), which has size \(n^4-n^3=n^3(n-1)\) and verifies in each of the four coordinate‐fixing cases (including \(n=1\)) that no forbidden \(n\)-tuple occurs.

problem:
Find all integer triples \((a, b, c)\) satisfying the equation

\[ 5a^2 + 9b^2 = 13c^2 \]
solution:
To solve the Diophantine equation

$$
5a^2 + 9b^2 = 13c^2,
$$

we aim to find all **integer triples** $(a, b, c)$ that satisfy this equation.

---

### Step 1: Consider the trivial solution

Clearly, if $a = b = c = 0$, the equation becomes:

$$
5(0)^2 + 9(0)^2 = 13(0)^2 \Rightarrow 0 = 0,
$$

which is true. So $(0, 0, 0)$ is a solution.

---

### Step 2: Assume a non-trivial solution exists

Suppose there exists a non-trivial solution, i.e., at least one of $a, b, c$ is non-zero. We will use **modular arithmetic** to analyze the equation and derive constraints on $a, b, c$.

---

### Step 3: Analyze the equation modulo 3

We reduce the original equation modulo 3:

$$
5a^2 + 9b^2 \equiv 13c^2 \pmod{3}.
$$

Since $9 \equiv 0 \pmod{3}$ and $13 \equiv 1 \pmod{3}$, the equation becomes:

$$
2a^2 \equiv c^2 \pmod{3}.
$$

Squares modulo 3 are only $0$ or $1$. So we consider:

- If $a^2 \equiv 0 \pmod{3}$, then $c^2 \equiv 0 \pmod{3}$, so $c \equiv 0 \pmod{3}$.
- If $a^2 \equiv 1 \pmod{3}$, then $2 \equiv c^2 \pmod{3}$, but 2 is not a square modulo 3.

Thus, the only possibility is $a \equiv 0 \pmod{3}$ and $c \equiv 0 \pmod{3}$.

---

### Step 4: Analyze the equation modulo 5

Now reduce the original equation modulo 5:

$$
5a^2 + 9b^2 \equiv 13c^2 \pmod{5}.
$$

Since $5 \equiv 0 \pmod{5}$ and $9 \equiv 4 \pmod{5}$, $13 \equiv 3 \pmod{5}$, we get:

$$
4b^2 \equiv 3c^2 \pmod{5}.
$$

Multiply both sides by the inverse of 4 modulo 5, which is 4 (since $4 \cdot 4 = 16 \equiv 1 \pmod{5}$):

$$
b^2 \equiv 2c^2 \pmod{5}.
$$

Now consider the possible values of $b^2$ and $c^2$ modulo 5. The quadratic residues modulo 5 are $0, 1, 4$.

- If $c^2 \equiv 0$, then $b^2 \equiv 0$.
- If $c^2 \equiv 1$, then $b^2 \equiv 2$, which is not a square modulo 5.
- If $c^2 \equiv 4$, then $b^2 \equiv 8 \equiv 3$, which is also not a square modulo 5.

Thus, the only possibility is $c \equiv 0 \pmod{5}$ and $b \equiv 0 \pmod{5}$.

---

### Step 5: Combine the results

From modulo 3 and 5:

- $a \equiv 0 \pmod{3}$,
- $b \equiv 0 \pmod{5}$,
- $c \equiv 0 \pmod{3}$ and $c \equiv 0 \pmod{5}$, so $c \equiv 0 \pmod{15}$.

Let us define:

$$
a = 3m, \quad b = 5n, \quad c = 15k,
$$

for some integers $m, n, k$.

Substitute into the original equation:

$$
5(3m)^2 + 9(5n)^2 = 13(15k)^2,
$$

$$
5 \cdot 9m^2 + 9 \cdot 25n^2 = 13 \cdot 225k^2,
$$

$$
45m^2 + 225n^2 = 2925k^2.
$$

Divide both sides by 45:

$$
m^2 + 5n^2 = 65k^2.
$$

---

### Step 6: Analyze the new equation modulo 5

Now consider:

$$
m^2 + 5n^2 \equiv 65k^2 \pmod{5}.
$$

Since $65 \equiv 0 \pmod{5}$ and $5n^2 \equiv 0 \pmod{5}$, we get:

$$
m^2 \equiv 0 \pmod{5} \Rightarrow m \equiv 0 \pmod{5}.
$$

So let $m = 5p$, and substitute back:

$$
(5p)^2 + 5n^2 = 65k^2 \Rightarrow 25p^2 + 5n^2 = 65k^2.
$$

Divide both sides by 5:

$$
5p^2 + n^2 = 13k^2.
$$

---

### Step 7: Analyze this new equation modulo 5 again

Reduce modulo 5:

$$
n^2 \equiv 13k^2 \equiv 3k^2 \pmod{5}.
$$

As before, the only way this is possible is if $k \equiv 0 \pmod{5}$, and then $n \equiv 0 \pmod{5}$.

Let $k = 5q$, $n = 5r$, and substitute:

$$
5p^2 + (5r)^2 = 13(5q)^2 \Rightarrow 5p^2 + 25r^2 = 13 \cdot 25q^2.
$$

Divide by 5:

$$
p^2 + 5r^2 = 65q^2.
$$

We are back to the same form as before: $x^2 + 5y^2 = 65z^2$.

---

### Step 8: Infinite descent

This process can be repeated indefinitely, each time reducing the size of the variables by a factor of 5 or 3. That is, from any solution $(a, b, c)$, we can find another solution $(m, n, k)$, and then $(p, r, q)$, and so on, with each new solution involving smaller integers.

This leads to an **infinite descent** — a contradiction unless the original solution is $(0, 0, 0)$. In other words, if there were any non-zero solution, we could always find a smaller non-zero solution, which is impossible in the integers.

---

### Conclusion

The only integer triple $(a, b, c)$ that satisfies the equation

$$
5a^2 + 9b^2 = 13c^2
$$

is the **trivial solution** where all variables are zero.

$$
\boxed{(0, 0, 0)}
$$
feedback: The solution is correct although it goes through some unnecessary conditions.
ground_truth_solution:
Solution. Observe that $(a, b, c)=(0,0,0)$ is a solution. Assume that the equation has a solution $\left(a_{0}, b_{0}, c_{0}\right) \neq(0,0,0)$. Let $d=\operatorname{gcd}\left(a_{0}, b_{0}, c_{0}\right)>0$. Let $(a, b, c)=\left(a_{0} / d, b_{0} / d, c_{0} / d\right)$.Then $\operatorname{gcd}(a, b, c)$ $=1$. From $5 a_{0}{ }^{2}+9 b_{0}{ }^{2}=13 c_{0}{ }^{2}$ it follows that:

$$
5 a^{2}+9 b^{2}=5\left(\frac{a_{0}}{d}\right)^{2}+9\left(\frac{b_{0}}{d}\right)^{2}=\frac{5 a_{0}{ }^{2}+9 b_{0}{ }^{2}}{d^{2}}=\frac{13 c_{0}{ }^{2}}{d^{2}}=13\left(\frac{c_{0}}{d}\right)^{2}=13 c^{2}
$$
hence $(a, b, c)$ is also a solution.
As $\left(a_{0}, b_{0}, c_{0}\right) \neq(0,0,0)$ it follows that $(a, b, c) \neq(0,0,0)$. Consider the equation modulo 5. It follows that $4 b^{2} \equiv 5 a^{2}+9 b^{2}=13 c^{2} \equiv 3 c^{2}(\bmod 5)$, that is $4 b^{2} \equiv 3 c^{2}(\bmod 5)$. Multiplying by $4$ gives:
$$
b^{2} \equiv 16 b^{2}=4 \cdot 4 b^{2} \equiv 4 \cdot 3 c^{2}=12 c^{2} \equiv 2 \cdot c^{2} \quad(\bmod 5)
$$

If $5 \mid c$ then $2 c^{2} \equiv 2 \cdot 0^{2}=0(\bmod 5)$ and therefore $a^{2} \equiv 0(\bmod 5)$, that is $5 \mid b^{2}$. As $5$ is prime it follows that $5 \mid b$. Hence $5$ divides $b$ and $c$. It follows that $5^{2} \mid 13 c^{2}-9 b^{2}=5 a^{2}$. Consequently $5$ divides $a^{2}$. As $5$ is prime, $5 \mid a$. This means that $5$ divides $a, b$ and $c$ contradicting the fact that $\operatorname{gcd}(a, b, c)=1$. We conclude that $5 \mid c$ does not hold.

As $5 \mid c$ does not hold and $5$ is a prime it follows that $c$ and $5$ are relative prime. Therefore there exists $x \in \mathbb{Z}$ such that $c \cdot x \equiv 1(\bmod 5)$. Multiplying by $x^{2}$ gives:

$$
(b \cdot x)^{2}=b^{2} \cdot x^{2} \equiv 2 \cdot c^{2} \cdot x^{2}=2 \cdot(c \cdot x)^{2} \equiv 2 \cdot 1^{2}=2 \quad(\bmod 5)
$$

That is $y^{2} \equiv 2(\bmod 5)$ where $y=b \cdot x$. As $y^{2} \equiv 2(\bmod 5)$ it follows that $y$ and $5$ are relative prime. By Fermat's little theorem it follows that $y^{4} \equiv 1(\bmod 5)$. Hence:

$$
1 \equiv y^{4}=\left(y^{2}\right)^{2} \equiv 2^{2}=4 \quad(\bmod 5)
$$
but $1 \not \equiv 4(\bmod 5)$ so we have a contradiction. We conclude that the equation $5 a^{2}+9 b^{2}=13 c^{2}$ has no solution besides the solution $(a, b, c)=(0,0,0)$.
llm_summary: The proof first observes the trivial solution (0,0,0) and then assumes a nonzero solution exists. It uses congruences modulo 3 to show 3 divides both a and c, and modulo 5 to show 5 divides both b and c. Writing a=3m, b=5n, c=15k yields the equation \(m^2+5n^2=65k^2\). A further modulo 5 argument gives m=5p and then n=5r, k=5q, leading to \(p^2+5r^2=65q^2\). The proof claims that one can repeat this process indefinitely (infinite descent), forcing only the trivial solution.

llm_issues.description: The proof asserts without justification that the new equation \(p^2+5r^2=65q^2\) admits the same modular reductions as the previous one, but does not show how to reapply the congruence arguments to restart the descent step by step.
llm_issues.text: "We are back to the same form as before... this process can be repeated indefinitely"

llm_issues.description: The proof never treats the possibility that \(c=0\) (in which case one must show directly that \(a=b=0\)), nor does it address negative values of \(a,b,c\) or comment on taking absolute values to ensure a well-founded descent.
This phrase is vague and misleading, since after the first reduction the descent only uses a factor of 5. It does not clarify which factor applies at each stage or how the factor of 3 is reused.
llm_issues.text: "each time reducing the size of the variables by a factor of 5 or 3"

llm_issues.description: The proof divides the Diophantine equations by 45 and then by 5 without explicitly verifying that the resulting triples remain integer solutions, omitting a check that the divisibility conditions ensure integrality at each step.
llm_issues.text: "Divide both sides by 45... Divide both sides by 5"

problem: Find all polynomials \( p \) with integer coefficients such that the number \( p(a) - p(b) \) is divisible by \( a+b \) for all integers \( a, b \), provided that \( a+b \neq 0 \).
solution:
Solution.

Throughout the proof “divides’’ means “divides in the ring ℤ’’ and all polynomials are assumed to have integer coefficients.

Problem.  Find all polynomials \(p\in\mathbb Z[x]\) such that  

\[
a+b \; \bigm\vert \; p(a)-p(b)\qquad\text{for every }a,b\in\mathbb Z\text{ with }a+b\ne 0.
\]

Answer.  Those and only those polynomials that contain even powers of \(x\) only, i.e.

\[
p(x)=c_{0}+c_{2}x^{2}+c_{4}x^{4}+\dots+c_{2m}x^{2m}\qquad
(c_{0},c_{2},\dots ,c_{2m}\in\mathbb Z,\;m\ge 0).
\]

We first prove that every such polynomial satisfies the required divisibility
and then show that no other polynomial can.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
1.  Even polynomials satisfy the condition
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Lemma 1 If \(k\) is even, then \(a+b\mid a^{k}-b^{k}\) for all integers \(a,b\)
with \(a+b\ne 0\).

Proof.  
Fix an integer \(b\) and consider the univariate polynomial in \(x\)

\[
F(x)=x^{k}-b^{k}\qquad(k\text{ even}).
\]

Because \(k\) is even we have \(F(-b)=(-b)^{k}-b^{k}=0\); thus \(x=-b\) is a
root of \(F\).  Hence \(x+b\) divides \(F(x)\) in the ring \(\mathbb Z[x]\).
Writing \(F(x)=(x+b)Q(x)\) and evaluating at \(x=a\) we obtain
\(a^{k}-b^{k}=(a+b)Q(a)\), so \(a+b\mid a^{k}-b^{k}\). ∎

Corollary 1 If \(p(x)=\sum_{j=0}^{m}c_{2j}x^{2j}\) (only even powers
occur), then \(a+b\mid p(a)-p(b)\) for every pair \((a,b)\) with
\(a+b\ne 0\).

Indeed, by Lemma 1 the required divisibility holds for every even monomial
\(x^{2j}\); hence it also holds for every integer linear combination of such
monomials.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
2.  Necessity: every admissible polynomial is even
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Suppose now that \(p\) obeys the divisibility requirement.  
Fix an arbitrary integer \(b\) and define  

\[
f_b(x)=p(x)-p(b)\in\mathbb Z[x].
\]

For every integer \(x\neq -b\) we have \(x+b\mid f_b(x)\); that is,
\(f_b(x)\equiv 0\pmod{x+b}\).
Divide \(f_b(x)\) by \(x+b\) in \(\mathbb Z[x]\):

\[
f_b(x)=(x+b)q_b(x)+r_b\qquad\bigl(q_b\in\mathbb Z[x],\;r_b\in\mathbb Z\bigr).
\]

Evaluating at the infinitely many integers \(x\neq -b\) we get  
\(x+b\mid r_b\).  Because the set \(\{\,|x+b|:x\in\mathbb Z,x\neq -b\}\)
is unbounded, the only integer divisible by all those numbers is \(r_b=0\).
Hence

\[
p(x)-p(b)=f_b(x)=(x+b)q_b(x)\qquad\text{for some }q_b\in\mathbb Z[x].
\]

Putting \(x=-b\) into this identity gives \(p(-b)-p(b)=0\); i.e.

\[
p(-b)=p(b)\qquad\text{for every }b\in\mathbb Z.
\]

Thus the two polynomials \(p(x)\) and \(p(-x)\) coincide at every integer
point, hence (by the identity theorem for polynomials)  

\[
p(x)=p(-x)\quad\text{in }\mathbb Z[x],
\]

so \(p\) is an even polynomial.  Consequently all odd–degree coefficients
of \(p\) are zero.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
3.  Conclusion
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Parts 1 and 2 together show that

• every polynomial containing only even powers of \(x\) satisfies the
required divisibility;

• every polynomial that satisfies the divisibility contains only even powers.

Therefore the set of all such polynomials is precisely

\[
\boxed{\,p(x)=c_{0}+c_{2}x^{2}+c_{4}x^{4}+\dots+c_{2m}x^{2m}\;
(m\ge 0,\;c_{2j}\in\mathbb Z)\,}.
\]

The constant polynomial (the case \(m=0\)) is included, and the zero
polynomial is obtained by choosing all coefficients equal to \(0\). ∎
ground_truth_solution:
Solution. The polynomials we are looking for are those whose every odd-degree term has zero coefficient.

Let $P(x)=P_{0}(x)+P_{1}(x)$, where $P_{0}$ and $P_{1}$ are polynomials whose all non-zero terms have either even or odd degree, respectively.

Then we can write $P_{0}(x)=Q\left(x^{2}\right)$, where polynomial $Q$ is obtained from polynomial $P_{0}$ by dividing degrees of all non-zero terms by $2$. Now, for any integers $a, b$ the number $P_{0}(a)-P_{0}(b)=Q\left(a^{2}\right)-Q\left(b^{2}\right)$

is divisible by $a^{2}-b^{2}$, and hence also by $a+b$. Thus, if every odd-degree term of $P$ has zero coefficient, then the condition of the problem is satisfied.

On the other hand, if polynomial $P$ satisfies the condition of the problem, then also $P-P_{0}=P_{1}$ must satisfy it. Note that for every real $x, P_{1}(-x)=-P_{1}(x)$, i.e. $P_{1}$ is an odd function. By substituting $b$ by $-b$ in the condition of the problem we obtain that $a-b \mid P_{1}(a)+P_{1}(b)$ holds for any distinct integers $a$ and $b$. Since also $a-b \mid P_{1}(a)-P_{1}(b)$, then for any integers $a, b$ we have $a-b \mid 2 P_{1}(a)$. But for any $a$ there exists such $b$ that $|a-b|>2 P_{1}(a)$. From this we conclude that $P_{1}(a)=0$ for any integer $a$. Altogether we have $P=P_{0}$, i.e. coefficients of all odd-degree terms are zero.
llm_summary: The proof first shows that any polynomial containing only even powers of x satisfies the divisibility condition by factoring \(x^{2j}-y^{2j}\) as \((x+y)Q(x,y)\). Then, for necessity, it considers \(f_b(x)=p(x)-p(b)\), divides by \(x+b\) in \(\mathbb Z[x]\) to deduce the remainder must vanish, yielding \(p(-b)=p(b)\) for all integers \(b\). By the identity theorem in an infinite integral domain, this implies \(p(x)=p(-x)\), so all odd coefficients are zero.

problem:
Let \(\Gamma\) be a circle in the plane and \(S\) be a point on \(\Gamma\). Mario and Luigi drive around the circle \(\Gamma\) with their go-karts. They both start at \(S\) at the same time. They both drive for exactly \(6\) minutes at constant speed counterclockwise around the track. During these \(6\) minutes, Luigi makes exactly one lap around \(\Gamma\) while Mario, who is three times as fast, makes three laps.

While Mario and Luigi drive their go-karts, Princess Daisy positions herself such that she is always exactly in the middle of the chord between them. When she reaches a point she has already visited, she marks it with a banana.

How many points in the plane, apart from \(S\), are marked with a banana by the end of the race?
solution:
Let Γ be the unit circle with centre O and let the starting point S be the point (1,0).
Introduce an orthonormal system with O as the origin and interpret points of the plane as
complex numbers.

1.  Where are Mario and Luigi?

   Denote the time in minutes by t (0 ≤ t ≤ 6).

   •  Luigi runs once round Γ in the 6 minutes, hence his angular speed is  
      ω = 2π / 6 = π/3  rad min⁻¹.  
      His position is  
      L(t) = e^{iωt}.                                       (1)

   •  Mario is three times as fast, so his angular speed is 3ω.  
      His position is  
      M(t) = e^{i3ωt}.                                       (2)

2.  Daisy’s position

   Daisy is always the midpoint of the chord LM, hence

      P(t) = ½(L(t)+M(t))
           = ½(e^{iωt}+e^{i3ωt}).                           (3)

   Put

      δ = ωt = πt/3.                                         (4)

   Because t runs from 0 to 6, δ runs from 0 to 2π.  
   With (4) equation (3) becomes

      P(δ) = ½(e^{iδ}+e^{i3δ})
            = e^{i2δ}·cos δ.                                 (5)

   In real coordinates

      P(δ) = (cos δ cos 2δ , cos δ sin 2δ).                  (6)

3.  When is a point visited twice?

   Suppose P(δ₁)=P(δ₂) with 0 ≤ δ₁<δ₂≤2π.

   (i)  If cos δ₁ = 0 (hence δ₁ = π/2 or 3π/2), equation (6) gives P(δ₁)=O.
        Equality therefore forces cos δ₂ = 0 as well, so δ₂ = 3π/2 or π/2.
        Consequently O is reached twice (at δ = π/2 and 3π/2).

   (ii) Assume now cos δ₁ ≠ 0.  
        Divide the equality P(δ₁)=P(δ₂) by cos δ₁e^{i2δ₁}:

           1 = (cos δ₂ / cos δ₁) · e^{i2(δ₂-δ₁)}.           (7)

        The right–hand side has modulus 1, hence

           |cos δ₂| = |cos δ₁|  and  e^{i2(δ₂-δ₁)} = ±1.     (8)

        Therefore
           2(δ₂-δ₁) ≡ 0 or π  (mod 2π),
        i.e.
           δ₂-δ₁ ∈ {0, π/2, π, 3π/2, 2π}.                  (9)

        •  δ₂-δ₁ = 0 or 2π   – same instant, or the start/end
           of the race.  This corresponds to the point S, which the
           problem tells us not to count.

        •  δ₂-δ₁ = π.  Then e^{i2(δ₂-δ₁)} = 1 while
           cos δ₂ = –cos δ₁, contradicting |cos δ₂| = |cos δ₁| unless
           cos δ₁ = 0, which is case (i). No new point arises.

        •  δ₂-δ₁ = π/2 or 3π/2.  Here e^{i2(δ₂-δ₁)} = –1, so
           cos δ₂ = –cos δ₁.  Using δ₂ = δ₁ + π/2 we get

              cos(δ₁+π/2) = –cos δ₁
            ⇒ –sin δ₁     = –cos δ₁
            ⇒ sin δ₁      =  cos δ₁                          (10)

           which is satisfied exactly for

              δ₁ = π/4 , 5π/4  (mod 2π).                    (11)

           With δ₂ = δ₁ + π/2 these give the pairs
           (π/4, 3π/4) and (5π/4, 7π/4).

           A completely analogous calculation for δ₂ = δ₁ – π/2
           yields

              δ₁ = 3π/4 , 7π/4,                             (12)

           which combine with (11) to the same two pairs.
           Thus there are precisely two further points that are
           visited twice.

4.  The three repeated points

   Evaluate P(δ) for the relevant values of δ.

   •  δ = π/2, 3π/2     ⇒  P = O                          (centre).

   •  δ = π/4 or 3π/4   ⇒  P = ( 0 ,  √2/2).

   •  δ = 5π/4 or 7π/4  ⇒  P = ( 0 , –√2/2).

   Besides the starting point S, Daisy therefore revisits exactly

      – the centre O,  
      – the point (0,  √2/2),  
      – the point (0, –√2/2).

5.  Bananas placed

   Each of those three points is met for the second time during the
   six-minute ride, so each receives a banana.  No other point is
   revisited, and S is excluded by the statement of the problem.

   Hence the number of points marked with a banana is

      3.

Answer: 3

ground_truth_solution:
Solution 1. Without loss of generality, we assume that $\Gamma$ is the unit circle and $S=(1,0)$. Three points are marked with bananas:
(i) After $45$ seconds, Luigi has passed through an arc with a subtended angle of $45^{\circ}$ and is at the point $(\sqrt{2} / 2, \sqrt{2} / 2)$, whereas Mario has passed through an arc with a subtended angle of $135^{\circ}$ and is at the point $(-\sqrt{2} / 2, \sqrt{2} / 2)$. Therefore Daisy is at the point $(0, \sqrt{2} / 2)$ after $45$ seconds. After $135$ seconds, Mario and Luigi's positions are exactly the other way round, so the princess is again at the point $(0, \sqrt{2} / 2)$ and puts a banana there.
(ii) Similarly, after $225$ seconds and after $315$ seconds, Princess Daisy is at the point $(0,-\sqrt{2} / 2)$ and puts a banana there.
(iii) After $90$ seconds, Luigi is at $(0,1)$ and Mario at $(0,-1)$, so that Daisy is at the origin of the plane. After $270$ seconds, Mario and Luigi's positions are exactly the other way round, hence Princess Daisy drops a banana at the point $(0,0)$.

We claim that no other point in the plane, apart from these three points and $S$, is marked with a banana. Let $t_{1}$ and $t_{2}$ be two different times when Daisy is at the same place. For $n \in\{1,2\}$ we write Luigis position at time $t_{n}$ as a complex number $z_{n}=\exp \left(i x_{n}\right)$ with $\left.x_{n} \in\right] 0,2 \pi[$. At this time, Mario is located at $z_{i}^{3}$ and Daisy at $\left(z_{i}^{3}+z_{i}\right) / 2$. According to our assumption we have $\left(z_{1}^{3}+z_{1}\right) / 2=\left(z_{2}^{3}+z_{2}\right) / 2$ or, equivalently, $\left(z_{1}-z_{2}\right)\left(z_{1}^{2}+z_{1} z_{2}+z_{2}^{2}+1\right)=0$. We have $z_{1} \neq z_{2}$, so that we must have $z_{1}^{2}+z_{1} z_{2}+z_{2}^{2}=-1$.

We proceed with an observation of the structure of $\Gamma$ as a set of complex numbers. Suppose that $z \in \Gamma \backslash\{S\}$. Then $z+1+z^{-1} \in \Gamma$ if and only if $z \in\{i,-1,-i\}$. For a proof of the observation note that $z+1+z^{-1}=z+1+\bar{z}$ is a real number for every $z \in \mathbb{C}$ with norm $|z|=1$. So it lies on the unit circle if and only if it is equal to $1$, in which case the real part of $z$ is equal to $0$, or it is equal to $-1$, in which case the real part of $z$ is equal to $-1$. We apply the observation to the number $z=z_{1} / z_{2}$, which satisfies the premise since $z+1+\bar{z}=-\overline{z_{1}} \cdot \overline{z_{2}} \in \Gamma$. Therefore, one of the following cases must occur.
(i) We have $z= \pm i$, that is, $z_{1}= \pm i z_{2}$. Without loss of generality we may assume $z_{2}=i z_{1}$. It follows that $-1=z_{1}^{2}+z_{1} z_{2}+z_{2}^{2}=i z_{1}^{2}$, so that $z_{1}=\exp (i \pi / 4)$ or $z_{1}=\exp (5 i \pi / 4)$. In the former case $\left(z_{1}, z_{2}\right)=(\exp (i \pi / 4), \exp (3 i \pi / 4))$, which matches case (1) above. In the latter case $\left(z_{1}, z_{2}\right)=(\exp (5 i \pi / 4), \exp (7 i \pi / 4))$, which matches case (2) above.
(ii) We have $z=-1$, that is, $z_{2}=-z_{1}$. It follows that $-1=z_{1}^{2}+z_{1} z_{2}+z_{2}^{2}=z_{1}^{2}$, so that $z_{1}=i$ or $z_{1}=-i$. This matches case (3) above.


Depiction of the path Daisy takes

Solution 2. We represent the position of Luigi and Mario by $(t, 3 t)(\bmod 1)$, so when Luigi is at angle $t \cdot 2 \pi$, Mario is at an angle $3 t \cdot 2 \pi$.

A chord (if it is not the diameter is determined by its midpoint. Therefore Daisy revisit a location only if

$$
(x, 3 x) \equiv(3 y, y) \quad(\bmod 1)
$$
for different value of $x, y(\bmod 1)$. By inspection, the three locations are visited twice.

problem: Let \(x, y \in \mathbb{R}\) be such that \(x = y(3-y)^{2}\) and \(y = x(3-x)^{2}\). Find all possible values of \(x+y\).
solution:
Here is a self‐contained proof, written in full detail.  We let \(x,y\in\mathbb{R}\) satisfy

\[
\begin{cases}
x = y\,(3 - y)^2,\\
y = x\,(3 - x)^2.
\end{cases}
\]

We wish to find all possible values of \(x+y\).

---

Proof.

Step 1.  The “obvious’’ case \(x=0\) or \(y=0\).  

• If \(y=0\), then the first equation gives
\[
x = 0\cdot(3-0)^2 = 0,
\]
so \((x,y)=(0,0)\).  We must check the second equation:
\[
y = x\,(3 - x)^2 \;\Longrightarrow\; 0 = 0\,(3 - 0)^2 = 0,
\]
which holds.  Thus \((0,0)\) is indeed a solution, and \(x+y=0\).  

• If instead \(x=0\), then by symmetry one also finds \(y=0\).  No new solutions arise.

Hence the only solution with \(x=0\) or \(y=0\) is \((x,y)=(0,0)\), giving \(x+y=0\).

---

From now on assume \(x\neq 0\) and \(y\neq 0\).  Then we may divide both equations by \(x\) or \(y\).  

Step 2.  Derivation of \(\,(3-x)(3-y)=\pm1\).

From 
\[
x = y\,(3 - y)^2
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\frac{x}{y} = (3-y)^2,
\]
and
\[
y = x\,(3 - x)^2
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\frac{y}{x} = (3-x)^2.
\]
Multiplying these two displayed equalities,
\[
\frac{x}{y}\,\frac{y}{x} \;=\;(3-y)^2\,(3-x)^2
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
1 = \bigl((3-x)(3-y)\bigr)^2.
\]
Hence
\[
(3-x)(3-y) = 1
\quad\text{or}\quad
(3-x)(3-y) = -1.
\]
We treat these two cases separately.

---

Case I.  \((3-x)(3-y)=1\).

Then
\[
3 - x = \frac1{\,3-y\,},
\]
so
\[
x = 3 - \frac1{3-y}.
\]
Substitute this into \(x = y\,(3-y)^2\):  
\begin{align*}
3 - \frac1{3-y} &= y\,(3-y)^2.
\end{align*}
Multiply both sides by \((3-y)\neq0\):
\[
3(3-y) - 1 = y\,(3-y)^3.
\]
Expand the left:
\[
9 - 3y - 1 = y\,(3-y)^3
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
8 - 3y = y\,(3-y)^3.
\]
Set 
\[
t = 3 - y.
\]
Then \(y = 3 - t\), and the equation becomes
\[
8 - 3(3 - t) = (3 - t)\,t^3,
\]
i.e.
\[
8 - 9 + 3t = 3t^3 - t^4,
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
3t - 1 = 3t^3 - t^4,
\]
or
\[
t^4 - 3t^3 + 3t - 1 = 0.
\]
We factor this quartic.  Notice \(t=1\) is a root since
\[
1^4 - 3\cdot1^3 + 3\cdot1 - 1 = 1 - 3 + 3 -1 = 0.
\]
By the Factor Theorem, divide \(t^4 - 3t^3 + 3t -1\) by \(t-1\).  A quick synthetic division yields
\[
t^4 - 3t^3 + 0\,t^2 + 3t -1
\;=\;(t-1)\,(t^3 -2t^2 -2t +1).
\]
Next observe \(t=-1\) is a root of the cubic \(t^3 -2t^2 -2t +1\):
\[
(-1)^3 -2(-1)^2 -2(-1) +1 = -1 -2 +2 +1 = 0.
\]
Dividing by \(t+1\) gives
\[
t^3 -2t^2 -2t +1 = (t+1)\,(t^2 -3t +1).
\]
Finally the quadratic
\[
t^2 -3t +1 = 0
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
t = \frac{3\pm\sqrt{9 - 4}}{2} = \frac{3\pm\sqrt5}{2}.
\]
Thus the four real roots of \(t^4 - 3t^3 + 3t - 1 = 0\) are
\[
t \in \Bigl\{\,1,\,-1,\;\tfrac{3+\sqrt5}2,\;\tfrac{3-\sqrt5}2\Bigr\}.
\]
For each such \(t\) we recover
\[
y = 3 - t,
\quad
x = 3 - \frac1t.
\]
We list all four:

1. \(t=1\):  \(y=2,\;\;x=3-1=2\).  Hence \((x,y)=(2,2)\), and \(x+y=4\).

2. \(t=-1\):  \(y=4,\;\;x=3-(-1)^{-1}=3+1=4\).  Hence \((x,y)=(4,4)\), and \(x+y=8\).

3. \(t=\tfrac{3+\sqrt5}2\):  
   \[
   y=3 - \frac{3+\sqrt5}2 = \frac{3-\sqrt5}2,
   \quad
   x = 3 - \frac2{3+\sqrt5}
       =3 - \frac{2(3-\sqrt5)}{9-5}
       =3 - \frac{3-\sqrt5}2
       = \frac{3+\sqrt5}2.
   \]
   Thus \(\bigl(x,y\bigr)=\bigl(\tfrac{3+\sqrt5}2,\tfrac{3-\sqrt5}2\bigr)\), and
   \[
     x+y = \frac{3+\sqrt5}2 + \frac{3-\sqrt5}2 = 3.
   \]

4. \(t=\tfrac{3-\sqrt5}2\):  by symmetry one finds
   \(\bigl(x,y\bigr)=\bigl(\tfrac{3-\sqrt5}2,\tfrac{3+\sqrt5}2\bigr)\), again
   \(x+y=3\).

No other real solutions arise in Case I.  Hence from this case we obtain the sums
\[
x+y \in \{\,4,\,8,\,3\}.
\]

---

Case II.  \((3-x)(3-y) = -1\).

Then
\[
3 - x = -\frac1{3-y},
\qquad
x = 3 + \frac1{3-y}.
\]
Substitute into \(x = y\,(3-y)^2\):
\[
3 + \frac1{3-y} = y\,(3-y)^2.
\]
Multiply by \((3-y)\neq0\):
\[
3(3-y) + 1 = y\,(3-y)^3
\;\Longrightarrow\;
9 - 3y + 1 = y\,(3-y)^3
\;\Longrightarrow\;
10 - 3y = y\,(3-y)^3.
\]
Again set \(t = 3-y\).  Then \(y=3-t\) and
\[
10 - 3(3 - t) = (3 - t)\,t^3
\;\Longrightarrow\;
10 - 9 + 3t = 3t^3 - t^4
\;\Longrightarrow\;
3t + 1 = 3t^3 - t^4
\;\Longrightarrow\;
t^4 - 3t^3 + 3t + 1 = 0.
\]
We factor the quartic 
\[
t^4 - 3t^3 + 3t + 1
\]
by seeking a decomposition \((t^2 + at + b)(t^2 + ct + d)\).  Equating coefficients leads to the system
\[
\begin{cases}
a + c = -3,\\
ac + b + d = 0,\\
ad + bc = 3,\\
bd = 1.
\end{cases}
\]
One finds the only integral solution is \(b=d=-1\), \(a=-1\), \(c=-2\).  Hence
\[
t^4 - 3t^3 + 3t + 1 = (t^2 - t - 1)\,(t^2 - 2t -1).
\]
These quadratics have the real roots
\[
t = \frac{1\pm\sqrt5}2
\quad\text{and}\quad
t = 1\pm\sqrt2,
\]
respectively.  Thus the four real roots are
\[
t \in \Bigl\{\tfrac{1+\sqrt5}{2},\;\tfrac{1-\sqrt5}{2},\;1+\sqrt2,\;1-\sqrt2\Bigr\}.
\]
For each such \(t\) we recover \(y=3-t\), \(x=3+1/t\).  A brief computation shows:

1. \(t=\tfrac{1+\sqrt5}{2}\) gives
   \((x,y)=\bigl(\tfrac{5+\sqrt5}2,\;\tfrac{5-\sqrt5}2\bigr)\), so
   \(x+y=5\).

2. \(t=\tfrac{1-\sqrt5}{2}\) gives
   \((x,y)=\bigl(\tfrac{5-\sqrt5}2,\;\tfrac{5+\sqrt5}2\bigr)\), so
   \(x+y=5\).

3. \(t=1+\sqrt2\) gives
   \((x,y)=(2+\sqrt2,\;2-\sqrt2)\), so \(x+y=4\).

4. \(t=1-\sqrt2\) gives
   \((x,y)=(2-\sqrt2,\;2+\sqrt2)\), so \(x+y=4\).

Hence Case II yields sums
\[
x+y \in \{\,5,\,4\}.
\]

---

Conclusion.  Collecting all solutions:

• From the trivial zero‐case \((0,0)\): \(x+y=0\).

• From Case I: \(x+y\in\{3,4,8\}\).

• From Case II: \(x+y\in\{4,5\}\).

Therefore the only possible values of \(x+y\) are
\[
\boxed{0,\;3,\;4,\;5,\;8}.
\]
This completes the proof.
ground_truth_solution:
Solution 1. The set $\{0,3,4,5,8\}$ contains all possible values for $x+y$. A pair $(x, x) \in \mathbb{R}^{2}$ satisfies the equations if and only if $x=x(3-x)^{2}$, and it is easy to see that this cubic equation has the solution set $\{0,2,4\}$. These pairs give us $0,4$ and $8$ as possible values for $x+y$.

Assuming $x \neq y$ let $s$ be the sum $x+y$ and $p$ be the product $x y$. Subtracting the first equation from the second and cancelling out the term $x-y$ we get

$$
p=s^{2}-6 s+10
$$

Adding the two equations gives

$$
0=s\left(s^{2}-3 p\right)-6\left(s^{2}-2 p\right)+8 s
$$

Together the equations give

$$
0=s^{3}-12 s^{2}+47 s-60=(s-3)(s-4)(s-5)
$$

The only possible values for $x+y$ when $x \neq y$ are therefore $3,4$ and $5$. We have already seen that $x+y=4$ has a solution $x=y=2$.

Next we investigate the case $x+y=3$. Here we can simplify the given equations as $x=y x^{2}$ and $y=x y^{2}$. The number $x$ cannot be zero in this case, since otherwise $y$ and $k$ would also be zero. We can conclude that $x y=1$. The equations $x+y=3$ and $x y=1$, according to Vieta's Theorem, imply that $x$ and $y$ are the solutions of the equation $\lambda^{2}-3 \lambda+1=0$. Hence

$$
(x, y)=\left(\frac{3+\sqrt{5}}{2}, \frac{3-\sqrt{5}}{2}\right) \quad \text { or } \quad(x, y)=\left(\frac{3-\sqrt{5}}{2}, \frac{3+\sqrt{5}}{2}\right)
$$
and it is easy to verify that both pairs satisfy the equations. These pairs give us $3$ as a possible value for $x+y$.

A simple calculation shows that if a pair $(x, y) \in \mathbb{R}^{2}$ satisfy the equations, then the pair $(4-x, 4-y)$ is solution to the equations. From the pairs we have just found, we can therefore construct pairs of solutions

$$
(x, y)=\left(\frac{5-\sqrt{5}}{2}, \frac{5+\sqrt{5}}{2}\right) \quad \text { and } \quad(x, y)=\left(\frac{5+\sqrt{5}}{2}, \frac{5-\sqrt{5}}{2}\right),
$$
which give us $5$ as a possible value for $x+y$.
llm_summary: The proof first handles the trivial case \(x=0\) or \(y=0\), yielding the solution \((0,0)\) and sum 0. Assuming \(x,y\neq0\), it divides the two equations to obtain \((3-x)(3-y)=\pm1\) and splits into Case I and Case II. In each case it sets \(t=3-y\), derives a quartic polynomial in \(t\), factors it (via synthetic division or by matching coefficients), recovers explicit \((x,y)\) pairs, and computes their sums. Collecting results gives \(x+y\in\{0,3,4,5,8\}\).
