problem:
Let \( n \) be a positive integer. A German set in an \( n \times n \) square grid is a set of \( n \) cells which contains exactly one cell in each row and column. Given a labeling of the cells with the integers from \( 1 \) to \( n^{2} \) using each integer exactly once, we say that an integer is a German product if it is the product of the labels of the cells in a German set.

(a) Let \( n=8 \). Determine whether there exists a labeling of an \( 8 \times 8 \) grid such that the following condition is fulfilled: The difference of any two German products is always divisible by \( 65 \).

(b) Let \( n=10 \). Determine whether there exists a labeling of a \( 10 \times 10 \) grid such that the following condition is fulfilled: The difference of any two German products is always divisible by \( 101 \).
solution:
Solution.  
Throughout the word “row’’ always means “row of the board’’ and “column’’ means “column of the board’’.  
A German set is therefore nothing else than a permutation of the columns, and there are  
\(n!=8!\) (respectively \(10!\)) German sets in an \(n\times n\) board.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
(a)  The case \(n=8\) and the modulus \(65=5\cdot 13\)

Assume for a contradiction that the numbers \(1,2,\dots ,64\) have been written in the
\(8\times 8\) board in such a way that the difference of any two German products is
always divisible by \(65\).
Hence every two German products are congruent modulo \(5\) and also
congruent modulo \(13\).

1.  The four numbers \(13,26,39,52\).  
   Denote by \(\mathcal M\) the set of the four cells that contain a multiple of \(13\).
   (They are the only integers in \(\{1,\dots ,64\}\) that are divisible by \(13\).)

2.  A German set avoiding \(\mathcal M\) exists.  
   Remove the four cells of \(\mathcal M\) from the board and put a 1 in each of the
   remaining \(60\) cells.
   Looking at this as a \(0\text{–}1\) matrix, every row and every column now contains
   at least \(7\) ones (because at most one cell has been deleted in each row and in
   each column).
   In a bipartite graph with parts of the same size \(n\), if
   every vertex has degree at least \(n/2\) then Hall’s condition is satisfied, so the
   graph contains a perfect matching.
   Applying this to the graph whose vertices are the rows and columns and whose
   edges are precisely the remaining ones, we obtain a perfect matching,
   i.e. a German set that uses no cell of \(\mathcal M\).
   Call this German set \(G_{0}\).

   Because no chosen entry is divisible by \(13\), the German product of \(G_{0}\) is
   not divisible by \(13\).

3.  A German set that contains a cell of \(\mathcal M\) also exists.
   Pick any cell \(P\in\mathcal M\) that lies in row \(r\) and column \(c\).
   Fix the choice “row \(r\) takes column \(c\)’’.  For the remaining
   seven rows and the remaining seven columns there are \((8-1)!=7!\) ways to
   complete a German set, hence such a completion certainly exists.
   Let \(G_{1}\) be one of them.
   Its product is divisible by \(13\).

4.  Contradiction modulo \(13\).  
   By construction the products of \(G_{0}\) and \(G_{1}\) are different modulo \(13\),
   so their difference is not a multiple of \(13\).  
   Consequently it is not a multiple of \(65=5\cdot 13\), contradicting the
   requirement of the problem.

Therefore there is no admissible labelling of an \(8\times 8\) board.

Answer to (a):  NO, such a labelling does not exist.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
(b)  The case \(n=10\) and the prime modulus \(101\)

Now \(101\) is prime and larger than the largest label \(100\).
We give an explicit construction that works.

Step 1.  A primitive root modulo \(101\).  
It is well–known (and easy to check directly) that \(2\) is a primitive root modulo
\(101\):  
\[
2^{100}\equiv1\pmod{101},\qquad
2^{50}\equiv100\not\equiv1,\quad
2^{25}\equiv10\not\equiv1,\quad
2^{20}\equiv95\not\equiv1,\quad
2^{10}\equiv14\not\equiv1,\quad
2^{5}\equiv32\not\equiv1 .
\]
Hence the powers \(2^{0},2^{1},\dots ,2^{99}\) give
all \(100\) non–zero residues modulo \(101\) once each.

Step 2.  The labelling.  
Number the rows and columns from \(0\) to \(9\).
Put in the cell of row \(i\) and column \(j\) (indices \(0\le i,j\le 9\))
the integer
\[
A_{i j}=2^{\,10i+j}\pmod{101}.
\]
Because the exponent \(10i+j\) runs through the complete set
\(\{0,1,\dots ,99\}\) the \(100\) numbers \(A_{i j}\) are exactly the
integers \(1,2,\dots ,100\), each used once.

Step 3.  All German products are equal modulo \(101\).  
Let \(\sigma\) be any permutation of \(\{0,1,\dots ,9\}\); the corresponding
German set is
\(\{(0,\sigma(0)),(1,\sigma(1)),\dots ,(9,\sigma(9))\}\).
Its German product is
\[
P(\sigma)=\prod_{i=0}^{9} 2^{\,10i+\sigma(i)}
          =2^{\sum_{i=0}^{9}(10i+\sigma(i))}.
\]
The exponent splits:
\[
\sum_{i=0}^{9}(10i+\sigma(i))
   =10\sum_{i=0}^{9}i+\sum_{i=0}^{9}\sigma(i)
   =10\cdot 45+45=495.
\]
(The identity \(\sum_{i=0}^{9}\sigma(i)=45\) holds because
\(\sigma\) is merely a rearrangement of \(0,1,\dots ,9\).)

Thus every German product equals \(2^{495}\) modulo \(101\).
In particular the difference of any two German products is divisible by \(101\).

Therefore the above labelling satisfies the required condition.

Answer to (b):  YES, such a labelling exists (an explicit one is given above).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
Summary.

(a)  No labelling of an \(8\times 8\) board works, because the four
     multiples of \(13\) force two German sets to have different residues modulo \(13\).

(b)  A labelling of a \(10\times 10\) board that works can be obtained by putting
     \(2^{\,10i+j}\pmod{101}\) in position \((i,j)\); then every German product
     equals \(2^{495}\pmod{101}\).
ground_truth_solution:
Solution:

(a) No, there is no such labelling.

On the contrary, we show that for every labelling there exist two German products whose difference is not divisible by $65$. Suppose that an $8 \times 8$ square grid is labelled with the numbers $1,2, \ldots, 64$ such that no number is used twice.

We can construct a German product that is divisible by $13$ by choosing a German set that includes the cell with the label $13$ and seven others in different rows and columns, but otherwise arbitrarily.

We can construct a German product that is not divisible by $13$ as follows. Notice that only four labels are divisible by 13, namely 13, 26, 39, and $52$. These four labels are located in at most four rows; we denote the index set of these rows $R \subseteq[1,8]$. Similarly, there are at least four columns that do not contain any of these four labels; we denote the index set of these columns $C \subseteq[1,8]$. Since $R \leq C$ it is possible to choose cells of a German set from rows $R$ using only columns from $C$. The remaining cells are chosen from the remaining rows accordingly to the definition, but otherwise arbitrarily. The resulting German product is not divisible by $13$ since the German set avoids the cells whose labels are divisible by $13$.

The difference of the two German products is not divisible by 13, since one German product is divisible by $13$ whereas the other one is not. Hence the difference is not divisible by $65$.

November $9$ to 13, $2023$
(b) Yes, there is such a labelling.

For $k \in[0,99]$ we define $a_{k}=2^{k}(\bmod 101)$; in other words, $a_{k}$ is the remainder of $2^{k}$ when divided by $101$. Note that $a_{k} \neq 0$ since no power of $2$ is divisible by $101$. Hence $1 \leq a_{k} \leq 100$ for all $k \in[0,99]$.

We label the cells of the square grid with the numbers $a_{k}$ as follows:

| $a_{0}$ | $a_{1}$ | $a_{2}$ | $\cdots$ | $a_{9}$ |
| :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: |
| $a_{10}$ | $a_{11}$ | $a_{12}$ | $\cdots$ | $a_{19}$ |
| $a_{20}$ | $a_{21}$ | $a_{22}$ | $\cdots$ | $a_{29}$ |
| $\vdots$ | $\vdots$ | $\vdots$ | $\ddots$ | $\vdots$ |
| $a_{90}$ | $a_{91}$ | $a_{92}$ | $\cdots$ | $a_{99}$ |

More precisely, if we label the rows and columns of the chessboard by $\{0,1,2, \ldots, 9\}$, then the cell with coordinates $(i, j)$ gets the label $a_{10 i+j}$.
Note that $a_{10 i+j} \equiv 2^{10 i+j}(\bmod 101)$ and that $2^{10 i+j}=\left(2^{10}\right)^{i} \cdot 2^{j}$. Hence for this labelling any rook product is congruent to

$$
\left(2^{10}\right)^{0+1+2+\ldots+9} \cdot 2^{0+1+2+\ldots+9}
$$
modulo 101. Hence the difference of any two German products is divisible by $101$ for this labelling.
It remains to show that the $a_{k}$ are pairwise different. (In more elaborate language, we would say that $2$ is a primitive root modulo 101.) To do this, we denote by $s$ the smallest positive integer such that $2^{s} \equiv 1(\bmod 101)$. Using long division, we may write $100=q s+r$ with non-negative integers $q$ and $r$ such that $0 \leq r \leq s-1$. By virtue of Fermat's little theorem we have
$$
1 \equiv 2^{100} \equiv 2^{q s+r} \equiv\left(2^{s}\right)^{q} \cdot 2^{r} \equiv 1^{q} \cdot 2^{r} \equiv 2^{r} \quad(\bmod 101) .
$$

Since $r<s$ and $s$ is the smallest positive integer with $2^{s} \equiv 1(\bmod 101)$, we must have $r=0$. In other words, $100$ is divisible by $s$; in other words, $s$ is a divisor of $100$.

We claim that $s=100$. If this was not the case, we would have $s \mid 20$ or $s \mid 50$, which implies that $2^{20} \equiv 1(\bmod 101)$ or $2^{50} \equiv 1(\bmod 101)$. However $2^{10}=1024 \equiv 14(\bmod 101)$, so that $2^{20} \equiv 14^{2} \equiv 196 \equiv-6 \equiv 1(\bmod 101)$ and $2^{50} \equiv\left(2^{20}\right)^{2} \cdot 2^{10} \equiv(-6)^{2} \cdot 14 \equiv 504 \equiv-1 \not 1(\bmod 101)$.

Now assume that $k, \ell \in[0,99]$ are positive integers with $k>\ell$ and $a_{k}=a_{\ell}$. Then we have $2^{k} \equiv 2^{\ell}(\bmod 101)$ and $0 \equiv 2^{k}-2^{\ell} \equiv 2^{\ell} \cdot\left(2^{k-\ell}-1\right)(\bmod 101)$. Since $2^{\ell}$ and $101$ are coprime, it follows that $2^{k-\ell}-1 \equiv 0(\bmod 101)$ and $2^{k-\ell} \equiv 1(\bmod 101)$. This cannot be true, since $k-\ell \in[1,99]$, but $s=100$ is the smallest positive integer with $2^{s} \equiv 1(\bmod 101)$. Hence $a_{k} \neq a_{\ell}$.

We conclude that the numbers $a_{k}$ with $k \in[0,99]$ are a hundred pairwise different numbers from the set $[1,100]$, hence they are a permutation of the set $[1,100]$ as it was required.

Definition: Let $p$ be a prime. Consider an $n \times n$ square grid of elements $a_{i, j} \in \mathbb{F}_{p}^{*}$ (for $i, j=1, \ldots, n$ ), which are not necessarily distinct. We call it rooky, if all its German products are equal as elements in $\mathbb{F}_{p}^{*}$.

We will provide a classification of all rooky square grids. Of course, most of this is not necessary when writing down a solution to the given problem, but it may still be interesting...

Lemma: A square grid is rooky if and only if for all $i, j, k, \ell$ :

$$
a_{i, j} \cdot a_{k, \ell}=a_{i, \ell} \cdot a_{k, j}
$$

Proof. If we swap the rows of two cells in a German set and keep their columns, it turns one valid German set into another. When comparing their German products, we can ignore all $n-2$ labels of cells that were not moved. The remaining values are $a_{i, j} \cdot a_{k, \ell}$ resp. $a_{i, \ell} \cdot a_{k, j}$ for certain $i, j, k, \ell$. This gives equality (1) for rooky square grids.

Conversely assume that (1) holds. Then we have to compare two arbitrary German products. But they can transformed into each other by a sequence of several swaps of two cells. Due to (1) the German product does not change at any of these steps, so the rook products of the original configurations are the same as well.

Lemma: A rooky square grid is uniquely determined by the elements of its first row and first column.

Proof. Indeed the previous lemma implies that

$$
a_{i, j} \cdot a_{1,1}=a_{i, 1} \cdot a_{1, j}
$$
which determines $a_{i, j}$ uniquely because $a_{1,1}$ is a unit.
One can actually prove directly that the square grid obtained that way is rooky, but it is simpler to continue directly to

Proposition: Let $\lambda_{i} \in \mathbb{F}_{p}^{*}(i=1, \ldots, n)$ and $\mu_{j} \in \mathbb{F}_{p}^{*}(j=1, \ldots, n)$ arbitrary elements. Then the square grid with

$$
a_{i, j}=\lambda_{i} \cdot \mu_{j}
$$
is rooky. Moreover any rooky square grid can be obtained this way.
Proof. The square grid with $a_{i, j}=\lambda_{i} \cdot \mu_{j}$ is rooky, because any German product has the value
$$
\prod_{i} \lambda_{i} \cdot \prod_{j} \mu_{j} .
$$

Let us prove the converse: By the previous lemma, it suffices to find $\lambda_{i} \mathrm{~S}$ and $\mu_{j} \mathrm{~S}$ that recreate the values of the first row and column. For this simply set $\lambda_{i}=a_{i, 1}$ and $\mu_{j}=\frac{a_{1, j}}{a_{1,1}}$.

Proposition: For any prime $p>n^{2}$, there exists a rooky square grid with only distinct elements.

Proof. Choose any primitive root $\alpha \in \mathbb{F}_{p}^{*}$. Then set $\lambda_{i}=\alpha^{i-1}, \mu_{j}=\alpha^{n \cdot(j-1)}$ and $a_{i, j}=\lambda_{i} \cdot \mu_{j}=\alpha^{i-1+n \cdot(j-1)}$. This provides indeed a rooky square grid. The values in the square are $\alpha^{0}, \alpha^{1}, \ldots, \alpha^{n^{2}-1}$. As we have chosen a primitive root, these are all distinct.

For $n=10, p=101$ and $\alpha=2$, this reproduces exactly the construction given in the previous solution.

In part (b), the proof exhibits an explicit labeling of a 10×10 grid by \(A_{ij}=2^{10i+j} mod101\), observes that 2 is a primitive root mod 101 so these labels are a permutation of 1…100, and shows every German product is \(2^{495} mod101\), hence all differences are divisible by 101.

problem: Let \( S(m) \) be the sum of the digits of the positive integer \( m \). Find all pairs \((a, b)\) of positive integers such that \( S\left(a^{b+1}\right) = a^{b} \).
solution:
Solution.  
Throughout the solution  

• \(S(n)\) denotes the (decimal) sum of the digits of \(n\);  
• all integers are supposed to be positive.

------------------------------------------------------------
1.  A congruence modulo \(9\)

A classical property of the digit sum is  

\[
S(n)\equiv n \pmod 9 \qquad(\forall n\in\mathbb N).
\]

Applying it to the equation of the statement we obtain  

\[
a^{\,b+1}\equiv S\!\bigl(a^{\,b+1}\bigr)=a^{\,b}\pmod 9
\Longrightarrow a^{\,b}(a-1)\equiv 0\pmod 9 .
\]

Hence

(1) \(9\mid a^{\,b}(a-1)\).

Because two consecutive integers can never both be divisible by \(3\),
it follows from (1) that  

\[
a\equiv 0 \pmod 9 \qquad\text{or}\qquad a\equiv 1\pmod 9 .
\tag{2}
\]

------------------------------------------------------------
2.  A general upper bound for \(S\bigl(a^{\,b+1}\bigr)\)

If \(n\) has \(d\) decimal digits, then \(10^{d-1}\le n<10^{d}\); hence
\(d\le\log_{10}n+1\) and therefore  

\[
S(n)\le 9d\le 9\bigl(\log_{10} n+1\bigr).
\]

With \(n=a^{\,b+1}\) we get  

\[
S\!\bigl(a^{\,b+1}\bigr)\le 9\Bigl((b+1)\log_{10}a+1\Bigr).
\tag{3}
\]

Because the left–hand side of (3) equals \(a^{\,b}\),
we find the fundamental inequality  

\[
a^{\,b}\le 9\Bigl((b+1)\log_{10}a+1\Bigr).
\tag{4}
\]

------------------------------------------------------------
3.  The case \(a\ge 10\) – non–existence of solutions

------------------------------------------------------------------
3.1  Preliminary simplifications  

For \(a\ge 10\) one has  

\[
\log_{10}a+1\le \frac a2
\]
(the function \(f(t)=t-2(\log_{10}t+1)\) is increasing and \(f(10)=6>0\)).
Insert this estimate in (4):

\[
a^{\,b}\le\frac{9}{2}(b+1)a.
\tag{5}
\]

------------------------------------------------------------------
3.2  The sub–case \(b\ge 2\)

Inequality (5) implies \(a\le \dfrac{9}{2}(b+1)\).
For \(b\ge 2\) this bound gives \(a\le 13\).
But we are in the sub-case \(a\ge 10\); hence \(a\in\{10,11,12,13\}\).

By the congruence (2) only \(a=10\) (because \(10\equiv 1\pmod 9\))
survives.  
For \(a=10\) the left–hand side of the original equation is
\(S(10^{\,b+1})=1\) while the right–hand side equals \(10^{\,b}\ge 100\),
a contradiction.  Thus no solution exists with \(a\ge 10,\;b\ge 2\).

------------------------------------------------------------------
3.3  The sub–case \(b=1\)

Then the required equality is \(S(a^{2})=a\).
Write \(a\) with \(d\;(d\ge 2)\) digits;  
\(a^{2}\) has at most \(2d\le 4\) digits because \(a\le 99\).
Hence \(S(a^{2})\le 36\).  
Consequently \(a\le 36\).

With this restriction and with (2) the only candidates are  

\[
a\in\{10,18,19,27,28,36\}.
\]

A direct calculation shows that none of them satisfies \(S(a^{2})=a\)
(\(10^{2}=100\Rightarrow S=1\), \(18^{2}=324\Rightarrow S=9\), etc.).
Therefore there is no solution with \(a\ge 10\).

------------------------------------------------------------
4.  The case \(1\le a\le 9\)

Because there are only finitely many small values to test, we shall
first reduce the range of \(b\) with the help of (4).

For \(2\le a\le 9\) we have \(\log_{10}a<1\);
hence (4) gives  

\[
a^{\,b}\le 9(b+1)+9=9b+18.
\tag{6}
\]

4.1  Bounding \(b\)

•  If \(a=8\) or \(7\): \(a^{2}=64,49>9\cdot2+18=36\),
so by (6) we must have \(b=1\).

•  If \(a=6,5,4\): \(a^{3}\ge 64>9\cdot3+18=45\);
hence \(b\le 2\).

•  If \(a=3\): \(3^{4}=81>9\cdot4+18=54\); hence \(b\le 3\).

•  If \(a=2\): inequality (6) yields \(2^{b}\le 9b+18\);
one checks that it fails for \(b\ge 7\),
so \(b\le 6\).

Thus a finite verification remains:
 (a,b) ∈   

  {2,…,9}×{1,…,6} for a=2,  

  {3}×{1,2,3}, {4,5,6}×{1,2}, {7,8}×{1}.

4.2  Exhaustive check

The table below lists \(a^{\,b}\) together with
\(S\bigl(a^{\,b+1}\bigr)\).

 a = 2  
 b=1 : \(2 ,\;S(4)=4\) ✗  
 b=2 : \(4 ,\;S(8)=8\) ✗  
 b=3 : \(8 ,\;S(16)=7\) ✗  
 b=4 : \(16,\;S(32)=5\) ✗  
 b=5 : \(32,\;S(64)=10\) ✗  
 b=6 : \(64,\;S(128)=11\)✗  

 a = 3  
 b=1 : \(3 ,\;S(9)=9\) ✗  
 b=2 : \(9 ,\;S(27)=9\) ✓  
 b=3 : \(27,\;S(81)=9\) ✗  

 a = 4  
 b=1 : \(4 ,\;S(16)=7\) ✗  
 b=2 : \(16,\;S(64)=10\) ✗  

 a = 5  
 b=1 : \(5 ,\;S(25)=7\) ✗  
 b=2 : \(25,\;S(125)=8\) ✗  

 a = 6  
 b=1 : \(6 ,\;S(36)=9\) ✗  
 b=2 : \(36,\;S(216)=9\) ✗  

 a = 7  
 b=1 : \(7 ,\;S(49)=13\) ✗  

 a = 8  
 b=1 : \(8 ,\;S(64)=10\) ✗  

 a = 9  
 b=1 : \(9 ,\;S(81)=9\) ✓  
 b≥2 : \(9^{\,b}\ge 81\) while \(S(9^{\,b+1})=9\) or \(18\), never equal.

4.3  The value \(a=1\)

Finally, for \(a=1\) we have
\(1^{\,b}=1\) and \(S(1^{\,b+1})=S(1)=1\) for every \(b\).

------------------------------------------------------------
5.  Conclusion

All the pairs \((a,b)\) that satisfy
\(S\!\bigl(a^{\,b+1}\bigr)=a^{\,b}\) are

• \((1,b)\) for every positive integer \(b\);  
• \((3,2)\);  
• \((9,1)\).

These are indeed solutions, and by the arguments above no other pair is
possible. ∎

Solution: Answer: $(a, b) \in\left\{(1, b) \mid b \in \mathbb{Z}^{+}\right\} \cup\{(3,2),(9,1)\}$.
Let $k$ denote the number of digits of $a$. Then $10^{k-1} \leq a<10^{k}$ and, therefore, $10^{(k-1) b} \leq a^{b}$ and $a^{b+1}<10^{k(b+1)}$. Of course, the digits are at most 9, so $S\left(a^{b+1}\right) \leq 9 \cdot k(b+1)$. We get

$$
10^{(k-1) b} \leq a^{b}=S\left(a^{b+1}\right) \leq 9 \cdot k(b+1) \text {, i.e. } 10^{(k-1) b} \leq 9 \cdot k(b+1) .
$$

Let us consider the case where $k \geq 2$. Then $k \leq 2(k-1)$ and note that $b+1 \leq 2 b$ as $b \geq 1$. Put $(k-1) b=: x$, then $k(b+1) \leq 4(k-1) b=4 x$. So $10^{x} \leq 36 x$. It is obvious that the only solutions in nonnegative integers to this inequality are $x=0$ and $x=1$. Indeed, for $x \geq 2$, the left hand side grows faster. Therefore, either $k=1$ or $k=2$ and $b=1$.

Now we have only two cases left.
Case 1: $b=1$ and $k=2$. We are left with the equation $S\left(a^{2}\right)=a$, for $10 \leq a<100$. Then $a^{2}<10^{4}$, so $a=S\left(a^{2}\right) \leq 9 \cdot 4=36$.

Moreover, taking into account the fact that the sum of digits does not change the number modulo $9, a^{2} \equiv a(\bmod 9)$, i.e., $a(a-1) \equiv 0(\bmod 9)$, therefore $a \equiv 0(\bmod 9)$ or $a \equiv 1(\bmod 9)$. So now we are left only with numbers $a \in$ $\{10,18,19,27,28,36\}$, which we can easily check by substitution and see that there are no solutions.

Case 2: $k=1$. In the same way, looking modulo 9, we get that $a^{b+1} \equiv a^{b}(\bmod 9)$ implies $a^{b}(a-1) \equiv 0(\bmod 9)$. Therefore either $a=1$ or $a$ is divisible by $3 . a=1$ is an obvious solution with all $b \in \mathbb{Z}^{+}$.

Otherwise, $a \in\{3,6,9\}$. But then $a^{b+1}<10^{b+1}$ and $S\left(a^{b+1}\right) \leq 9(b+1)$. Therefore, $3^{b} \leq a^{b}=S\left(a^{b+1}\right) \leq 9(b+1)$. But from $3^{b} \leq 9(b+1)$, we can conclude $b \leq 3$. Indeed, for $b \geq 4$, the left hand side increases faster. So we are left with $a \in\{3,6,9\}$ and $b \leq 3$. We check all these cases to determine that only $(a, b)=(3,2)$ or $(a, b)=(9,1)$ are solutions.
llm_summary: The proof uses the well–known fact that a number is congruent to its digit sum modulo 9 to deduce that a≡0 or 1 mod 9.  It then bounds S(a^{b+1}) by 9(digits of a^{b+1})≤9((b+1)log_{10}a+1) to derive the key inequality a^b≤9((b+1)log_{10}a+1).  Splitting into the cases a≥10 (handled by further elementary bounds and small searches) and 1≤a≤9 (handled by bounding b for each a and an exhaustive check), the proof finds exactly the solutions (1,b),(3,2),(9,1).

problem: Let \( ABC \) be a triangle with circumcenter \( O \). The points \( D, E, F \) lie in the interiors of the sides \( BC, CA, AB \) respectively, such that \(\overline{DE} \perp \overline{CO}\) and \(\overline{DF} \perp \overline{BO}\). Let \( K \) be the circumcenter of triangle \( AFE \). Prove that the lines \(\overline{DK}\) and \(\overline{BC}\) are perpendicular.
solution:
Let the circumcircle of \( \triangle ABC \) be denoted by \( (ABC) \).

1.  Tangents.

   Because \(O\) is the circumcenter, the tangent to \( (ABC) \) at  
   a vertex is perpendicular to the radius through that vertex.  
   Hence

   •  the tangent at \(B\;(t_B)\) is perpendicular to \(BO\);  
   •  the tangent at \(C\;(t_C)\) is perpendicular to \(CO\).

   By hypothesis \(DF\perp BO\) and \(DE\perp CO\); therefore  

   \[
   DF\parallel t_B ,\qquad DE\parallel t_C .\tag{1}
   \]

2.  The angle \( \angle FDE\).

   From (1) the angle between \(DF\) and \(DE\) equals the angle between the two tangents:

   \[
   \angle FDE=\angle(t_B,t_C)=\angle BOC .
   \]

   Since \(O\) is the circumcenter, \( \angle BOC = 2\angle BAC\).  Hence  

   \[
   \boxed{\;\angle FDE = 2\angle BAC\;}. \tag{2}
   \]

3.  The angle \( \angle FKE\).

   The points \(A,E,F\) lie on the circle \((AFE)\) with centre \(K\).  
   In that circle the central angle subtending chord \(FE\) is twice the corresponding inscribed angle:

   \[
   \angle FKE = 2\angle FAE .
   \]

   Because \(F\in AB\) and \(E\in AC\), we have \( \angle FAE = \angle BAC\).  Hence  

   \[
   \boxed{\;\angle FKE = 2\angle BAC\;}. \tag{3}
   \]

4.  A cyclic quadrilateral.

   By (2) and (3)  
   \( \angle FDE = \angle FKE\).  
   The two equal angles stand on the same segment \(FE\); consequently the four points

   \[
   D,\;E,\;F,\;K
   \]

   are concyclic.  (If two distinct points subtend equal angles from the same chord, they are on the same circle with that chord.)

5.  Computing \( \angle KDF\).

   In the cyclic quadrilateral \(DFEK\) equal angles subtend the same arc; in particular  

   \[
   \angle KDF = \angle KEF .\tag{4}
   \]

   Let \( \ell\) be the tangent to \((AFE)\) at \(E\).  
   Because \(K\) is the centre of \((AFE)\), \(KE\perp\ell\).  
   By the tangent–chord theorem  

   \[
   \angle(\ell,EF)=\angle FAE=\angle BAC .
   \]

   Therefore  

   \[
   \angle KEF = 90^{\circ}-\angle BAC .\tag{5}
   \]

   Combining (4) and (5),

   \[
   \boxed{\;\angle KDF = 90^{\circ}-\angle BAC\;}. \tag{6}
   \]

6.  Computing \( \angle FDB\).

   Using (1) again, \(DF\parallel t_B\).  
   Applying the tangent–chord theorem at \(B\) (with chord \(BC\)) gives

   \[
   \angle(t_B,BC)=\angle BAC .
   \]

   Since \(DB\subset BC\),

   \[
   \boxed{\;\angle FDB = \angle BAC\;}. \tag{7}
   \]

7.  The right angle at \(D\).

   At the vertex \(D\)

   \[
   \angle KDB
         = \angle KDF + \angle FDB          \quad (\text{adjacent angles})
         = \bigl(90^{\circ}-\angle BAC\bigr)+\angle BAC
         = 90^{\circ}.
   \]

   Thus \(DK\perp DB\).  Because \(D\) lies on \(BC\), we obtain  

   \[
   DK\perp BC ,
   \]

   completing the proof. ∎
feedback: The solution is correct. A minor comment is that when we are not working with directed angles some issues may arise with the claim that if two angles are equal, a respective quadrilateral is cyclic, but this is minor.

## Problem statement

Let $A B C$ be a triangle with circumcenter $O$. The points $D, E, F$ lie in the interiors of the sides $B C, C A, A B$ respectively, such that $\overline{D E} \perp \overline{C O}$ and $\overline{D F} \perp \overline{B O}$. Let $K$ be the circumcenter of triangle $A F E$. Prove that the lines $\overline{D K}$ and $\overline{B C}$ are perpendicular.

First, note $\measuredangle E D F=180^{\circ}-\measuredangle B O C=180^{\circ}-2 A$, so $\measuredangle F D E=2 A$.

Observe that $\measuredangle F K E=2 A$ as well; hence $K F D E$ is cyclic. Hence

$$
\begin{aligned}
\measuredangle K D B & =\measuredangle K D F+\measuredangle F D B \\
& =\measuredangle K E F+\left(90^{\circ}-\measuredangle D B O\right) \\
& =\left(90^{\circ}-A\right)+\left(90^{\circ}-\left(90^{\circ}-A\right)\right) \\
& =90^{\circ} .
\end{aligned}
$$

and the proof ends here.
llm_summary: The proof begins by noting that the tangents t_B and t_C to the circumcircle (ABC) at B and C satisfy DF⊥BO and DE⊥CO, so DF∥t_B and DE∥t_C, hence \(\angle FDE=\angle(t_B,t_C)=\angle BOC=2\angle BAC\). Since K is the circumcenter of (AFE), its central angle gives \(\angle FKE=2\angle FAE=2\angle BAC\), so D,E,F,K are concyclic. Finally, the tangent–chord theorem at E yields \(\angle KDF=90^\circ-\angle BAC\) and at B gives \(\angle FDB=\angle BAC\), whose sum is \(90^\circ\), proving \(DK\perp BC\).

problem:
Let \( n \) be a positive integer. Find the greatest possible integer \( m \), in terms of \( n \), with the following property: a table with \( m \) rows and \( n \) columns can be filled with real numbers in such a manner that for any two different rows \([a_{1}, a_{2}, \ldots, a_{n}]\) and \([b_{1}, b_{2}, \ldots, b_{n}]\) the following holds:

\[
\max \left(\left|a_{1}-b_{1}\right|,\left|a_{2}-b_{2}\right|, \ldots,\left|a_{n}-b_{n}\right|\right)=1
\]
solution:
Here is a fully self‐contained proof that the largest possible number of rows is 
\[
m_{\max}(n)\;=\;2^n.
\]

Proof.  
We shall exhibit (i) a construction with \(2^n\) rows, and then (ii) prove by induction on \(n\) that no larger set can exist.

1.  Construction of size \(2^n\).  
Label the columns \(1,2,\dots,n\).  For each binary vector 
\[
v=(v_1,v_2,\dots,v_n)\in\{0,1\}^n
\]
use \(v\) as a row of the table.  Thus there are exactly \(2^n\) rows.  If 
\(\,v\neq w\in\{0,1\}^n\), then for each \(i\), \(\lvert v_i-w_i\rvert\) is either \(0\) or \(1\), and since \(v\neq w\) there is at least one coordinate \(i\) with \(\lvert v_i-w_i\rvert=1\).  Hence
\[
\max_{1\le i\le n}\Bigl\lvert v_i-w_i\Bigr\rvert \;=\;1,
\]
as required.

2.  Optimality: no more than \(2^n\) rows are possible.  
Let \(S\subset\Bbb R^n\) be any set of points (to serve as rows) with the property
\[
\forall\;x\neq y\in S:\quad
\max_{1\le i\le n}\bigl\lvert x_i-y_i\bigr\rvert \;=\;1.
\]
We must show \(\lvert S\rvert\le2^n\).  We argue by induction on \(n\).

Base case \(n=1\).  Then \(S\subset\Bbb R\) and the condition says any two distinct points differ by exactly \(1\).  Clearly no three real numbers can all be at mutual distance \(1\) (if \(a<b<c\), then \(\lvert a-b\rvert=\lvert b-c\rvert=1\) forces \(\lvert a-c\rvert=2\)).  Hence \(\lvert S\rvert\le2=2^1\).

Inductive step.  Suppose the claim holds in dimension \(n-1\).  Let us prove it in dimension \(n\).

(a)  Let
\[
A \;=\;\{\,x_1 : x=(x_1,x_2,\dots,x_n)\in S\}\subset\Bbb R
\]
be the set of first coordinates of points of \(S\).  Since for any \(x,y\in S\)
\(\lvert x_1-y_1\rvert\le\max_i\lvert x_i-y_i\rvert=1,\)
the set \(A\) lies in some closed interval of length at most \(1\).  Let
\[
a\;=\;\inf A,\qquad b\;=\;\sup A,
\]
so \(0\le b-a\le1\).

(b)  Case 1: \(b-a<1\).  Then for every \(x,y\in S\) we have \(\lvert x_1-y_1\rvert<1\), so the condition
\(\max_{1\le i\le n}\lvert x_i-y_i\rvert=1\)
must be witnessed in one of the last \(n-1\) coordinates.  In other words, the projection
\[
\pi: \Bbb R^n\longrightarrow\Bbb R^{\,n-1},\qquad
\pi(x_1,x_2,\dots,x_n)=(x_2,\dots,x_n),
\]
carries \(S\) bijectively onto a set \(\pi(S)\subset\Bbb R^{\,n-1}\) which is again an “equilateral” set in the \(\ell_\infty\)‐metric of side length \(1\).  By the inductive hypothesis
\(\lvert S\rvert=\lvert\pi(S)\rvert\le 2^{\,n-1}<2^n\),
as desired.

(c)  Case 2: \(b-a=1\).  Then there are points in \(S\) whose first coordinate is exactly \(a\), and others whose first coordinate is exactly \(b=a+1\).  Partition
\[
L=\{x\in S:x_1=a\},\quad
H=\{x\in S:x_1=b\},\quad
M=S\setminus(L\cup H).
\]
Note that for any \(u\in M\) and any \(x\in L\), we have
\(\lvert u_1-x_1\rvert<1\), so the required distance \(\max_i\lvert u_i-x_i\rvert=1\)
must occur in one of the last \(n-1\) coordinates; hence
\(\pi(u)\) and \(\pi(x)\) are at \(\ell_\infty\)‐distance \(1\) in \(\Bbb R^{n-1}\).  Equally, for any \(u\in M\) and any \(y\in H\), the same holds.  Finally, if \(x,x'\in L\), then \(x_1=x'_1\) forces their distance also to be realized in coordinates \(2,\dots,n\), so \(\pi(x)\) and \(\pi(x')\) are also at distance \(1\); and likewise for any two points in \(H\).

Thus both
\[
\pi(L\cup M)\quad\text{and}\quad\pi(H\cup M)
\]
are equilateral sets of side‐length \(1\) in \(\Bbb R^{\,n-1}\).  By the inductive hypothesis,
\[
\lvert L\rvert+\lvert M\rvert=\bigl\lvert\pi(L\cup M)\bigr\rvert\;\le\;2^{\,n-1},
\quad
\lvert H\rvert+\lvert M\rvert=\bigl\lvert\pi(H\cup M)\bigr\rvert\;\le\;2^{\,n-1}.
\]
Adding these two inequalities gives
\[
\bigl(\lvert L\rvert+\lvert M\rvert\bigr)
+\bigl(\lvert H\rvert+\lvert M\rvert\bigr)
\;\le\;2\cdot2^{\,n-1}=2^n,
\]
i.e. \(\lvert L\rvert+\lvert H\rvert+2\lvert M\rvert\le2^n\).  Hence
\[
\lvert S\rvert=\lvert L\rvert+\lvert H\rvert+\lvert M\rvert
\;=\;\bigl(\lvert L\rvert+\lvert H\rvert+2\lvert M\rvert\bigr)
-\lvert M\rvert
\;\le\;2^n-\lvert M\rvert
\;\le\;2^n.
\]
This completes the induction.

Combining (1) and (2), the answer is
\[
\boxed{m_{\max}(n)=2^n}.
\]

## Problem statement

Let $n$ be a positive integer. Find the greatest possible integer $m$, in terms of $n$, with the following property: a table with $m$ rows and $n$ columns can be filled with real numbers in such a manner that for any two different rows $\left[a_{1}, a_{2}, \ldots, a_{n}\right]$ and $\left[b_{1}, b_{2}, \ldots, b_{n}\right]$ the following holds:

$$
\max \left(\left|a_{1}-b_{1}\right|,\left|a_{2}-b_{2}\right|, \ldots,\left|a_{n}-b_{n}\right|\right)=1
$$
\I Answer. The largest $m$ is $m(n)=2^{n}$.
\ा Construction. Choose the table with all $2^{n}$ binary vectors.

Bound. We will proceed by induction on $n$, with the base case $n=1$ being immediate. Take the first column, and assume the entries lie in some interval $I=[r, r+1]$. Then the rows with first entry equal to $r$ form an $(n-1)$-table, hence at most $m(n-1)$ of them. The rows with first entry not equal to $r$ also form an $(n-1)$-table, hence at most $m(n-1)$ of them. So

$$
m(n) \leq \underbrace{m(n-1)}_{\text {first entry } r}+\underbrace{m(n-1)}_{\text {first entry not } r}=2 m(n-1)
$$
and we're done by induction.
llm_summary: The proof gives a two‐part argument. First, it shows by explicit construction that labeling each row with a binary vector in \(\{0,1\}^n\) yields \(2^n\) rows satisfying the max‐norm distance condition. Second, it proves by induction on \(n\) that any set \(S\subset\mathbb R^n\) with the property that any two distinct points have \(\ell_\infty\)‐distance exactly 1 can have at most \(2^n\) points. The base case \(n=1\) is handled by noting no three reals can be mutually at distance 1. In the inductive step, one considers the range of first coordinates (of length \(<1\) or exactly 1), projects onto the last \(n-1\) coordinates, and applies the inductive hypothesis in each case to bound \(|S|\).

problem:
The numbers \( p \) and \( q \) are prime and satisfy

\[
\frac{p}{p+1}+\frac{q+1}{q}=\frac{2 n}{n+2}
\]

for some positive integer \( n \). Find all possible values of \( q-p \).
solution:
Let  

\[
\frac{p}{p+1}+\frac{q+1}{q}=\frac{2n}{n+2}\qquad (1)
\]

where \(p , q\) are primes and \(n\) is a positive integer.  
We have to determine every possible value of \(q-p\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
1.  A convenient reformulation
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Write the two fractions on the left–hand side of (1) as  

\[
\frac{p}{p+1}=1-\frac1{p+1},\qquad 
\frac{q+1}{q}=1+\frac1q .
\]

Hence  

\[
2+\frac1q-\frac1{p+1}=\frac{2n}{n+2}\Longrightarrow 
\frac1q-\frac1{p+1}=-\frac4{n+2}.     \tag{2}
\]

Multiply (2) by \(q(p+1)(n+2)\):

\[
(n+2)\bigl((p+1)-q\bigr)=4q(p+1).
\]

Put  

\[
s:=q-(p+1)\qquad (s>0),
\qquad 
m:=p+1 .
\]

Because \(q=p+1+s=m+s\), the last equality becomes  

\[
(n+2)s=4qm=4(m+s)m.   \tag{3}
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
2.  A first divisibility conclusion
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Equation (3) shows that \(s\mid 4qm\).  
Since \(q\) is prime and \(s<q\), the two integers \(s\) and \(q\) are coprime:

\[
\gcd(s,q)=\gcd\bigl(q-m,\;q\bigr)=\gcd(m,q)=1 .
\]

(Indeed a common divisor of \(s\) and \(q\) would also divide
\(q-(q-m)=m\);
but \(q\) is prime, bigger than \(m\), so that common divisor must be \(1\).)

Because \(s\) is coprime to \(q\) yet divides \(4qm\),
it must divide the remaining factor \(4m\):

\[
s\mid 4m. \tag{4}
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
3.  Coprimality with \(m\)
--------------------------------------------------------------------
If a prime \(d\) divides both \(s\) and \(m\), then it divides their sum
\(q=m+s\) as well.
Since \(1<d\le m<q\) and \(q\) itself is prime,
that cannot happen.  Therefore  

\[
\gcd(s,m)=1 . \tag{5}
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
4.  Determining \(s\)
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Combine (4) and (5).  
All prime divisors of \(s\) come from the factor \(4m\);
none of them can divide \(m\) (by (5)),
hence they must come from \(4=2^{2}\).
Consequently

\[
s\mid 4\quad\Longrightarrow\quad s\in\{1,2,4\}.  \tag{6}
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
5.  The desired differences
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Recall that  

\[
q-p=(m+s)-p=(p+1+s)-p=s+1.
\]

With (6) this yields

\[
q-p\in\{2,\,3,\,5\}.  \tag{7}
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
6.  Realising each value
--------------------------------------------------------------------
It remains to show that every number in (7) really occurs.

• \(q-p=2\) (that is \(s=1\)):
   take \(p=3,\;q=5\).
   From (3) one obtains \(n+2=80\), whence \(n=78\).
   A direct check shows that (1) is satisfied.

• \(q-p=3\) (\(s=2\)):
   choose \(p=2,\;q=5\);\; (3) gives \(n+2=30\), i.e. \(n=28\).

• \(q-p=5\) (\(s=4\)):
   choose \(p=2,\;q=7\);\; (3) gives \(n+2=21\), i.e. \(n=19\).

Thus every value listed in (7) actually occurs.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
7.  Conclusion
--------------------------------------------------------------------
The only possible values of \(q-p\) are

\[
\boxed{\;2,\;3,\;5\;}.
\]
ground_truth_solution:
## Problem statement

The numbers $p$ and $q$ are prime and satisfy

$$
\frac{p}{p+1}+\frac{q+1}{q}=\frac{2 n}{n+2}
$$
for some positive integer $n$. Find all possible values of $q-p$.

We clean up the numerators as

$$
\left(1-\frac{1}{p+1}\right)+\left(1+\frac{1}{q}\right)=2-\frac{4}{n+2}
$$
which simplifies as
$$
\frac{4}{n+2}=\frac{1}{p+1}-\frac{1}{q}
$$

which reduces as

$$
\frac{4}{n+2}=\frac{q-p-1}{q(p+1)}
$$

At this point $n$ is a free parameter. So, this motivates us to rewrite the equation as

$$
n+2=\frac{4 q(p+1)}{(q-p)-1}
$$

This implies that $q-p-1 \mid 4 q(p+1)$. Since $n$ is positive, we have $0<q-p-1<q$. Because $q$ is prime, this implies $q-p-1 \mid 4(p+1)$. But now $q-p-1 \mid 4(p+1)+4(q-p-1)=4 q$. Again, $q$ is prime, so $q-p-1 \mid 4$. This implies $q-p \in\{2,3,5\}$.

It is easy to construct working examples: say $(p, q)$ is $(3,5),(2,5)$ and $(2,7)$.
llm_summary:
The proof rewrites the given equation as
\[
1/q - 1/(p+1) = -4/(n+2)
\]
and then multiplies through to obtain
\[(n+2)s = 4q(p+1),\]
where \(s = q-(p+1)\).  Using the fact that \(s\) is coprime to both \(q\) and \(p+1\), it concludes that \(s\) divides 4, so \(s\in\{1,2,4\}\) and hence \(q-p = s+1\in\{2,3,5\}\).  Finally, it exhibits one prime example for each difference to show these values occur.

llm_issues.description:
When you multiply
\(1/q - 1/(p+1) = -4/(n+2)\)
by \(q(p+1)(n+2)\), the correct result is
\((n+2)((p+1)-q) = -4q(p+1)\).  The proof omits or mis-handles this sign change and does not explain how the negative sign is absorbed before defining \(s\).
The proof asserts without justification that \(s>0\), i.e. that \(q>p+1\).  No argument is given to rule out \(q\le p+1\) before introducing \(s>0\).
The proof invokes \(s<q\) without justification (it depends on the same unproven assumption \(q>p+1\)).
llm_issues.location: In the argument for coprimality of \(s\) and \(q\)
llm_issues.text: Since \(q\) is prime and \(s<q\), the two integers \(s\) and \(q\) are coprime

llm_issues.description: Each example is asserted to satisfy the original equation by “direct check,” but the proof omits all details of these verifications.
llm_issues.text: Direct check shows that (1) is satisfied.

problem:
There are infinitely many people registered on the social network Mugbook. Some pairs of (different) users are registered as friends, but each person has only finitely many friends. Every user has at least one friend. (Friendship is symmetric; that is, if \(A\) is a friend of \(B\), then \(B\) is a friend of \(A\).) Each person is required to designate one of their friends as their best friend. If \(A\) designates \(B\) as her best friend, then it does not follow that \(B\) necessarily designates \(A\) as her best friend. Someone designated as a best friend is called a 1-best friend. More generally, if \(n>1\) is a positive integer, then a user is an \(n\)-best friend provided that they have been designated the best friend of someone who is an \((n-1)\)-best friend. Someone who is a \(k\)-best friend for every positive integer \(k\) is called popular.

(a) Prove that every popular person is the best friend of a popular person.

(b) Show that if people can have infinitely many friends, then it is possible that a popular person is not the best friend of a popular person.
solution:
Let us first introduce a convenient notation.  
Write \(X\longrightarrow Y\) if the user \(X\) has designated the user \(Y\) as her best friend.  
Because each person designates exactly one best friend, every vertex of the directed graph
formed by the arrows has out–degree \(1\); the in–degree can be any (finite or infinite) cardinality.

A directed path  

\[
U_{m}\longrightarrow U_{m-1}\longrightarrow\cdots\longrightarrow U_{1}\longrightarrow U_{0}
\]

containing \(m\ge 1\) arrows will be called an \(m\)-chain and we say that
\(U_{0}\) is reached by that \(m\)-chain.  
If \(U_{0}\) is reached by some \(m\)-chain, then \(U_{0}\) is an \(m\)-best friend
according to the recursive definition given in the statement.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
(a)  Every popular person is the best friend of a popular person
--------------------------------------------------------------------

Assume that every user has only finitely many friends and let \(P\) be a popular user.
Thus for every positive integer \(k\) there exists a \(k\)-chain ending at \(P\).
Fix such a \(k\)-chain and denote its penultimate vertex by \(V_{k}\):
\[
U_{k}\longrightarrow\cdots\longrightarrow U_{2}\longrightarrow
\underbrace{V_{k}}_{\text{friend of }P}\;\longrightarrow P .
\]
Consequently \(V_{k}\longrightarrow P\); in particular \(V_{k}\) is a friend of \(P\).

Because \(P\) has only finitely many friends, the finite set  
\[
F=\{\,\text{friends of }P\,\}
\]
contains the whole infinite sequence \(\{V_{1},V_{2},V_{3},\dots\}\).
By the pigeon-hole principle some element of \(F\) occurs infinitely
often in that sequence; call that element \(Q\).  
Hence there are arbitrarily long chains whose last arrow is \(Q\longrightarrow P\).

Let \(n\) be an arbitrary positive integer.
Choose a chain whose length is at least \(n+1\) and whose last arrow is \(Q\longrightarrow P\):
\[
W_{n}\longrightarrow\cdots\longrightarrow W_{1}\longrightarrow
\underbrace{Q}_{\text{best friend }P}\;\longrightarrow P .
\]
There are \(n\) arrows before \(Q\); consequently \(Q\) is an \(n\)-best friend.
Because \(n\) was arbitrary, \(Q\) is an \(n\)-best friend for every \(n\), i.e. \(Q\) is popular.

Finally, \(Q\longrightarrow P\), so \(P\) is indeed the best friend of the popular
user \(Q\).  This proves part (a).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
(b)  If users may have infinitely many friends, the statement can fail
--------------------------------------------------------------------

We construct an explicit example.  
All friendships listed are understood to be symmetric.

Users  
• one special user \(A\) (he will be popular);  
• for every integer \(n\ge 0\) a user \(B_{n}\);  
• for every integer \(n\ge 1\) and every integer \(1\le k\le n\) a user \(C_{n,k}\).

Friendships  
• \(A\) is friends with every \(B_{n}\) (hence with infinitely many people);  
• for each \(n\ge 0\) the pair \(B_{n},C_{n,1}\) are friends;  
• for each \(n\ge 1\) and \(2\le k\le n\) the pair \(C_{n,k},C_{n,k-1}\) are friends.

(Every user just listed has at least one friend; many have exactly one or two.)

Best friends  
• \(A\) designates \(B_{0}\) as best friend;  
• every \(B_{n}\) (\(n\ge 0\)) designates \(A\) as best friend, so \(B_{n}\longrightarrow A\);  
• for each \(n\ge 0\) the user \(C_{n,1}\) designates \(B_{n}\) as best friend;  
• for \(n\ge 1\) and \(2\le k\le n\) the user \(C_{n,k}\) designates \(C_{n,k-1}\) as best friend.

Verification that \(A\) is popular  
------------------------------------------------
For \(k=1\) the arrow \(B_{0}\longrightarrow A\) itself is a \(1\)-chain, 
so \(A\) is a \(1\)-best friend.

Fix \(m\ge 2\) and consider the chain  
\[
C_{m,m}\longrightarrow C_{m,m-1}\longrightarrow\cdots\longrightarrow
C_{m,1}\longrightarrow B_{m}\longrightarrow A ,
\]
which has \(m+1\) arrows; hence \(A\) is an \((m+1)\)-best friend.
Because \(m\) was arbitrary, \(A\) is an \(r\)-best friend for every positive
integer \(r\); thus \(A\) is popular.

The users who choose \(A\) as best friend are precisely the \(B_{n}\,(n\ge 0)\).
We show that none of them is popular.

Limited popularity of each \(B_{n}\)  
------------------------------------
User \(B_{n}\) is the endpoint of exactly one family of chains, namely  
\[
C_{n,n}\longrightarrow C_{n,n-1}\longrightarrow\cdots\longrightarrow
C_{n,1}\longrightarrow B_{n}.
\]
The longest such chain contains \(n\) arrows, so \(B_{n}\) is an
\(n\)-best friend, but it is not an \((n+1)\)-best friend.
Therefore \(B_{n}\) fails to be popular.

Consequently \(A\) is a popular person who is not the best friend of any
popular person.  (Every user with \(A\) as best friend is some \(B_{n}\),
and none of the \(B_{n}\) are popular.)  This establishes part (b).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
Conclusion
--------------------------------------------------------------------
(a) With only finitely many friends per user, the pigeon-hole argument
shows that a popular person must be the best friend of a popular person.  
(b) Allowing users to have infinitely many friends, the explicit
construction above exhibits a popular user who is not the best friend of
any popular user, showing that the finiteness assumption in part (a) is essential.
feedback: The solution is correct and clear.

## Problem statement

There are infinitely many people registered on the social network Mugbook. Some pairs of (different) users are registered as friends, but each person has only finitely many friends. Every user has at least one friend. (Friendship is symmetric; that is, if $A$ is a friend of $B$, then $B$ is a friend of $A$.) Each person is required to designate one of their friends as their best friend. If $A$ designates $B$ as her best friend, then (unfortunately) it does not follow that $B$ necessarily designates $A$ as her best friend. Someone designated as a best friend is called a 1-best friend. More generally, if $n>1$ is a positive integer, then a user is an $n$-best friend provided that they have been designated the best friend of someone who is an $(n-1)$-best friend. Someone who is a $k$-best friend for every positive integer $k$ is called popular.
(a) Prove that every popular person is the best friend of a popular person.
(b) Show that if people can have infinitely many friends, then it is possible that a popular person is not the best friend of a popular person.

First note the following statement is true by induction:
Claim - Someone who is an $n$-best friend is also a $k$-best friend for all $1 \leq k<n$.
Proof. Induction on $(k, n)$.
For part (a), suppose Dan is a popular person. Let the friends of Dan be $P_{1}, P_{2}, \ldots$, $P_{m}$. For each $n$, one of the $P_{i}$ 's must be an $n$-best friend. By pigeonhole, one of the $P_{i}$ 's is an $n$-best friend for infinitely many $n \geq 1$. Hence be the claim above they are popular too.

For part (b), consider a social graph defined by having $\operatorname{Dan}(D)$ and the following chains of best friends:

$$
\begin{aligned}
& D \longleftarrow P_{11} \\
& D \longleftarrow P_{21} \longleftarrow P_{22} \\
& D \longleftarrow P_{31} \longleftarrow P_{32} \longleftarrow P_{33} \\
& D \longleftarrow P_{41} \longleftarrow P_{42} \longleftarrow P_{43} \longleftarrow P_{44}
\end{aligned}
$$

Then Dan is the only popular person in the entire network. This gives the construction promised.

In part (b) it gives an explicit construction of users \(A,B_n,C_{n,k}\), with \(A\) having infinitely many friends, to exhibit a popular user \(A\) whose only best friends \(B_n\) each fail to be popular.

problem: The side \( BC \) of the triangle \( ABC \) is extended beyond \( C \) to \( D \) so that \( CD = BC \). The side \( CA \) is extended beyond \( A \) to \( E \) so that \( AE = 2CA \). Prove that if \( AD = BE \) then the triangle \( ABC \) is right-angled.
solution:
To prove that if \(AD = BE\) then triangle \(ABC\) is right-angled, we use vector geometry with point \(A\) as the origin. This simplifies the position vectors and allows us to work with vectors directly. We denote the position vectors of points as follows:

- Let \(\vec{A} = \vec{0}\), the origin.
- Let \(\vec{B}\) be the position vector of point \(B\).
- Let \(\vec{C}\) be the position vector of point \(C\).

### Step 1: Define points \(D\) and \(E\)
- Point \(D\) is defined by extending \(BC\) beyond \(C\) such that \(CD = BC\).  
  The vector \(BC = \vec{C} - \vec{B}\), so \(CD = BC = \vec{C} - \vec{B}\).  
  Thus, the position vector of \(D\) is:  
  \[
  \vec{D} = \vec{C} + CD = \vec{C} + (\vec{C} - \vec{B}) = 2\vec{C} - \vec{B}.
  \]

- Point \(E\) is defined by extending \(CA\) beyond \(A\) such that \(AE = 2CA\).  
  The vector \(CA = \vec{A} - \vec{C} = -\vec{C}\) (since \(\vec{A} = \vec{0}\)).  
  Thus, \(AE = 2 \cdot CA = 2 \cdot (-\vec{C}) = -2\vec{C}\).  
  Therefore, the position vector of \(E\) is:  
  \[
  \vec{E} = \vec{A} + AE = \vec{0} + (-2\vec{C}) = -2\vec{C}.
  \]

### Step 2: Express vectors \(AD\) and \(BE\)
- Vector \(AD\) is the vector from \(A\) to \(D\):  
  \[
  \vec{AD} = \vec{D} - \vec{A} = (2\vec{C} - \vec{B}) - \vec{0} = 2\vec{C} - \vec{B}.
  \]  
  The length \(AD\) is the magnitude of this vector:  
  \[
  |AD| = |2\vec{C} - \vec{B}|.
  \]

- Vector \(BE\) is the vector from \(B\) to \(E\):  
  \[
  \vec{BE} = \vec{E} - \vec{B} = (-2\vec{C}) - \vec{B} = -2\vec{C} - \vec{B}.
  \]  
  The length \(BE\) is the magnitude of this vector:  
  \[
  \[|BE| = |-2\vec{C} - \vec{B}| = |-(2\vec{C} + \vec{B})| = |2\vec{C} + \vec{B}|,\]
  \]  
  since the magnitude is invariant under negation.

### Step 3: Apply the condition \(AD = BE\)
Given \(AD = BE\), we have:  
\[
|2\vec{C} - \vec{B}| = |2\vec{C} + \vec{B}|.
\]

To eliminate the magnitudes, we square both sides:  
\[
|2\vec{C} - \vec{B}|^2 = |2\vec{C} + \vec{B}|^2.
\]

The squared magnitude of a vector \(\vec{V}\) is \(\vec{V} \cdot \vec{V}\), so we compute both sides using the dot product.

- Left side:  
  \[
  |2\vec{C} - \vec{B}|^2 = (2\vec{C} - \vec{B}) \cdot (2\vec{C} - \vec{B}).
  \]  
  Expand the dot product:  
  \[
  (2\vec{C} - \vec{B}) \cdot (2\vec{C} - \vec{B}) = (2\vec{C}) \cdot (2\vec{C}) - (2\vec{C}) \cdot \vec{B} - \vec{B} \cdot (2\vec{C}) + (-\vec{B}) \cdot (-\vec{B}).
  \]  
  Since the dot product is commutative and distributive:  
  \[
  = 4(\vec{C} \cdot \vec{C}) - 4(\vec{C} \cdot \vec{B}) + (\vec{B} \cdot \vec{B}) = 4|\vec{C}|^2 - 4(\vec{C} \cdot \vec{B}) + |\vec{B}|^2.
  \]

- Right side:  
  \[
  |2\vec{C} + \vec{B}|^2 = (2\vec{C} + \vec{B}) \cdot (2\vec{C} + \vec{B}).
  \]  
  Expand the dot product:  
  \[
  (2\vec{C} + \vec{B}) \cdot (2\vec{C} + \vec{B}) = (2\vec{C}) \cdot (2\vec{C}) + (2\vec{C}) \cdot \vec{B} + \vec{B} \cdot (2\vec{C}) + \vec{B} \cdot \vec{B} = 4|\vec{C}|^2 + 4(\vec{C} \cdot \vec{B}) + |\vec{B}|^2.
  \]

Set the squared magnitudes equal:  
\[
4|\vec{C}|^2 - 4(\vec{C} \cdot \vec{B}) + |\vec{B}|^2 = 4|\vec{C}|^2 + 4(\vec{C} \cdot \vec{B}) + |\vec{B}|^2.
\]

### Step 4: Simplify the equation
Subtract common terms from both sides:  
\[
(4|\vec{C}|^2 - 4(\vec{C} \cdot \vec{B}) + |\vec{B}|^2) - (4|\vec{C}|^2 + 4(\vec{C} \cdot \vec{B}) + |\vec{B}|^2) = 0.
\]

Simplify:  
\[
4|\vec{C}|^2 - 4(\vec{C} \cdot \vec{B}) + |\vec{B}|^2 - 4|\vec{C}|^2 - 4(\vec{C} \cdot \vec{B}) - |\vec{B}|^2 = -8(\vec{C} \cdot \vec{B}) = 0.
\]

Thus:  
\[
-8(\vec{C} \cdot \vec{B}) = 0 \implies \vec{C} \cdot \vec{B} = 0.
\]

### Step 5: Interpret the result
Since \(\vec{A} = \vec{0}\), the vector \(\vec{B}\) represents \(\overrightarrow{AB}\) and \(\vec{C}\) represents \(\overrightarrow{AC}\). The dot product \(\vec{B} \cdot \vec{C} = 0\) means that \(\overrightarrow{AB}\) and \(\overrightarrow{AC}\) are perpendicular. Therefore, the angle at vertex \(A\) is a right angle.

### Conclusion
We have shown that if \(AD = BE\), then \(\overrightarrow{AB} \cdot \overrightarrow{AC} = 0\), which implies that triangle \(ABC\) has a right angle at \(A\). Thus, triangle \(ABC\) is right-angled.

\boxed{\text{The triangle } ABC \text{ is right- is right-angled at } A.}

problem: Determine all real constants \( t \) such that whenever \( a, b, \) and \( c \) are the lengths of sides of a triangle, then so are \( a^{2}+b c t, b^{2}+c a t, c^{2}+a b t \).
solution:
Let $a,b,c$ be the side lengths of a triangle. This means $a,b,c > 0$ and they satisfy the triangle inequalities $a+b>c$, $a+c>b$, and $b+c>a$.
Let $a' = a^2+bct$, $b' = b^2+cat$, and $c' = c^2+abt$. We want to find all real $t$ such that $a',b',c'$ are also side lengths of a triangle.
This requires $a',b',c' > 0$ and $a'+b'>c'$, $a'+c'>b'$, $b'+c'>a'$.

Step 1: Positivity of $a', b', c'$.
If $a=b=c=x$ for some $x>0$ (an equilateral triangle), then $a'=b'=c'=x^2+x^2t = x^2(1+t)$.
For $a'>0$, we must have $x^2(1+t)>0$, which implies $1+t>0$, so $t>-1$.

Suppose $t<0$. Let $t = -k$ for some $k>0$. Then $a' = a^2-kbc > 0$. This means $k < a^2/(bc)$.
This inequality must hold for any triangle. Consider the triangle with sides $(\epsilon, 1, 1)$ where $\epsilon>0$ is very small. (This forms a valid triangle as $1+1>\epsilon$ and $\epsilon+1>1$).
For this triangle, $a=\epsilon, b=1, c=1$. We need $k < \epsilon^2/(1 \cdot 1) = \epsilon^2$.
Since this must hold for any such $\epsilon$, $k$ must be smaller than any positive number. This implies $k \le 0$.
This contradicts $k>0$. So $t$ cannot be negative. Thus $t \ge 0$.

If $t=0$, then $a'=a^2, b'=b^2, c'=c^2$. Consider the right triangle $(a,b,c)=(3,4,5)$. Then $(a',b',c')=(9,16,25)$.
The triangle inequality $a'+b'>c'$ becomes $9+16>25$, which is $25>25$, false. (Sides must form a non-degenerate triangle).
Therefore, $t \ne 0$.
Combining these results, we must have $t>0$. If $t>0$, then $a,b,c>0$ implies $a^2, bct >0$, so $a^2+bct>0$ is always true. Same for $b'$ and $c'$. So condition $a',b',c'>0$ means $t>0$.

Step 2: Triangle inequalities for $a', b', c'$.
Let's analyze $a'+b'>c'$:
$(a^2+bct) + (b^2+cat) > c^2+abt$
$(a^2+b^2-c^2) + t(bc+ca-ab) > 0$.
Let $X_1 = a^2+b^2-c^2$ and $Y_1 = bc+ca-ab$. The condition is $X_1+tY_1>0$.
By symmetry, the other two inequalities are:
$X_2+tY_2 > 0$, where $X_2 = a^2+c^2-b^2$ and $Y_2 = bc+ab-ca$. (for $a'+c'>b'$)
$X_3+tY_3 > 0$, where $X_3 = b^2+c^2-a^2$ and $Y_3 = ca+ab-bc$. (for $b'+c'>a'$)

Step 3: Finding a lower bound for $t$.
Consider a "degenerate" triangle where $c \to a+b$. (e.g. $a, b, a+b-\epsilon$ for small $\epsilon>0$).
$X_1 = a^2+b^2-c^2 \to a^2+b^2-(a+b)^2 = a^2+b^2-(a^2+2ab+b^2) = -2ab$.
$Y_1 = bc+ca-ab \to b(a+b)+a(a+b)-ab = ab+b^2+a^2+ab-ab = a^2+ab+b^2$.
The inequality $X_1+tY_1>0$ becomes (in the limit) $-2ab + t(a^2+ab+b^2) \ge 0$.
Since $a,b>0$, $a^2+ab+b^2>0$. So $t \ge \frac{2ab}{a^2+ab+b^2}$.
Let $k=a/b$. Then $t \ge \frac{2(a/b)}{(a/b)^2+(a/b)+1} = \frac{2k}{k^2+k+1}$.
The function $f(k)=\frac{2k}{k^2+k+1}$ for $k>0$ has derivative $f'(k) = \frac{2(k^2+k+1)-2k(2k+1)}{(k^2+k+1)^2} = \frac{-2k^2+2}{(k^2+k+1)^2}$.
$f'(k)=0$ implies $-2k^2+2=0 \implies k=1$.
The maximum value is $f(1)=2/(1+1+1)=2/3$.
So we must have $t \ge 2/3$.
If $t=2/3$, the condition becomes $-2ab + (2/3)(a^2+ab+b^2) > 0$ for triangles $a,b,c$ where $c$ is very close to $a+b$.
This simplifies to $2a^2-4ab+2b^2 > 0$, or $2(a-b)^2 > 0$.
This inequality $2(a-b)^2>0$ holds if $a \ne b$. If $a=b$, it becomes $0>0$, which is false.
This suggests $t=2/3$ might be a solution, but we need to check carefully for $a=b$ and $c \approx 2a$.
Let $a=b=1$. Let $c=2-\epsilon$ for $\epsilon>0$ small.
$X_1 = 1^2+1^2-(2-\epsilon)^2 = 2-(4-4\epsilon+\epsilon^2) = -2+4\epsilon-\epsilon^2$.
$Y_1 = 1(2-\epsilon)+1(2-\epsilon)-1\cdot 1 = 4-2\epsilon-1 = 3-2\epsilon$.
The condition $X_1+tY_1 > 0$ becomes $(-2+4\epsilon-\epsilon^2) + t(3-2\epsilon) > 0$.
If $t=2/3$: $(-2+4\epsilon-\epsilon^2) + (2/3)(3-2\epsilon) > 0$
$-2+4\epsilon-\epsilon^2 + 2-(4/3)\epsilon > 0$
$(4-4/3)\epsilon-\epsilon^2 > 0 \implies (8/3)\epsilon-\epsilon^2 > 0 \implies \epsilon(8/3-\epsilon)>0$.
This is true for $0 < \epsilon < 8/3$. So $t=2/3$ works for these triangles.

Step 4: Finding an upper bound for $t$.
Consider a "degenerate" isosceles triangle $a=b=1, c=\epsilon$ for small $\epsilon>0$.
$X_1 = 1^2+1^2-\epsilon^2 = 2-\epsilon^2$.
$Y_1 = 1\cdot\epsilon + 1\cdot\epsilon - 1\cdot 1 = 2\epsilon-1$.
The inequality $X_1+tY_1>0$ becomes $(2-\epsilon^2) + t(2\epsilon-1) > 0$.
For $\epsilon$ small enough (e.g. $\epsilon < 1/2$), $Y_1 = 2\epsilon-1 < 0$.
So $t(2\epsilon-1) > -(2-\epsilon^2)$ implies $t < \frac{-(2-\epsilon^2)}{2\epsilon-1} = \frac{2-\epsilon^2}{1-2\epsilon}$.
We need $t$ to be less than all such values. We should find the minimum of $g(\epsilon)=\frac{2-\epsilon^2}{1-2\epsilon}$ for $\epsilon \in (0,1/2)$.
$g'(\epsilon) = \frac{-2\epsilon(1-2\epsilon) - (2-\epsilon^2)(-2)}{(1-2\epsilon)^2} = \frac{-2\epsilon+4\epsilon^2+4-2\epsilon^2}{(1-2\epsilon)^2} = \frac{2\epsilon^2-2\epsilon+4}{(1-2\epsilon)^2}$.
The quadratic $2\epsilon^2-2\epsilon+4$ has discriminant $(-2)^2-4(2)(4) = 4-32 = -28 < 0$. Since the leading coefficient is positive, the numerator is always positive.
So $g'(\epsilon)>0$ for $\epsilon \in (0,1/2)$. Thus $g(\epsilon)$ is increasing on this interval.
The minimum value is approached as $\epsilon \to 0^+$. $\lim_{\epsilon \to 0^+} g(\epsilon) = \frac{2-0}{1-0} = 2$.
So we must have $t \le 2$.
Let's check $t=2$. The condition is $(2-\epsilon^2) + 2(2\epsilon-1)>0$.
$2-\epsilon^2+4\epsilon-2 > 0 \implies 4\epsilon-\epsilon^2 > 0 \implies \epsilon(4-\epsilon)>0$.
This is true for $0 < \epsilon < 4$. So $t=2$ works for these triangles.
If $t > 2$, say $t=2+\eta$ for $\eta>0$. The condition is $(2-\epsilon^2) + (2+\eta)(2\epsilon-1) > 0$.
$2-\epsilon^2 + 4\epsilon-2+2\eta\epsilon-\eta > 0 \implies -\eta+(4+2\eta)\epsilon-\epsilon^2 > 0$.
For sufficiently small $\epsilon>0$, the term $-\eta$ dominates, and the inequality is false.
E.g., if $\epsilon < \eta/(4+2\eta)$, and $\eta$ is small, this implies the inequality is false. More precisely, for a fixed $\eta>0$, choose $\epsilon$ small enough such that $(4+2\eta)\epsilon-\epsilon^2 < \eta$. Then $-\eta+(4+2\eta)\epsilon-\epsilon^2 < 0$.
Thus, $t \le 2$ is necessary.

Step 5: Verifying for $t \in [2/3, 2]$.
Let $a=x+y, b=y+z, c=z+x$ for $x,y,z>0$ (Ravi substitution).
$a^2+b^2-c^2 = (x+y)^2+(y+z)^2-(z+x)^2 = 2y^2+2xy+2yz-2zx$.
$bc+ca-ab = (y+z)(z+x)+(z+x)(x+y)-(x+y)(y+z) = x^2-y^2+z^2+xy+3yz+xz$.
The inequality $X_1+tY_1>0$ becomes
$(2y^2+2xy+2yz-2zx) + t(x^2-y^2+z^2+xy+3yz+xz) > 0$.
Let $F_1(x,y,z; t)$ be the expression on the left side.
$F_1(x,y,z; t) = tx^2+(2-t)y^2+tz^2+(2+t)xy+(2+3t)yz+(t-2)xz$.
The other two inequalities are $F_2(x,y,z;t) = F_1(y,z,x;t)>0$ and $F_3(x,y,z;t)=F_1(z,x,y;t)>0$.
(These correspond to cyclic permutation $a \to b \to c \to a$, so $x \to y \to z \to x$).
Let's check $t=2/3$:
$F_1(x,y,z; 2/3) = (2/3)x^2+(4/3)y^2+(2/3)z^2+(8/3)xy+4yz-(4/3)xz$.
Multiplying by $3/2$: $x^2+2y^2+z^2+4xy+6yz-2xz$. There was a typo in thoughts with $4yz$ instead of $6yz$.
$2+3t = 2+3(2/3) = 2+2 = 4$. So $(2+3t)yz = 4yz$.
Correcting $F_1(x,y,z;t)$:
$X_1 = 2y^2+2xy+2yz-2zx$.
$Y_1 = (y+z)(z+x) + (z+x)(x+y) - (x+y)(y+z)$
$= (yz+xy+z^2+xz) + (zx+zy+x^2+xy) - (xy+xz+y^2+yz)$
$= z^2+x^2-y^2+xy+yz+3xz$. (Mistake in coefficient of $yz$ and $xz$ earlier too. $y(z+x- (y+z)) + c(a-b)+ab = y(x-y) + (z+x)(x+y-(y+z)) = xy-y^2+(z+x)(x-z)=xy-y^2+x^2-z^2 $... this is not working. Let's re-evaluate $Y_1$).
$Y_1 = bc+ca-ab = (y+z)(z+x) + (z+x)(x+y) - (x+y)(y+z)$.
Term $x^2$: From $(z+x)(x+y)$, so $x^2$.
Term $y^2$: From $-(x+y)(y+z)$, so $-y^2$.
Term $z^2$: From $(y+z)(z+x)$, so $z^2$.
Term $xy$: $x(z+x)$, $x(x+y)$, $-(x+y)y \rightarrow xz+x^2+x^2+xy-xy-y^2$. $(y+z)(z+x) \implies xy$. $(z+x)(x+y) \implies xy$. $-(x+y)(y+z) \implies -xy$. So $xy$.
Term $yz$: $(y+z)z$, $(z+x)y$, $-(x+y)z \implies yz+z^2+xy+yz - (xz+yz)$. $(y+z)(z+x) \implies yz$. $(z+x)(x+y) \implies yz$. $-(x+y)(y+z) \implies -yz$. So $yz$.
Term $xz$: $(y+z)x$, $z(x+y)$, $-x(y+z) \implies xz$. $z(z+x) \implies xz$. $(x+y)(z+x) \implies xz$. $-(x+y)(y+z) \implies -xz$. So $3xz$.
$Y_1 = x^2-y^2+z^2+xy+yz+3xz$. The previous calculation $(x^2-y^2+z^2+xy+3yz+xz)$ had $3yz$ not $yz$. Let me verify again.
$bc = (y+z)(z+x) = yz+yx+z^2+zx$
$ca = (z+x)(x+y) = zx+zy+x^2+xy$
$ab = (x+y)(y+z) = xy+xz+y^2+yz$
$Y_1 = (yz+xy+z^2+zx) + (zx+zy+x^2+xy) - (xy+xz+y^2+yz)$
$= yz+xy+z^2+zx + zx+zy+x^2+xy - xy-xz-y^2-yz$
$= x^2-y^2+z^2 + (xy+xy-xy) + (yz+zy-yz) + (zx+zx-xz)$
$= x^2-y^2+z^2+xy+yz+zx$.
So $F_1(x,y,z; t) = (2y^2+2xy+2yz-2zx) + t(x^2-y^2+z^2+xy+yz+zx)$
$= tx^2+(2-t)y^2+tz^2+(2+t)xy+(2+t)yz+(t-2)zx$.

For $t=2/3$:
$F_1(x,y,z; 2/3) = (2/3)x^2+(4/3)y^2+(2/3)z^2+(8/3)xy+(8/3)yz+(-4/3)zx$.
Multiplying by $3/2$: $x^2+2y^2+z^2+4xy+4yz-2zx$.
This can be written as $(x-z)^2+2y^2+4xy+4yz+2xz-2xz = (x-z)^2+2y(y+2x+2z)$.
Since $x,y,z>0$, $y>0$ and $(y+2x+2z)>0$. So $2y(y+2x+2z)>0$.
Also $(x-z)^2 \ge 0$. So $(x-z)^2+2y(y+2x+2z)>0$.
Thus $t=2/3$ works.

For $t=2$:
$F_1(x,y,z; 2) = 2x^2+(0)y^2+2z^2+4xy+4yz+(0)zx$.
$= 2x^2+2z^2+4xy+4yz = 2(x^2+z^2+2xy+2yz)$.
This is $2(x(x+2y)+z(z+2y))$. Since $x,y,z>0$, this expression is strictly positive.
Thus $t=2$ works.

Let $f(t) = X_1+tY_1$. We know $f(2/3)>0$ and $f(2)>0$.
Since $f(t)$ is linear in $t$, for any $t \in (2/3,2)$, we can write $t = \alpha(2/3) + (1-\alpha)(2)$ for some $\alpha \in (0,1)$.
Then $f(t) = \alpha f(2/3) + (1-\alpha)f(2)$. (This is incorrect, it should be $t = (1-\lambda)t_1 + \lambda t_2$. $f(t) = X_1 + ((1-\lambda)t_1+\lambda t_2)Y_1 = (1-\lambda)(X_1+t_1Y_1) + \lambda(X_1+t_2Y_1) - (1-\lambda)X_1 - \lambda X_1 + X_1 = (1-\lambda)f(t_1) + \lambda f(t_2)$.)
Yes, $f(t)$ is a convex combination of $f(t_1)$ and $f(t_2)$.
So $f(t) > 0$ for $t \in (2/3,2)$ provided $Y_1$ does not change sign in a problematic way. But $f(t)$ is just a line in $t$.
If $f(t_1)>0$ and $f(t_2)>0$, then $f(t)>0$ for all $t$ between $t_1$ and $t_2$, unless $Y_1=0$.
If $Y_1=0$, then $f(t)=X_1$. We need $X_1 > 0$.
$Y_1 = x^2-y^2+z^2+xy+yz+zx=0$.
$X_1 = 2y^2+2xy+2yz-2zx$.
If $Y_1=0$, then $x^2+z^2+xy+yz+zx=y^2$. This means $y^2$ must be large compared to $x,z$.
E.g., $x=1, z=1$. $1-y^2+1+y+y+1=0 \implies 3+2y-y^2=0 \implies y^2-2y-3=0 \implies (y-3)(y+1)=0$. So $y=3$.
$(x,y,z)=(1,3,1)$. $a=4, b=4, c=2$. This is an isosceles triangle.
$Y_1 = 1-9+1+3+3+1 = 0$.
$X_1 = 2(9)+2(3)+2(3)-2(1) = 18+6+6-2 = 28 > 0$.
This holds. In general, when $Y_1=0$, $X_1=2y^2+2xy+2yz-2zx = 2y^2+2y(x+z)-2zx$. If $Y_1=0$, then $y^2 = x^2+z^2+xy+yz+zx$. $X_1>0$ unless $z,x$ are large and $y$ small, but this seems to contradict $Y_1=0$.
The argument that $f(t) = (1-\lambda)f(t_1)+\lambda f(t_2)$ is correct. If $f(2/3)>0$ and $f(2)>0$, then $f(t)>0$ for all $t \in [2/3,2]$. This applies to $F_1, F_2, F_3$.

Thus, $t \in [2/3, 2]$ are the solutions.

Final check on the conditions and derivations:
1.  Positivity of $a',b',c'$ implies $t>0$. (Used $t \ge 0$ from $\epsilon,1,1$ and $t \ne 0$ from $3,4,5$).
2.  $a'+b'>c'$ (and its permutations).
    Limit $c \to a+b$ gives $t \ge 2/3$. (The equality $2(a-b)^2=0$ is avoided as $F_1(x,y,z;2/3)>0$ by Ravi substitution).
    Limit $c \to 0$ for $a=b=1$ gives $t \le 2$. (The equality $\epsilon(4-\epsilon)=0$ is avoided as $F_1(x,y,z;2)>0$).
3.  Ravi substitution transforms the inequalities for $a',b',c'$ into $F_1>0, F_2>0, F_3>0$.
    $F_1(x,y,z;t) = tx^2+(2-t)y^2+tz^2+(2+t)xy+(2+t)yz+(t-2)zx$.
    $F_1(x,y,z;2/3) = (2/3)x^2+(4/3)y^2+(2/3)z^2+(8/3)xy+(8/3)yz+(-4/3)zx = (2/3)((x-z)^2+2y(y+2x+2z)) > 0$.
    $F_1(x,y,z;2) = 2x^2+2z^2+4xy+4yz = 2(x(x+2y)+z(z+2y)) > 0$.
    The permutations $F_2, F_3$ are similarly positive at $t=2/3$ and $t=2$.
    For any fixed $(x,y,z)$, $F_1(x,y,z;t)$ is a linear function of $t$. If it is positive at $t=2/3$ and $t=2$, it must be positive for all $t \in [2/3,2]$. Same for $F_2, F_3$.

The range of $t$ is $[2/3, 2]$.

The final answer is $\boxed{[2/3, 2]}$.
ground_truth_solution:
Answer. We will show the answer is exactly

$$
2 / 3 \leq t \leq 2
$$

【 Proof. Apply the substitution $a=y+z, b=z+x, c=x+y$. We need the inequality

$$
\begin{gathered}
a^{2}+b c t<b^{2}+c a t+c^{2}+a b t \\
(y+z)^{2}+(x+y)(x+z) t<(x+y)^{2}+(x+z)^{2}+(y+z)(2 x+y+z) t \\
\Longleftrightarrow\left[x^{2}-\left(x y+x z+y z+y^{2}+z^{2}\right)\right] t<2 x^{2}+2 x y+2 x z-2 y z
\end{gathered}
$$

to be true for all $(x, y, z) \in \mathbb{R}_{>0}^{3}$ (checking only one inequality is enough by symmetry). Writing this is a quadratic in $x$, we want

$$
Q(x):=(2-t) x^{2}+(2+t)(y+z) x+\left(\left(y^{2}+y z+z^{2}\right) t-2 y z\right)>0 .
$$

Claim - Except when $t=2$, the quadratic $Q$ always has two real roots.

Proof. The discriminant is

$$
\begin{aligned}
D & =[(2+t)(y+z)]^{2}-4(2-t)\left(\left(y^{2}+y z+z^{2}\right) t-2 y z\right) \\
& =\left((2+t)^{2}-4(2-t) t\right)\left(y^{2}+z^{2}\right)+\left(2(2+t)^{2}-4(2-t)(t-2)\right) y z \\
& =\left(5 t^{2}-4 t+4\right)\left(y^{2}+z^{2}\right)+\left(6 t^{2}-8 t+24\right) y z>0
\end{aligned}
$$

which means $Q$ always has two real roots (aside for the single exceptional case $t=2$, in which $Q$ is not a quadratic).

Now, we make a few closing observations.

- It is clear we need $t \leq 2$, since a negative leading coefficient will cause the inequality to fail for $x \gg y, z$.
- The case $t=2$ obviously has $Q>0$ always.
- For $t<2$, as $Q$ always has two real roots, the assertion is true if and only if all coefficients of $Q$ are nonnegative.
- When $t \geq \frac{2}{3}$, we have $(2+t)(y+z)>0$ obviously, and from

$$
\frac{y^{2}+y z+z^{2}}{3} \geq y z
$$
the constant coefficient is nonnegative as well. Thus when $\frac{2}{3} \leq t \leq 2$ we indeed have $Q(x)>0$ for $x, y, z>0$.
- If $t<\frac{2}{3}$, then by letting $y=z$ fails the condition.
llm_summary: The proof first shows positivity of a′,b′,c′ forces t>0 by testing an equilateral triangle and a near-degenerate (ε,1,1) triangle, and excludes t=0 via the (3,4,5) example. It then derives the lower bound t≥2/3 by examining a′+b′>c′ as c→a+b and optimizing over a/b, and the upper bound t≤2 by doing the same for a=b=1,c→0. Finally, it applies the Ravi substitution a=x+y, b=y+z, c=z+x to rewrite the inequalities in the form F₁(x,y,z;t)>0 (and its cyclic permutations) and verifies F₁>0 at t=2/3 and t=2, arguing by linearity that positivity holds for all t∈[2/3,2].

llm_issues.description: The proof derives both lower and upper bounds on t by analyzing only the inequality a′+b′>c′ in specific degenerate triangles, but does not check the other two inequalities (a′+c′>b′, b′+c′>a′) in those limits. It appeals to symmetry without justification that those cases impose no further restrictions.

The derivation of the expressions for Y₁ and F₁(x,y,z;t) is presented in a disorganized way with aborted attempts and self-critical commentary, rather than a clear, step-by-step algebraic computation.

problem: Determine all positive integers \( n \geq 2 \) for which there exist integers \( x_{1}, x_{2}, \ldots, x_{n-1} \) satisfying the condition that if \( 0<i<n, 0<j<n, i \neq j \) and \( n \) divides \( 2i+j \), then \( x_{i}<x_{j} \).
solution:
Let \(S = \{1, 2, \ldots, n-1\}\). The condition is that if \(0 < i < n\), \(0 < j < n\), \(i \neq j\), and \(n \mid (2i+j)\), then \(x_i < x_j\). Let \(R\) be the set of such pairs \((i,j)\). Such integers \(x_1, \ldots, x_{n-1}\) exist if and only if the directed graph \(G_n = (S, R)\) is a directed acyclic graph (DAG). This means there is no cycle \(i_1 \to i_2 \to \ldots \to i_k \to i_1\) such that \((i_m, i_{m+1}) \in R\) for \(m=1,\ldots,k-1\) and \((i_k, i_1) \in R\). Such a cycle would imply \(x_{i_1} < x_{i_2} < \ldots < x_{i_k} < x_{i_1}\), which is impossible.

The condition \(n \mid (2i+j)\) implies \(2i+j = cn\) for some integer \(c\). Since \(i, j \in S\), \(0 < i,j < n\). Thus \(0 < 2i+j < 3n\). So \(c\) can be 1 or 2.
Let \(j_1 = n-2i\) and \(j_2 = 2n-2i\).
If \(0 < j_1 < n\) and \(j_1 \neq i\), then \((i, j_1) \in R\). This means \(x_i < x_{j_1}\). This occurs when \(i < n/2\). If \(j_1=0\), i.e. \(i=n/2\), this edge is not formed. If \(j_1=i\), then \(3i=n\); this edge is not formed because \(i \neq j\).
If \(0 < j_2 < n\) and \(j_2 \neq i\), then \((i, j_2) \in R\). This means \(x_i < x_{j_2}\). This occurs when \(i > n/2\). (More precisely, \(2n-2i < n \implies n < 2i \implies i > n/2\). And \(2n-2i > 0 \implies i < n\).) If \(j_2=i\), then \(3i=2n\); this edge is not formed.

Let's define a function \(f: S \to S \cup \{0, n/2\}\) (codomain will be refined).
If \(i=n/2\) (which implies \(n\) is even): \(2i+j = n+j\). So \(n \mid (n+j)\) implies \(n \mid j\). Since \(0 < j < n\), this is impossible. So, if \(i=n/2\), there is no \(j\) such that \((i,j) \in R\). So \(n/2\) is a sink node in \(G_n\).

If \(i \neq n/2\):
Define \(j \equiv -2i \pmod n\). We require \(j \in S\), so \(1 \le j \le n-1\).
If \(-2i \pmod n = 0\), then \(n \mid 2i\).
  If \(n\) is odd, then \(n \mid i\). This is not possible as \(i \in S\).
  If \(n\) is even, then \(n/2 \mid i\). So \(i=n/2\) (which we excluded) or \(i=n\) (not in \(S\)).
So for \(i \in S \setminus \{n/2\}\), \(-2i \pmod n\) is in \(S\). Let \(f(i) = (-2i) \pmod n\), with the result taken in \(\{1, \ldots, n-1\}\).
The actual relations are:
1. If \(0 < i < n/2\): \(2i < n\). Then \(2i+j=n \implies j=n-2i\). Since \(0 < 2i < n\), \(0 < n-2i < n\). So \(j=n-2i\). This is \(f(i)\).
2. If \(n/2 < i < n\): \(n < 2i < 2n\). Then \(2i+j=kn\). If \(k=1\), \(j=n-2i < 0\), impossible. So \(k=2\), \(j=2n-2i\). Since \(n < 2i < 2n\), \(0 < 2n-2i < n\). So \(j=2n-2i\). This is \(f(i)\).

So for \(i \in S \setminus \{n/2\}\), if \(f(i) \neq i\), there is an edge \((i, f(i)) \in R\).
A cycle \(i_1 \to i_2 \to \ldots \to i_k \to i_1\) means \(i_{m+1} = f(i_m)\) for all \(m\) (with \(i_{k+1}=i_1\)). Also \(i_m \neq i_{m+1}\) for all \(m\). If \(i_m = f(i_m)\) for some \(m\), then \(i_m = (-2i_m) \pmod n \implies 3i_m \equiv 0 \pmod n\). This means \(i_m=n/3\) or \(i_m=2n/3\) (if they are integers). These "self-loops" \((i_m,i_m)\) are not in \(R\) due to the \(i \neq j\) condition.
Thus, we are looking for \(n\) such that there is no cycle \(i_1 \to \dots \to i_k \to i_1\) where \(i_m \in S \setminus \{n/2\}\), \(i_m\) are distinct, and \(k \ge 2\), or \(k=1\) if \(i_1 \neq f(i_1)\) (impossible, \(k=1\) means \(i_1=f(i_1)\)).
The condition for a cycle becomes \(i_1 = f^{(k)}(i_1) = (-2)^k i_1 \pmod n\), so \( ((-2)^k-1)i_1 \equiv 0 \pmod n\). The elements \(i_m\) must be distinct and none can be \(n/2\).

Case 1: \(n\) is odd.
Then \(n/2\) is not an integer, so \(S \setminus \{n/2\} = S\). The map \(f(i) = (-2i) \pmod n\) is a permutation of \(S\), because \(\gcd(-2,n)=1\).
Thus, the graph defined by edges \((i, f(i))\) is a collection of disjoint cycles.
If \(n\) is not divisible by 3: Then \(3i \not\equiv 0 \pmod n\) for \(i \in S\). So \(f(i) \neq i\) for all \(i \in S\). This means all cycles have length \(k \ge 2\). Any such cycle is a forbidden cycle in \(G_n\). Thus, if \(n\) is odd and not divisible by 3, \(n\) is not a solution. E.g. \(n=5\) is not a solution.
If \(n\) is divisible by 3: Then \(f(i)=i\) for \(i=n/3\) and \(i=2n/3\). These are not edges in \(R\). For any other \(i \in S' = S \setminus \{n/3, 2n/3\}\), \(f(i) \neq i\). If \(S'\) is not empty, then \(f\) restricted to \(S'\) is a permutation of \(S'\). All elements in \(S'\) belong to cycles of length \(k \ge 2\). Any such cycle is forbidden. So \(n\) can be a solution only if \(S'\) is empty.
\(S'\) is empty if \(S=\{n/3, 2n/3\}\). Since \(S=\{1, \ldots, n-1\}\), this means \(n-1=2\), so \(n=3\).
The elements are \(1,2\). \(n/3=1, 2n/3=2\). So \(S=\{1,2\}\). \(S'\) is empty.
For \(n=3\), \(R\) is empty. Thus \(n=3\) is a solution.

Case 2: \(n\) is even. Let \(n=2^a m\), where \(m\) is odd and \(a \ge 1\).
As noted, \(n/2\) is a sink.
The map is \(f(i)=(-2i) \pmod n\) for \(i \in S_0 = S \setminus \{n/2\}\).
The values \(f(i)\) are in \(S\). If \(f(i)=n/2\), then the path \(i \to n/2\) terminates at \(n/2\). This happens if \((-2i) \pmod n = n/2\), which means \(2i \equiv -n/2 \pmod n \equiv n/2 \pmod n\). So \(n \mid (2i - n/2)\). Let \(2i-n/2 = cn\). \(2i = (c+1/2)n\). This requires \(n\) to be even, so \(c+1/2\) must make sense. \(4i = (2c+1)n\). So \(n\) must be a multiple of 4, and \(2c+1\) must be such that \(i<n\). So \(i=n/4\) (for \(2c+1=1\)) or \(i=3n/4\) (for \(2c+1=3\)).
So if \(a \ge 2\) (i.e. \(n\) is a multiple of 4), then \(n/4\) and \(3n/4\) map to \(n/2\). These paths are not cycles.
Fixed points \(n/3, 2n/3\) (if \(m\) is a multiple of 3) are not in \(R\).

Consider a cycle \(i_1 \to i_2 \to \ldots \to i_k \to i_1\) in \(G_n\). All \(i_j \in S_0\). None of \(i_j\) can map to \(n/2\), so \(i_j \notin \{n/4, 3n/4\}\) (if \(a \ge 2\)). Also \(i_j \neq n/3, 2n/3\).
Let \(i_j' = i_j \pmod m\). Then \(i_{j+1}' \equiv -2i_j' \pmod m\). This defines a cycle \(i_1' \to \ldots \to i_k' \to i_1'\) in \(\{0,1,\ldots,m-1\}\).
If \(m>3\): Then \(m\) is odd and not divisible by 3 (e.g. \(m=5,7,\dots\)), or \(m\) is odd and divisible by 3 but larger than 3 (e.g. \(m=9,15,\dots\)). In either case, similar to Case 1, there exists a cycle of elements \(p_1 \to \ldots \to p_k \to p_1\) in \(\{1,\ldots,m-1\}\) such that \(p_j \neq m/3, 2m/3\).
We can choose \(i_1 = p_1\). Then define \(i_j = f^{(j-1)}(i_1)\). Then \(i_j \pmod m = p_j\). So \(p_j \neq 0\).
This means \(i_j\) is not a multiple of \(m\). So \(i_j \neq n/2 = 2^{a-1}m\). Also \(i_j \neq n/4 = 2^{a-2}m\) and \(i_j \neq 3n/4 = 3 \cdot 2^{a-2}m\) (if \(a \ge 2\)).
Also \(i_j \pmod m = p_j\), and \(p_j \not\in \{0, m/3, 2n/3\}\). This means \(i_j\) is not one of the fixed points \(n/3\) or \(2n/3\). (If \(i_j=n/3\), then \(i_j \pmod m = (2^a m/3) \pmod m\). This is \(m/3\) if \(2^a \equiv 1 \pmod 3\) or \(2m/3\) if \(2^a \equiv 2 \pmod 3\). But \(p_j\) is not \(m/3\) or \(2m/3\).)
Thus, this cycle \(i_1 \to \ldots \to i_k \to i_1\) does not contain \(n/2\), does not terminate at \(n/2\), and does not involve fixed points. This is a forbidden cycle.
Therefore, for \(n\) to be a solution, we must have \(m=1\) or \(m=3\).

So \(n\) must be of the form \(2^a\) or \(3 \cdot 2^a\).
If \(n=2^a\) for \(a \ge 1\): For any \(i \in S_0 = S \setminus \{2^{a-1}\}\), let \(i = 2^s k\) where \(k\) is odd and \(s < a-1\).
Then \(f(i) = (-2i) \pmod{2^a} = (-2^{s+1}k) \pmod{2^a}\). The power of 2 dividing \(f(i)\) is \(s+1\).
Repeatedly applying \(f\), the power of 2 in the image increases by 1 at each step (unless it has reached \(2^{a-1}\)).
Eventually, any path reaches an element \(x = 2^{a-1}k'\) where \(k'\) is odd.
Then \(f(x) = (-2 \cdot 2^{a-1}k') \pmod{2^a} = (-2^a k') \pmod{2^a} = 0\).
However, \(f(i)\) is defined to be in \(\{1, \ldots, n-1\}\).
The definition of $f(i)$ is $n-2i$ or $2n-2i$. If $x=2^{a-1}k'$, then $2x = 2^a k'$.
If $x < n/2=2^{a-1}$, this is impossible. (It requires $k'<1$).
If $x > n/2=2^{a-1}$: $f(x)=2n-2x = 2 \cdot 2^a - 2^a k' = 2^a(2-k')$. Since \(k'\) is odd, \(2-k'\) is odd. For \(f(x)\) to be in \(S\), \(2-k'\) must be positive, so \(k'=1\). Then \(f(x)=2^a=n\), which is not in \(S\).
There is some confusion here with \(f(i)\) vs \((-2i)\pmod n\). If \((-2i) \pmod n = 0\), then \(i=n/2\). But \(n/2\) has no outgoing edge.
The argument is simpler: any \(i \in S_0\). Iteratively apply \(f\). Sequence \(i_0=i, i_1=f(i_0), \dots\).
\(v_2(i_{j+1}) = v_2(2i_j) = v_2(i_j)+1\), as long as \(v_2(i_j) < a-1\).
So eventually for some \(t\), \(v_2(i_t) \ge a-1\).
If \(v_2(i_t) = a-1\), then \(i_t = 2^{a-1}k\) for some odd \(k\). Since \(i_t < n=2^a\), \(k\) must be 1. So \(i_t=2^{a-1}=n/2\).
At this point, the path terminates at \(n/2\). So there are no cycles within \(S_0\).
Thus, all \(n=2^a\) for \(a \ge 1\) are solutions. (e.g. \(2, 4, 8, \ldots\)).

If \(n=3 \cdot 2^a\) for \(a \ge 0\):
\(n=3\) (for \(a=0\)) is a solution as shown in Case 1.
Let \(a \ge 1\). \(n\) is even. Fixed points are \(n/3=2^a\) and \(2n/3=2 \cdot 2^a\).
Paths can terminate at \(n/2=3 \cdot 2^{a-1}\) (from \(n/4=3 \cdot 2^{a-2}\) and \(3n/4=9 \cdot 2^{a-2}\), if \(a \ge 2\)).
Let \(i \in S_0\). If \(i\) is one of \(n/4, 3n/4, n/3, 2n/3\), it either terminates or is a fixed point (not in R).
Otherwise, consider \(i_0=i\). The sequence \(i_j = f^{(j)}(i_0)\).
Let \(i_j = 2^{s_j} k_j\) where \(k_j\) is odd. Then \(s_{j+1} = s_j+1\) as long as \(s_j < a-1\).
So eventually \(s_t \ge a-1\).
If \(s_t=a-1\): \(i_t=2^{a-1}k_t\).
  If \(k_t\) is a multiple of 3, \(k_t=3k'\). Then \(i_t = 2^{a-1}3k' = (n/2)k'\). Since \(i_t < n\), \(k'\) must be 1. So \(i_t=n/2\). Path terminates. (This includes \(n/4\) and \(3n/4\): for \(n/4 = 3 \cdot 2^{a-2}\), \(s=a-2\), after one step it becomes $2^{a-1} \cdot 3 = n/2$).
  If \(k_t\) is not a multiple of 3: \(i_t=2^{a-1}k_t\). Then \(f(i_t) = (-2 \cdot 2^{a-1}k_t) \pmod{3 \cdot 2^a} = (-2^a k_t) \pmod{3 \cdot 2^a}\).
  Since \(k_t\) is not a multiple of 3, \(-k_t \pmod 3\) is either 1 or 2.
  So \((-2^a k_t) \pmod{3 \cdot 2^a}\) will be \(2^a \cdot 1 = n/3\) or \(2^a \cdot 2 = 2n/3\).
  These are the fixed points of \(f\). So the path terminates at a fixed point.
Since all paths eventually lead to \(n/2\) or a fixed point \(\{n/3, 2n/3\}\), there are no cycles of length \(k \ge 2\).
Thus, all \(n=3 \cdot 2^a\) for \(a \ge 0\) are solutions. (e.g. \(3, 6, 12, \ldots\)).

Combining these, the integers \(n\) are those of the form \(2^a\) for \(a \ge 1\) or \(3 \cdot 2^a\) for \(a \ge 0\).

Final list of solutions:
From \(2^a, a \ge 1\): \(2, 4, 8, 16, \ldots\)
From \(3 \cdot 2^a, a \ge 0\): \(3 \cdot 2^0=3\), \(3 \cdot 2^1=6\), \(3 \cdot 2^2=12\), \(3 \cdot 2^3=24, \ldots\)

The set of all positive integers \(n \ge 2\) for which the condition holds is the set of integers of the form \(2^a\) for \(a \ge 1\) and integers of the form \(3 \cdot 2^a\) for \(a \ge 0\).

The final answer is $\boxed{n=2^a \text{ for } a\ge 1 \text{ or } n=3 \cdot 2^a \text{ for } a\ge 0}$.
ground_truth_solution:
The answer is $n=2^{k}$ and $n=3 \cdot 2^{k}$, for each $k \geq 0$ (excluding $n=1$ ).
We work with the set $S=\{1,2, \ldots, n-1\} \bmod n$ of nonzero residues modulo $n$ instead. We define the relation $\prec$ on $S$ to mean that $2 i+j \equiv 0(\bmod n)$ and $i \neq j$, for $i, j \in S$. Then the problem satisfies the conditions if and only if $\prec$ has no cycles, i.e. $\prec$ imposes a partial order on $S$.

The existence of a cycle for $\prec$ is equivalent to some choice of $t_{1} \in S$ and an integer $m \geq 2$ such that

$$
t_{1} \prec t_{2} \prec \cdots \prec t_{m} \prec t_{1}
$$

Unwinding the definition, this is equivalent to two conditions:

- We need $t_{i} \not \equiv t_{i+1}(\bmod n)$ for $i=1, \ldots, m\left(\right.$ where $\left.t_{m+1}=t_{1}\right)$. This is equivalent to

$$
3 \cdot 2^{i-1} \cdot t_{1} \equiv 0 \quad(\bmod n) \quad(ऽ)
$$
- For $t_{m} \prec t_{1}$ to be true, we need
$$
(-2)^{m} t_{1} \equiv t_{1} \quad(\bmod n) \Longleftrightarrow\left((-2)^{m}-1\right) t_{1} \equiv 0 \quad(\bmod n) .
$$

We now analyze three cases:

- Let $n=2^{k}$. Suppose for contradiction some cycle exists. Then $(-2)^{m}-1$ is coprime to $n$, so $(\boldsymbol{\phi})$ would imply $t_{1} \equiv 0(\bmod n)$, contradiction.
- Let $n=3 \cdot 2^{k}$. Suppose for contradiction some cycle exists. If ( $\boldsymbol{\sim}$ ) holds for some $m$, then $2^{k} \mid t_{1}$, so the only possibility is that $t_{1} \equiv \pm 2^{k}(\bmod n)$ and $3 \mid(-2)^{m}-1$. However, in that case ( $\Omega$ ) is violated for $i=1$, contradiction.
- Suppose $n$ had an $n$ has an odd divisor $d \mid n$ and $d \geq 5$. Then taking $t_{1}=n / d$ and $m=\varphi(d)$, the equation $(\boldsymbol{Q})$ is true. Moreover, $(\Omega)$ is true because there is at least one odd prime $p$ with $\nu_{p}(n)>\nu_{p}\left(3 t_{1}\right)=\nu_{p}(3 n / d)$ (since $d \geq 5$ is odd). So indeed it's possible to construct a cycle.

Thus these are all the answers and the only answers.
llm_summary: The proof reformulates the condition as acyclicity of the directed graph Gₙ with vertices {1,…,n−1} and edges i→j whenever n divides 2i+j. It shows this graph is a functional graph given by the map f(i)=−2i mod n (with special sink at i=n/2 and excluded self‐loops at i=n/3,2n/3), then analyzes cycles of f via the congruence (−2)^k i≡i mod n, splitting into odd n (yielding only n=3) and even n (yielding n=2^a or 3·2^a), and finally argues that for these n every path terminates at a sink or fixed point, so no directed cycle exists.
