llm_issues.text: On the other hand the clockwise angle from \(P_B\) to \(P_C\) is less than \(\pi\), so the clockwise angle from \(P_C\) to \(P_B\) exceeds \(\pi\); hence \(P_B\) and \(P_C\) cannot both have the remaining two vertices inside their right half-planes.

llm_issues.description: The proof invokes a separation argument without justification, assuming the existence of a line through the origin that places all three vertices strictly on one side.
llm_issues.text: Because \(O\) is outside \(\Delta\), the three vertices lie in some open half-plane \(H\) bounded by a line through \(O\); denote its boundary by \(\ell\).

llm_issues.description: The notion of the “right” side of a line through the origin is not formally defined, making the construction of each half-plane \(H(P_i)\) ambiguous.
llm_issues.text: rotate a line \(\ell\) through \(O\) clockwise until exactly \(m\) other points lie strictly to the right of \(\ell\). Denote by \(H(P_i)\) the open half-plane situated to the right of that position of \(\ell\).

llm_issues.description: The lemma covers triangles with the origin on an edge (interior not containing \(O\)) but its proof assumes \(O\) is strictly outside, failing to handle the boundary case when \(O\) lies exactly on one side of the triangle.
llm_issues.text: Let \(\Delta = ABC\) be a triangle whose interior does not contain \(O\).

problem:
Does there exist a nonnegative integer \(a\) for which the equation

\[
\left\lfloor\frac{m}{1}\right\rfloor+\left\lfloor\frac{m}{2}\right\rfloor+\left\lfloor\frac{m}{3}\right\rfloor+\cdots+\left\lfloor\frac{m}{m}\right\rfloor=n^{2}+a
\]

has more than one million different solutions \((m, n)\) where \(m\) and \(n\) are positive integers?
solution:
Yes, such a non-negative integer \(a\) exists.  
(In fact one can show that some \(a\le 1.3\cdot 10^{9}\) already works.)

--------------------------------------------------------------------
Notation
--------------------------------------------------------------------
For every positive integer \(m\) write  

\[
S(m)=\sum_{k=1}^{m}\Bigl\lfloor\frac{m}{k}\Bigr\rfloor .
\]

With this notation the equation in the statement becomes  

\[
S(m)=n^{2}+a .
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
1.  Two elementary estimates
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Lemma 1.  \(m\;\le\;S(m)\;\le\;m(1+\ln m)\) for every \(m\ge 1\).

Proof.  The left inequality is obvious because the first summand of
\(S(m)\) equals \(m\).
For the right inequality use \(\lfloor m/k\rfloor\le m/k\) :

\[
S(m)\le m\sum_{k=1}^{m}\frac1k
        = m\,H_{m}\le m\bigl(1+\ln m\bigr),
\]
where \(H_{m}\) is the \(m\)-th harmonic number and the last
inequality is standard. ∎



Lemma 2.  For every real \(x\ge 0\) and \(t=\lfloor\sqrt{x}\rfloor\)

\[
0\;\le\;x-t^{2}\;\le\;2\sqrt{x}.
\]

Proof.  From \(t^{2}\le x<(t+1)^{2}=t^{2}+2t+1\) we obtain  
\(0\le x-t^{2}<2t+1\le 2(t+1)\le 2\sqrt{x}+2\).  Because both sides are
integers, the strict inequality may be replaced by \(\le\),
and removing the harmless “\( +2\)” gives the stated bound. ∎



--------------------------------------------------------------------
2.  Bounding the possible remainders \(S(m)-\lfloor\sqrt{S(m)}\rfloor^{2}\)
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Fix a very large integer \(N\) (to be specified later) and
set  

\[
B:=\Bigl\lfloor 2\sqrt{\,N\bigl(1+\ln N\bigr)}\Bigr\rfloor .
\]

For every \(m\le N\) put  

\[
r(m):=S(m)-\Bigl\lfloor\sqrt{S(m)}\Bigr\rfloor^{2}.
\]

By Lemma 1, \(S(m)\le N(1+\ln N)\); applying Lemma 2 gives  

\[
0\le r(m)\le 2\sqrt{S(m)}
           \le 2\sqrt{N\bigl(1+\ln N\bigr)}\le B.
\]

Hence each \(r(m)\) lies in the finite set
\(\{0,1,\dots ,B\}\), which contains exactly \(B+1\) elements.



--------------------------------------------------------------------
3.  A pigeonhole count
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Among the first \(N\) positive integers there are \(N\) values
\(r(1),r(2),\dots ,r(N)\) and only \(B+1\) possible
values they can assume.
Therefore, by the pigeonhole principle, some value
\(a\in\{0,1,\dots ,B\}\) occurs at least  

\[
\Bigl\lceil\frac{N}{B+1}\Bigr\rceil
\quad\text{times.}
\]

Call an index \(m\le N\) “good’’ if \(r(m)=a\).
For every good \(m\) put  

\[
n=\Bigl\lfloor\sqrt{S(m)}\Bigr\rfloor .
\]

By definition of \(r(m)\) we have
\(S(m)=n^{2}+a\); consequently every good \(m\) produces a
solution \((m,n)\) of the required equation.



--------------------------------------------------------------------
4.  Choosing \(N\) so that there are more than one million good indices
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Because \(B+1\le 2\sqrt{N(1+\ln N)}+1\le 3\sqrt{N(1+\ln N)}\) for large
\(N\),

\[
\frac{N}{B+1}\ge
\frac{N}{3\sqrt{N(1+\ln N)}}=
\frac{\sqrt{N}}{3\sqrt{1+\ln N}}.
\]

We want the right-hand side to exceed \(10^{6}\):

\[
\frac{\sqrt{N}}{3\sqrt{1+\ln N}}>10^{6}
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
N>9\cdot 10^{12}(1+\ln N).
\]

Taking \(N=10^{16}\) fulfils this inequality, because  
\(1+\ln 10^{16}\approx 37\) and
\(9\cdot10^{12}\cdot 37\approx 3.3\cdot 10^{14}\ll 10^{16}\).

With this choice

\[
\frac{N}{B+1}\;>\;
\frac{10^{16}}{2\sqrt{10^{16}\cdot 37}+1}
\;=\;
\frac{10^{16}}{2\cdot 6.1\cdot10^{8}+1}
\;>\;8\times 10^{6}.
\]

Hence at least \(8\,000\,000>1\,000\,000\) indices \(m\le 10^{16}\)
are good.



--------------------------------------------------------------------
5.  Finishing the proof
--------------------------------------------------------------------
For the value of \(a\) singled out in Section 3 we have produced more
than one million distinct positive integers \(m\) (the good indices)
and, for each of them, a positive integer \(n\) such that
\(S(m)=n^{2}+a\).
Therefore the given equation possesses more than a million different
solutions \((m,n)\).

Finally, note that by construction  

\[
0\le a\le B\le 2\sqrt{10^{16}(1+\ln 10^{16})}<1.3\cdot 10^{9},
\]

so \(a\) is indeed a non-negative integer.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
Conclusion
--------------------------------------------------------------------
There does exist a non-negative integer \(a\) (for instance some
\(a\le 1.3\cdot 10^{9}\)) for which the equation  

\[
\sum_{k=1}^{m}\Bigl\lfloor\frac{m}{k}\Bigr\rfloor
      \;=\;n^{2}+a
\]

has more than one million distinct positive-integer solutions
\((m,n)\).
ground_truth_solution:
## Problem statement

Does there exist a nonnegative integer $a$ for which the equation

$$
\left\lfloor\frac{m}{1}\right\rfloor+\left\lfloor\frac{m}{2}\right\rfloor+\left\lfloor\frac{m}{3}\right\rfloor+\cdots+\left\lfloor\frac{m}{m}\right\rfloor=n^{2}+a
$$
has more than one million different solutions $(m, n)$ where $m$ and $n$ are positive integers?

The answer is yes. In fact, we prove the following general version:

Claim — Consider any function $f: \mathbb{N} \rightarrow \mathbb{N}$ satisfying $f(m)=o\left(m^{2}\right)$. Then for some $a$, the equation

$$
f(m)=n^{2}+a
$$
has at least $1000000$ solutions $(m, n)$.

Proof. We consider triples $(m, n, a)$ satisfying the equation with the additional property that

$$
n=\lfloor\sqrt{f(m)}\rfloor^{2} \Longrightarrow a=f(m)-n^{2} \in[0,2 \sqrt{f(m)}]
$$

Now, let $M$ be large enough that $\max _{m=1}^{M} f(m)<\frac{M^{2}}{2 \cdot 10^{12}}$. Then there are $M$ triples, but $a<\frac{M}{10^{6}}$ in each triple. So some $a$ appears $10^{6}$ times.
llm_summary: The proof defines \(S(m)=\sum_{k=1}^{m}\lfloor m/k\rfloor\) and studies the remainders \(r(m)=S(m)-\lfloor\sqrt{S(m)}\rfloor^2\), showing by two lemmas that \(0\le r(m)\le B\). By the pigeonhole principle on the first \(N\) values and choosing \(N=10^{16}\) so that \(N/(B+1)>10^6\), one finds a remainder \(a\) occurring over a million times, each yielding a solution \((m,n)\) with \(n=\lfloor\sqrt{S(m)}\rfloor\). Finally, it verifies that \(a\le1.3\times10^9\).

llm_issues.description: Lemma 2 is stated for all real \(x\) but its proof relies on the integrality of \(x\) to convert a strict inequality into a non-strict one and to drop the “+2”. The generalization to real \(x\) and the removal of +2 are oversimplified.
llm_issues.text: For every real \(x\ge 0\) and \(t=\lfloor\sqrt{x}\rfloor\) … removing the harmless "+2" gives the stated bound.

llm_issues.description: The inequality \(2\sqrt{N(1+\ln N)}+1\le3\sqrt{N(1+\ln N)}\) is asserted for “large \(N\)” without specifying or verifying the threshold where it holds, making the argument slightly non-rigorous.
llm_issues.text: Because \(B+1\le 2\sqrt{N(1+\ln N)}+1\le 3\sqrt{N(1+\ln N)}\) for large \(N\),

problem:
Let \( f \) be continuous and nowhere monotone on \([0,1]\). Show that the set of points on which \( f \) attains local minima is dense in \([0,1]\).

(A function is nowhere monotone if there exists no interval where the function is monotone. A set is dense if each non-empty open interval contains at least one element of the set.)
solution:
Let  

\[
L=\Bigl\{x\in[0,1]\; ;\; \exists \,\varepsilon>0\;\text{with}\;
          f(x)\le f(t)\;\text{for every }t\in[0,1]\cap(x-\varepsilon ,x+\varepsilon )
     \Bigr\}
\]

be the set of points where \(f\) attains a (strict or flat) local minimum.
We have to prove that \(L\) is dense in \([0,1]\); i.e. that every non-empty
open sub-interval of \([0,1]\) contains at least one point of \(L\).

Throughout the proof \(f:[0,1]\longrightarrow\mathbb R\) is assumed
continuous and \emph{nowhere monotone}:  
for no sub-interval \(J\subset[0,1]\) is \(f\) monotone on \(J\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
Lemma 1 (A continuous function without local extrema is monotone).
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Let \(I=(\alpha ,\beta)\subset\mathbb R\) be open and let
\(g:I\to\mathbb R\) be continuous.
If \(g\) has neither a local maximum nor a local minimum in \(I\),
then \(g\) is monotone on \(I\).

Proof.
Assume, for a contradiction, that \(g\) is \emph{not} monotone.
Then there exist \(x<y<z\) in \(I\) such that one of the two
inequalities  

\[
g(x)<g(y)>g(z)\qquad\text{or}\qquad g(x)>g(y)<g(z)
\]

holds.  Consider the first possibility; the second is treated in the
same way after changing the sign of \(g\).

Because \(g\) is continuous on the compact interval \([x,z]\), it
attains a maximum at some point \(c\in[x,z]\).
Since \(g(x)<g(y)\) and \(g(z)<g(y)\), that maximum
satisfies \(g(c)\ge g(y)>\max\{g(x),g(z)\}\); hence \(c\) cannot be one
of the endpoints \(x\) or \(z\).  Consequently \(c\in(x,z)\subset I\)
and \(c\) is a \emph{local maximum} of \(g\), contradicting the
hypothesis.  Therefore the assumed non-monotonicity is impossible and
\(g\) must be monotone on \(I\).
\(\square\)

--------------------------------------------------------------------
Lemma 2 (Two maxima force a minimum).
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Let \(g\) be continuous on an interval and suppose \(p<q\) are both
local maxima of \(g\).  Then there exists
\(r\in(p,q)\) which is a local minimum of \(g\).

Proof.
On the compact set \([p,q]\) the continuous function \(g\) attains a
minimum at some \(r\in[p,q]\).
Because \(g(p)\) and \(g(q)\) are local (hence strictly) bigger than all
sufficiently near points,  
\[
g(r)<\max\{g(p),g(q)\}=g(p)=g(q),
\]
so \(r\neq p,q\) and \(r\in(p,q)\).
Being the absolute minimum on \([p,q]\), \(r\) is also a local minimum.
\(\square\)

--------------------------------------------------------------------
Main proof (density of local minima).
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Take an arbitrary non-empty open sub-interval  
\[
I=(a,b)\subset(0,1).
\]
We shall show that \(L\cap I\neq\varnothing\).

Assume the contrary, namely that \(I\) contains \emph{no} local
minimum of \(f\).

Step 1.  If \(I\) also contained no local \emph{maximum}, then by Lemma
1 the restriction \(f|_{I}\) would be monotone, contradicting the
hypothesis that \(f\) is nowhere monotone.  Hence \(I\) must contain at
least one local maximum.

Step 2.  Because \(I\) carries no local minima, Lemma 2 shows that it
can carry \emph{at most one} local maximum—otherwise two maxima would
force a minimum between them.  Denote this unique local maximum by
\(m\in I\).

Step 3.  At least one of the intervals \((a,m)\) or \((m,b)\) is
non-empty; assume, for definiteness, that \(J=(a,m)\neq\varnothing\).
By construction \(J\subset I\).

•  \(J\) contains no local minimum (that was our standing assumption
about \(I\)).  
•  \(J\) contains no local maximum either, because \(m\) is the only
local maximum in \(I\) and \(m\notin J\).

Consequently \(f\) has \emph{no} local extrema on \(J\).
Applying Lemma 1 to the continuous function \(f|_{J}\) we conclude that
\(f\) is monotone on \(J\).

But \(J\) is a non-degenerate sub-interval of \([0,1]\), contradicting
the fact that \(f\) is nowhere monotone.

The contradiction shows that our assumption was false: the open
interval \(I\) must indeed contain a point of \(L\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
Conclusion.
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Every open sub-interval of \([0,1]\) contains a point where \(f\)
achieves a local minimum; equivalently, the set \(L\) of local minima is
dense in \([0,1]\).
\(\blacksquare\)
source: International Mathematics Competition for University Students
ground_truth_solution:
Solution. Let $(x-\alpha, x+\alpha) \subset[0,1]$ be an arbitrary non-empty open interval. The function $f$ is not monoton in the intervals $[x-\alpha, x]$ and $[x, x+\alpha]$, thus there exist some real numbers $x-\alpha \leq p<q \leq x, x \leq r<s \leq x+\alpha$ so that $f(p)>f(q)$ and $f(r)<f(s)$.

By Weierstrass' theorem, $f$ has a global minimum in the interval $[p, s]$. The values $f(p)$ and $f(s)$ are not the minimum, because they are greater than $f(q)$ and $f(s)$, respectively. Thus the minimum is in the interior of the interval, it is a local minimum. So each nonempty interval $(x-\alpha, x+\alpha) \subset[0,1]$ contains at least one local minimum.
llm_summary: The proof defines L as the set of local minima of f and proceeds by contradiction: given any open interval I⊂(0,1) with no local minimum, it first shows I must contain at least one local maximum (else f|I would be monotone by Lemma 1), then argues there can be at most one maximum in I (else Lemma 2 would produce a minimum), and finally restricts to a subinterval J without any extrema to conclude f is monotone on J by Lemma 1, contradicting the nowhere-monotone hypothesis. Hence every open subinterval contains a local minimum and L is dense.

problem:
(a) Show that for each function \( f: \mathbb{Q} \times \mathbb{Q} \rightarrow \mathbb{R} \), there exists a function \( g: \mathbb{Q} \rightarrow \mathbb{R} \) such that \( f(x, y) \leq g(x) + g(y) \) for all \( x, y \in \mathbb{Q} \).

(b) Find a function \( f: \mathbb{R} \times \mathbb{R} \rightarrow \mathbb{R} \) for which there is no function \( g: \mathbb{R} \rightarrow \mathbb{R} \) such that \( f(x, y) \leq g(x) + g(y) \) for all \( x, y \in \mathbb{R} \).
solution:
Part (a): Show that for each function \( f: \mathbb{Q} \times \mathbb{Q} \rightarrow \mathbb{R} \), there exists a function \( g: \mathbb{Q} \rightarrow \mathbb{R} \) such that \( f(x, y) \leq g(x) + g(y) \) for all \( x, y \in \mathbb{Q} \).

Proof:
Let \(\mathbb{Q}\) be the set of rational numbers. We know that \(\mathbb{Q}\) is countable. Let \(\{q_n\}_{n=0}^{\infty}\) be an enumeration of \(\mathbb{Q}\).
We want to construct a function \(g: \mathbb{Q} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}\) such that for all \(x, y \in \mathbb{Q}\), \(f(x, y) \leq g(x) + g(y)\).

We define the values \(g(q_n)\) by induction on \(n\).

Base case: For \(n=0\), we define \(g(q_0)\). The condition \(f(q_0, q_0) \leq g(q_0) + g(q_0)\) must hold.
Let us define \(g(q_0) = \frac{f(q_0, q_0)}{2}\).
Then \(f(q_0, q_0) \leq 2g(q_0)\) becomes \(f(q_0, q_0) \leq 2 \frac{f(q_0, q_0)}{2}\), which is \(f(q_0, q_0) \leq f(q_0, q_0)\). This is true.

Inductive step: Assume that \(g(q_0), g(q_1), \ldots, g(q_{n-1})\) have been defined for \(n \geq 1\). We now define \(g(q_n)\).
The value \(g(q_n)\) must satisfy the following inequalities for all \(k < n\):
1. \(f(q_k, q_n) \leq g(q_k) + g(q_n) \implies g(q_n) \geq f(q_k, q_n) - g(q_k)\)
2. \(f(q_n, q_k) \leq g(q_n) + g(q_k) \implies g(q_n) \geq f(q_n, q_k) - g(q_k)\)
Also, \(g(q_n)\) must satisfy the inequality for \(x=y=q_n\):
3. \(f(q_n, q_n) \leq g(q_n) + g(q_n) \implies g(q_n) \geq \frac{f(q_n, q_n)}{2}\)

To ensure these conditions are met, we define \(g(q_n)\) as follows.
Let \(S_n\) be the set of lower bounds for \(g(q_n)\) imposed by already defined values:
\[ S_n = \left\{ \frac{f(q_n, q_n)}{2} \right\} \cup \bigcup_{k=0}^{n-1} \{ f(q_k, q_n) - g(q_k), f(q_n, q_k) - g(q_k) \} \]
Since \(n\) is finite, the set \(\{q_0, \ldots, q_{n-1}\}\) is finite. Thus \(S_n\) is a finite, non-empty set of real numbers.
Define \(g(q_n) = \max S_n\). Since \(S_n\) is a finite non-empty set, its maximum exists and is a real number.
This completes the inductive definition of \(g(q_n)\) for all \(n \in \mathbb{N}\). Thus \(g(x)\) is defined for all \(x \in \mathbb{Q}\).

Now we verify that \(f(x,y) \leq g(x)+g(y)\) for all \(x,y \in \mathbb{Q}\).
Let \(x=q_k\) and \(y=q_m\) for some integers \(k, m \geq 0\).

Case 1: \(k=m\). So \(x=y=q_k\).
By construction:
If \(k=0\), \(g(q_0) = f(q_0, q_0)/2\). So \(2g(q_0) = f(q_0, q_0)\), which means \(f(q_0, q_0) \leq g(q_0)+g(q_0)\).
If \(k>0\), \(g(q_k) = \max S_k\). One element of \(S_k\) is \(f(q_k, q_k)/2\).
So \(g(q_k) \geq f(q_k, q_k)/2\), which implies \(2g(q_k) \geq f(q_k, q_k)\).
Thus, \(f(q_k, q_k) \leq g(q_k)+g(q_k)\) holds for all \(k\).

Case 2: \(k \neq m\).
Assume without loss of generality that \(m > k\).
When \(g(q_m)\) was defined, we had \(g(q_m) = \max S_m\).
The set \(S_m\) contains the value \(f(q_k, q_m) - g(q_k)\) because \(k < m\).
So, by definition of maximum, \(g(q_m) \geq f(q_k, q_m) - g(q_k)\).
Rearranging this inequality gives \(g(q_m) + g(q_k) \geq f(q_k, q_m)\).
This is exactly \(f(q_k, q_m) \leq g(q_k)+g(q_m)\).
If we assumed \(k > m\), then \(g(q_k)\) would be defined based on \(g(q_m)\).
The set \(S_k\) contains \(f(q_k, q_m) - g(q_m)\) because \(m < k\).
So \(g(q_k) \geq f(q_k, q_m) - g(q_m)\), which rearranges to \(g(q_k)+g(q_m) \geq f(q_k, q_m)\).

Thus, for all pairs \((q_k, q_m)\), the condition \(f(q_k, q_m) \leq g(q_k)+g(q_m)\) is satisfied.
The function \(g: \mathbb{Q} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}\) has been constructed as required.

Part (b): Find a function \( f: \mathbb{R} \times \mathbb{R} \rightarrow \mathbb{R} \) for which there is no function \( g: \mathbb{R} \rightarrow \mathbb{R} \) such that \( f(x, y) \leq g(x) + g(y) \) for all \( x, y \in \mathbb{R} \).

Proof:
Let's define the function \(f: \mathbb{R} \times \mathbb{R} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}\) as follows:
\[ f(x,y) = \begin{cases} \frac{1}{|x-y|} & \text{if } x \neq y \\ 0 & \text{if } x=y \end{cases} \]
Assume, for the sake of contradiction, that there exists a function \(g: \mathbb{R} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}\) such that \(f(x,y) \leq g(x)+g(y)\) for all \(x,y \in \mathbb{R}\).

For \(x=y\), the condition is \(f(x,x) \leq g(x)+g(x)\), which means \(0 \leq 2g(x)\), so \(g(x) \geq 0\) for all \(x \in \mathbb{R}\).

For \(x \neq y\), the condition is \(\frac{1}{|x-y|} \leq g(x)+g(y)\).
Since \(|x-y| > 0\), we have \(\frac{1}{|x-y|} > 0\). This implies \(g(x)+g(y) > 0\).

Consider the interval \([0,1]\). This interval is uncountable.
For each \(N \in \mathbb{N}\), define the set \(A_N = \{x \in [0,1] : g(x) \leq N\}\).
Since \(g(x)\) is a finite real number for each \(x \in [0,1]\), for each \(x\) there is some \(N\) such that \(g(x) \leq N\). (Specifically, we can choose \(N = \lceil g(x) \rceil\) if \(g(x) \geq 0\). If \(g(x)\) were allowed to be negative, we would pick \(N = \lceil |g(x)| \rceil\), but we've shown \(g(x) \geq 0\)).
Thus, \([0,1] = \bigcup_{N=1}^{\infty} A_N\).

Let \(x, y\) be two distinct points in \(A_N\). So \(x \in [0,1]\), \(y \in [0,1]\), \(x \neq y\).
Since \(x, y \in A_N\), we have \(g(x) \leq N\) and \(g(y) \leq N\).
From the condition \(f(x,y) \leq g(x)+g(y)\), we have:
\[ \frac{1}{|x-y|} \leq g(x)+g(y) \leq N+N = 2N \]
This implies \(|x-y| \geq \frac{1}{2N}\).
This means that any two distinct points in \(A_N\) must be separated by a distance of at least \(\frac{1}{2N}\).

Now we show that \(A_N\) must be a finite set.
Let \(A_N = \{p_1, p_2, \ldots, p_k\}\) where the points are ordered \(0 \leq p_1 < p_2 < \ldots < p_k \leq 1\).
If \(k \geq 2\), then \(p_{j+1} - p_j \geq \frac{1}{2N}\) for \(j=1, \ldots, k-1\).
Then \(1 \geq p_k - p_1 = (p_k - p_{k-1}) + (p_{k-1} - p_{k-2}) + \ldots + (p_2 - p_1)\).
There are \(k-1\) terms in this sum. So \(1 \geq \sum_{j=1}^{k-1} (p_{j+1}-p_j) \geq (k-1) \frac{1}{2N}\).
Thus, \(1 \geq \frac{k-1}{2N}\), which implies \(2N \geq k-1\), or \(k \leq 2N+1\).
If \(k=1\) or \(k=0\), \(A_N\) is finite. In all cases, \(A_N\) contains at most \(2N+1\) points. Hence, \(A_N\) is a finite set for each \(N \in \mathbb{N}\).

We have \([0,1] = \bigcup_{N=1}^{\infty} A_N\). This means that \([0,1]\) is a countable union of finite sets.
A countable union of finite sets is a countable set.
This would imply that \([0,1]\) is countable.
However, it is a well-known result (e.g., by Cantor's diagonal argument) that the interval \([0,1]\) is uncountable.
This is a contradiction.

Therefore, our initial assumption must be false: there is no function \(g: \mathbb{R} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}\) satisfying \(f(x,y) \leq g(x)+g(y)\) for the chosen function \(f\).

Summary of argument for part (b):
1. Define \(f(x,y) = 1/|x-y|\) for \(x \neq y\) and \(f(x,x)=0\).
2. Assume such a \(g\) exists. Then \(g(x) \geq 0\) for all \(x\).
3. For distinct \(x,y\), \(1/|x-y| \leq g(x)+g(y)\).
4. Define \(A_N = \{x \in [0,1] : g(x) \leq N\}\). Then \([0,1] = \bigcup_{N=1}^\infty A_N\).
5. Show that each \(A_N\) is finite (specifically, \(|A_N| \leq 2N+1\)).
6. This implies \([0,1]\) is a countable union of finite sets, so \([0,1]\) is countable.
7. This contradicts the known uncountability of \([0,1]\).
8. Conclude that no such \(g\) exists.

The final answer is $\boxed{f(x,y) = \frac{1}{|x-y|} \text{ for } x \neq y \text{ and } f(x,x)=0}$.
source: International Mathematics Competition for University Students
ground_truth_solution:
Solution. a) Let $\varphi: \mathbb{Q} \rightarrow \mathbb{N}$ be a bijection. Define $g(x)=\max \{|f(s, t)|: s, t \in \mathbb{Q}, \varphi(s) \leq$ $\varphi(x), \varphi(t) \leq \varphi(x)\}$. We have $f(x, y) \leq \max \{g(x), g(y)\} \leq g(x)+g(y)$.
b) We shall show that the function defined by $f(x, y)=\frac{1}{|x-y|}$ for $x \neq y$ and $f(x, x)=0$ satisfies the problem. If, by contradiction there exists a function $g$ as above, it results, that $g(y) \geq \frac{1}{|x-y|}-f(x)$ for $x, y \in \mathbb{R}, x \neq y$; one obtains that for each $x \in \mathbb{R}, \lim _{y \rightarrow x} g(y)=\infty$. We show, that there exists no function $g$ having an infinite limit at each point of a bounded and closed interval $[a, b]$.

For each $k \in \mathbb{N}^{+}$denote $A_{k}=\{x \in[a, b]:|g(x)| \leq k\}$.
We have obviously $[a, b]=\cup_{k=1}^{\infty} A_{k}$. The set $[a, b]$ is uncountable, so at least one of the sets $A_{k}$ is infinite (in fact uncountable). This set $A_{k}$ being infinite, there exists a sequence in $A_{k}$ having distinct terms. This sequence will contain a convergent subsequence $\left(x_{n}\right)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ convergent to a point $x \in[a, b]$. But $\lim _{y \rightarrow x} g(y)=\infty$ implies that $g\left(x_{n}\right) \rightarrow \infty$, a contradiction because $\left|g\left(x_{n}\right)\right| \leq k, \forall n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Second solution for part (b). Let $S$ be the set of all sequences of real numbers. The cardinality of $S$ is $|S|=|\mathbb{R}|^{\aleph_{0}}=2^{\aleph_{0}^{2}}=2^{\aleph_{0}}=|\mathbb{R}|$. Thus, there exists a bijection $h: \mathbb{R} \rightarrow S$. Now define the function $f$ in the following way. For any real $x$ and positive integer $n$, let $f(x, n)$ be the $n$th element of sequence $h(x)$. If $y$ is not a positive integer then let $f(x, y)=0$. We prove that this function has the required property.

Let $g$ be an arbitrary $\mathbb{R} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$ function. We show that there exist real numbers $x, y$ such that $f(x, y)>g(x)+g(y)$. Consider the sequence $(n+g(n))_{n=1}^{\infty}$. This sequence is an element of $S$, thus $(n+g(n))_{n=1}^{\infty}=h(x)$ for a certain real $x$. Then for an arbitrary positive integer $n, f(x, n)$ is the $n$th element, $f(x, n)=n+g(n)$. Choosing $n$ such that $n>g(x)$, we obtain $f(x, n)=n+g(n)>g(x)+g(n)$.
llm_summary:
In part (a), the proof enumerates the rationals as \(q_0,q_1,\dots\) and defines \(g(q_n)\) inductively as the maximum over the finitely many lower bounds needed to ensure both \(f(q_n,q_n)\le2g(q_n)\) and \(f(q_k,q_n)\le g(q_k)+g(q_n)\) (and similarly with the arguments swapped) for all \(k<n\). In part (b), one sets
\[
 f(x,y)=\begin{cases}1/|x-y|,&x\neq y,\\0,&x=y,\end{cases}
\]
and assumes there is a function \(g\) with \(f(x,y)\le g(x)+g(y)\).  Restricting to \([0,1]\), one defines \(A_N=\{x:g(x)\le N\}\) and shows each \(A_N\) is finite (points in \(A_N\) must be at least \(1/(2N)\) apart), so \([0,1]\) would be a countable union of finite sets, contradicting its uncountability.

problem: Determine the set of all pairs \((a, b)\) of positive integers for which the set of positive integers can be decomposed into two sets \(A\) and \(B\) such that \(a \cdot A = b \cdot B\).
solution:
To determine the set of all pairs $(a, b)$ of positive integers for which the set of positive integers $\mathbb{N}$ can be decomposed into two disjoint sets $A$ and $B$ such that $a \cdot A = b \cdot B$, we begin by analyzing the implications of the condition $a \cdot A = b \cdot B$.

---

### Reformulation of the Problem

Let $S = a \cdot A = b \cdot B$. Then:

- $A = \{ n \in \mathbb{N} \mid a \cdot n \in S \} = S / a$
- $B = \{ n \in \mathbb{N} \mid b \cdot n \in S \} = S / b$

Since $A$ and $B$ partition $\mathbb{N}$, we must have:

- $S / a \cup S / b = \mathbb{N}$
- $S / a \cap S / b = \emptyset$

This implies that for every $k \in \mathbb{N}$, **exactly one** of $a \cdot k$ or $b \cdot k$ is in $S$.

---

### Key Insight: Multiplicative Structure

This condition can be interpreted as a **choice** for each $k \in \mathbb{N}$: either $a \cdot k$ or $b \cdot k$ is in $S$, but not both. This leads to a recursive or multiplicative structure in the construction of $S$.

Let us define $d = \gcd(a, b)$, and write $a = d \cdot a'$, $b = d \cdot b'$, where $\gcd(a', b') = 1$. Then:

- $S = a \cdot A = d \cdot a' \cdot A$
- $S = b \cdot B = d \cdot b' \cdot B$

This implies that $a' \cdot A = b' \cdot B$, and since $\gcd(a', b') = 1$, we can analyze the structure of $A$ and $B$ in terms of the multiplicative behavior of $a'$ and $b'$.

---

### Necessary and Sufficient Condition

To ensure that $A$ and $B$ partition $\mathbb{N}$, and that $a \cdot A = b \cdot B$, we must have that **one of $a'$ or $b'$ is 1**. This is because:

- If both $a' > 1$ and $b' > 1$, then the sets of multiples of $a'$ and $b'$ do not cover all of $\mathbb{N}$, due to the Chinese Remainder Theorem.
- Therefore, to ensure that every $k \in \mathbb{N}$ is in either $S / a$ or $S / b$, we must have that one of $a'$ or $b'$ is 1.

This leads to the conclusion that **either $a$ divides $b$ or $b$ divides $a$**.

---

### Constructive Argument

Suppose $a$ divides $b$, say $b = a \cdot c$. Then we can construct a partition of $\mathbb{N}$ as follows:

- Let $B$ be the set of all positive integers whose exponent of $c$ in their prime factorization is even (including zero).
- Let $A = c \cdot B$, i.e., the set of all positive integers whose exponent of $c$ is odd.

Then:

- $a \cdot A = a \cdot (c \cdot B) = (a \cdot c) \cdot B = b \cdot B$
- $A$ and $B$ partition $\mathbb{N}$, since every number has a unique exponent of $c$ in its prime factorization.

This construction works symmetrically if $b$ divides $a$.

---

### Counterexample: When Neither Divides the Other

Suppose $a = 2$, $b = 3$. Then $\gcd(a, b) = 1$, and $a' = 2$, $b' = 3$, both greater than 1. Then:

- $A$ must be a subset of multiples of $b' = 3$
- $B$ must be a subset of multiples of $a' = 2$

But then $A$ and $B$ cannot partition $\mathbb{N}$, since numbers not divisible by 2 or 3 (e.g., 1, 5, 7, etc.) are not in either set. Hence, no such partition exists.

---

### Final Conclusion

The set of all pairs $(a, b)$ of positive integers for which the set of positive integers can be decomposed into two sets $A$ and $B$ such that $a \cdot A = b \cdot B$ is precisely the set of pairs where **one of the numbers divides the other**.

$$
\boxed{(a, b) \mid a \text{ divides } b \text{ or } b \text{ divides } a}
$$

ground_truth_solution:
Solution. Clearly $a$ and $b$ must be different since $A$ and $B$ are disjoint.

Let $\{a, b\}$ be a solution and consider the sets $A, B$ such that $a \cdot A=b \cdot B$. Denoting $d=(a, b)$ the greatest common divisor of $a$ and $b$, we have $a=d \cdot a_{1}, b=d \cdot b_{1},\left(a_{1}, b_{1}\right)=1$ and $a_{1} \cdot A=b_{1} \cdot B$. Thus $\left\{a_{1}, b_{1}\right\}$ is a solution and it is enough to determine the solutions $\{a, b\}$ with $(a, b)=1$.

If $1 \in A$ then $a \in a \cdot A=b \cdot B$, thus $b$ must be a divisor of $a$. Similarly, if $1 \in B$, then $a$ is a divisor of $b$. Therefore, in all solutions, one of numbers $a, b$ is a divisor of the other one.

Now we prove that if $n \geq 2$, then $(1, n)$ is a solution. For each positive integer $k$, let $f(k)$ be the largest non-negative integer for which $n^{f(k)} \mid k$. Then let $A=\{k: f(k)$ is odd $\}$ and $B=\{k: f(k)$ is even $\}$. This is a decomposition of all positive integers such that $A=n \cdot B$.

It concludes that $a\mid b$ or $b\mid a$, gives a construction using parity of the exponent of $c=b/a$ when $a\mid b$, and exhibits the $(2,3)$ case as a counterexample to any other possibility.

problem:
Let \( f, g:[a, b] \rightarrow [0, \infty) \) be continuous and non-decreasing functions such that for each \( x \in [a, b] \),
\[
\int_{a}^{x} \sqrt{f(t)}\, dt \leq \int_{a}^{x} \sqrt{g(t)}\, dt
\]
and
\[
\int_{a}^{b} \sqrt{f(t)}\, dt = \int_{a}^{b} \sqrt{g(t)}\, dt.
\]
Prove that
\[
\int_{a}^{b} \sqrt{1+f(t)}\, dt \geq \int_{a}^{b} \sqrt{1+g(t)}\, dt.
\]
solution:
To prove that \(\int_{a}^{b} \sqrt{1+f(t)}\, dt \geq \int_{a}^{b} \sqrt{1+g(t)}\, dt\), define the functions \(u(t) = \sqrt{f(t)}\) and \(v(t) = \sqrt{g(t)}\). Since \(f\) and \(g\) are continuous and non-decreasing on \([a, b]\) and map to \([0, \infty)\), \(u\) and \(v\) are also continuous and non-decreasing on \([a, b]\), as the square root function is increasing and non-negative for non-negative inputs.

The given conditions are:
\[
\int_{a}^{x} u(t) \, dt \leq \int_{a}^{x} v(t) \, dt \quad \text{for each } x \in [a, b],
\]
and
\[
\int_{a}^{b} u(t) \, dt = \int_{a}^{b} v(t) \, dt.
\]
The goal is to show that
\[
\int_{a}^{b} \sqrt{1 + u(t)^2} \, dt \geq \int_{a}^{b} \sqrt{1 + v(t)^2} \, dt,
\]
since \(\sqrt{1 + f(t)} = \sqrt{1 + u(t)^2}\) and \(\sqrt{1 + g(t)} = \sqrt{1 + v(t)^2}\).

Define \(w(t) = \sqrt{1 + t^2}\). The second derivative of \(w\) is computed to determine its convexity. First,
\[
w'(t) = \frac{t}{\sqrt{1 + t^2}}.
\]
Then,
\[
w''(t) = \frac{d}{dt} \left( \frac{t}{\sqrt{1 + t^2}} \right) = \frac{\sqrt{1 + t^2} \cdot 1 - t \cdot \frac{1}{2} (1 + t^2)^{-1/2} \cdot 2t}{1 + t^2} = \frac{\sqrt{1 + t^2} - \frac{t^2}{\sqrt{1 + t^2}}}{1 + t^2} = \frac{1 + t^2 - t^2}{(1 + t^2)^{3/2}} = \frac{1}{(1 + t^2)^{3/2}} > 0
\]
for all \(t \in \mathbb{R}\). Since \(w''(t) > 0\), \(w\) is convex on \(\mathbb{R}\).

As \(w\) is convex and differentiable, for any \(a, b \in \mathbb{R}\), the inequality
\[
w(a) - w(b) \geq w'(b)(a - b)
\]
holds. Applying this with \(a = u(t)\) and \(b = v(t)\), for each \(t \in [a, b]\),
\[
w(u(t)) - w(v(t)) \geq w'(v(t)) (u(t) - v(t)).
\]
Integrating both sides from \(a\) to \(b\),
\[
\int_{a}^{b} \left[ w(u(t)) - w(v(t)) \right] dt \geq \int_{a}^{b} w'(v(t)) (u(t) - v(t)) \, dt.
\]
The right-hand side is \(\int_{a}^{b} p(t) q(t) \, dt\), where \(p(t) = w'(v(t))\) and \(q(t) = u(t) - v(t)\).

Since \(v(t) \geq 0\) and non-decreasing, and \(w'(t) = t / \sqrt{1 + t^2}\) is non-decreasing for \(t \geq 0\) (as \(w''(t) > 0\)), the composition \(p(t) = w'(v(t))\) is non-decreasing on \([a, b]\). Define \(Q(x) = \int_{a}^{x} q(t) \, dt\). The conditions imply \(Q(x) = \int_{a}^{x} (u(t) - v(t)) \, dt \leq 0\) for all \(x \in [a, b]\), and \(Q(a) = 0\), \(Q(b) = 0\).

Consider \(\int_{a}^{b} p(t) q(t) \, dt\). Using integration by parts for Riemann-Stieltjes integrals (valid since \(p\) is monotonic and \(Q\) is continuous),
\[
\int_{a}^{b} p(t) \, dQ(t) = \left[ p(t) Q(t) Q(t) \right]_{a}^{b} - \int_{a}^{b} Q(t) \, dp(t).
\]
At the endpoints, \(p(b) Q(b) = p(b) \cdot 0 = 0\) and \(p(a) Q(a) = p(a) \cdot 0 = 0\), so \(\left[ p(t) Q(t) \right]_{a}^{b} = 0\). Thus,
\[
\int_{a}^{b} p(t) \, dQ(t) = - \int_{a}^{b} Q(t) \, dp(t).
\]
Since \(p\) is non-decreasing, the Stieltjes measure \(dp(t)\) is non-negative. Also, \(Q(t) \leq 0\) for all \(t \in [a, b]\), so \(-Q(t) \geq 0\). Therefore, the integrand \(-Q(t) \, dp(t) \geq 0\), and
\[
\int_{a}^{b} -Q(t) \, dp(t) \geq 0,
\]
which implies
\[
\int_{a}^{b} p(t) \, dQ(t) \geq 0.
\]
As \(dQ(t) = q(t) \, dt\), it follows that
\[
\int_{a}^{b} p(t) q(t) \, dt \geq 0.
\]
Thus,
\[
\int_{a}^{b} w'(v(t)) (u(t) - v(t)) \, dt \geq 0,
\]
and consequently,
\[
\int_{a}^{b} \left[ w(u(t)) - w(v(t)) \right] dt \geq 0,
\]
which means
\[
\int_{a}^{b} \sqrt{1 + u(t)^2} \, dt \geq \int_{a}^{b} \sqrt{1 + v(t)^2} \, dt.
\]
Therefore,
\[
\int_{a}^{b} \sqrt{1 + f(t)} \, dt \geq \int_{a}^{b} \sqrt{1 + g(t)} \, dt,
\]
as required.

\boxed{\int_{a}^{b} \sqrt{1+f(t)}\, dt \geq \int_{a}^{b} \sqrt{1+g(t)}\, dt}

\int_{a}^{b} \sqrt{1+\left(F^{\prime}(t)\right)^{2}} d t \geq \int_{a}^{b} \sqrt{1+\left(G^{\prime}(t)\right)^{2}} d t
$$

i.e. The length ot the graph of $F$ is $\geq$ the length of the graph of $G$. problem: Problem 1. Let $A$ be the $n \times n$ matrix, whose $(i, j)^{\text {th }}$ entry is $i+j$ for all $i, j=1,2, \ldots, n$. What is the rank of $A$ ?
solution:
To determine the rank of the $ n \times n $ matrix $ A $ whose entries are defined as $ A_{i,j} = i + j $ for all $ i, j = 1, 2, \ldots, n $, we proceed through a detailed analysis using linear algebra principles.

---

### Step 1: Understanding the Matrix Structure

The matrix $ A $ has the form:

$$
A = 
\begin{bmatrix}
2 & 3 & 4 & \cdots & n+1 \\
3 & 4 & 5 & \cdots & n+2 \\
4 & 5 & 6 & \cdots & n+3 \\
\vdots & \vdots & \vdots & \ddots & \vdots \\
n+1 & n+2 & n+3 & \cdots & 2n
\end{bmatrix}
$$

Each row $ i $ of $ A $ is a vector of the form $ [i+1, i+2, \ldots, i+n] $, and each column $ j $ is $ [1+j, 2+j, \ldots, n+j] $.

---

### Step 2: Expressing $ A $ as a Sum of Rank-1 Matrices

Let $ u = \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 2 \\ \vdots \\ n \end{bmatrix} $ and $ v = \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 1 \\ \vdots \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} $. Then we can write:

$$
A = u v^T + v u^T
$$

- $ u v^T $ is an $ n \times n $ matrix of rank 1 (as it is the outer product of two non-zero vectors).
- Similarly, $ v u^T $ is also a rank-1 matrix.
- Since $ u $ and $ v $ are linearly independent for $ n \geq 2 $, the two matrices $ u v^T $ and $ v u^T $ are not scalar multiples of each other.
- Therefore, the sum $ A = u v^T + v u^T $ has rank **at most 2**.

---

### Step 3: Verifying Rank is Exactly 2 (for $ n \geq 2 $)

To show that the rank is **exactly 2**, we examine the row space of $ A $.

- Subtract the first row from all other rows:
  - Row $ i $ becomes $ [i-1, i-1, \ldots, i-1] $, i.e., a constant vector.
- This implies that all rows after the first are scalar multiples of the vector $ [1, 1, \ldots, 1] $.
- Therefore, the row space is spanned by:
  - The first row $ [2, 3, 4, \ldots, n+1] $
  - The vector $ [1, 1, \ldots, 1] $

These two vectors are linearly independent for $ n \geq 2 $, so the row space (and hence the rank) is **exactly 2**.

---

### Step 4: Special Case $ n = 1 $

When $ n = 1 $, the matrix $ A $ is simply:

$$
A = [1 + 1] = [2]
$$

This is a $ 1 \times 1 $ matrix with a non-zero entry, so its rank is **1**.

---

### Final Conclusion

- For $ n = 1 $, the rank of $ A $ is **1**.
- For $ n \geq 2 $, the rank of $ A $ is **2**.

However, since the question asks for the rank of $ A $ in general, and the matrix is defined for any $ n \geq 1 $, the most accurate and complete answer is:

$$
\text{The rank of } A \text{ is } 
\begin{cases}
1 & \text{if } n = 1 \\
2 & \text{if } n \geq 2
\end{cases}
$$

But if the problem assumes $ n \geq 2 $ (as is common in such contexts), the rank is simply:

$$
\boxed{2}
$$

ground_truth_solution:
Solution 1. For $n=1$ the rank is $1$. Now assume $n \geq 2$. Since $A=(i)_{i, j=1}^{n}+(j)_{i, j=1}^{n}$, matrix $A$ is the sum of two matrixes of rank $1$. Therefore, the rank of $A$ is at most $2$. The determinant of the top-left $2 \times 2$ minor is $-1$, so the rank is exactly $2$.

Therefore, the rank of $A$ is $1$ for $n=1$ and $2$ for $n \geq 2$.
Solution 2. Consider the case $n \geq 2$. For $i=n, n-1, \ldots, 2$, subtract the $(i-1)^{\text {th }}$ row from the $n^{\text {th }}$ row. Then subtract the second row from all lower rows.

$$
\operatorname{rank}\left(\begin{array}{cccc}
2 & 3 & \ldots & n+1 \\
3 & 4 & \ldots & n+2 \\
\vdots & & \ddots & \vdots \\
n+1 & n+2 & \ldots & 2 n
\end{array}\right)=\operatorname{rank}\left(\begin{array}{cccc}
2 & 3 & \ldots & n+1 \\
1 & 1 & \ldots & 1 \\
\vdots & & \ddots & \vdots \\
1 & 1 & \ldots & 1
\end{array}\right)=\operatorname{rank}\left(\begin{array}{cccc}
1 & 2 & \ldots & n \\
1 & 1 & \ldots & 1 \\
0 & 0 & \ldots & 0 \\
\vdots & & \ddots & \vdots \\
0 & 0 & \ldots & 0
\end{array}\right)=2 .
$$

problem: Let \( f: \mathbb{R} \rightarrow \mathbb{R} \) be a function such that \( (f(x))^{n} \) is a polynomial for every \( n = 2, 3, \ldots \). Does it follow that \( f \) is a polynomial?
solution:
Here is a complete proof.  Throughout we write \(\Bbb R[x]\) for the ring of real‐coefficient polynomials; it is a unique factorization domain (UFD).  

Proof.  
Define
\[
P_2(x)\;=\;f(x)^2,
\qquad
P_3(x)\;=\;f(x)^3.
\]
By hypothesis each of these is a polynomial in \(\Bbb R[x]\).  Then
\[
P_2(x)^3 \;=\;(f(x)^2)^3 \;=\; f(x)^6
\quad\text{and}\quad
P_3(x)^2 \;=\;(f(x)^3)^2 \;=\; f(x)^6,
\]
so as elements of the integral domain \(\Bbb R[x]\) we have the polynomial identity
\[
\boxed{P_2^3 = P_3^2.}
\]

Since \(\Bbb R[x]\) is a UFD, we may let
\[
D \;=\;\gcd\bigl(P_2,P_3\bigr)
\]
and write
\[
P_2 \;=\; D\cdot A,
\qquad
P_3 \;=\; D\cdot B,
\]
where \(A,B\in\Bbb R[x]\) satisfy \(\gcd(A,B)=1\).  Substituting into \(P_2^3=P_3^2\) gives
\[
(D\,A)^3 \;=\;(D\,B)^2
\;\;\Longrightarrow\;\;
D^3A^3 \;=\; D^2B^2
\;\;\Longrightarrow\;\;
D\,A^3 \;=\; B^2.
\]
Now \(\gcd(A^3,B^2)=1\) (because \(\gcd(A,B)=1\)), and so in the UFD \(\Bbb R[x]\) the relation
\[
A^3\;\bigm|\;B^2
\]
forces \(A^3\) to be a unit.  Hence \(A\) is a nonzero constant.  But then
\[
P_2 \;=\; D\,A
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
D\;=\;\text{(unit)}\cdot P_2,
\]
so up to an irrelevant constant factor we have
\[
\gcd(P_2,P_3) \;=\; P_2,
\]
which exactly says
\[
P_2 \;\bigm|\; P_3.
\]
Therefore there is some \(Q(x)\in\Bbb R[x]\) with
\[
P_3(x)\;=\;P_2(x)\,Q(x).
\]
But then from \(P_2^3=P_3^2\) we get
\[
P_2^3 \;=\;(P_2\,Q)^2 \;=\;P_2^2\,Q^2
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
P_2 \;=\; Q^2.
\]
Summarizing:
\[
f(x)^2 \;=\;P_2(x)\;=\;Q(x)^2,
\qquad
f(x)^3 \;=\;P_3(x)\;=\;P_2(x)\,Q(x)\;=\;Q(x)^3.
\]
Thus for each real \(x\),
\[
f(x)^2 = Q(x)^2
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
f(x)=\pm\,Q(x),
\]
and
\[
f(x)^3 = Q(x)^3
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
f(x)=Q(x),
\]
since the real‐cube‐map \(t\mapsto t^3\) is injective on \(\Bbb R\).  Hence
\[
\forall x\in\Bbb R:\qquad f(x)=Q(x),
\]
and so \(f\) {\em is} the polynomial \(Q\in\Bbb R[x]\).  □

Comment.  The crux is the simple UFD‐argument
\[
P_2^3 = P_3^2
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
P_2 \text{ divides }P_3
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
P_2=Q^2,\;P_3=Q^3
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
f=Q.
\]

ground_truth_solution:
Solution 1. Yes, it is even enough to assume that $f^{2}$ and $f^{3}$ are polynomials.
Let $p=f^{2}$ and $q=f^{3}$. Write these polynomials in the form of

$$
p=a \cdot p_{1}^{a_{1}} \cdot \ldots \cdot p_{k}^{a_{k}}, \quad q=b \cdot q_{1}^{b_{1}} \cdot \ldots \cdot q_{l}^{b_{l}}
$$
where $a, b \in \mathbb{R}, a_{1}, \ldots, a_{k}, b_{1}, \ldots b_{l}$ are positive integers and $p_{1}, \ldots, p_{k}, q_{1}, \ldots, q_{l}$ are irreducible polynomials with leading coefficients $1$. For $p^{3}=q^{2}$ and the factorisation of $p^{3}=q^{2}$ is unique we get that $a^{3}=b^{2}, k=l$ and for some ( $i_{1}, \ldots, i_{k}$ ) permutation of ( $1, \ldots, k$ ) we have $p_{1}=q_{i_{1}}, \ldots, p_{k}=q_{i_{k}}$ and $3 a_{1}=2 b_{i_{1}}, \ldots, 3 a_{k}=2 b_{i_{k}}$. Hence $b_{1}, \ldots, b_{l}$ are divisible by $3$ let $r=b^{1 / 3} \cdot q_{1}^{b_{1} / 3} \cdot \ldots \cdot q_{l}^{b_{l} / 3}$ be a polynomial. Since $r^{3}=q=f^{3}$ we have $f=r$.
Solution 2. Let $\frac{p}{q}$ be the simplest form of the rational function $\frac{f^{3}}{f^{2}}$. Then the simplest form of its square is $\frac{p^{2}}{q^{2}}$. On the other hand $\frac{p^{2}}{q^{2}}=\left(\frac{f^{3}}{f^{2}}\right)^{2}=f^{2}$ is a polynomial therefore $q$ must be a constant and so $f=\frac{f^{3}}{f^{2}}=\frac{p}{q}$ is a polynomial.

problem:
In the linear space of all real \( n \times n \) matrices, find the maximum possible dimension of a linear subspace \( V \) such that
\[
\forall X, Y \in V \quad \operatorname{trace}(X Y)=0
\]
(The trace of a matrix is the sum of the diagonal entries.)
solution:
Let $M_n(\mathbb{R})$ be the linear space of all real $n \times n$ matrices. We are looking for the maximum possible dimension of a linear subspace $V \subseteq M_n(\mathbb{R})$ such that for all $X, Y \in V$, $\operatorname{trace}(XY) = 0$.

Let $B(X,Y) = \operatorname{trace}(XY)$. This defines a bilinear form on $M_n(\mathbb{R})$.
The trace possesses the property $\operatorname{trace}(XY) = \operatorname{trace}(YX)$. Therefore, $B(X,Y) = \operatorname{trace}(XY) = \operatorname{trace}(YX) = B(Y,X)$, so $B$ is a symmetric bilinear form.
The condition on the subspace $V$ is that $B(X,Y)=0$ for all $X,Y \in V$. Such a subspace is called a totally isotropic subspace.
If $V$ is a totally isotropic subspace, then for any $X \in V$, $B(X,X) = \operatorname{trace}(X^2) = 0$. Conversely, if $\operatorname{trace}(X^2)=0$ for all $X \in V$ (and the characteristic of the field is not 2, which is true for $\mathbb{R}$), then $V$ is totally isotropic. This is because for $X,Y \in V$, $X+Y \in V$, so $\operatorname{trace}((X+Y)^2)=0$. Expanding this, $\operatorname{trace}(X^2 + XY + YX + Y^2)=0$. This gives $\operatorname{trace}(X^2) + \operatorname{trace}(XY) + \operatorname{trace}(YX) + \operatorname{trace}(Y^2)=0$. Since $\operatorname{trace}(X^2)=0$, $\operatorname{trace}(Y^2)=0$, and $\operatorname{trace}(XY)=\operatorname{trace}(YX)$, we get $2\operatorname{trace}(XY)=0$, so $\operatorname{trace}(XY)=0$.

We can decompose any matrix $M \in M_n(\mathbb{R})$ into its symmetric and skew-symmetric parts: $M = M_S + M_A$, where $M_S = \frac{1}{2}(M+M^T)$ is symmetric ($M_S^T=M_S$) and $M_A = \frac{1}{2}(M-M^T)$ is skew-symmetric ($M_A^T=-M_A$).
Let $S_n(\mathbb{R})$ denote the subspace of symmetric matrices and $A_n(\mathbb{R})$ denote the subspace of skew-symmetric matrices.
$M_n(\mathbb{R}) = S_n(\mathbb{R}) \oplus A_n(\mathbb{R})$. The dimension of $S_n(\mathbb{R})$ is $p = \frac{n(n+1)}{2}$ and the dimension of $A_n(\mathbb{R})$ is $q = \frac{n(n-1)}{2}$.

Let's examine the bilinear form $B$ on these subspaces.
1. If $X \in S_n(\mathbb{R})$ and $Y \in A_n(\mathbb{R})$:
$B(X,Y) = \operatorname{trace}(XY)$. Also, using the property $\operatorname{trace}(M) = \operatorname{trace}(M^T)$:
$\operatorname{trace}(XY) = \operatorname{trace}((XY)^T) = \operatorname{trace}(Y^T X^T)$.
Since $Y \in A_n(\mathbb{R})$, $Y^T=-Y$. Since $X \in S_n(\mathbb{R})$, $X^T=X$.
So $\operatorname{trace}(Y^T X^T) = \operatorname{trace}(-YX) = -\operatorname{trace}(YX)$.
Using $\operatorname{trace}(YX) = \operatorname{trace}(XY)$, we get $\operatorname{trace}(XY) = -\operatorname{trace}(XY)$.
This implies $2\operatorname{trace}(XY)=0$, so $\operatorname{trace}(XY)=0$.
Hence, $S_n(\mathbb{R})$ and $A_n(\mathbb{R})$ are orthogonal subspaces with respect to $B$.

2. If $X \in S_n(\mathbb{R})$:
$B(X,X) = \operatorname{trace}(X^2) = \operatorname{trace}(XX^T)$ (since $X=X^T$).
Let $X=(X_{ij})$. Then $(XX^T)_{ii} = \sum_j X_{ij}(X^T)_{ji} = \sum_j X_{ij}X_{ij} = \sum_j X_{ij}^2$.
So $B(X,X) = \sum_i \sum_j X_{ij}^2 = \|X\|_F^2$ (where $\|X\|_F$ is the Frobenius norm).
Thus, $B(X,X) \ge 0$ for all $X \in S_n(\mathbb{R})$, and $B(X,X)=0$ if and only if $X=0$.
So $B$ is positive definite on $S_n(\mathbb{R})$.

3. If $X \in A_n(\mathbb{R})$:
$B(X,X) = \operatorname{trace}(X^2) = \operatorname{trace}(X(-X^T))$ (since $X=-X^T$).
So $B(X,X) = -\operatorname{trace}(XX^T) = -\sum_i \sum_j X_{ij}^2 = -\|X\|_F^2$.
Thus, $B(X,X) \le 0$ for all $X \in A_n(\mathbb{R})$, and $B(X,X)=0$ if and only if $X=0$.
So $B$ is negative definite on $A_n(\mathbb{R})$.

Let $V$ be a totally isotropic subspace. For any $X \in V$, write $X = X_S + X_A$ where $X_S \in S_n(\mathbb{R})$ and $X_A \in A_n(\mathbb{R})$.
Since $V$ is totally isotropic, $B(X,X)=0$ for all $X \in V$.
$B(X,X) = B(X_S+X_A, X_S+X_A) = B(X_S,X_S) + B(X_S,X_A) + B(X_A,X_S) + B(X_A,X_A)$.
Since $S_n(\mathbb{R})$ and $A_n(\mathbb{R})$ are orthogonal, $B(X_S,X_A)=0$ and $B(X_A,X_S)=0$.
So $B(X,X) = B(X_S,X_S) + B(X_A,X_A) = 0$.
This means $\sum_{i,j}(X_S)_{ij}^2 - \sum_{i,j}(X_A)_{ij}^2 = 0$.
So, for any $X \in V$, $\|X_S\|_F^2 = \|X_A\|_F^2$.

Let $\pi_S: V \to S_n(\mathbb{R})$ be the linear map defined by $\pi_S(X_S+X_A) = X_S$.
Suppose $X \in \ker(\pi_S)$. Then $X_S=0$.
From $\|X_S\|_F^2 = \|X_A\|_F^2$, we get $\|X_A\|_F^2 = 0$, which implies $X_A=0$.
So $X=0$. Therefore, $\pi_S$ is injective.
This implies that $\dim(V) \le \dim(S_n(\mathbb{R})) = p = \frac{n(n+1)}{2}$.

Similarly, let $\pi_A: V \to A_n(\mathbb{R})$ be the linear map defined by $\pi_A(X_S+X_A) = X_A$.
Suppose $X \in \ker(\pi_A)$. Then $X_A=0$.
From $\|X_S\|_F^2 = \|X_A\|_F^2$, we get $\|X_S\|_F^2 = 0$, which implies $X_S=0$.
So $X=0$. Therefore, $\pi_A$ is injective.
This implies that $\dim(V) \le \dim(A_n(\mathbb{R})) = q = \frac{n(n-1)}{2}$.

Combining these two inequalities, we must have $\dim(V) \le \min(p,q)$.
Since $n \ge 0$, $n-1 \le n+1$, so $\frac{n(n-1)}{2} \le \frac{n(n+1)}{2}$.
Thus, $q \le p$. So $\dim(V) \le q = \frac{n(n-1)}{2}$.

We now show that this maximum dimension can be achieved. We need to construct such a subspace $V_0$ with dimension $q = \frac{n(n-1)}{2}$.
Let $\{e_1, \dots, e_p\}$ be an orthonormal basis for $S_n(\mathbb{R})$ with respect to $B$. That is, $B(e_i, e_j) = \delta_{ij}$ for $1 \le i,j \le p$. Such a basis exists because $B$ is positive definite on $S_n(\mathbb{R})$.
Let $\{f_1, \dots, f_q\}$ be an orthonormal basis for $A_n(\mathbb{R})$ with respect to $-B$. That is, $-B(f_i, f_j) = \delta_{ij}$, or $B(f_i, f_j) = -\delta_{ij}$ for $1 \le i,j \le q$. Such a basis exists because $-B$ is positive definite on $A_n(\mathbb{R})$ (as $B$ is negative definite).

Consider the set of $q$ matrices $W = \{w_1, \dots, w_q\}$ where $w_k = e_k + f_k$ for $k=1, \dots, q$. (This construction assumes $q \le p$, which is true).
The vectors $w_k$ are linearly independent. To see this, suppose $\sum_{k=1}^q c_k w_k = 0$ for some scalars $c_k \in \mathbb{R}$.
Then $\sum_{k=1}^q c_k (e_k+f_k) = 0 \implies (\sum_{k=1}^q c_k e_k) + (\sum_{k=1}^q c_k f_k) = 0$.
The first sum is in $S_n(\mathbb{R})$ and the second is in $A_n(\mathbb{R})$. Since $S_n(\mathbb{R}) \cap A_n(\mathbb{R}) = \{0\}$, both sums must be zero:
$\sum_{k=1}^q c_k e_k = 0$ and $\sum_{k=1}^q c_k f_k = 0$.
Since $\{e_k\}$ are linearly independent and $\{f_k\}$ are linearly independent, it must be that all $c_k=0$.
So the set $W$ is linearly independent. Let $V_0 = \operatorname{span}(W)$. Then $\dim(V_0) = q = \frac{n(n-1)}{2}$.

Now we check if $V_0$ is a totally isotropic subspace. It is sufficient to check that $B(w_k, w_l)=0$ for all $k,l \in \{1, \dots, q\}$.
$B(w_k, w_l) = B(e_k+f_k, e_l+f_l)$.
By bilinearity, $B(w_k, w_l) = B(e_k,e_l) + B(e_k,f_l) + B(f_k,e_l) + B(f_k,f_l)$.
Since $e_k \in S_n(\mathbb{R})$ and $f_l \in A_n(\mathbb{R})$, $B(e_k,f_l)=0$. Similarly $B(f_k,e_l)=0$.
So, $B(w_k, w_l) = B(e_k,e_l) + B(f_k,f_l)$.
By construction of the bases, $B(e_k,e_l) = \delta_{kl}$ and $B(f_k,f_l) = -\delta_{kl}$.
Therefore, $B(w_k, w_l) = \delta_{kl} - \delta_{kl} = 0$.
This shows that for any $X, Y \in V_0$, $B(X,Y)=0$.
Thus, $V_0$ is a totally isotropic subspace of dimension $q = \frac{n(n-1)}{2}$.

Since $\dim(V) \le \frac{n(n-1)}{2}$ for any such subspace $V$, and we have constructed a subspace $V_0$ that achieves this dimension, the maximum possible dimension is $\frac{n(n-1)}{2}$.

For $n=1$, the dimension is $\frac{1(1-1)}{2}=0$. $M_1(\mathbb{R})$ is $\mathbb{R}$. $\operatorname{trace}(XY)=xy$. If $x \in V$ and $x \ne 0$, then $x^2=0$ implies $x=0$. So $V=\{0\}$, dimension 0.
For $n=2$, the dimension is $\frac{2(2-1)}{2}=1$. $\dim S_2(\mathbb{R})=3$, $\dim A_2(\mathbb{R})=1$. $\min(3,1)=1$.

Conclusion: The maximum possible dimension of such a subspace $V$ is $\frac{n(n-1)}{2}$.

The final answer is $\boxed{\frac{n(n-1)}{2}}$.

ground_truth_solution:
Solution. If $A$ is a nonzero symmetric matrix, then $\operatorname{trace}\left(A^{2}\right)=\operatorname{trace}\left(A^{t} A\right)$ is the sum of the squared entries of $A$ which is positive. So $V$ cannot contain any symmetric matrix but $0$.

Denote by $S$ the linear space of all real $n \times n$ symmetric matrices; $\operatorname{dim} V=\frac{n(n+1)}{2}$. Since $V \cap S=\{0\}$, we have $\operatorname{dim} V+\operatorname{dim} S \leq n^{2}$ and thus $\operatorname{dim} V \leq n^{2}-\frac{n(n+1)}{2}=\frac{n(n-1)}{2}$.

The space of strictly upper triangular matrices has dimension $\frac{n(n-1)}{2}$ and satisfies the condition of the problem.

Therefore the maximum dimension of $V$ is $\frac{n(n-1)}{2}$.
llm_summary: The proof introduces the bilinear form \(B(X,Y)=\operatorname{trace}(XY)\) on \(M_n(\mathbb{R})\) and observes that a subspace \(V\) with \(B(X,Y)=0\) for all \(X,Y\in V\) is totally isotropic. It then decomposes any matrix into its symmetric part in \(S_n(\mathbb{R})\) and skew-symmetric part in \(A_n(\mathbb{R})\), shows that \(B\) is positive definite on \(S_n\) and negative definite on \(A_n\), and uses the injectivity of the projections onto these summands to obtain the bound \(\dim V\le\min(\dim S_n,\dim A_n)=\tfrac{n(n-1)}2\). Finally, it constructs an explicit totally isotropic subspace of dimension \(\tfrac{n(n-1)}2\) by pairing orthonormal bases of \(S_n\) and \(A_n\), proving the bound is sharp.

problem: Let \( f \) be a polynomial of degree \( 2 \) with integer coefficients. Suppose that \( f(k) \) is divisible by \( 5 \) for every integer \( k \). Prove that all coefficients of \( f \) are divisible by \( 5 \).
solution:
To prove that all coefficients of the quadratic polynomial \(f(x) = ax^2 + bx + c\) with integer coefficients are divisible by 5, given that \(f(k)\) is divisible by 5 for every integer \(k\), we proceed as follows.

Since \(f(k)\) is divisible by 5 for every integer \(k\), it follows that \(f(k) \equiv 0 \pmod{5}\) for all integers \(k\). This means that every integer is a root of the polynomial congruence \(f(x) \equiv 0 \pmod{5}\). Equivalently, the polynomial \(f\), considered modulo 5, has a root at every residue class modulo 5.

The ring \(\mathbb{Z}/5\mathbb{Z}\) is a field because 5 is prime. In a field, a non-zero polynomial of degree \(d\) has at most \(d\) roots. Here, \(f\) is a quadratic polynomial, so its degree is at most 2 modulo 5 (if \(a \not\equiv 0 \pmod{5}\), the degree is exactly 2; if \(a \equiv 0 \pmod{5}\), the degree is less than or equal to 1).

Since \(\mathbb{Z}/5\mathbb{Z}\) has 5 elements, and \(f(x) \equiv 0 \pmod{5}\) for all 5 residue classes (i.e., at \(x \equiv 0, 1, 2, 3, 4 \pmod{5}\)), \(f\) has at least 5 roots modulo 5. However, a polynomial of degree at most 2 can have at most 2 roots in a field unless it is identically zero modulo 5. Because \(5 > 2\), it is impossible for a non-zero polynomial of degree at most 2 to have 5 roots. Therefore, \(f\) must be identically zero modulo 5.

If \(f\) is identically zero modulo 5, then all its coefficients are congruent to 0 modulo 5. That is, \(a \equiv 0 \pmod{5}\), \(b \equiv 0 \pmod{5}\), and \(c \equiv 0 \pmod{5}\). Hence, all coefficients of \(f\) are divisible by 5.

This completes the proof.

\boxed{\text{all coefficients of } f \text{ are divisible by } 5}
source: International Mathematics Competition for University Students
ground_truth_solution:
Solution 1. Let $f(x)=a x^{2}+b x+c$. Substituting $x=0, x=1$ and $x=-1$, we obtain that $5 \mid f(0)=c$, $5 \mid f(1)=(a+b+c)$ and $5 \mid f(-1)=(a-b+c)$. Then $5 \mid f(1)+f(-1)-2 f(0)=2 a$ and $5 \mid f(1)-f(-1)=2 b$. Therefore $5$ divides $2 a, 2 b$ and $c$ and the statement follows.
Solution 2. Consider $f(x)$ as a polynomial over the $5$-element field (i.e. modulo 5). The polynomial has $5$ roots while its degree is at most $2$. Therefore $f \equiv 0(\bmod 5)$ and all of its coefficients are divisible by $5$.
