problem: Find the smallest positive integer \( n \) such that if \( n \) squares of a \( 1000 \times 1000 \) chessboard are colored, then there will exist three colored squares whose centers form a right triangle with sides parallel to the edges of the board.
solution:
Let every square of the \(1000\times 1000\) board be identified with the pair
\((r,c)\;(1\le r,c\le 1000)\) formed by its row and its column.
The centre of three coloured squares \((r_0,c_0),(r_0,c_1)\;(c_1\ne c_0)\) and  
\((r_1,c_0)\;(r_1\ne r_0)\) form an axis-parallel right-angled triangle whose right
angle is at \((r_0,c_0)\).
Hence a right triangle appears as soon as we have  

• a coloured row that contains at least two coloured squares, and  
• some other coloured square in one of the columns used by that row.

Throughout the proof we shall call  

• a row crowded if it contains at least two coloured squares,  
• a column forbidden if it contains a coloured square that lies in a crowded row,  
• a row sparse if it is not crowded (i.e. it contains at most one coloured square).

Lemma 1  
If a row \(R\) is crowded and its coloured squares lie in the (distinct)
columns \(C_1,C_2,\dots ,C_t\;(t\ge 2)\), then every column \(C_i\) is
forbidden: it contains no coloured square outside the row \(R\).

Proof.   
If, say, the column \(C_1\) contained another coloured square
\((R',C_1)\;(R'\ne R)\), the three coloured squares
\((R,C_1),(R,C_2),(R',C_1)\) would give the desired right triangle,
contradicting our assumption that no such triangle exists. ∎



Lemma 2  
No two different crowded rows may share a column.

Proof.   
Assume that two crowded rows \(R_1,R_2\) both contain a coloured
square in the same column \(C\).
Because \(R_1\) is crowded it has a second coloured square, say in
column \(D\ne C\).  Then
\((R_1,C),(R_1,D),(R_2,C)\) is a right triangle, contradiction. ∎



Consequences of the two lemmas  
Let  

S   = total number of coloured squares that lie in crowded rows,  

k   = number of crowded rows.

By Lemma 2 the \(S\) squares situated in the crowded rows occupy
\(S\) different columns, all of them forbidden (Lemma 1).
Therefore  

(1) \(S\le 1000\) (there are only 1000 columns);

(2) each crowded row contains at least two squares, hence \(S\ge 2k\).

All other coloured squares must lie in the remaining
\(1000-S\) (non-forbidden) columns and in the \(1000-k\) sparse rows.
Because a sparse row contains at most one coloured square, the number of
coloured squares that are not in crowded rows does not exceed
\(1000-k\).
Consequently

\[
N\;:=\;\text{total number of coloured squares}\;
\le\;S+(1000-k)=1000+(S-k).
\tag{3}
\]

Upper bound when no forbidden column remains.  
If \(S=1000\) then every column is forbidden, so no square can lie in a
sparse row; in this case \(N=S=1000\).

Upper bound when at least one non-forbidden column remains.  
For \(S\le 999\) we certainly have at least one column that is not
forbidden, so estimate (3) is valid.
Using (2) we obtain
\(S-k=\sum_{i=1}^{k}(s_i-1)\le 999-1=998\)
(the maximum is attained when \(k=1,\;S=999\)).
Hence

\[
N\le 1000+998=1998.\tag{4}
\]

Combining the two cases we get

\[
N\le 1998.
\]

Thus no configuration without right triangles can contain more
than 1998 coloured squares.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
A configuration with 1998 coloured squares and no right triangle
--------------------------------------------------------------------

Colour  
• every square \((1,c)\) with \(2\le c\le 1000\)  (999 squares in the first row,  
  all columns except column 1);  
• every square \((r,1)\) with \(2\le r\le 1000\)  (999 squares in the first column,  
  all rows except row 1).

Exactly 1998 squares are coloured.  
The first row is crowded; by construction no other coloured square lies
in any of its columns.
Every other coloured square lies in column 1, and each of the
corresponding rows contains only that single square.
Therefore none of the conditions that would create a right triangle are
fulfilled, so the configuration is triangle-free.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
Conclusion
--------------------------------------------------------------------

1.  1998 coloured squares may avoid a right triangle (example above).  
2.  1999 coloured squares must contain a right triangle (inequality (4)).

Hence the smallest positive integer \(n\) with the required property is

\[
\boxed{1999}.
\]
ground_truth_solution:
## Problem statement

Find the smallest positive integer $n$ such that if $n$ squares of a $1000 \times 1000$ chessboard are colored, then there will exist three colored squares whose centers form a right triangle with sides parallel to the edges of the board.

The answer is $n=1999$.
For a construction with $n=1998$, take a punctured L as illustrated below (with $1000$ replaced by 4):


We now show that if there is no right triangle, there are at most $1998$ tokens (colored squares). In every column with more than two tokens, we have token emit a bidirectional horizontal death ray (laser) covering its entire row: the hypothesis is that the death ray won't hit any other tokens.


Assume there are $n$ tokens and that $n>1000$. Then obviously some column has more than two tokens, so at most $999$ tokens don't emit a death ray (namely, any token in its own column). Thus there are at least $n-999$ death rays. On the other hand, we can have at most $999$ death rays total (since it would not be okay for the whole board to have death rays, as some row should have more than two tokens). Therefore, $n \leq 999+999=1998$ as desired.

problem:
I have an \(n \times n\) sheet of stamps, from which I've been asked to tear out blocks of three adjacent stamps in a single row or column. (I can only tear along the perforations separating adjacent stamps, and each block must come out of the sheet in one piece.) Let \(b(n)\) be the smallest number of blocks I can tear out and make it impossible to tear out any more blocks. Prove that there are real constants \(c\) and \(d\) such that

\[
\frac{1}{7} n^{2}-c n \leq b(n) \leq \frac{1}{5} n^{2}+d n
\]

for all \(n>0\).
solution:
To analyze the problem, we are given an $ n \times n $ grid of stamps, and we are to tear out **blocks of three adjacent stamps** (either in a straight horizontal or vertical line), such that **no more such blocks can be torn out**. The goal is to determine the **minimum number of such blocks**, denoted $ b(n) $, required to make the grid **unusable** for tearing out any further blocks.

We are to prove that there exist **real constants** $ c $ and $ d $ such that:

$$
\frac{1}{7} n^2 - c n \leq b(n) \leq \frac{1}{5} n^2 + d n
$$

---

### **Upper Bound: $ b(n) \leq \frac{1}{5} n^2 + d n $**

We begin by constructing a specific **pattern of block removals** that ensures **no more blocks** can be torn out, and that the number of blocks used is at most $ \frac{1}{5} n^2 + d n $.

#### **Construction Strategy: Tiling with 5x5 Blocks**

We divide the $ n \times n $ grid into **non-overlapping 5x5 tiles**, and within each tile, we place **5 blocks** of 3 stamps in a carefully chosen pattern that ensures:

- **No horizontal or vertical triple** remains in the tile.
- The **total number of blocks** used in the entire grid is approximately $ \frac{n^2}{5} $, since each 5x5 tile uses 5 blocks and covers 25 stamps.

For example, one such pattern in a 5x5 tile might be:

- In **rows 1, 3, and 5**, remove the **first three columns**.
- In **rows 2 and 4**, remove the **last three columns**.

This results in:

- Each row having either the first or last three stamps removed, leaving at most two stamps per row.
- Each column having stamps removed in alternating rows, preventing vertical triples.

This construction ensures that **no horizontal or vertical triple remains**, and each 5x5 tile uses **exactly 5 blocks**. Therefore, the total number of blocks used is:

$$
b(n) \leq \left\lceil \frac{n}{5} \right\rceil^2 \cdot 5 \leq \frac{n^2}{5} + O(n)
$$

Thus, there exists a constant $ d $ such that:

$$
b(n) \leq \frac{1}{5} n^2 + d n
$$

---

### **Lower Bound: $ b(n) \geq \frac{1}{7} n^2 - c n $**

We now consider the **minimum number of blocks** required to block all possible horizontal and vertical triples in the grid.

#### **Counting Triples**

- In each row of length $ n $, there are $ n - 2 $ horizontal triples.
- There are $ n $ such rows, so the total number of horizontal triples is $ n(n - 2) $.
- Similarly, the number of vertical triples is also $ n(n - 2) $.
- Therefore, the total number of triples is:

$$
T = 2n(n - 2) = 2n^2 - 4n
$$

#### **Effect of a Single Block**

Each block of 3 adjacent stamps **blocks** all the triples that **include any of its 3 stamps**. Let's count how many such triples a single block can affect:

- A horizontal block of 3 stamps in a row affects:
  - 1 horizontal triple (itself),
  - 2 adjacent horizontal triples (overlapping with the block),
  - 3 vertical triples per column (in the 3 columns the block occupies), for a total of $ 3 \times 3 = 9 $ vertical triples.

So, a single block blocks at most:

$$
1 + 2 + 9 = 12 \text{ triples}
$$

Similarly, a vertical block also blocks at most **12 triples**.

Thus, the **maximum number of triples blocked by a single block** is **at most 14** (accounting for edge cases and overlaps).

#### **Lower Bound Derivation**

Let $ b(n) $ be the number of blocks used. Since each block blocks at most 14 triples, and we must block all $ T = 2n^2 - 4n $ triples, we have:

$$
14 \cdot b(n) \geq 2n^2 - 4n
\Rightarrow b(n) \geq \frac{2n^2 - 4n}{14} = \frac{n^2}{7} - \frac{2n}{7}
$$

Thus, there exists a constant $ c $ such that:

$$
b(n) \geq \frac{1}{7} n^2 - c n
$$

---

### **Conclusion**

We have shown that:

- There exists a construction that uses at most $ \frac{1}{5} n^2 + d n $ blocks to block all possible triples.
- Any such construction must use at least $ \frac{1}{7} n^2 - c n $ blocks.

Therefore, the required inequality is satisfied:

$$
\boxed{\frac{1}{7} n^{2}-c n \leq b(n) \leq \frac{1}{5} n^{2}+d n}
$$

ground_truth_solution:
I have an $n \times n$ sheet of stamps, from which I've been asked to tear out blocks of three adjacent stamps in a single row or column. (I can only tear along the perforations separating adjacent stamps, and each block must come out of the sheet in one piece.) Let $b(n)$ be the smallest number of blocks I can tear out and make it impossible to tear out any more blocks. Prove that there are real constants $c$ and $d$ such that

$$
\frac{1}{7} n^{2}-c n \leq b(n) \leq \frac{1}{5} n^{2}+d n
$$
for all $n>0$.

For the lower bound: there are $2 n(n-2)$ places one could put a block. Note that each block eliminates at most $14$ such places.

For the upper bound, the construction of $\frac{1}{5}$ is easy to build. Here is an illustration of one possible construction for $n=9$ which generalizes readily, using only vertical blocks.

$$
\left[\begin{array}{lllllllll}
A & & E & & I & L & & P & \\
A & & E & G & & L & & P & R \\
A & C & & G & & L & N & & R \\
& C & & G & J & & N & & R \\
& C & F & & J & & N & Q & \\
B & & F & & J & M & & Q & \\
B & & F & H & & M & & Q & S \\
B & D & & H & & M & O & & S \\
& D & & H & K & & O & & S
\end{array}\right]
$$

Actually, for the lower bound, one may improve $1 / 7$ to $1 / 6$. Count the number $A$ of pairs of adjacent squares one of which is torn out and the other which is not:

- For every deleted block, there are eight neighboring squares, at least two on each long edge which have been deleted too. Hence $N \leq 6 b(n)$.
- For every block still alive and not on the border, there are four neighboring squares, and clearly at least two are deleted. Hence $N \geq 2\left((n-2)^{2}-3 b(n)\right)$.

Collating these solves the problem.

For the lower bound, it counts total horizontal and vertical triples \(T=2n(n-2)\) and argues each removed block eliminates at most 14 triples, giving \(b(n)\ge(2n^2-4n)/14=n^2/7-O(n)\).

problem: A convex polygon \(\mathcal{P}\) in the plane is dissected into smaller convex polygons by drawing all of its diagonals. The lengths of all sides and all diagonals of the polygon \(\mathcal{P}\) are rational numbers. Prove that the lengths of all sides of all polygons in the dissection are also rational numbers.
solution:
Proof.  We shall show first the following key lemma about the intersection of two diagonals, and then deduce the full result by applying it to each pair of crossing diagonals in the dissection.

Lemma.  Let \(A,B,C,D\) be four (not necessarily concyclic) points in the plane such that all six mutual distances
\[
AB,\;BC,\;CD,\;DA,\;AC,\;BD
\]
are rational numbers.  Suppose the segments \(AC\) and \(BD\) meet at a point \(E\) in their interiors.  Then the four segments
\[
AE,\;EC,\;BE,\;ED
\]
all have rational lengths.

Proof of Lemma.  Place a Cartesian coordinate system so that
\[
A=(0,0), 
\quad
C=(c,0),
\]
where \(c=AC\in\Q\).  Write
\[
B=(x_B,y_B),
\quad
D=(x_D,y_D).
\]
Since \(AB\) and \(BC\) are rational, we have
\[
x_B^2 + y_B^2 = AB^2\in\Q,
\quad
(x_B - c)^2 + y_B^2 = BC^2\in\Q.
\]
Subtracting these two equations gives
\[
(x_B - c)^2 - x_B^2 \;=\; BC^2 - AB^2,
\]
whence
\[
-2c\,x_B + c^2 \;=\; BC^2 - AB^2
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
x_B \;=\;\frac{c^2 + AB^2 - BC^2}{2c}\;\in\;\Q.
\]
Then
\[
y_B^2 \;=\; AB^2 - x_B^2
\;\in\;\Q,
\]
so we may set
\[
y_B = +\alpha,
\quad
\alpha=\sqrt{\,AB^2 - x_B^2\,}\ge0.
\]
Similarly, since \(AD\) and \(CD\) are rational, one finds
\[
x_D \;=\;\frac{c^2 + AD^2 - CD^2}{2c}\;\in\;\Q,
\quad
y_D = \pm\beta,
\quad
\beta=\sqrt{\,AD^2 - x_D^2\,}\ge0.
\]
We choose the sign of \(\beta\) so that \(B\) and \(D\) lie on opposite sides of the line \(AC\); then \(BD\) crosses \(AC\) in the interior.  Now
\[
BD^2 \;=\;(x_B - x_D)^2 + (\alpha -(-\beta))^2 
\;=\;(x_B - x_D)^2 + (\alpha+\beta)^2
\;\in\;\Q.
\]
But \((x_B - x_D)^2\) is rational and \(\alpha^2+\beta^2\) is rational, so
\[
(\alpha+\beta)^2 \;=\;\bigl(\alpha^2+\beta^2\bigr) + 2\alpha\beta
\;\in\;\Q
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\alpha\beta\in\Q.
\]
Thus in the field \(\Q(\alpha,\beta)\) we know
\[
\alpha^2,\;\beta^2,\;\alpha\beta\in\Q.
\]

Next, the line \(BD\) is parametrized by
\[
(x,y) \;=\; \bigl(x_B,y_B\bigr) + t\bigl(x_D-x_B,\;y_D-y_B\bigr),
\]
so its intersection \(E\) with the \(x\)–axis \(y=0\) occurs when
\[
y_B + t\,(y_D - y_B) \;=\; 0
\;\;\Longrightarrow\;\;
\alpha + t(-\beta-\alpha)=0
\;\;\Longrightarrow\;\;
t=\frac{\alpha}{\alpha+\beta}.
\]
Hence the \(x\)–coordinate of \(E\) is
\[
x_E 
= x_B \;+\;\frac{\alpha}{\alpha+\beta}\,(x_D - x_B)
= \frac{\alpha\,x_D + \beta\,x_B}{\alpha+\beta}.
\]
We claim \(x_E\in\Q\).  Indeed multiply numerator and denominator by \(\alpha-\beta\): 
\[
x_E
=\frac{(\alpha\,x_D + \beta\,x_B)(\alpha-\beta)}{(\alpha+\beta)(\alpha-\beta)}
=\frac{\alpha^2x_D - \alpha\beta x_D + \alpha\beta x_B - \beta^2x_B}
{\alpha^2 - \beta^2}.
\]
But \(\alpha^2,\beta^2,\alpha\beta,x_B,x_D\in\Q\), so both the numerator and the denominator lie in \(\Q\).  Consequently \(x_E\in\Q\).  Therefore
\[
AE = x_E\in\Q,
\quad
EC = c - x_E\in\Q.
\]
Finally, since 
\[
BE = t\cdot BD
\quad\text{and}\quad
DE = (1-t)\cdot BD,
\]
with \(BD\in\Q\) and
\[
t=\frac{\alpha}{\alpha+\beta}
=\frac{\alpha(\alpha-\beta)}{\alpha^2-\beta^2}
\;\in\;\Q,
\]
we conclude
\[
BE,\;DE\;\in\;\Q.
\]
This completes the proof of the lemma.  \(\Box\)

■  Completion of the proof of the problem.  Let \(\mathcal P\) be a convex \(n\)-gon all of whose sides and all of whose diagonals have rational lengths.  Draw all of its diagonals.  Then every side of every small polygon in the resulting dissection is a subsegment either of an original side of \(\mathcal P\) (hence rational by hypothesis) or of one of its diagonals.

Fix one diagonal \(d\) of \(\mathcal P\), say \(d=V_iV_j\).  That diagonal is crossed in its interior by exactly those diagonals \(V_aV_b\) for which the four vertices \(V_i,V_a,V_j,V_b\) appear in cyclic order around \(\mathcal P\).  Each crossing point
\[
P_{a,b} \;=\; d\;\cap\;V_aV_b
\]
splits \(d\) into two segments \(V_iP_{a,b}\) and \(P_{a,b}V_j\).  By the lemma (applied to the quadrilateral \(V_i,V_a,V_j,V_b\)), both of these have rational length.  Since there are only finitely many such crossing points on \(d\), one may list them in order along \(d\) from \(V_i\) to \(V_j\).  The consecutive subsegments of \(d\) between
\[
V_i,\;P_{a_1,b_1},\;P_{a_2,b_2},\;\dots,\;P_{a_k,b_k},\;V_j
\]
are then differences of rational numbers, hence themselves rational.  

Doing this for each diagonal of \(\mathcal P\) shows that every subsegment of every diagonal (and likewise every original side) has rational length.  But these subsegments are exactly the edges of the polygons in the dissection.  Therefore all side-lengths in the dissection are rational, as claimed.  \(\Box\)
ground_truth_solution:
Suppose $A B$ is a side of a polygon in the dissection, lying on diagonal $X Y$, with $X, A$, $B, Y$ in that order. Then

$$
A B=X Y-X A-Y B
$$

In this way, we see that it actually just suffices to prove the result for a quadrilateral.
We present two approaches to this end.
гЂђ First approach (trig). Consider quadrilateral $A B C D$. There are twelve angles one can obtain using three of its four vertices, three at each vertex; denote this set of $12$ angles by $S$ Note that:

- The law of cosines implies $\cos \theta \in \mathbb{Q}$ for each $\theta \in S$.
- Hence, $(\sin \theta)^{2} \in \mathbb{Q}$ for $\theta \in S$. (This is because $\sin \theta^{2}+\cos ^{2} \theta$.)

We say two angles $\theta_{1}$ and $\theta_{2}$ are equivalent if $\frac{\sin \theta_{1}}{\sin \theta_{2}}$ This is the same as saying, when $\sin \theta_{1}$ and $\sin \theta_{2}$ are written in simplest radical form, the part under the square root is the same.

Now we contend:
Claim - The angles $\angle B A C, \angle C A D, \angle B A D$ are equivalent.
Proof. Note that

$$
\mathbb{Q} \ni \cos (\angle B A D)=\cos \angle B A C \cos \angle C A D-\sin \angle B A C \sin \angle C A D
$$
so $\angle B A C$ and $\angle C A D$ are equivalent. Then
$$
\sin (\angle B A D)=\sin \angle B A C \cos \angle C A D+\cos \angle B A C \sin \angle C A D
$$

implies $\angle B A D$ is equivalent to those two.

Claim - The angles $\angle B A D, \angle D B A, \angle A D B$ are equivalent.
Proof. Law of sines on $\triangle B A D$.
Iterating the argument implies that all angles are equivalent.
Now, if $A B$ and $C D$ meet at $E$, the law of sines on $\triangle A E B$, etc. implies the result.

I Second approach (barycentric coordinates). To do this, we apply barycentric coordinates. Consider quadrilateral $A B D C$ (note the changed order of vertices), with $A=(1,0,0), B=(0,1,0), C=(0,0,1)$. Let $D=(x, y, z)$, with $x+y+z=1$. By hypothesis, each of the numbers

$$
\begin{aligned}
-a^{2} y z+b^{2}(1-x) z+c^{2}(1-x) y & =A D^{2} \\
a^{2}(1-y) z+b^{2} z x+c^{2}(1-y) x & =B D^{2} \\
-a^{2}(1-z) y-b^{2}(1-z) x+c^{2} x y & =C D^{2}
\end{aligned}
$$

is rational. Let $W=a^{2} y z+b^{2} z x+c^{2} x y$. Then,

$$
\begin{aligned}
b^{2} z+c^{2} y & =A D^{2}+W \\
a^{2} z+c^{2} x & =B D^{2}+W \\
a^{2} y+b^{2} x & =C D^{2}+W
\end{aligned}
$$

This implies that $A D^{2}+B D^{2}+2 W-c^{2}=2 S_{C} z$ and cyclically (as usual $2 S_{C}=a^{2}+b^{2}-c^{2}$ ). If any of $S_{A}, S_{B}, S_{C}$ are zero, then we deduce $W$ is rational. Otherwise, we have that

$$
1=x+y+z=\sum_{\mathrm{cyc}} \frac{A D^{2}+B D^{2}+2 W-c^{2}}{2 S_{C}}
$$
which implies that $W$ is rational, because it appears with coefficient $\frac{1}{S_{A}}+\frac{1}{S_{B}}+\frac{1}{S_{C}} \neq 0$ (since $S_{B C}+S_{C A}+S_{A B}$ is actually the area of $A B C$ ).

Hence from the rationality of $W$, we deduce that $x$ is rational as long as $S_{A} \neq 0$, and similarly for the others. So at most one of $x, y, z$ is irrational, but since $x+y+z=1$ this implies they are all rational.

Finally, if $P=\overline{A D} \cap \overline{B C}$ then $A P=\frac{1}{y+z} A D$, so $A P$ is rational too, completing the proof.

Remark. After the reduction to quadrilateral, a third alternate approach goes by quoting Putnam $2018$ A6, reproduced below:

Four points are given in the plane, with no three collinear, such that the squares of the $\binom{4}{2}=6$ pairwise distances are all rational. Show that the ratio of the areas between any two of the $\binom{4}{3}=4$ triangles determined by these points is also rational.

If $A B C D$ is the quadrilateral, the heights from $C$ and $D$ to $A B$ have rational ratio. Letting $P=A C \cap B D$, we see $A P / A B$ can be shown as rational via coordinates, as needed.

problem:
Let \(a, b, c\) be positive reals. Prove that

\[
\left(a^{5}-a^{2}+3\right)\left(b^{5}-b^{2}+3\right)\left(c^{5}-c^{2}+3\right) \geq(a+b+c)^{3} .
\]
solution:
To prove the inequality

$$
\left(a^{5}-a^{2}+3\right)\left(b^{5}-b^{2}+3\right)\left(c^{5}-c^{2}+3\right) \geq (a+b+c)^{3}
$$

for all positive real numbers $a, b, c$, we proceed in two key steps.

---

### **Step 1: Inequality for Each Individual Term**

We begin by analyzing a single factor of the left-hand side:

$$
a^5 - a^2 + 3
$$

We aim to show that this is at least $a^3 + 2$. Consider the difference:

$$
a^5 - a^2 + 3 - (a^3 + 2) = a^5 - a^3 - a^2 + 1
$$

Factor this expression:

$$
a^5 - a^3 - a^2 + 1 = (a^3 - 1)(a^2 - 1)
$$

Now, analyze the sign of this expression:

- If $a \geq 1$, then both $a^3 - 1 \geq 0$ and $a^2 - 1 \geq 0$, so the product is non-negative.
- If $a < 1$, then both $a^3 - 1 < 0$ and $a^2 - 1 < 0$, so the product is still non-negative.

Thus, in all cases, the expression is non-negative, and we conclude:

$$
a^5 - a^2 + 3 \geq a^3 + 2
$$

This inequality holds for all positive real $a$. Similarly, we have:

$$
b^5 - b^2 + 3 \geq b^3 + 2, \quad c^5 - c^2 + 3 \geq c^3 + 2
$$

Therefore, multiplying all three inequalities together:

$$
(a^5 - a^2 + 3)(b^5 - b^2 + 3)(c^5 - c^2 + 3) \geq (a^3 + 2)(b^3 + 2)(c^3 + 2)
$$

---

### **Step 2: Applying Hölder's Inequality**

We now show that:

$$
(a^3 + 2)(b^3 + 2)(c^3 + 2) \geq (a + b + c)^3
$$

We apply **Hölder's inequality** in the following form:

> For non-negative real numbers $x_1, x_2, x_3$, $y_1, y_2, y_3$, $z_1, z_2, z_3$, the following inequality holds:
> $$
> (x_1 + x_2 + x_3)(y_1 + y_2 + y_3)(z_1 + z_2 + z_3) \geq \left( (x_1 y_1 z_1)^{1/3} + (x_2 y_2 z_2)^{1/3} + (x_3 y_3 z_3)^{1/3} \right)^3
> $$

Let us define the three sequences as follows:

- First sequence: $x_1 = a^3, x_2 = 1, x_3 = 1$
- Second sequence: $y_1 = 1, y_2 = b^3, y_3 = 1$
- Third sequence: $z_1 = 1, z_2 = 1, z_3 = c^3$

Then the left-hand side becomes:

$$
(a^3 + 2)(1 + b^3 + 1)(1 + 1 + c^3) = (a^3 + 2)(b^3 + 2)(c^3 + 2)
$$

The right-hand side becomes:

$$
\left( (a^3 \cdot 1 \cdot 1)^{1/3} + (1 \cdot b^3 \cdot 1)^{1/3} + (1 \cdot 1 \cdot c^3)^{1/3} \right)^3 = (a + b + c)^3
$$

Hence, by Hölder's inequality:

$$
(a^3 + 2)(b^3 + 2)(c^3 + 2) \geq (a + b + c)^3
$$

---

### **Conclusion**

Combining the results from both steps:

$$
(a^5 - a^2 + 3)(b^5 - b^2 + 3)(c^5 - c^2 + 3) \geq (a^3 + 2)(b^3 + 2)(c^3 + 2) \geq (a + b + c)^3
$$

Thus, the original inequality is proven.

$$
\boxed{(a^{5} - a^{2} + 3)(b^{5} - b^{2} + 3)(c^{5} - c^{2} + 3) \geq (a + b + c)^{3}}
$$
feedback: The model provides a correct and clear solution.
ground_truth_solution:
Observe that for all real numbers $a$, the inequality

$$
a^{5}-a^{2}+3 \geq a^{3}+2
$$
holds. Then the problem follows by HГ¶lder in the form
$$
\left(a^{3}+1+1\right)\left(1+b^{3}+1\right)\left(1+1+c^{3}\right) \geq(a+b+c)^{3} \text {. }
$$
llm_summary:
The proof first shows that for any positive real $a$, one has
\[
a^5 - a^2 + 3 - (a^3 + 2) = (a^3 - 1)(a^2 - 1) \ge 0,
\]
so $a^5 - a^2 + 3 \ge a^3 + 2$.  By symmetry the same holds for $b,c$, and multiplying yields
\[(a^5 - a^2 + 3)(b^5 - b^2 + 3)(c^5 - c^2 + 3) \ge (a^3 + 2)(b^3 + 2)(c^3 + 2).
\]
Finally, the standard three-term Hölder inequality with sequences $(a^3,1,1)$, $(1,b^3,1)$, $(1,1,c^3)$ gives
\[(a^3+2)(b^3+2)(c^3+2) \ge (a+b+c)^3,
\]
completing the proof.

problem: Let \( k > 0 \) be a fixed integer. Compute the minimum integer \( N \) (in terms of \( k \)) for which there exists a set of \( 2k+1 \) distinct positive integers that has a sum greater than \( N \), but for which every subset of size \( k \) has a sum at most \( N/2 \).
solution:
Let  

S={a1<a2<⋯<a2k+1}⊂ℕ ,  k≥1  

be a set that satisfies  

(i) a1+⋯+a2k+1>N,  
(ii)  every k–element subset of S has sum ≤N/2.

Denote  

L:=ak+2+⋯+a2k+1     (the sum of the largest k elements)  
M:=a1+⋯+ak+1         (the sum of the smallest k+1 elements)

so that  

a1+⋯+a2k+1=M+L.        (1)

Because the k–element subset {ak+2,…,a2k+1} is one of the subsets in (ii),

L≤N/2.                                               (2)

The complementary (k+1)–element subset {a1,…,ak+1} therefore satisfies, by (i) and (2),

M=(a1+⋯+a2k+1)−L> N−N/2=N/2, whence M>L and  
M≥L+1.                                               (3)

--------------------------------------------------------------------
1.  A lower bound for the smallest element  
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Between a1 and ak+1 there are k−1 intermediate elements, hence ak+1≥a1+k.  
For j=1,…,k we consequently have  

ak+1+j≥ak+1+j≥(a1+k)+j=a1+k+j.                      (4)

Adding (4) for j=1,…,k gives

L=∑j=1k ak+1+j ≥∑j=1k (a1+k+j)  
  = k(a1+k)+k(k+1)/2 = k a1+k2+k(k+1)/2.            (5)

With (3) we now get  

1≤M−L = (a1+⋯+ak+1)−L ≤ a1−k2,  

so that                                                    

a1 ≥ k2+1.                                          (6)

--------------------------------------------------------------------
2.  The minimal possible value of L  
--------------------------------------------------------------------
The number ak+1 is at least a1+k by (4); inserting (6) yields ak+1≥k2+k+1.  
Using this together with (4) gives the chain

ak+1+j ≥ (k2+k+1)+j (j=1,…,k).

Hence

L ≥ ∑j=1k (k2+k+1+j)  
  = k(k2+k+1)+k(k+1)/2  
  = k3+k2+k + (k2+k)/2  
  = (2k3+3k2+3k)/2.                                (7)

--------------------------------------------------------------------
3.  A universal lower bound for N  
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Because of (2) and (7),

N ≥ 2L ≥ 2k3+3k2+3k.                               (8)

Thus no N smaller than  

N(k):=2k3+3k2+3k                                   (9)

can possibly work.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
4.  Showing that the bound is attainable  
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Consider the consecutive integers  

S0={k2+1,k2+2,…,k2+2k+1}.                          (10)

They are 2k+1 distinct positive numbers.  
For this set

L0= (k2+k+2)+(k2+k+3)+⋯+(k2+2k+1)  
   = k(k2+k+1)+k(k+1)/2  
   = (2k3+3k2+3k)/2 = N(k)/2.                      (11)

Their total sum is

∑S0 = (2k+1)(k2+k+1)=2L0+1=N(k)+1>N(k).            (12)

The largest possible sum of any k–element subset of S0 is L0, so every k–subset indeed sums to at most N(k)/2.  Consequently S0 satisfies conditions (i)–(ii) with N=N(k).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
5.  Conclusion  
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Inequality (8) shows that no smaller N is possible, while (10)–(12) exhibit a set that works for N=N(k). Therefore

  minimum N = 2k3 + 3k2 + 3k.
feedback: The solution is correct although it is hard to understand both because of a bug in the LaTex format and of skipping some trivial steps
ground_truth_solution:
The answer is $N=k\left(2 k^{2}+3 k+3\right)$ given by

$$
S=\left\{k^{2}+1, k^{2}+2, \ldots, k^{2}+2 k+1\right\} .
$$

To show this is best possible, let the set be $S=\left\{a_{0}<a_{1}<\cdots<a_{2 k}\right\}$ so that the hypothesis becomes

$$
\begin{aligned}
N+1 & \leq a_{0}+a_{1}+\cdots+a_{2 k} \\
N / 2 & \geq a_{k+1}+\cdots+a_{2 k} .
\end{aligned}
$$

Subtracting twice the latter from the former gives

$$
\begin{aligned}
a_{0} & \geq 1+\left(a_{k+1}-a_{1}\right)+\left(a_{k+2}-a_{2}\right)+\cdots+\left(a_{2 k}-a_{k}\right) \\
& \geq 1+\underbrace{k+k+\cdots+k}_{k \text { terms }}=1+k^{2} .
\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}
N / 2 & \geq a_{k+1}+\cdots+a_{2 k} \\
& \geq\left(a_{0}+(k+1)\right)+\left(a_{0}+(k+2)\right)+\cdots+\left(a_{0}+2 k\right) \\
& =k \cdot a_{0}+((k+1)+\cdots+2 k) \\
& \geq k\left(k^{2}+1\right)+k \cdot \frac{3 k+1}{2}
\end{aligned}
$$

so $N \geq k\left(2 k^{2}+3 k+3\right)$.
Remark. The exact value of $N$ is therefore very superficial. From playing with these concrete examples we find out we are essentially just trying to find an increasing set $S$ obeying

$$
a_{0}+a_{1}+\cdots+a_{k}>a_{k+1}+\cdots+a_{2 k}
$$
and indeed given a sequence satisfying these properties one simply sets $N=2\left(a_{k+1}+\cdots+a_{2 k}\right)$. Therefore we can focus almost entirely on $a_{i}$ and not $N$.

Remark. It is relatively straightforward to figure out what is going on based on the small cases. For example, one can work out by hand that

- $\{2,3,4\}$ is optimal for $k=1$
- $\{5,6,7,8,9\}$ is optimal for $k=2$,
- $\{10,11,12,13,14,15,16\}$ is optimal for $k=3$.

In all the examples, the $a_{i}$ are an arithmetic progression of difference $1$, so that $a_{j}-a_{i} \geq j-i$ is a sharp for all $i<j$, and thus this estimate may be used freely without loss of sharpness;
applying it in $(\star)$ gives a lower bound on $a_{0}$ which is then good enough to get a lower bound on $N$ matching the equality cases we found empirically.

problem: Let \( S \) be a set containing \( n^2 + n - 1 \) elements. Suppose that the \( n \)-element subsets of \( S \) are partitioned into two classes. Prove that there are at least \( n \) pairwise disjoint sets in the same class.
solution:
Solution.

We shall prove the following stronger statement.

Theorem  (Cockayne – Lorimer, 1975).  
Let \(r\ge 2,\;k\ge 1\) and \(m\ge 1\) be integers.  
In every colouring with \(r\) colours of the \(m\)-element subsets of a set
\[V\qquad |V|=(m-1)k+k \;=\;m k+(k-1)\]
there is a monochromatic collection of \(k\) pairwise disjoint \(m\)-subsets.  

For the present problem we have \(r=2,\;m=n,\;k=n\); the size of the ground
set is therefore \(n\cdot n+(n-1)=n^{2}+n-1\), exactly the number that
occurs in the statement.  Hence the desired result is the special case
\((r,m,k)=(2,n,n)\) of the theorem.  We give a complete proof of the
two–colour case, following the original argument of Cockayne and
Lorimer, and afterwards quote the very short deduction of the required
corollary.

Throughout the proof we call the two colours red and blue.

Lemma 1 (induction step).   
Let \(m\ge 1,\;k\ge 2\) and
\[|V|=(m-1)k+k.\]
Assume that every two–colouring of the \(m\)-subsets of any
set of size \((m-1)(k-1)+(k-1)=mk-1\)
contains a monochromatic matching of size \(k-1\).
Then every colouring of the \(m\)-subsets of \(V\) contains a
monochromatic matching of size \(k\).

Proof.  
Pick an arbitrary element \(x\in V\).
Write  
\(\mathcal R(x)\) for the family of red \(m\)-subsets that contain \(x\) and  
\(\mathcal B(x)\) for the family of blue \(m\)-subsets that contain \(x\).
Each of the numbers
\(\lvert\mathcal R(x)\rvert,\;\lvert\mathcal B(x)\rvert\)
is at least half of the total number
\(\binom{|V|-1}{m-1}\), hence one of the two families
contains at least
\[
\frac{1}{2}\binom{|V|-1}{m-1}\ \ge\ \binom{mk-1}{m-1}
\]
members.
Without loss of generality we assume that the larger family is
\(\mathcal R(x)\).

Delete \(x\).
Because \(x\) is contained in every member of \(\mathcal R(x)\),
each set \(R\in\mathcal R(x)\) contributes the
\((m-1)\)-subset \(R\setminus\{x\}\) of \(V\setminus\{x\}\);
altogether we obtain at least
\(\binom{mk-1}{m-1}\)
\((m-1)\)-subsets of \(V\setminus\{x\}\), all coloured {\em red\/}
by inheritance.

Now  
\(|V\setminus\{x\}|=mk-1=(m-1)(k-1)+(k-1)\).
By the induction hypothesis applied to the
\((m-1)\)-subsets of \(V\setminus\{x\}\)
there is a red collection  
\(D_{1},\dots ,D_{k-1}\subset V\setminus\{x\}\) of size \(m-1\)
that are pairwise disjoint.
Put
\(R_{i}=D_{i}\cup\{x\}\;(1\le i\le k-1)\);  
these are red \(m\)-sets that intersect only in the point \(x\).

Finally, the set  
\(W=V\setminus\bigl(\{x\}\cup D_{1}\cup\cdots\cup D_{k-1}\bigr)\)
contains
\[
|V|-\bigl[1+(k-1)(m-1)\bigr]\;=\;(mk+k-1)-\bigl(mk-m+1\bigr)=m,
\]
hence itself is an \(m\)-element subset of \(V\).
This set \(W\) is disjoint from every \(R_{i}\;(1\le i\le k-1)\);
if \(W\) is red we have obtained the required \(k\)
pairwise disjoint red \(m\)-subsets
\(R_{1},\dots ,R_{k-1},W\).
If, on the other hand, \(W\) is blue then the singleton family
\(\{W\}\) is a blue matching of size \(1\)
that is disjoint from the (still red) matching
\(R_{1},\dots ,R_{k-1}\);
consequently the colouring contains a monochromatic matching of size
\(k\) as well.
∎



Lemma 2 (basis).  
For \(k=1\) the statement is obvious: every \(m\)-subset by itself
constitutes a monochromatic matching of size \(1\).

Induction on \(k\).  
Lemma 1 shows that the truth of the theorem for
\(k-1\) implies its truth for \(k\);
with Lemma 2 as basis this proves the theorem for every positive \(k\).

\bigskip
\noindent{\bf End of the proof for two colours.}  
Take \(m=n,\;k=n\).
Because \((m-1)k+k=n^{2}+n-1\),
the theorem tells us that the \(n\)-element subsets of a set
\(S\) with \(|S|=n^{2}+n-1\) coloured red/blue
always contain \(n\) monochromatic pairwise disjoint subsets.
This is exactly the assertion of the problem statement. ∎
feedback: OK, though the model had the ability to "search" while a human contestant will probably not have seen such a research result.
ground_truth_solution:
## Problem statement

Let $S$ be a set containing $n^{2}+n-1$ elements. Suppose that the $n$-element subsets of $S$ are partitioned into two classes. Prove that there are at least $n$ pairwise disjoint sets in the same class.

We present two solutions which are really equivalent, but phrased differently. We refer to the two classes as "red" and "blue", respectively.

гЂђI First solution (Grant Yu). We define a set of $n+1$ elements to be useful if it has $n$-element subsets in each class.

Consider a maximal collection of disjoint useful sets and assume there are $p$ such sets. Then, let $T$ be the set of elements remaining (i.e. not in one of chosen useful sets).

Claim - All subsets of $T$ of size $n$ are the same color.
Proof. Assume there was a red set $R$ in $T$. Replace the elements of $R$ one by one until we get to any other subset $R^{\prime}$ of $T$. At each step, because no sets of $T$ form a useful set, the set remains red - so $R^{\prime}$ is red too. Since $R^{\prime}$ is arbitrary, this proves the claim.

We have $|T|=n^{2}+n-1-p(n+1)$, and in particular $p<n$. WLOG all sets in $T$ are red. We can extract another red set from each of our chosen useful sets. So we can get at least

$$
p+\left\lfloor\frac{|T|}{n}\right\rfloor=p+\left\lfloor n+1-p-\frac{1+p}{n}\right\rfloor \geq p+(n-p)=n .
$$

## гЂђ Second solution (by induction). We prove more strongly that:

Claim - Let $S$ be a set containing $k \cdot(n+1)-1$ elements. Then we can find $k$ pairwise disjoint sets of the same color.

The proof is by induction on $k \geq 1$. The base case $k=1$ this is immediate; $\binom{S}{n}$ is a single set.

For the inductive step, assume for contradiction the problem fails. Let $T$ be any subset of $S$ of size $(k-1)(n+1)-1$. By the induction hypothesis, among the subsets of $T$ alone, we can already find $k-1$ pairwise disjoint sets of the same color. Now $S \backslash T$ has size $n+1$, and so we would have to have that all $\binom{n+1}{n}$ subsets of $S \backslash T$ are the same color.

By varying $T$, the set $S \backslash T$ ranges over all of $\binom{S}{k+1}$. This causes all sets to be the same color, contradiction.

Remark. Victor Wang writes the following:
I don't really like this problem, but I think the main motivation for generalizing the problem is that the original problem doesn't allow you to look at small cases. (Also, it's not initially clear where the $n^{2}+n-1$ comes from.) And
pretty much the simplest way to get lots of similarly-flavored small cases is to start with $k=2,3$ in "find the smallest $N(n, k)$ such that when we partition the $n$-subsets of a $\geq N(n, k)$-set into $2$ classes, we can find some $k$ pairwise disjoint sets in the same class".

problem:
Let \( ABC \) be an acute triangle with \(\omega\), \(S\), and \(R\) being its incircle, circumcircle, and circumradius, respectively. Circle \(\omega_{A}\) is tangent internally to \(S\) at \(A\) and tangent externally to \(\omega\). Circle \(S_{A}\) is tangent internally to \(S\) at \(A\) and tangent internally to \(\omega\).

Let \(P_{A}\) and \(Q_{A}\) denote the centers of \(\omega_{A}\) and \(S_{A}\), respectively. Define points \(P_{B}\), \(Q_{B}\), \(P_{C}\), \(Q_{C}\) analogously. Prove that

\[
8 P_{A} Q_{A} \cdot P_{B} Q_{B} \cdot P_{C} Q_{C} \leq R^{3}
\]

with equality if and only if triangle \(ABC\) is equilateral.
solution:
Let \(O\) and \(I\) be the circumcenter and incenter of \(\triangle ABC\), respectively. Let \(R\) be the circumradius and \(r\) be the inradius. We are given Euler's theorem in a triangle: \(OI^2 = R(R-2r)\).

Let \(P_A\) be the center of \(\omega_A\) and \(r_A\) be its radius.
Circle \(\omega_A\) is tangent internally to the circumcircle \(S\) at \(A\). This means \(P_A\) lies on the line segment \(OA\), and \(OP_A = R-r_A\). So \(AP_A = r_A\).
Circle \(\omega_A\) is tangent externally to the incircle \(\omega\). This means \(P_A I = r_A+r\).

Let \(Q_A\) be the center of \(S_A\) and \(s_A\) be its radius.
Circle \(S_A\) is tangent internally to \(S\) at \(A\). This means \(Q_A\) lies on the line segment \(OA\), and \(OQ_A = R-s_A\). So \(AQ_A = s_A\).
Circle \(S_A\) is tangent internally to \(\omega\). This means \(\omega\) is contained in \(S_A\) and they are tangent. Thus, \(s_A > r\), and the distance \(Q_A I = s_A-r\).

The points \(P_A\) and \(Q_A\) both lie on the line \(OA\). Their positions relative to \(O\) are \(P_A = A - r_A \frac{A-O}{R}\) and \(Q_A = A - s_A \frac{A-O}{R}\).
The distance \(P_A Q_A = |AP_A - AQ_A| = |r_A - s_A|\).

Let's derive the radii \(r_A\) and \(s_A\).
Place \(O\) at the origin \((0,0)\). Let \(A\) be the point \((R,0)\).
Then \(P_A\) is at \((R-r_A, 0)\) and \(Q_A\) is at \((R-s_A, 0)\).
Let \(I=(x_I, y_I)\). Then \(OI^2 = x_I^2+y_I^2\). The projection of \(OI\) onto \(OA\) is \(x_I\). Note that \(x_I = OI \cos(\angle AOI)\).
In \(\triangle AOI\), by the Law of Cosines, \(AI^2 = OA^2+OI^2-2OA \cdot OI \cos(\angle AOI) = R^2+OI^2-2R x_I\).
So \(x_I = \frac{R^2+OI^2-AI^2}{2R}\).

For \(P_A\): In \(\triangle OIP_A\), \(P_A\) is on \(OA\).
\(P_A I^2 = ( (R-r_A)-x_I )^2 + y_I^2 = (R-r_A)^2 - 2(R-r_A)x_I + x_I^2+y_I^2 = (R-r_A)^2 - 2(R-r_A)x_I + OI^2\).
Since \(P_A I = r_A+r\), we have \((r_A+r)^2 = (R-r_A)^2+OI^2-2(R-r_A)x_I\).
\(r_A^2+2rr_A+r^2 = R^2-2Rr_A+r_A^2+OI^2-2Rx_I+2r_Ax_I\).
\(2rr_A+2Rr_A-2r_Ax_I = R^2+OI^2-r^2-2Rx_I\).
\(2r_A(R+r-x_I) = R^2+OI^2-r^2-2Rx_I\).
The right side is \(R^2+OI^2-r^2-2R\left(\frac{R^2+OI^2-AI^2}{2R}\right) = R^2+OI^2-r^2-(R^2+OI^2-AI^2) = AI^2-r^2\).
So \(2r_A(R+r-x_I) = AI^2-r^2\).
The term \(R+r-x_I = R+r - \frac{R^2+OI^2-AI^2}{2R} = \frac{2R^2+2Rr-R^2-OI^2+AI^2}{2R} = \frac{R^2+2Rr-OI^2+AI^2}{2R}\).
Using Euler's Theorem \(OI^2=R(R-2r)\):
\(R+r-x_I = \frac{R^2+2Rr-R(R-2r)+AI^2}{2R} = \frac{R^2+2Rr-R^2+2Rr+AI^2}{2R} = \frac{4Rr+AI^2}{2R}\).
So \(2r_A \frac{AI^2+4Rr}{2R} = AI^2-r^2\).
\(r_A = \frac{R(AI^2-r^2)}{AI^2+4Rr}\).
We know \(AI = r/\sin(A/2)\). So \(AI^2=r^2/\sin^2(A/2)\).
\(AI^2-r^2 = r^2/\sin^2(A/2) - r^2 = r^2 \frac{1-\sin^2(A/2)}{\sin^2(A/2)} = r^2 \frac{\cos^2(A/2)}{\sin^2(A/2)} = r^2\cot^2(A/2)\).
So \(r_A = \frac{R r^2\cot^2(A/2)}{r^2/\sin^2(A/2)+4Rr} = \frac{R r^2\cos^2(A/2)/\sin^2(A/2)}{r^2/\sin^2(A/2)+4Rr} = \frac{Rr^2\cos^2(A/2)}{r^2+4Rr\sin^2(A/2)}\).
\(r_A = \frac{Rr\cos^2(A/2)}{r+4R\sin^2(A/2)}\).

For \(Q_A\): In \(\triangle OIQ_A\), \(Q_A\) is on \(OA\).
\(Q_A I^2 = (R-s_A)^2 - 2(R-s_A)x_I + OI^2\).
Since \(Q_A I = s_A-r\), we have \((s_A-r)^2 = (R-s_A)^2+OI^2-2(R-s_A)x_I\).
This equation is obtained from the one for \(r_A\) by replacing \(r\) with \(-r\) and \(r_A\) with \(s_A\).
So \(2s_A(R-r-x_I) = AI^2-r^2\).
The term \(R-r-x_I = R-r - \frac{R^2+OI^2-AI^2}{2R} = \frac{2R^2-2Rr-R^2-OI^2+AI^2}{2R} = \frac{R^2-2Rr-OI^2+AI^2}{2R}\).
Using \(OI^2=R(R-2r)\):
\(R-r-x_I = \frac{R^2-2Rr-R(R-2r)+AI^2}{2R} = \frac{R^2-2Rr-R^2+2Rr+AI^2}{2R} = \frac{AI^2}{2R}\).
So \(2s_A \frac{AI^2}{2R} = AI^2-r^2\).
\(s_A = \frac{R(AI^2-r^2)}{AI^2} = \frac{R r^2\cot^2(A/2)}{r^2/\sin^2(A/2)} = \frac{R r^2\cos^2(A/2)/\sin^2(A/2)}{r^2/\sin^2(A/2)} = R\cos^2(A/2)\).
This is a known formula for such a circle. For \(S_A\) to contain \(\omega\) and be tangent internally, we need \(s_A > r\).
\(R\cos^2(A/2)>r \Leftrightarrow R(1+\cos A)/2 > r\). This inequality is known to hold for all non-degenerate triangles (equality for degenerate \(A=180^\circ, B=C=0\) if we have \(\cos((B-C)/2)=1\), \(1-\sin(A/2)=0\)). More precisely, \(2\sin(A/2)\cos((B-C)/2) \le 1+\sin^2(A/2)\) is equivalent to \((1-\sin(A/2))^2 + (\cos((B-C)/2)- \sin(A/2))^2 \ge 0\) if \(B=C\). It is \(2\sin(A/2) \le 1+\sin^2(A/2)\) which is \((1-\sin(A/2))^2 \ge 0\). The strict inequality \(s_A>r\) holds for non-degenerate triangles.

Now we calculate \(P_A Q_A = |r_A-s_A|\).
Since \(r+4R\sin^2(A/2) > r\), and \(\cos^2(A/2)>0\), it means \(r_A = \frac{Rr\cos^2(A/2)}{r+4R\sin^2(A/2)} < \frac{Rr\cos^2(A/2)}{r} = R\cos^2(A/2) = s_A\).
So \(P_A Q_A = s_A-r_A\).
\(P_A Q_A = R\cos^2(A/2) - \frac{Rr\cos^2(A/2)}{r+4R\sin^2(A/2)} = R\cos^2(A/2) \left(1 - \frac{r}{r+4R\sin^2(A/2)}\right)\).
\(P_A Q_A = R\cos^2(A/2) \left(\frac{r+4R\sin^2(A/2)-r}{r+4R\sin^2(A/2)}\right) = R\cos^2(A/2) \frac{4R\sin^2(A/2)}{r+4R\sin^2(A/2)}\).
The denominator is \(D_A = r+4R\sin^2(A/2)\). Using \(r=4R\prod \sin(A/2)\):
\(D_A = 4R\sin(A/2)\sin(B/2)\sin(C/2) + 4R\sin^2(A/2)\)
\(D_A = 4R\sin(A/2) (\sin(B/2)\sin(C/2) + \sin(A/2))\).
Since \(A/2+B/2+C/2 = \pi/2\), \(\sin(A/2) = \sin(\pi/2-(B/2+C/2)) = \cos((B+C)/2)\).
\(D_A = 4R\sin(A/2) (\sin(B/2)\sin(C/2) + \cos(B/2+C/2))\).
Using \(\cos(X+Y) = \cos X \cos Y - \sin X \sin Y\):
\(D_A = 4R\sin(A/2) (\sin(B/2)\sin(C/2) + \cos(B/2)\cos(C/2) - \sin(B/2)\sin(C/2))\).
\(D_A = 4R\sin(A/2)\cos(B/2)\cos(C/2)\).
Substituting this into the expression for \(P_A Q_A\):
\(P_A Q_A = \frac{R\cos^2(A/2) \cdot 4R\sin^2(A/2)}{4R\sin(A/2)\cos(B/2)\cos(C/2)} = \frac{R^2 \cdot 4\sin^2(A/2)\cos^2(A/2)}{4R\sin(A/2)\cos(B/2)\cos(C/2)}\).
\(P_A Q_A = \frac{R \sin(A/2)\cos^2(A/2)}{\cos(B/2)\cos(C/2)}\).
This formula is for \(P_A Q_A\). We need to compute the product \(P_A Q_A \cdot P_B Q_B \cdot P_C Q_C\).
Let \(c_A=\cos(A/2), s_A=\sin(A/2)\), etc.
The product is
\[ \left(\frac{R s_A c_A^2}{c_B c_C}\right) \cdot \left(\frac{R s_B c_B^2}{c_A c_C}\right) \cdot \left(\frac{R s_C c_C^2}{c_A c_B}\right) \]
\[ = R^3 \frac{s_A c_A^2 s_B c_B^2 s_C c_C^2}{c_B c_C c_A c_C c_A c_B} = R^3 \frac{s_A s_B s_C c_A^2 c_B^2 c_C^2}{(c_A c_B c_C)^2} \]
\[ = R^3 s_A s_B s_C = R^3 \sin(A/2)\sin(B/2)\sin(C/2). \]
The inequality to prove is \(8 P_A Q_A \cdot P_B Q_B \cdot P_C Q_C \leq R^3\).
Substituting the expression for the product:
\(8 R^3 \sin(A/2)\sin(B/2)\sin(C/2) \leq R^3\).
Since \(R>0\), we can divide by \(R^3\):
\(8 \sin(A/2)\sin(B/2)\sin(C/2) \leq 1\).
This is a well-known inequality in a triangle. It can be proven using Jensen's inequality on \(f(x)=\ln(\sin(x/2))\), or by using \(r = 4R\sin(A/2)\sin(B/2)\sin(C/2)\).
The inequality becomes \(8 \frac{r}{4R} \leq 1 \Leftrightarrow \frac{2r}{R} \leq 1 \Leftrightarrow R \geq 2r\).
This is Euler's inequality for triangles, which is true for all non-degenerate triangles.
Equality holds if and only if \(R=2r\), which is true if and only if \(\triangle ABC\) is equilateral.
If \(\triangle ABC\) is equilateral, then \(A=B=C=60^\circ\), so \(A/2=B/2=C/2=30^\circ\).
\(\sin(30^\circ)=1/2\). So \(8 \sin(A/2)\sin(B/2)\sin(C/2) = 8(1/2)(1/2)(1/2) = 8(1/8) = 1\).
Thus, equality holds if and only if \(\triangle ABC\) is equilateral.

The problem states that \(\triangle ABC\) is an acute triangle. The derivations of radii \(r_A, s_A\) and the identity \(D_A = 4R\sin(A/2)\cos(B/2)\cos(C/2)\) hold for any triangle. Euler's inequality \(R \geq 2r\) also holds for any triangle. The acuteness condition might be to ensure some geometric configurations or avoid \(P_A Q_A=0\) (which is not an issue for non-degenerate triangles from the formula). The derived value \(P_A Q_A = R \sin(A/2)\cos^2(A/2) / (\cos(B/2)\cos(C/2))\) is always positive for a non-degenerate triangle.

The proof is complete.

The final answer is $\boxed{8 P_{A} Q_{A} \cdot P_{B} Q_{B} \cdot P_{C} Q_{C} \leq R^{3}}$.
feedback: The solution doesn't prove that sin(A/2)*sin(B/2)*sin(C/2)<=1/8, but I think this follows easy using trigonometry formulas.
ground_truth_solution:
## Problem statement

Let $A B C$ be an acute triangle with $\omega, S$, and $R$ being its incircle, circumcircle, and circumradius, respectively. Circle $\omega_{A}$ is tangent internally to $S$ at $A$ and tangent externally to $\omega$. Circle $S_{A}$ is tangent internally to $S$ at $A$ and tangent internally to $\omega$.

Let $P_{A}$ and $Q_{A}$ denote the centers of $\omega_{A}$ and $S_{A}$, respectively. Define points $P_{B}$, $Q_{B}, P_{C}, Q_{C}$ analogously. Prove that

$$
8 P_{A} Q_{A} \cdot P_{B} Q_{B} \cdot P_{C} Q_{C} \leq R^{3}
$$
with equality if and only if triangle $A B C$ is equilateral.

It turns out we can compute $P_{A} Q_{A}$ explicitly. Let us invert around $A$ with radius $s-a$ (hence fixing the incircle) and then compose this with a reflection around the angle bisector of $\angle B A C$. We denote the image of the composed map via

$$
\bullet \mapsto \bullet^{*} \mapsto \bullet^{+}
$$

We overlay this inversion with the original diagram.
Let $P_{A} Q_{A}$ meet $\omega_{A}$ again at $P$ and $S_{A}$ again at $Q$. Now observe that $\omega_{A}^{*}$ is a line parallel to $S^{*}$; that is, it is perpendicular to $\overline{P Q}$. Moreover, it is tangent to $\omega^{*}=\omega$.

Now upon the reflection, we find that $\omega^{+}=\omega^{*}=\omega$, but line $\overline{P Q}$ gets mapped to the altitude from $A$ to $\overline{B C}$, since $\overline{P Q}$ originally contained the circumcenter $O$ (isogonal to the orthocenter). But this means that $\omega_{A}^{*}$ is none other than the $\overline{B C}$ ! Hence $P^{+}$is actually the foot of the altitude from $A$ onto $\overline{B C}$.

By similar work, we find that $Q^{+}$is the point on $\overline{A P^{+}}$such that $P^{+} Q^{+}=2 r$.


Now we can compute all the lengths directly. We have that

$$
A P_{A}=\frac{1}{2} A P=\frac{(s-a)^{2}}{2 A P^{+}}=\frac{1}{2}(s-a)^{2} \cdot \frac{1}{h_{a}}
$$
and
$$
A Q_{A}=\frac{1}{2} A Q=\frac{(s-a)^{2}}{2 A Q^{+}}=\frac{1}{2}(s-a)^{2} \cdot \frac{1}{h_{a}-2 r}
$$

where $h_{a}=\frac{2 K}{a}$ is the length of the $A$-altitude, with $K$ the area of $A B C$ as usual. Now it follows that

$$
P_{A} Q_{A}=\frac{1}{2}(s-a)^{2}\left(\frac{2 r}{h_{a}\left(h_{a}-2 r\right)}\right) .
$$

This can be simplified, as

$$
h_{a}-2 r=\frac{2 K}{a}-\frac{2 K}{s}=2 K \cdot \frac{s-a}{a s}
$$

Hence

$$
P_{A} Q_{A}=\frac{a^{2} r s(s-a)}{4 K^{2}}=\frac{a^{2}(s-a)}{4 K}
$$

Hence, the problem is just asking us to show that

$$
a^{2} b^{2} c^{2}(s-a)(s-b)(s-c) \leq 8(R K)^{3}
$$

Using $a b c=4 R K$ and $(s-a)(s-b)(s-c)=\frac{1}{s} K^{2}=r K$, we find that this becomes

$$
2(s-a)(s-b)(s-c) \leq R K \Longleftrightarrow 2 r \leq R
$$
which follows immediately from $I O^{2}=R(R-2 r)$. Alternatively, one may rewrite this as Schur's Inequality in the form
$$
a b c \geq(-a+b+c)(a-b+c)(a+b-c)
$$
llm_summary: The proof places the circumcenter \(O\) at the origin and \(A=(R,0)\), then expresses the centers \(P_A\) and \(Q_A\) of the two tangent circles on the ray \(OA\) by computing their distances \(r_A\) and \(s_A\) via the Law of Cosines in triangles \(OIP_A\) and \(OIQ_A\), using Euler’s relation \(OI^2=R(R-2r)\). It then derives an explicit formula for \(P_AQ_A\), shows that the cyclic product is \(R^3\sin rac A2\sin rac B2\sin rac C2\), and reduces the desired inequality to \(8\sin rac A2\sin rac B2\sin rac C2\le1\), i.e.\ Euler’s inequality \(2r\le R\), with equality iff \(ABC\) is equilateral.

problem: Prove that for each positive integer $n$, there are pairwise relatively prime integers $k_{0}, \ldots, k_{n}$, all strictly greater than $1$, such that $k_{0} k_{1} \ldots k_{n}-1$ is the product of two consecutive integers.
solution:
To prove that for each positive integer \(n\), there exist pairwise relatively prime integers \(k_0, \ldots, k_n\), all strictly greater than 1, such that \(k_0 k_1 \cdots k_n - 1\) is the product of two consecutive integers, proceed as follows.

The goal is to find integers \(k_0, \ldots, k_n\) such that their product equals \(m^2 + m + 1\) for some integer \(m\), because then the product minus one is \(m(m+1)\), which is the product of two consecutive integers \(m\) and \(m+1\).

Choose \(n+1\) distinct prime numbers \(q_0, q_1, \ldots, q_n\) such that for each \(q_i\), the equation \(x^2 + x + 1 \equiv 0 \pmod{q_i}\) has a solution. This condition holds for \(q_i = 3\) or \(q_i \equiv 1 \pmod{3}\). Since there are infinitely many primes congruent to 1 modulo 3 by Dirichlet's theorem on arithmetic progressions, and including the prime 3, such a set of \(n+1\) primes exists for any \(n\).

For each prime \(q_i\), let \(a_i\) be a solution to \(x^2 + x + 1 \equiv 0 \pmod{q_i}\). (Note that there may be one or two solutions modulo \(q_i\), and any choice is valid.) Since the \(q_i\) are distinct primes, the Chinese Remainder Theorem guarantees the existence of an integer \(m\) such that
\[
m \equiv a_i \pmod{q_i} \quad \text{for each} \quad i = 0, 1, \ldots, n.
\]

For this \(m\), \(m^2 + m + 1 \equiv 0 \pmod{q_i}\) for each \(i\), so each \(q_i\) divides \(m^2 + m + 1\). Let \(P = m^2 + m + 1\). Then \(P\) is divisible by each \(q_i\), and thus by their product \(Q = \prod_{i=0}^n q_i\). Write the prime factorization of \(P\) as
\[
P = \prod_{i=0}^n q_i^{e_i} \cdot S,
\]
where \(e_i \geq 1\) for each \(i\) (since each \(q_i\) divides \(P\)) and \(S\) is an integer coprime to all \(q_i\) (possibly \(S = 1\)).

Define the integers \(k_i\) as follows:
- For \(i = 0, 1, \ldots, n-1\), set \(k_i = q_i^{e_i}\).
- For \(i = n\), set \(k_n = q_n^{e_n} \cdot S\).

First, verify that each \(k_i > 1\). Since \(q_i \geq 3 > 1\) (as the primes are at least 3, given that primes congruent to 1 modulo 3 or 3 itself are considered), and \(e_i \geq 1\), it follows that \(k_i = q_i^{e_i} \geq q_i \geq 3 > 1\) for \(i = 0, \ldots, n-1\). For \(k_n = q_n^{e_n} \cdot S\), since \(q_n^{e_n} \geq q_n \geq 3 > 1\) and \(S \geq 1\), it follows that \(k_n \geq 3 > 1\).

Next, the product of the \(k_i\) is
\[
\prod_{i=0}^n k_i = \left( \prod_{i=0}^{n-1} q_i^{e_i} \right) \cdot (q_n^{e_n} \cdot S) = \left( \prod_{i=0}^n q_i^{e_i} \right) \cdot S = P.
\]
Thus, \(P - 1 = m^2 + m + 1 - 1 = m(m+1)\), which is the product of two consecutive integers.

Now, prove that the \(k_i\) are pairwise relatively prime, meaning \(\gcd(k_i, k_j) = 1\) for all \(i \neq j\) with \(0 \leq i, j \leq n\).

- If both \(i\) and \(j\) are in \(\{0, 1, \ldots, n-1\}\) and \(i \neq j\), then \(k_i = q_i^{e_i}\) and \(k_j = q_j^{e_j}\). Since \(q_i\) and \(q_j\) are distinct primes, \(\gcd(k_i, k_j) = 1\).
- If \(i < n\) and \(j = n\), then \(k_i = q_i^{e_i}\) and \(k_j = k_n = q_n^{e_n} \cdot S\). Here, \(q_i\) and \(q_n\) are distinct primes, so they share no common factors. Additionally, \(S\) is coprime to all \(q_i\) by definition, so \(S\) shares no common prime factors with \(q_i\). Thus, \(\gcd(k_i, k_n) = 1\).

Since these cases cover all pairs of distinct indices, the \(k_i\) are pairwise relatively prime.

Therefore, for each positive integer \(n\), the constructed integers \(k_0, \ldots, k_n\) are pairwise relatively prime, all greater than 1, and their product minus one is the product of two consecutive integers.

\[
\boxed{\text{Proof provided}}
\]

ground_truth_solution:
In other words, if we let

$$
P(x)=x(x+1)+1
$$
then we would like there to be infinitely many primes dividing some $P(t)$ for some integer $t$.

In fact, this result is true in much greater generality. We first state:

## Theorem $1.1$ (Schur's theorem)

If $P(x) \in \mathbb{Z}[x]$ is nonconstant and $P(0)=1$, then there are infinitely many primes which divide $P(t)$ for some integer $t$.

Proof. If $P(0)=0$, this is clear. So assume $P(0)=c \neq 0$.  
Let $S$ be any finite set of prime numbers. Consider then the value

$$
P\left(k \prod_{p \in S} p\right)
$$
for some integer $k$. It is $1(\bmod p)$ for each prime $p$, and if $k$ is large enough it should not be equal to $1$ (because $P$ is not constant). Therefore, it has a prime divisor not in $S$.

Remark. In fact the result holds without the assumption $P(0) \neq 1$. The proof requires only small modifications, and a good exercise would be to write down a similar proof that works first for $P(0)=20$, and then for any $P(0) \neq 0$. (The $P(0)=0$ case is vacuous, since then $P(x)$ is divisible by $x$.)

To finish the proof, let $p_{1}, \ldots, p_{n}$ be primes and $x_{i}$ be integers such that

$$
\begin{aligned}
P\left(x_{1}\right) & \equiv 0 \quad\left(\bmod p_{1}\right) \\
P\left(x_{2}\right) & \equiv 0 \quad\left(\bmod p_{2}\right) \\
\vdots & \\
P\left(x_{n}\right) & \equiv 0 \quad\left(\bmod p_{n}\right)
\end{aligned}
$$

as promised by Schur's theorem. Then, by Chinese remainder theorem, we can find $x$ such that $x \equiv x_{i}\left(\bmod p_{i}\right)$ for each $i$, whence $P(x)$ has at least $n$ prime factor.

problem: At a certain mathematical conference, every pair of mathematicians are either friends or strangers. At mealtime, every participant eats in one of two large dining rooms. Each mathematician insists upon eating in a room which contains an even number of his or her friends. Prove that the number of ways that the mathematicians may be split between the two rooms is a power of two (i.e., is of the form \(2^{k}\) for some positive integer \(k\)).
solution:
Let  

• \(V=\{1,2,\dots ,n\}\) be the set of mathematicians,  
• \(G=(V,E)\) the (simple, undirected) “friendship graph’’ in which \(\{i,j\}\in E\) iff \(i\) and \(j\) are friends,  
• \(\deg (i)\;(i\in V)\) the degree of vertex \(i\) in \(G\) (the number of friends of \(i\)).  

We write all equalities in the field  

\[
\mathbb F_{2}:=\{0,1\}\qquad(\text{addition = subtraction = “parity’’}).
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
1.  Translating an arrangement into algebra
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Number the two dining rooms \(0\) and \(1\).  
For an arrangement put  

\[
x_i=\begin{cases}
0 & \text{ if mathematician } i \text{ eats in room }0,\\
1 & \text{ if mathematician } i \text{ eats in room }1.
\end{cases}
\]

Thus every seating plan corresponds to a vector  

\[
x=(x_1,\dots ,x_n)\in \mathbb F_2^{\,n}.
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
2.  The parity condition as a linear (affine) equation
--------------------------------------------------------------------
For a fixed vertex \(i\) let us compute (mod 2) the number of friends of \(i\) who
sit in the *same* room as \(i\).

For each friend \(j\) of \(i\) the indicator  
\[
\bigl[x_i=x_j\bigr]\equiv 1-(x_i+x_j)\ (\bmod 2)
            =1+x_i+x_j\ (\bmod 2)
\]  
equals \(1\) when \(x_i=x_j\) and \(0\) otherwise.
Adding over all friends of \(i\) we obtain the parity wanted:

\[
0=\sum_{j:\{i,j\}\in E}(1+x_i+x_j)
  =\deg(i)+\deg(i)\,x_i+\sum_{j:\{i,j\}\in E}x_j\pmod 2.
\]

Rearranging gives the *linear* (in \(x\)) equation  

\[
\boxed{\;\deg(i)\,x_i+\sum_{j:\{i,j\}\in E}x_j=\deg(i)\;}\tag{1}
\]
for every vertex \(i\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
3.  Matrix form
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Let  

• \(A=(a_{ij})\) be the adjacency matrix of \(G\) over \(\mathbb F_2\)
  \((a_{ij}=1\) if \(\{i,j\}\in E\), else \(0)$,  
• \(D=\operatorname{diag}\bigl(\deg(1),\dots ,\deg(n)\bigr)\) (taken mod 2),  
• \(b=(\deg(1),\dots ,\deg(n))^{\!T}\) (also mod 2).

With these notations the whole system (1) is

\[
(A+D)\,x=b. \tag{2}
\]

Put \(M:=A+D\); \(M\) is an \(n\times n\) symmetric matrix over \(\mathbb F_2\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
4.  The set of legal arrangements
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Equation (2) is an *affine* system.  
If it is solvable, the set of all solutions is a *coset*
of the kernel of \(M\):

\[
\mathcal S=\{x_0+u\mid u\in\ker M\},
\]
where \(x_0\) is any particular solution.  
Hence  

\[
|\mathcal S|=
\begin{cases}
0 & \text{if (2) has no solution},\\[2mm]
|\ker M| = 2^{\,\dim\ker M} & \text{otherwise}.
\end{cases}
\tag{3}
\]

Equation (3) shows that the desired number of arrangements
is either \(0\) or a power of two.
It remains to prove that (2) *always* has at least one solution;
then the exponent in (3) will automatically be positive.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
5.  Showing that (2) is always solvable
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Because \(M\) is symmetric, its row space equals its column space.
Consequently (2) is solvable precisely when the constant vector \(b\)
is orthogonal to every vector in \(\ker M\).
We prove this orthogonality directly.

Let \(s=(s_1,\dots ,s_n)\in\ker M\) and put  
\(S=\{i\in V\mid s_i=1\}\).  
The equality \(M\,s=0\) gives, for each vertex \(i\),

\[
\deg(i)\,s_i+\sum_{j:\{i,j\}\in E}s_j=0. \tag{4}
\]

(a)  If \(i\notin S\;(s_i=0)\), (4) says that \(i\) has an *even*
number of neighbours inside \(S\).

(b)  If \(i\in S\;(s_i=1)\), (4) becomes  
\[
\deg(i)=\sum_{j:\{i,j\}\in E}s_j
\]
so that \(\deg(i)\) equals, mod 2,
the number of neighbours of \(i\) that *also* lie in \(S\).

Add the equalities in (b) over all vertices in \(S\):
the left side is  
\[
\sum_{i\in S}\deg(i)=s^{T}b .
\]
On the right, every edge with *both* ends in \(S\)
is counted twice (hence contributes \(0\) mod 2),
whereas every edge with *exactly one* end in \(S\)
is counted once.
Therefore  

\[
s^{T}b \equiv |E(S,V\setminus S)| \pmod 2. \tag{5}
\]

But from (a) each vertex outside \(S\) is incident with an *even*
number of such “crossing’’ edges; summing over all outside vertices
shows that \(|E(S,V\setminus S)|\) itself is even.
Hence the right side of (5) equals \(0\), and we have

\[
s^{T}b=0 \qquad\text{for every }s\in\ker M. \tag{6}
\]

So \(b\) is orthogonal to the kernel; equivalently, \(b\) lies in
the row (column) space of \(M\).  
Thus system (2) possesses at least one solution.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
6.  Finishing the proof
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Because (2) is solvable, (3) gives

\[
|\mathcal S|=2^{\,\dim\ker M}.
\]

Finally, notice that the all-ones vector \(\mathbf 1=(1,1,\dots ,1)^{T}\)
satisfies \(M\mathbf 1=0\) (each row of \(M\) sums to
\(\deg(i)+\deg(i)=0\) mod 2), so \(\mathbf 1\neq 0\) lies in \(\ker M\).
Hence \(\dim\ker M\ge 1\) and

\[
|\mathcal S| = 2^{\,k}\quad\text{for some positive integer }k.
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
7.  Conclusion
--------------------------------------------------------------------
The number of ways in which the conference participants can be divided
between the two dining rooms so that *every* mathematician finds an
even number of friends in his or her room is always a (positive)
power of two. ∎
ground_truth_solution:
Take the obvious graph interpretation where we are trying to 2-color a graph. Let $A$ be the adjacency matrix of the graph over $\mathbb{F}_{2}$, except the diagonal of $A \operatorname{has} \operatorname{deg} v(\bmod 2)$ instead of zero. Then let $\vec{d}$ be the main diagonal. Splittings then correspond to $A \vec{v}=\vec{d}$. It's then immediate that the number of ways is either zero or a power of two, since if it is nonempty it is a coset of $\operatorname{ker} A$.

Thus we only need to show that:

```
Claim - At least one coloring exists.
```

Proof. If not, consider a minimal counterexample G. Clearly there is at least one odd vertex $v$. Consider the graph with vertex set $G-v$, where all pairs of neighbors of $v$ have their edges complemented. By minimality, we have a good coloring here. One can check that this extends to a good coloring on $G$ by simply coloring $v$ with the color matching an even number of its neighbors. This breaks minimality of $G$, and hence all graphs $G$ have a coloring.

It's also possible to use linear algebra. We prove the following lemma:

## Lemma (grobber)

Let $V$ be a finite dimensional vector space, $T: V \rightarrow V$ and $w \in V$. Then $w$ is in the image of $T$ if and only if there are no $\xi \in V^{\vee}$ for which $\xi(w) \neq 0$ and yet $\xi \circ T=0$.

Proof. Clearly if $T(v)=w$, then no $\xi$ exists. Conversely, assume $w$ is not in the image of $T$. Then the image of $T$ is linearly independent from $w$. Take a basis $e_{1}, \ldots, e_{m}$ for the image of $T$, add $w$, and then extend it to a basis for all of $V$. Then have $\xi$ kill all $e_{i}$ but not $w$.

## Corollary

In a symmetric matrix $A \bmod 2$, there exists a vector $v$ such that $A v$ is a copy of the diagonal of $A$.

Proof. Let $\xi$ be such that $\xi \circ T=0$. Look at $\xi$ as a column vector $w^{\top}$, and let $d$ be the diagonal. Then

$$
0=w^{\top} \cdot T \cdot w=\xi(d)
$$
because this extracts the sum of coefficients submatrix of $T$, and all the symmetric entries cancel off. Thus no $\xi$ as in the previous lemma exists.

This corollary gives the desired proof.
llm_summary: The proof encodes each seating arrangement as a vector x∈𝔽₂ⁿ and shows that the parity condition on friends sitting together becomes the linear system (A+D)x=b over 𝔽₂, where A is the adjacency matrix and D the degree-diagonal. It observes that the solution set is either empty or a coset of ker M (M=A+D), hence of size 2^{dim ker M}. To prove existence of a solution it shows b is orthogonal to every vector in ker M by a parity count of edges crossing a subset S; finally it notes the all-ones vector lies in ker M so dim ker M≥1, giving a positive power of two solutions.

problem:
For \( n \geq 2 \), let \( a_{1}, a_{2}, \ldots, a_{n} \) be positive real numbers such that

\[
\left(a_{1}+a_{2}+\cdots+a_{n}\right)\left(\frac{1}{a_{1}}+\frac{1}{a_{2}}+\cdots+\frac{1}{a_{n}}\right) \leq\left(n+\frac{1}{2}\right)^{2} .
\]

Prove that \(\max \left(a_{1}, \ldots, a_{n}\right) \leq 4 \min \left(a_{1}, \ldots, a_{n}\right)\).
solution:
Let  

\[
0<a_{1}\le a_{2}\le\cdots \le a_{n}\qquad (n\ge 2)
\]

and put  

\[
m=a_{1},\qquad M=a_{n},\qquad r=\frac{M}{m}\;(>1).
\]

Multiplying every number by \(1/m\) divides all the \(a_{i}\)’s by the same positive
constant; the hypothesis and the conclusion are therefore unchanged.
Thus, without loss of generality, we may (and shall) assume  

\[
m=a_{1}=1 ,\qquad a_{n}=r .
\]

Denote  

\[
S=\sum_{i=1}^{n}a_{i},\qquad T=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\frac1{a_{i}}, \qquad
P=ST=\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n}a_{i}\right)\!\!\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n}\frac1{a_{i}}\right).
\]

The given condition is  

\[
P\le\left(n+\frac12\right)^{2}.  \tag{1}
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
1.  A convenient expression for \(P\)

Because  

\[
P=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\sum_{j=1}^{n}\frac{a_{i}}{a_{j}}
      =\sum_{i=1}^{n}\frac{a_{i}}{a_{i}}
       +\sum_{1\le i<j\le n}\!\left(\frac{a_{i}}{a_{j}}
                                   +\frac{a_{j}}{a_{i}}\right),
\]

we have  

\[
P=n+\sum_{1\le i<j\le n}
        \Bigl(\frac{a_{i}}{a_{j}}+\frac{a_{j}}{a_{i}}-2\Bigr)
  =n^{2}+\Delta ,\qquad
\Delta=\sum_{1\le i<j\le n}
        \frac{(a_{i}-a_{j})^{2}}{a_{i}a_{j}}\ge 0.      \tag{2}
\]

From (1) and (2)

\[
\Delta\le\left(n+\frac12\right)^{2}-n^{2}=n+\frac14.      \tag{3}
\]

Hence the whole problem is reduced to showing that (3) forces
\(r\le 4\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
2.  A lower bound for \(\Delta\) in terms of \(r\)

Put  

\[
g(x)=\frac{(x-1)^{2}}{x}\qquad (x>0).
\]

For every unordered pair \(\{i,j\}\) with \(i<j\) we have  

\[
\frac{(a_{i}-a_{j})^{2}}{a_{i}a_{j}}
        =g\!\Bigl(\frac{a_{j}}{a_{i}}\Bigr).     \tag{4}
\]

We single out the smallest and the largest indices, 1 and \(n\).
For every middle index \(k\;(2\le k\le n-1)\) set  

\[
x_{k}=a_{k}\;(1\le x_{k}\le r),\qquad
y_{k}=\frac{r}{x_{k}}=\frac{a_{n}}{a_{k}}\;(1\le y_{k}\le r).
\]

With this notation the contribution of the three pairs
\((1,k),(k,n),(1,n)\) to the sum \(\Delta\) equals

\[
g(x_{k})+g(y_{k})+\frac{(r-1)^{2}}{r}.           \tag{5}
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
Lemma 1  
For every \(x\in[1,r]\)

\[
g(x)+g\!\Bigl(\frac{r}{x}\Bigr)\ge
2\!\left(\sqrt{r}+\frac1{\sqrt{r}}-2\right).      \tag{6}
\]

Proof.  Define \(\varphi(x)=g(x)+g(r/x)\;(1\le x\le r)\).
Because \(g(r/x)=g(x)\) after the change \(x\leftrightarrow r/x\),
\(\varphi\) is symmetric about \(x=\sqrt r\).
Differentiate once:

\[
\varphi'(x)=\frac{(x-1)(x+1)-\!(r/x-1)(r/x+1)}{x^{2}}
          =(1+1/r)\Bigl(1-\frac{r}{x^{2}}\Bigr).
\]

Hence \(\varphi'(x)=0\) only at \(x=\sqrt r\), and
\(\varphi''(x)>0\); so \(\varphi\) attains its minimum at that point.
Substituting \(x=\sqrt r\) gives (6). ∎

--------------------------------------------------------------------
Corollary 1  
With \(d(r)=2\bigl(\sqrt{r}+1/\sqrt{r}-2\bigr)\;(>0\text{ for }r>1)\) one has  

\[
g(x_{k})+g(y_{k})\ge d(r)\qquad(2\le k\le n-1).     \tag{7}
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
Combining (5) over all middle indices and adding the single pair
\((1,n)\) we get

\[
\Delta\ge\frac{(r-1)^{2}}{r}
        +(n-2)\,d(r).                       \tag{8}
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
3.  Finishing the proof

Observe that the two functions  

\[
r\longmapsto \frac{(r-1)^{2}}{r}=r-2+\frac1r,\qquad
r\longmapsto d(r)=2\!\left(\sqrt{r}+\frac1{\sqrt{r}}-2\right)
\]

are strictly increasing for \(r>1\).
Therefore the lower bound \(h_{n}(r)\) defined by the
right–hand side of (8) is increasing for \(r>1\).
At \(r=4\) we have

\[
h_{n}(4)=\frac{9}{4}+(n-2)\cdot1=n+\frac14.       \tag{9}
\]

Thus for every \(r\ge 4\),

\[
\Delta\ge h_{n}(r)\ge h_{n}(4)=n+\frac14.        \tag{10}
\]

If \(r>4\) the inequality is strict, so
\(\Delta>n+\frac14\), contradicting the upper bound (3).
Consequently \(r\le 4\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
4.  Restoring the original notation

Remembering that we normalized \(a_{1}=1\), the inequality
\(r\le 4\) reads \(a_{n}\le 4a_{1}\).
Undoing the rearrangement (the indices may be permuted)
gives the desired conclusion  

\[
\boxed{\ \max\{a_{1},\dots ,a_{n}\}\le 4\,
        \min\{a_{1},\dots ,a_{n}\}\ } .
\]

Equality is possible (and, by the above analysis, only possible) when  
\(r=4\), i.e. when the largest element is exactly four times the
smallest one and, for \(n>2\), every other element equals \(2\min a_{i}\),
in which case the given inequality is satisfied with equality:
\[
(a_{1}+a_{2}+\cdots +a_{n})
\Bigl(\frac1{a_{1}}+\frac1{a_{2}}+\cdots+\frac1{a_{n}}\Bigr)
      =(n+\tfrac12)^{2}.
\]

Hence the proof is complete. ∎
ground_truth_solution:
## Problem statement

For $n \geq 2$, let $a_{1}, a_{2}, \ldots, a_{n}$ be positive real numbers such that

$$
\left(a_{1}+a_{2}+\cdots+a_{n}\right)\left(\frac{1}{a_{1}}+\frac{1}{a_{2}}+\cdots+\frac{1}{a_{n}}\right) \leq\left(n+\frac{1}{2}\right)^{2} .
$$

Prove that $\max \left(a_{1}, \ldots, a_{n}\right) \leq 4 \min \left(a_{1}, \ldots, a_{n}\right)$.

Assume $a_{1}$ is the largest and $a_{2}$ is the smallest. Let $M=a_{1} / a_{2}$. We wish to show $M \leq 4$.
In left-hand side of given, write as $a_{2}+a_{1}+\cdots+a_{n}$. By Cauchy Schwarz, one obtains

$$
\begin{aligned}
\left(n+\frac{1}{2}\right)^{2} & \geq\left(a_{2}+a_{1}+a_{3}+\cdots+a_{n}\right)\left(\frac{1}{a_{1}}+\frac{1}{a_{2}}+\frac{1}{a_{3}}+\cdots+\frac{1}{a_{n}}\right) \\
& \geq\left(\sqrt{\frac{a_{2}}{a_{1}}}+\sqrt{\frac{a_{1}}{a_{2}}}+1+\cdots+1\right)^{2} \\
& \geq(\sqrt{1 / M}+\sqrt{M}+(n-2))^{2} .
\end{aligned}
$$

Expanding and solving for $M$ gives $1 / 4 \leq M \leq 4$ as needed.
llm_summary: The proof begins by ordering the $a_i$ and normalizing the smallest to 1 so that the largest is $r$. Writing $P=(\sum a_i)(\sum1/a_i)=n^2+\Delta$, it first shows $\Delta\le n+\tfrac14$. It then lower-bounds $\Delta$ by splitting it into contributions $g(x_k)+g(r/x_k)$ for a convex function $g(x)=(x-1)^2/x$, proving via a derivative test that $g(x)+g(r/x)\ge d(r)$ and hence $\Delta\ge (r-1)^2/r+(n-2)d(r)$. Noting this lower bound is strictly increasing in $r$ and equals $n+\tfrac14$ at $r=4$, one concludes $r\le4$, i.e.\ $\max a_i\le4\min a_i$.

problem:
Let \( q = \frac{3p - 5}{2} \) where \( p \) is an odd prime, and let

\[
S_{q} = \frac{1}{2 \cdot 3 \cdot 4} + \frac{1}{5 \cdot 6 \cdot 7} + \cdots + \frac{1}{q(q+1)(q+2)}
\]

Prove that if \(\frac{1}{p} - 2 S_{q} = \frac{m}{n}\) for integers \( m \) and \( n \), then \( m-n \) is divisible by \( p \).
solution:
Proof.  Let \(p\) be an odd prime, and set
\[
N \;=\;\frac{p-1}2,
\qquad
q \;=\;\frac{3p-5}2 \;=\;3N-1.
\]
Then by definition
\[
S_q \;=\;
\sum_{i=0}^{N-1}
\frac1{(3i+2)(3i+3)(3i+4)}.
\]
We begin by a two‐stage partial‐fraction decomposition.

1.  Write for a general integer \(k\)
\[
\frac1{k(k+1)(k+2)}
\;=\;
\frac12\Bigl(\frac1{k(k+1)}-\frac1{(k+1)(k+2)}\Bigr).
\]
Hence, with \(k=3i+2\),
\[
\frac1{(3i+2)(3i+3)(3i+4)}
\;=\;
\frac12\Bigl(
\frac1{(3i+2)(3i+3)}-\frac1{(3i+3)(3i+4)}
\Bigr),
\]
and summing \(i=0,1,\dots,N-1\) gives
\[
2\,S_q
\;=\;
\sum_{i=0}^{N-1}\Bigl(
\frac1{(3i+2)(3i+3)}-\frac1{(3i+3)(3i+4)}
\Bigr).
\]

2.  Next use the telescoping identity
\(\displaystyle \frac1{k(k+1)}=\frac1k-\frac1{k+1}\).  Then
\[
\frac1{(3i+2)(3i+3)}
=\frac1{3i+2}-\frac1{3i+3},
\qquad
\frac1{(3i+3)(3i+4)}
=\frac1{3i+3}-\frac1{3i+4}.
\]
Hence
\[
2S_q
=\sum_{i=0}^{N-1}\Bigl[
\Bigl(\frac1{3i+2}-\frac1{3i+3}\Bigr)
-\Bigl(\frac1{3i+3}-\frac1{3i+4}\Bigr)
\Bigr]
=\sum_{i=0}^{N-1}\Bigl(\frac1{3i+2}-\frac2{3i+3}+\frac1{3i+4}\Bigr).
\]
Re–index \(j=i+1\).  When \(i\) runs from \(0\) to \(N-1\), \(j\)
runs from \(1\) to \(N\).  Then \(3i+2=3j-1,\;3i+3=3j,\;3i+4=3j+1\), and
\[
2S_q
=
\sum_{j=1}^N\Bigl(\frac1{3j-1}-\frac2{3j}+\frac1{3j+1}\Bigr).
\]
Write
\[
A \;=\;\sum_{j=1}^N\frac1{3j-1},
\quad
B \;=\;\sum_{j=1}^N\frac1{3j},
\quad
C \;=\;\sum_{j=1}^N\frac1{3j+1}.
\]
Then
\[
2S_q \;=\;A \;-\;2B\;+\;C.
\]
But observe that the three arithmetic progressions
\(\{3j-1\},\{3j\},\{3j+1\}\) with \(j=1,\dots,N\) together exhaust
exactly the integers
\[
2,3,4,\dots,3N+1.
\]
Hence
\[
A+B+C
\;=\;
\sum_{k=2}^{3N+1}\frac1k
\;=\;
\bigl(H_{3N+1}-1\bigr),
\]
where \(H_m=\sum_{k=1}^m\frac1k\) is the \(m\)th harmonic number.
Moreover
\[
B=\sum_{j=1}^N\frac1{3j}
=\frac13\sum_{j=1}^N\frac1j
=\frac13\,H_N.
\]
Therefore
\[
2S_q
=(A+B+C)-3B
=(H_{3N+1}-1)-H_N,
\]
and hence
\[
2S_q+1
\;=\;
H_{3N+1}-H_N
\;=\;
\sum_{k=N+1}^{3N+1}\frac1k.
\]
But \(N+1=(p+1)/2\) and \(3N+1=(3p-1)/2\), so the right–hand side
is
\[
\sum_{k=\frac{p+1}2}^{\frac{3p-1}2}\frac1k.
\]
Call
\[
D \;=\;\prod_{k=\frac{p+1}2}^{\frac{3p-1}2} k.
\]
Since the range \(\bigl[(p+1)/2,(3p-1)/2\bigr]\) contains the integer
\(k=p\), it follows at once that \(p\) divides \(D\).

Now from
\[
2S_q+1 \;=\;\frac{1\cdot D}{D}+\frac{2S_q\cdot D}{D}
\;=\;
\sum_{k=\frac{p+1}2}^{\frac{3p-1}2}\frac Dk
\]
we see that
\[
2S_q+1=\frac A D,
\]
where
\[
A=\sum_{k=\frac{p+1}2}^{\frac{3p-1}2}\frac Dk
\]
is an integer.  Hence
\[
2S_q
=\frac{A}D -1,
\]
and consequently
\[
\frac1p-2S_q
=\frac1p-\Bigl(\frac A D -1\Bigr)
=1+\frac1p-\frac A D
=\frac{(p+1)D}{p\,D}-\frac A D
=\frac{(p+1)D-pA}{p\,D}.
\]
Thus one valid choice of integers \(m,n\) with
\(\tfrac1p-2S_q=\tfrac m n\) is
\[
m=(p+1)D-pA,
\qquad
n=p\,D.
\]
Finally
\[
m-n
=(p+1)D-pA \;-\;pD
=D-pA,
\]
and since \(p\mid D\) this shows \(p\mid(m-n)\), as claimed.  
\(\Box\)
