problem: The first \( k \) terms \( a_{1}, a_{2}, \ldots, a_{k} \) of the sequence \( (a_{n}) \) are distinct natural numbers, and for \( n > k \), the number \( a_{n} \) is the smallest natural number that cannot be represented as the sum of several (possibly one) of the numbers \( a_{1}, a_{2}, \ldots, a_{n-1} \). Prove that \( a_{n} = 2 a_{n-1} \) for all sufficiently large \( n \).
solution:
Let \(k\) be fixed and write  
\[
s_n=a_1+a_2+\dots +a_n\qquad (n\ge 1)
\]
for the partial sums of the sequence.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
Step 1.  A first (and permanent) lower bound  
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Claim:  For every \(n>k\)
\[
a_{n+1}\;\ge\;2a_n . \tag{1}
\]

Proof.  
With the first \(n\) terms at our disposal we can certainly form every
integer
\(1,2,\dots ,a_n-1\); otherwise \(a_n\) would not have been the smallest
unrepresentable number when it was chosen.  
Adding \(a_n\) to those representations gives all integers
\(a_n+1,a_n+2,\dots ,2a_n-1\).  Thus every positive integer
\(\le 2a_n-1\) is representable with the first \(n\) terms,
so the next
smallest unrepresentable integer—namely \(a_{\,n+1}\)—must satisfy
\(a_{n+1}\ge 2a_n\).
\(\square\)

Iterating (1) we get, for \(m\ge 0\),
\[
a_{k+2+m}\;\ge\;2^{\,m}\,a_{k+2},
\]
so the sequence grows at least exponentially and is therefore unbounded.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
Step 2.  A useful inequality for later terms  
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Fix an index \(r\ge k\).  
Because of (1) we have \(a_{i+1}\ge 2a_i\) for every \(i\ge r+1\).
We now show that for all \(n\ge r+1\)
\[
\sum_{i=r+1}^{n-1}a_i\;\le\;a_n-a_{\,r+1}. \tag{2}
\]

Proof by induction on \(n\).

• Base case \(n=r+1\): the left–hand side is \(0\), equality holds.

• Induction step:  
Assume (2) is true for some \(n\ge r+1\).  Then
\[
\sum_{i=r+1}^{n}a_i
      =a_n+\sum_{i=r+1}^{\,n-1}a_i
      \le a_n+\bigl(a_n-a_{\,r+1}\bigr)
      =2a_n-a_{\,r+1}
      \le a_{\,n+1}-a_{\,r+1},
\]
because \(a_{\,n+1}\ge 2a_n\) by (1).  Hence (2) also holds for \(n+1\);
the induction is complete.  \(\square\)

--------------------------------------------------------------------
Step 3.  Choosing a starting index  
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Let  
\[
C \;=\; s_k=a_1+\dots +a_k .
\]
Because the sequence is unbounded, there is an index  
\[
R\; \ge\; k
\qquad\text{ with }\qquad 
a_{\,R+1} \;>\; C. \tag{3}
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
Step 4.  Eventually each new term exceeds the sum of all earlier ones  
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Combine (2) with (3).  
For any \(n\ge R+1\),
\[
s_{\,n-1}=C+\sum_{i=R+1}^{\,n-1}a_i
        < a_{\,R+1}+\bigl(a_n-a_{\,R+1}\bigr)
        =a_n. \tag{4}
\]

Thus from index \(R+1\) onwards every term of the sequence is
strictly larger than the sum of all its predecessors.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
Step 5.  Consequence of (4): the next term must be \(2a_n\)  
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Lemma.  If \(s_{\,n-1}<a_n\) for some \(n\), then
\[
a_{\,n+1}=2a_n .
\]

Proof.  
As in Step 1 the integers \(1,2,\dots ,a_n-1\) are representable with the
first \(n-1\) terms.  
Adding \(a_n\) to them yields every
integer from \(a_n+1\) up to \(2a_n-1\).
Because the largest possible
subset–sum of the first \(n\) terms is \(s_{\,n-1}+a_n<2a_n\),
the number \(2a_n\) itself is not representable.
All smaller positive integers are,
so \(2a_n\) is the smallest non-representable integer:
\(a_{\,n+1}=2a_n\).
\(\square\)

Applying the lemma to \(n=R+1\) (where (4) holds) gives  
\[
a_{\,R+2}=2a_{\,R+1}. \tag{5}
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
Step 6.  Doubling continues forever  
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Because
\(s_{\,R+1}=s_{\,R}+a_{\,R+1}<2a_{\,R+1}=a_{\,R+2}\),
the hypothesis of the lemma is true for \(n=R+2\) as well; hence
\(a_{\,R+3}=2a_{\,R+2}\).
Repeating this argument inductively yields

\[
a_{n}=2a_{n-1}\qquad\text{for every }n\ge R+2. \tag{6}
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
Conclusion  
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Equality (6) shows that from the fixed index \(N=R+2\) onward the
sequence simply doubles at each step.
Therefore

  \(a_{n}=2a_{\,n-1}\) for all sufficiently large \(n\),

which is exactly what had to be proven.  \(\blacksquare\)
ground_truth_solution:
**Solution.** For each \( n \geqslant k \), consider the set of all natural numbers not exceeding \( a_{1} + a_{2} + \cdots + a_{n} \), and those among them that are not sums of several elements of the set \( \{a_{1}, a_{2}, \ldots, a_{n}\} \) will be called holes. If the set of holes is non-empty, then \( a_{n+1} \) is the smallest of them; otherwise, \( a_{n+1} = a_{1} + a_{2} + \cdots + a_{n} + 1 \). We will prove that as \( n \) increases by \( 1 \), the number of holes decreases by at least \( 1 \).

Notice that if the number \( t \leqslant S = a_{1} + a_{2} + \cdots + a_{n} \) is a sum of one or several of the numbers \( a_{1}, a_{2}, \ldots, a_{n} \), then the number \( S - t \) is also such a sum: it is the sum of all \( a_{i} \) not included in the sum equal to \( t \).
The fact that \( a_{n+1} \) is the smallest hole means that all numbers from \( 1 \) to \( a_{n+1} - 1 \) are sums of several of the numbers \( a_{1}, a_{2}, \ldots, a_{n} \). Therefore, all numbers from \( a_{1} + \cdots + a_{n} - a_{n+1} \) to \( a_{1} + \cdots + a_{n} \)

are also such sums. Adding \( a_{n+1} \), we obtain that all numbers from \( a_{1} + \cdots + a_{n} \) to \( a_{1} + \cdots + a_{n} + a_{n+1} \) are sums of some of the numbers \( a_{1}, a_{2}, \ldots, a_{n+1} \). Thus, when replacing \( n \) with \( n + 1 \), no new holes have appeared, and at least one old one (specifically \( a_{n+1} \)) has disappeared, which is what we needed to prove.
Therefore, starting from some point, there will be no holes left.
Thus, for all sufficiently large \( n \), the equality \( a_{n+1} = a_{1} + \cdots + a_{n} + 1 \) holds. Then \( a_{n+2} = a_{1} + \cdots + a_{n} + a_{n+1} + 1 = \left(a_{1} + \cdots + a_{n} + 1\right) + a_{n+1} = 2 a_{n+1} \), which is what we needed to prove. (matol.kz)
llm_summary: The proof introduces the partial sums \(s_n=\sum_{i=1}^n a_i\) and first shows via the minimality of each \(a_n\) that \(a_{n+1}\ge2a_n\), giving exponential growth.  It then fixes an index \(R\) so that \(a_{R+1}>s_k\) and uses an inductive inequality on \(\sum_{i=R+1}^{n-1}a_i\) to conclude that for all \(n\ge R+1\), \(s_{n-1}<a_n\).  A second minimality argument then yields \(a_{n+1}=2a_n\), and by induction this doubling continues for all sufficiently large \(n\).

problem: Prove that there exist infinitely many pairs \((m, n)\) of positive integers such that \(m+n\) divides \((m!)^{n}+(n!)^{m}+1\).
solution:
To prove that there exist **infinitely many pairs** $(m, n)$ of positive integers such that  
$$
m + n \mid (m!)^n + (n!)^m + 1,
$$  
we construct an infinite family of such pairs using a clever combination of number theory and factorial properties.

---

### **Key Observations and Strategy**

We aim to find **infinitely many** pairs $(m, n)$ such that the sum $m + n$ divides the expression  
$$
(m!)^n + (n!)^m + 1.
$$

Let’s define $k$ to be an even integer greater than or equal to 4. For such $k$, we define:
- $n = k$,
- $t = k! + 1$,
- $m = t - k = k! + 1 - k$.

We will show that for **infinitely many** such $k$, the pair $(m, n) = (t - k, k)$ satisfies the required divisibility condition.

---

### **Step 1: Constructing the Pair**

Let $k$ be an even integer with $k \geq 4$. Define:
- $n = k$,
- $t = k! + 1$,
- $m = t - k = k! + 1 - k$.

We will show that:
$$
m + n = t = k! + 1 \mid (m!)^n + (n!)^m + 1.
$$

---

### **Step 2: Properties of $t = k! + 1$**

- Since $k$ is even and $k \geq 4$, $k!$ is even, so $t = k! + 1$ is **odd**.
- $t = k! + 1$ is **composite** for infinitely many such $k$. This is because for infinitely many primes $p$, $k = p - 1$ is even, and by **Wilson's Theorem**, $k! \equiv -1 \pmod{p}$, so $p \mid k! + 1$, making $k! + 1$ composite.

Thus, for infinitely many even $k$, $t = k! + 1$ is a **composite number**.

---

### **Step 3: Divisibility of $m!$ by $t$**

We now show that $t \mid m!$, where $m = t - k = k! + 1 - k$.

- Since $t = k! + 1$, and $m = t - k = k! + 1 - k$, we have:
  $$
  m = k! + 1 - k = k! - k + 1.
  $$
- Since $k \geq 4$, $k!$ is much larger than $k$, so $m = k! - k + 1$ is a large number.
- $t = k! + 1$ is a composite number, and all its prime factors are **greater than $k$** (since $k!$ is divisible by all integers up to $k$, and $k! + 1$ is not divisible by any of them).
- Therefore, all prime factors of $t$ are **less than or equal to $m$** (since $m = k! - k + 1 > k$), and hence divide $m!$.
- Thus, $t \mid m!$.

---

### **Step 4: Evaluating the Expression Modulo $t$**

We now evaluate the expression modulo $t = k! + 1$:
$$
(m!)^n + (n!)^m + 1 \equiv 0 \pmod{t}.
$$

- Since $t \mid m!$, we have $(m!)^n \equiv 0 \pmod{t}$.
- Since $n = k$, we have $n! = k!$, and by construction, $k! \equiv -1 \pmod{t}$, so:
  $$
  (n!)^m = (k!)^m \equiv (-1)^m \pmod{t}.
  $$
- Therefore, the expression becomes:
  $$
  (m!)^n + (n!)^m + 1 \equiv 0 + (-1)^m + 1 \pmod{t}.
  $$
- Since $m = t - k = k! + 1 - k$, and $k$ is even, $t = k! + 1$ is odd, so $m = t - k$ is **odd**.
- Thus, $(-1)^m = -1$, and the expression becomes:
  $$
  -1 + 1 = 0 \pmod{t}.
  $$

Hence, the divisibility condition is satisfied.

---

### **Step 5: Infinitely Many Such Pairs**

We now show that there are **infinitely many** such $k$ for which the above construction works.

- For each prime $p \geq 5$, define $k = p - 1$, which is even and $\geq 4$.
- Then $k! + 1$ is divisible by $p$, and since $k! + 1 > p$, it is **composite**.
- Therefore, for each such $k$, the pair $(m, n) = (t - k, k)$ satisfies the divisibility condition.
- Since there are **infinitely many primes**, there are **infinitely many such $k$**.

---

### **Conclusion**

We have constructed an infinite family of pairs $(m, n)$ such that:
$$
m + n \mid (m!)^n + (n!)^m + 1.
$$
Each such pair is of the form:
$$
m = k! + 1 - k, \quad n = k,
$$
for infinitely many even integers $k \geq 4$.

Thus, the proof is complete.

$$
\boxed{(m, n) \text{ such that } m = (k! + 1) - k \text{ and } n = k \text{ for infinitely many even } k}
$$
ground_truth_solution:
Solution. We shall find a pair such that $m+n=p$ is prime and $n$ is even. Applying Wilson's theorem we have

$$
m!=(p-n)!=\frac{(p-1)!}{(p-n+1) \ldots(p-2)(p-1)} \equiv \frac{-1}{-(n-1) \ldots(-2)(-1)} \equiv \frac{1}{(n-1)!} \equiv \frac{n}{n!} \quad(\bmod p)
$$

It follows from Fermat's Little Theorem that $(n!)^{p} \equiv n!(\bmod p)$, therefore

$$
(m!)^{n}+(n!)^{m}+1 \equiv\left(\frac{n}{n!}\right)^{n}+(n!)^{p-n}+1 \equiv \frac{n^{n}+n!+(n!)^{n}}{(n!)^{n}} \quad(\bmod p)
$$
thus it suffices to prove that the number $n^{n}+n!+(n!)^{n}$ has a prime divisor $p>n$ for infinitely many even $n$.
We prove that this condition is satisfied, for instance, by all the numbers of the form $n=2 q$, where $q>2$ is prime. Let $A=(2 q)^{2 q}+(2 q)!+((2 q)!)^{2 q}$. For a prime $p$ and integer $k$ we denote by $v_{p}(k)$ the largest integer $\ell$ such that $p^{\ell}$ divides $k$.

If $r<2 q$ is prime and $r \notin\{2, q\}$ then $A \equiv(2 q)^{2 q} \not \equiv 0(\bmod r)$. The largest degree of $q$ dividing $(2 q)!$ is $q^{2}$, while for $(2 q)^{2 q}$ and $((2 q)!)^{2 q}$ it is $2 q$ and $4 q$ respectively, therefore $v_{q}(A)=2$.

Finally, $v_{2}((2 q)!)=\left[\frac{2 q}{2}\right]+\left[\frac{2 q}{4}\right]+\left[\frac{2 q}{8}\right]+\cdots<\frac{2 q}{2}+\frac{2 q}{4}+\frac{2 q}{8}+\cdots=2 q$, so $v_{2}((2 q)!)<v_{2}\left((2 q)^{2 q}\right)$ and obviously $v_{2}((2 q)!)<v_{2}\left((2 q)!^{2 q}\right)$, thus $v_{2}(A) \leq 2 q-1$. On the other hand, $A>(2 q)^{2 q}>2^{2 q-1} q^{2}$, therefore $A$ has a prime divisor $p>2 q$, q.e.d.

It then claims all prime divisors of t exceed k and are ≤ m, so t | m! and thus (m!)^n ≡ 0 (mod t). Since k! ≡ −1 (mod t) and m is odd, (n!)^m ≡ (−1)^m = −1, yielding (m!)^n + (n!)^m + 1 ≡ 0 (mod t). Varying over infinitely many primes p produces infinitely many such pairs.

problem: The Crocodile thought of four unit squares of a $2018 \times 2018$ grid forming a rectangle with sides $1$ and $4$. The Bear can choose any square formed by $9$ unit squares (i.e., a $3 \times 3$ square) and ask whether it contains at least one of the four Crocodile's squares. What is the minimum number of questions he must ask to be sure of at least one affirmative answer?
solution:
To determine the minimum number of $3 \times 3$ squares the Bear must ask about to guarantee that at least one contains at least one unit square from any $1 \times 4$ rectangle chosen by the Crocodile, consider the possible orientations of the rectangle. The rectangle can be either horizontal (occupying one row and four columns) or vertical (occupying four rows and one column). The Bear must ensure coverage for both orientations with the same set of $3 \times 3$ squares.

For a horizontal $1 \times 4$ rectangle, the top-left corner is at position $(r, c)$ with $r$ ranging from 1 to 2018 (rows) and $c$ ranging from 1 to 2015 (columns, since $c + 3 \leq 2018$). A $3 \times 3$ square with top-left corner at $(i, j)$ intersects this rectangle if $r \in [i, i+2]$ and the column intervals $[c, c+3]$ and $[j, j+2]$ overlap, which occurs when $c \in [j-3, j+2]$. To cover all such $(r, c)$, the minimum number of $i$ values needed to cover all rows $r$ is $\lceil 2018 / 3 \rceil = 673$, and the minimum number of $j$ values needed to cover all columns $c$ is $\lceil 2015 / 6 \rceil = 336$. Thus, the product set size for horizontal rectangles is $673 \times 336$.

For a vertical $1 \times 4$ rectangle, the top-left corner is at $(r, c)$ with $r$ ranging from 1 to 2015 (rows, since $r + 3 \leq 2018$) and $c$ ranging from 1 to 2018 (columns). A $3 \times 3$ square at $(i, j)$ intersects this rectangle if $|i - r| \leq 2$ and $|j - c| \leq 2$. To cover all such $(r, c)$, the minimum number of $i$ values needed to cover all rows $r$ is $\lceil 2015 / 3 \rceil = 672$, and the minimum number of $j$ values needed to cover all columns $c$ is $\lceil 2018 / 6 \rceil = 337$. Thus, the product set size for vertical rectangles is $672 \times 337$.

The set size for vertical rectangles, $672 \times 337 = 226464$, is larger than that for horizontal rectangles ($673 \times 336 = 226128$). Moreover, a set designed to cover all vertical rectangles also covers all horizontal rectangles, because if every $c$ has a $j$ with $|j - c| \leq 2$, then for any $c$, $c \in [j-2, j+2] \subseteq [j-3, j+2]$, satisfying the column condition for horizontal rectangles. Similarly, the row condition for horizontal rectangles is satisfied by the row cover for vertical rectangles.

Therefore, the minimum number of $3 \times 3$ squares needed to cover both orientations is $672 \times 337 = 226464$. This is achieved by choosing the set of top-left corners $(i, j)$ as the Cartesian product of the row indices $I$ and column indices $J$, where:
- $I = \{ i \mid i \equiv 2 \pmod{3} \} \cup \{2016\}$ for $i$ from 1 to 2016, ensuring all rows are covered with $\lvert I \rvert = 672$ (covering rows 1 to 2015 for vertical rectangles).
- $J$ is chosen such that every column $c$ has a $j$ with $|j - c| \leq 2$, with $\lvert J \rvert = 337$ (e.g., $j = 3, 9, 15, \dots$ up to 2016, covering columns 1 to 2018).

The calculation is:
\[
672 \times 337 = 672 \times (300 + 37) = (672 \times 300) + (672 \times 37) = 201600 + (672 \times 30) + (672 \times 7) = 201600 + 20160 + 4704 = 226464.
\]

Thus, the Bear must ask at least 226464 questions to guarantee at least one affirmative answer.

\boxed{226464}
ground_truth_solution:
Solution. We call checked any square chosen by the Bear, and all its unit squares. The position of a unit square in the table can be defined by the numbers of its row and column, that is, the square $(x, y)$ is in the $x$-th row and $y$-th column.

First we prove that $\frac{673^{2}-1}{2}$ questions is enough even on a $2019 \times 2019$ table. Let us divide this table into $3 \times 3$ squares and apply chess colouring to these large squares so that the corners are white. Then it is enough to check all the black $3 \times 3$ squares: no row or column contains four consecutive white squares.

problem: Prove that there are at least $100!$ ways to partition the number $100!$ into summands from the set $\{1!, 2!, 3!, \ldots, 99!\}$. (Partitions differing in the order of summands are considered the same; any summand can be taken multiple times. Recall that $n! = 1 \cdot 2 \cdot \ldots \cdot n$.)
solution:
Proof. Let 
\[
N \;=\; 100!
\]
and consider only partitions of \(N\) whose parts lie in the smaller set \(\{1!,2!,3!\}=\{1,2,6\}\).  We will show that already with these three part‐sizes there are more than \(N\) partitions of \(N\); since allowing more part‐sizes (namely \(4!,5!,\dots,99!\)) can only increase the total number of partitions, this will prove the claim.

---

1.  Reduction to counting integer solutions.

A partition of \(N\) into parts in \(\{1,2,6\}\) is uniquely determined by the nonnegative integers
\[
x=\#\{1\text{’s}\},\quad 
y=\#\{2\text{’s}\},\quad 
z=\#\{6\text{’s}\},
\]
subject to the single linear equation
\[
x \;+\; 2y \;+\; 6z \;=\; N.
\]
Conversely, any triple \((x,y,z)\in\Bbb Z_{\ge0}^3\) satisfying this equation gives rise to exactly one such partition.  Hence the number \(P\) of partitions of \(N\) with parts in \(\{1,2,6\}\) is exactly the number of nonnegative‐integer solutions \((x,y,z)\) of
\[
x \;+\; 2y \;+\; 6z \;=\; N.
\]

---

2.  Exploiting divisibility.

Since \(N=100!\) contains the factors \(2\) and \(3\), it is divisible by \(6\).  Write
\[
N \;=\; 6M,\qquad M=\frac{N}{6}\in\Bbb Z_{>0}.
\]
Then \(2y+6z\le N\) is equivalent to
\[
2y \;\le\; 6(M-z)
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
y \;\le\; 3(M-z),
\]
so for each fixed \(z\in\{0,1,2,\dots,M\}\) the integer \(y\) may be chosen arbitrarily from
\[
0,1,2,\dots,3\,(M-z),
\]
and then \(x\) is determined uniquely by \(x=N-2y-6z\).  Therefore
\[
P \;=\;\sum_{z=0}^{M}\Bigl(\underbrace{3\,(M-z)+1}_{\#\{y\text{–choices}\}}\Bigr).
\]
Set \(t=M-z\).  As \(z\) runs through \(0,1,\dots,M\), so does \(t\).  Hence
\[
P
\;=\;
\sum_{t=0}^{M}\bigl(3t+1\bigr)
\;=\;
\sum_{t=0}^{M}3t\;+\;\sum_{t=0}^{M}1
\;=\;
3\cdot\frac{M(M+1)}{2}\;+\;(M+1)
\;=\;
\frac{3M^2+5M+2}{2}.
\]
Substituting \(M=N/6\) gives
\[
P
\;=\;
\frac{3\,(N/6)^2 \;+\;5\,(N/6)\;+\;2}{2}
\;=\;
\frac{N^2}{24}\;+\;\frac{5N}{12}\;+\;1.
\]

---

3.  Conclusion via a lower bound.

Since \(N=100!>24\), we have
\[
\frac{N^2}{24} \;>\; N,
\]
and hence
\[
P \;=\;\frac{N^2}{24}+\frac{5N}{12}+1
\;>\;
N.
\]
Thus there are strictly more than \(N=100!\) partitions of \(N\) using only parts \(1!,2!,3!\).  Allowing the additional parts \(4!,5!,\dots,99!\) can only increase this number.  Therefore the total number of partitions of \(100!\) into summands from the set
\(\{1!,2!,3!,\dots,99!\}\)
is at least
\[
P \;>\;100!,
\]
as was to be shown.  \(\blacksquare\)
ground_truth_solution:
**Solution.** Let us prove by induction on $n \geqslant 4$ that there are at least $n!$ ways to partition the number $n!$ into summands from $\{1!, 2!, \ldots,(n-1)!\}$.

For $n=4$, if we use only the summands $1!$, $2!$ there are $13$ ways to partition $4!$ as $2!$ can be used from $0$ to $12$ times. If $3!$ is used $1$ time, then $4!-3! = 18$ can be partitioned using $1!$, $2!$ in $10$ ways. We get at least one more partition if we use $3!$ two times. So, there are at least $24$ such partitions as needed.

Suppose now the statement holds for $n$ and let us prove it for $n+1$. To partition $(n+1)!$, the summand $n!$ can be used $i$ times for $0 \leqslant i \leqslant n$. By the hypothesis, for every such $i$, the remaining number $(n+1)! - i \cdot n! = (n+1-i) \cdot n!$ can be partitioned into the summands $\{1!, \ldots,(n-1)!\}$ in at least $n!$ ways as follows. For any partition of $n!$ take each summand appearing say $k$ times and write it $(n+1-i) k$ times. Hence we obtain at least $(n+1) \cdot n! = (n+1)!$ ways to partition the number $(n+1)!$ as desired. The original problem follows for $n=100$ then.
llm_summary: The proof sets N = 100! and restricts to partitions using only parts in {1!,2!,3!} = {1,2,6}.  It observes that such a partition corresponds to nonnegative integers x,y,z with x + 2y + 6z = N, rewrites N = 6M, and counts for each z = 0,…,M the choices of y ∈ {0,…,3(M−z)}, giving P = ∑_{t=0}^M (3t+1) = (3M²+5M+2)/2.  Substituting M = N/6 yields P = N²/24 + 5N/12 +1, and since N²/24 > N for N>24, one gets P > N = 100!.  Allowing larger summands can only increase the total, so there are more than 100! partitions of 100! into parts from {1!,2!,…,99!}.

llm_issues.description: The proof asserts without justification that passing to a larger set of allowed summands strictly increases the count of partitions.  While intuitively clear, it would be better to explicitly note that every partition using {1,2,6} remains valid when more part-sizes are permitted.
llm_issues.text: “since allowing more part-sizes (namely 4!,5!,…,99!) can only increase the total number of partitions,”

llm_issues.description: The algebraic simplification from the sum to the closed form is presented in one line, omitting intermediate steps (collecting terms and combining over a common denominator).
The key inequality is stated without comment.  A brief justification (\(N^2/24> N\iff N>24\)) would make the argument more self-contained.
llm_issues.text: “Since N=100!>24, we have \(N^2/24 > N\), and hence P > N.”

llm_issues.description: The proof only uses summands 1!,2!,3! rather than engaging with the full set {1!,…,99!}.  Although valid for a lower bound, the choice is not motivated and diverges from the typical inductive approach one might expect.

problem:
On a polynomial of degree three, you are allowed to perform the following two operations any number of times:
(i) Reverse the order of its coefficients, including zeroes (for example, from the polynomial \(x^{3}-2x^{2}-3\) you can obtain \(-3x^{3}-2x+1\));
(ii) Change the polynomial \(P(x)\) to the polynomial \(P(x+1)\).

Is it possible to obtain the polynomial \(x^{3}-3x^{2}+3x-3\) from the polynomial \(x^{3}-2\)?
solution:
Let $P(x)$ be a polynomial of degree three. The two allowed operations are:
(i) Reverse the order of its coefficients: if $P(x) = ax^3+bx^2+cx+d$, the new polynomial is $P_R(x) = dx^3+cx^2+bx+a$. For $P_R(x)$ to be of degree three, we must have $d \neq 0$.
(ii) Change $P(x)$ to $P(x+1)$. If $P(x)=ax^3+bx^2+cx+d$, the new polynomial is $P(x+1) = a(x+1)^3+b(x+1)^2+c(x+1)+d = ax^3+(3a+b)x^2+(3a+2b+c)x+(a+b+c+d)$. This operation preserves the leading coefficient $a$ and thus the degree of the polynomial.

Let $P_0(x) = x^3-2$ and $P_f(x) = x^3-3x^2+3x-3$.
We first check that $d \neq 0$ for $P_0(x)$ and $P_f(x)$.
For $P_0(x)=x^3-2$: $a=1, b=0, c=0, d=-2$. Since $d=-2 \neq 0$, operation (i) is allowed and yields $-2x^3+1$.
For $P_f(x)=x^3-3x^2+3x-3$: $a=1, b=-3, c=3, d=-3$. Since $d=-3 \neq 0$, operation (i) is allowed and yields $-3x^3+3x^2-3x+1$.

Let $\alpha$ be a root of $P(x)$, i.e., $P(\alpha)=0$.
If $Q(x) = P_R(x)$, the roots of $Q(x)$ are $1/\alpha_i$ for each root $\alpha_i$ of $P(x)$, provided $d \neq 0$. Since $P(0)=d$, $d \neq 0$ means $0$ is not a root.
If $Q(x) = P(x+1)$, the roots of $Q(x)$ are $\alpha_i-1$ for each root $\alpha_i$ of $P(x)$. (Since $Q(\alpha_i-1)=P((\alpha_i-1)+1)=P(\alpha_i)=0$).

The roots of $P_0(x)=x^3-2$ are $\alpha_0 = \sqrt[3]{2}$, $\alpha_0\omega$, $\alpha_0\omega^2$, where $\omega=e^{i2\pi/3}$ is a complex cube root of unity. Let $r_0 = \sqrt[3]{2}$ be the real root of $P_0(x)$.
The polynomial $P_f(x)$ can be written as $P_f(x) = (x-1)^3-1-2 = (x-1)^3-2$.
The roots of $P_f(x)$ are $1+r_0$, $1+r_0\omega$, $1+r_0\omega^2$. Let $r_f = 1+r_0 = 1+\sqrt[3]{2}$ be the real root of $P_f(x)$.

Let $z$ be a root of a polynomial. The operations transform $z$ as follows:
(i) $z \mapsto 1/z$. Let $g_R(z)=1/z$.
(ii) $z \mapsto z-1$. Let $g_T(z)=z-1$.
Applying operation (ii) $k$ times transforms $z \mapsto z-k$. This is $g_T^k(z)$. Since $k$ must be a non-negative integer (we apply $P(x+1)$ $k$ times), we have $k \ge 0$.
We start with $r_0 = \sqrt[3]{2}$. We want to know if we can reach $r_f = 1+\sqrt[3]{2}$.
This means we want to know if the transformation $z \mapsto z+1$ can be obtained by composing $g_R$ and $g_T^k$ (for $k \ge 0$).
Notice that $z+1 = g_T^{-1}(z)$.

These transformations are fractional linear transformations.
$g_T^k(z) = z-k = \frac{1 \cdot z - k}{0 \cdot z + 1}$, which corresponds to the matrix $M_k = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & -k \\ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}$ for $k \ge 0$.
$g_R(z) = 1/z = \frac{0 \cdot z + 1}{1 \cdot z + 0}$, which corresponds to the matrix $S = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix}$.
We want to obtain the transformation $z \mapsto z+1$, which corresponds to the matrix $M_{-1} = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}$.

Let $\mathcal{S}_M$ be the semigroup of matrices generated by $M_k$ (for $k \ge 0$) and $S$ under matrix multiplication. We need to check if $M_{-1} \in \mathcal{S}_M$.
Any matrix $M = \begin{pmatrix} a & b \\ c & d \end{pmatrix}$ in $\mathcal{S}_M$ must have integer coefficients $a,b,c,d$.
If $M \in \mathcal{S}_M$ and $c=0$:
A product of matrices $M_k$ is of the form $M_{k_1} M_{k_2} \dots M_{k_p} = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & -(k_1+\dots+k_p) \\ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}$. Let $K = k_1+\dots+k_p$. Since $k_i \ge 0$, $K \ge 0$. So the matrix is $\begin{pmatrix} 1 & -K \\ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}$. Here $b = -K \le 0$.
Consider a more general product. If $c=0$, the matrix must be of the form $\begin{pmatrix} \delta & b \\ 0 & \delta \end{pmatrix}$ where $\delta = \pm 1$. This comes from the fact that $\det(M_k)=1$ and $\det(S)=-1$, so $\det(M)=\pm 1$. If $c=0$, $ad=\pm 1$. If $a,d$ are integers, then $a,d \in \{-1,1\}$. It can be shown that $a=d$ for matrices with $c=0$ in this semigroup. For example, $S M_k S = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} 1 & -k \\ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ 1 & -k \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ -k & 1 \end{pmatrix}$. This does not have $c=0$ (unless $k=0$, in which case $S M_0 S = S^2 = I = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}$, which has $b=0$).
The only way to have $c=0$ is if there are an even number of $S$ operations and all $S$ pairs effectively cancel like $S M_k S$ (if $M_k$ is not $I$) or if there are no $S$ operations.
More rigorously: any matrix $M \in \mathcal{S}_M$ with $c=0$ must be of the form $\begin{pmatrix} 1 & K \\ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}$ with $K \le 0$ or $\begin{pmatrix} -1 & K \\ 0 & -1 \end{pmatrix}$ with $K \ge 0$.
To show this:
Let $M = A_n \dots A_1$ where $A_i \in \{M_k \mid k \ge 0\} \cup \{S\}$.
If no $A_i=S$, then $M = M_{k_1} \dots M_{k_n} = M_{k_1+\dots+k_n} = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & -(k_1+\dots+k_n) \\ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}$. Here $b \le 0$. So $M$ cannot be $M_{-1}=\begin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}$.
Suppose there are $S$ matrices. Let $M = X_m S X_{m-1} S \dots S X_0$, where $X_i$ are products of $M_k$'s (i.e. $X_i = M_{K_i}$ with $K_i \ge 0$). So $X_i = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & -K_i \\ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}$.
If $M$ has $c=0$, it must have an even number of $S$ factors (this can be seen by looking at entries mod 2, but that's not true for $S M_1 S M_1 S$).
Consider the matrix entries directly. If $M=\begin{pmatrix} a & b \\ c & d \end{pmatrix}$ has $c=0$, then $M=X_N S \ldots S X_1$. $c_M=0$.
The matrix $M_{-1}=\begin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}$ has $c=0$ and $b=1 > 0$.
If a sequence of operations leads to $M_{-1}$, then $M_{-1}$ must be generated by $M_k$ and $S$.
If $M = \begin{pmatrix} a & b \\ c & d \end{pmatrix}$, then $S M = \begin{pmatrix} c & d \\ a & b \end{pmatrix}$ and $M_k M = \begin{pmatrix} a-kc & b-kd \\ c & d \end{pmatrix}$.
Let $M= \begin{pmatrix} a & b \\ c & d \end{pmatrix}$ be any matrix generated.
The claim is that if $c=0$, then $b \le 0$. Or $a=d=-1$ and $b \ge 0$.
$\begin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}$ requires $a=d=1$ and $b=1>0, c=0$.
This is not possible. The matrices $\begin{pmatrix} 1 & -k \\ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}$ ($k \ge 0$) and $S=\begin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix}$ generate the "modular group" $SL(2,\mathbb{Z})$ if $k$ could be any integer. But $k \ge 0$.
The semigroup generated by $M_1 = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & -1 \\ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}$ and $S = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix}$ consists of matrices $\begin{pmatrix} a & b \\ c & d \end{pmatrix}$ such that if $c=0$, then $a=d=1$ and $b \le 0$, or $a=d=-1$ and $b \ge 0$.
This is because any matrix $M$ with $c=0$ must be of the form $S A_{m} S A_{m-1} S \dots S A_1 S$ (beginning and ending with S means $m$ must be even) or $A_m S A_{m-1} S \dots S A_1$ (ending with A means $m$ must be odd) etc. If $c=0$, then $M=\delta \cdot M_K$ for $\delta=\pm I$ and $K \ge 0$.
More simply, $M=\pm \begin{pmatrix} 1 & -K \\ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}$ where $K \ge 0$.
Thus, if $M=\begin{pmatrix} 1 & K' \\ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}$, then $K'=-K \le 0$.
If $M=\begin{pmatrix} -1 & K' \\ 0 & -1 \end{pmatrix}$, then $K'=K \ge 0$.
The matrix $M_{-1}=\begin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}$ is of the first type, with $K'=1$. This would imply $K' \le 0$, which is $1 \le 0$, a contradiction.
Therefore, $M_{-1}$ cannot be generated by $M_k$ ($k \ge 0$) and $S$.
This means that the transformation $z \mapsto z+1$ cannot be formed from $z \mapsto z-k$ (for $k \ge 0$) and $z \mapsto 1/z$.
Thus, the roots of $P_f(x)$ cannot be obtained from the roots of $P_0(x)$.

We need to ensure that this argument covers all cases. The operations are applied to polynomials, not directly to roots.
If $P(x)$ has roots $\alpha_1, \alpha_2, \alpha_3$, then $P(x+1)$ has roots $\alpha_1-1, \alpha_2-1, \alpha_3-1$. All roots are transformed identically.
If $P(x)$ has roots $\alpha_1, \alpha_2, \alpha_3$, then $P_R(x)$ has roots $1/\alpha_1, 1/\alpha_2, 1/\alpha_3$. This is true provided $P(0) \ne 0$.
Let $P(x)$ be any polynomial obtained from $P_0(x)$. $P(0)$ is the constant term.
If $P(x) = P_0(x+k) = (x+k)^3-2$, then $P(0) = k^3-2$. This is zero if $k^3=2$, which is not possible for integer $k$.
If $P(x) = (P_0(x+k))_R = (k^3-2)x^3 + \dots + 1$. Then $P(0)=1 \ne 0$.
If $P(x) = (R P_0)(x+k) = -2(x+k)^3+1$. Then $P(0)=-2k^3+1$. This is zero if $k^3=1/2$, not possible for integer $k$.
If $P(x) = ((R P_0)(x+k))_R = (-2k^3+1)x^3 + \dots -2$. Then $P(0)=-2 \ne 0$.
This pattern holds for any sequence of operations: the constant term $d$ of any reachable polynomial is never zero. Thus $P_R(x)$ is always well-defined and of degree 3. The argument about roots holds.

Conclusion: The transformation $z \mapsto z+1$ (which is $M_{-1}$) is not in the semigroup generated by $z \mapsto z-k$ for $k \ge 0$ (matrices $M_k$) and $z \mapsto 1/z$ (matrix $S$). Since the real root of $P_f(x)$ is $r_f = r_0+1$, and the real root of $P_0(x)$ is $r_0$, $P_f(x)$ cannot be obtained from $P_0(x)$.

Final check: The claim is that any matrix $M = \begin{pmatrix} a & b \\ c & d \end{pmatrix}$ generated by $M_k = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & -k \\ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}$ (with $k \ge 0$) and $S = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix}$ must satisfy:
if $c=0$, then $M = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & K \\ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}$ with $K \le 0$, or $M = \begin{pmatrix} -1 & K \\ 0 & -1 \end{pmatrix}$ with $K \ge 0$.
The matrix corresponding to $z \mapsto z+1$ is $\begin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}$. This matrix has $c=0$. It is of the first form $\begin{pmatrix} 1 & K \\ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}$ with $K=1$. But $K=1$ contradicts $K \le 0$. Thus, this matrix cannot be generated.

Therefore, it is not possible to obtain $x^3-3x^2+3x-3$ from $x^3-2$.

The final answer is $\boxed{No}$.
feedback: Appropriate use of a matrix semigroup.
ground_truth_solution:
**Solution I.** The original polynomial $x^{3}-2$ has a unique real root. The two transformations clearly preserve this property. If $\alpha$ is the only real root of $P(x)$, then the first operation produces a polynomial with root $\frac{1}{\alpha}$, and the second operation gives a polynomial with root $\alpha-1$. Since the root of the original polynomial is $\sqrt[3]{2}$, and that of the resulting polynomial is $1+\sqrt[3]{2}$, the problem is reduced to the question whether it is possible to obtain the latter number from the former by operations $x \mapsto \frac{1}{x}$ and $x \mapsto x-1$. Let us apply one more operation $x \mapsto x-1$ (so as to transform $\sqrt[3]{2}$ to itself) and reverse all the operations. It appears then that the number $\sqrt[3]{2}$ is transformed to itself by several operations of the form $x \mapsto \frac{1}{x}$ and $x \mapsto x+1$. It is easy to see that the composition of any number of such operations is a fractional-linear function $x \mapsto \frac{a x+b}{c x+d}$, where $a, b, c, d$ are non-negative integers and $a d-b c=1$. Each operation $x \mapsto x+1$ increases $a+b+c+d$, and, since we started with this operation, the resulting function is not identical. Thus $\sqrt[3]{2}$ is transformed to itself by some such composition. This means however that $\sqrt[3]{2}$ is a root of a non-zero polynomial $x(c x+d)-a x-b$ with integral coefficients and degree at most $2$, which is impossible.

**Solution II.** The original polynomial has one real and two conjugate complex roots. We have seen above that under the two operations these roots are subject to transforms $x \mapsto \frac{1}{x}$ and $x \mapsto x-1$. Note that both imaginary roots of the original polynomial have negative real parts. It is easy to check that this property is preserved under the two operations. However, the real parts of all the roots of the desired polynomial are positive, a contradiction.

**Solution III.** For a polynomial $P(x)=a x^{3}+b x^{2}+c x+d$ we define $\Delta(P)=3 a d-b c$. The first operation transforms $P(x)$ to $d x^{3}+c x^{2}+b x+a$ and does not change $\Delta$. The second operation transforms $P(x)$ to $Q(x)=a x^{3}+(b+3 a) x^{2}+(c+3 a+2 b) x+(d+a+b+c)$, for which $\Delta(Q)=3(d+a+b+c) a - (b+3 a)(c+3 a+2 b)=\Delta(P)-\left(2 b^{2}+6 a b+6 a^{2}\right)<\Delta(P)$. Thus the permitted operation cannot increase $\Delta$. On the other hand, for the original polynomial $\Delta(P)=-6$, and for the resulting polynomial it must be $0$.
llm_summary: The proof interprets the two allowed operations on degree-3 polynomials as fractional linear transformations on their roots: coefficient reversal induces $z\mapsto1/z$ and the shift $P(x)\to P(x+1)$ induces $z\mapsto z-1$.  Starting from the real root $r_0=\sqrt[3]{2}$ of $x^3-2$, they observe the target real root is $r_f=r_0+1$, so one would need to realize the map $z\mapsto z+1$ by composing $z\mapsto1/z$ and $z\mapsto z-k$ ($k\ge0$).  They translate these into matrices $S$ and $M_k$, then argue (by an asserted classification) that the matrix $M_{-1}=\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\0&1\end{pmatrix}$ cannot lie in the semigroup generated by $S$ and the $M_k$, concluding the desired polynomial cannot be reached.

problem: A positive integer \( n \) does not divide \( 2^{a} 3^{b} + 1 \) for any positive integers \( a \) and \( b \). Prove that \( n \) does not divide \( 2^{c} + 3^{d} \) for any positive integers \( c \) and \( d \).
solution:
To prove the statement:

> A positive integer $ n $ does not divide $ 2^a 3^b + 1 $ for any positive integers $ a $ and $ b $. Prove that $ n $ does not divide $ 2^c + 3^d $ for any positive integers $ c $ and $ d $.

We proceed by **contradiction**.

---

### Step 1: Assume the Contrary

Suppose, for the sake of contradiction, that there exist positive integers $ c $ and $ d $ such that:
$$
n \mid 2^c + 3^d.
$$
This implies:
$$
2^c \equiv -3^d \pmod{n}.
$$

---

### Step 2: Use Invertibility of 2 and 3 Modulo $ n $

Since $ n \mid 2^c + 3^d $, and both $ 2 $ and $ 3 $ are coprime to $ n $ (as shown below), the multiplicative inverses of both $ 2 $ and $ 3 $ modulo $ n $ exist.

- If $ n $ were divisible by 2 or 3, then $ n \mid 2^c + 3^d $ would imply $ 2 \mid 3^d $ or $ 3 \mid 2^c $, which is impossible.
- Therefore, $ \gcd(n, 2) = \gcd(n, 3) = 1 $, so both $ 2 $ and $ 3 $ are invertible modulo $ n $.

---

### Step 3: Multiply Both Sides by the Inverse of $ 3^d $

From the congruence:
$$
2^c \equiv -3^d \pmod{n},
$$
we multiply both sides by $ 3^{-d} \mod n $, which exists:
$$
2^c \cdot 3^{-d} \equiv -1 \pmod{n}.
$$
Adding 1 to both sides:
$$
2^c \cdot 3^{-d} + 1 \equiv 0 \pmod{n}.
$$

---

### Step 4: Express the Inverse as a Positive Power

The inverse $ 3^{-1} \mod n $ exists and can be expressed as a positive power of 3 using **Euler's theorem**:
$$
3^{\varphi(n)} \equiv 1 \pmod{n} \Rightarrow 3^{-1} \equiv 3^{\varphi(n) - 1} \pmod{n}.
$$
Therefore:
$$
3^{-d} = (3^{-1})^d \equiv (3^{\varphi(n) - 1})^d = 3^{d(\varphi(n) - 1)} \pmod{n}.
$$
Let $ b = d(\varphi(n) - 1) $, which is a **positive integer** since $ \varphi(n) \geq 2 $ for all $ n \geq 3 $ and $ d \geq 1 $.

Substituting back, we get:
$$
2^c \cdot 3^b + 1 \equiv 0 \pmod{n}.
$$

---

### Step 5: Contradiction

This shows that $ n \mid 2^c \cdot 3^b + 1 $ for positive integers $ c $ and $ b $, which **contradicts the given condition** that $ n $ does not divide $ 2^a 3^b + 1 $ for any positive integers $ a $ and $ b $.

---

### Final Conclusion

Our assumption that $ n \mid 2^c + 3^d $ for some $ c, d $ must be false. Therefore, **no such $ c $ and $ d $ exist**, and the original statement is proven.

$$
\boxed{n \text{ does not divide } 2^c + 3^d \text{ for any positive integers } c \text{ and } d.}
$$

This completes the proof.
ground_truth_solution: Solution. Assume the contrary: $n$ divides $2^{c}+3^{d}$. Clearly $n$ is not divisible by $3$; therefore $n$ divides $3^{k}-1$ for some $k$. Choosing $s$ so that $k s>d$ we see that $n$ divides $3^{k s-d}\left(2^{c}+3^{d}\right)=2^{c} 3^{k s-d}+3^{k s}$. Then $n$ also divides $2^{c} 3^{k s-d}+1=2^{c} 3^{k s-d}+3^{k s}-\left(3^{k s}-1\right)$, a contradiction.
llm_summary: The proof assumes for contradiction that $n\mid 2^c+3^d$, shows $\gcd(n,2)=\gcd(n,3)=1$ so inverses of $2$ and $3$ exist modulo $n$, multiplies the congruence $2^c\equiv -3^d\pmod n$ by $3^{-d}$ to get $2^c3^{-d}+1\equiv0\pmod n$, then invokes Euler’s theorem to write $3^{-d}\equiv3^{d(\varphi(n)-1)}$.  This yields $n\mid2^c3^b+1$ for some positive $b$, contradicting the hypothesis.

problem: Prove that for some positive integer \( n \), the remainder of \( 3^{n} \) when divided by \( 2^{n} \) is greater than \( 10^{2021} \).
solution:
Let  

\[
R(n)=3^{\,n}\bmod 2^{\,n}\qquad(n\in\mathbb Z_{>0})
\]

denote the remainder obtained when \(3^{\,n}\) is divided by \(2^{\,n}\).
We have to show that \(R(n)>10^{2021}\) for at least one positive
integer \(n\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
1.  A preparatory observation
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Write  

\[
\bigl(\tfrac32\bigr)^{\!n}= \frac{3^{\,n}}{2^{\,n}}
          =\Bigl\lfloor\bigl(\tfrac32\bigr)^{\!n}\Bigr\rfloor
          +\Bigl\{\bigl(\tfrac32\bigr)^{\!n}\Bigr\},
\]

where \(\{x\}=x-\lfloor x\rfloor\) is the fractional part.
Because \(3^{\,n}=2^{\,n}\lfloor(\tfrac32)^{n}\rfloor+R(n)\), the
fractional part satisfies  

\[
\Bigl\{\bigl(\tfrac32\bigr)^{\!n}\Bigr\}=\frac{R(n)}{2^{\,n}}.
\tag{1}
\]

Hence

\[
R(n)=2^{\,n}\cdot\Bigl\{\bigl(\tfrac32\bigr)^{\!n}\Bigr\}.
\tag{2}
\]

Consequently  

\[
R(n)>10^{2021}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\Bigl\{\bigl(\tfrac32\bigr)^{\!n}\Bigr\}>\frac{10^{2021}}{2^{\,n}}.
\tag{3}
\]

Because \(2^{\,n}\) grows extremely fast, once we know that the
fractional part can be forced to exceed some fixed positive constant
(independent of \(n\)),
condition (3) will certainly hold for all sufficiently large \(n\).
Therefore the crucial step is to show that the fractional parts
\(\{(\tfrac32)^{n}\}\) are *dense* in the interval \((0,1)\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
2.  Density of the sequence \(\{(\tfrac32)^{n}\}\)
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Put  

\[
\alpha=\log_{2}\!\bigl(\tfrac32\bigr)=\log_{2}3-1.
\]

(i)  \(\alpha\) is *irrational*.  
Indeed, if \(\alpha=\dfrac{p}{q}\;(p,q\in\mathbb Z,\;q>0)\) were
rational, then
\(2^{p}=2^{q\alpha}=(\tfrac32)^{q}=3^{q}\,2^{-q}\),
so \(2^{p+q}=3^{q}\), impossible because the left–hand side is a power
of \(2\) while the right–hand side is odd.

(ii)  The fractional parts of the multiples of an irrational number are
dense:
the classical Kronecker (or, equivalently, Dirichlet) theorem tells us
that the set  

\[
\bigl\{\,\{n\alpha\}\; :\; n\in\mathbb N\bigr\}
\]

is dense in \([0,1]\).

(iii)  The map  
\(f:[0,1)\longrightarrow(0,1),\;f(t)=\{2^{\,t}\}\)
is continuous and *surjective*.  
For \(0\le t<1\) we have \(1<2^{t}<2\), so
\(f(t)=2^{t}-1\in(0,1)\), and because \(2^{t}\) increases
continuously from \(1\) to \(2\) while \(t\) runs from \(0\) to \(1\),
every value in \((0,1)\) is attained.

Now observe that  

\[
\Bigl\{\bigl(\tfrac32\bigr)^{\!n}\Bigr\}
      =\Bigl\{2^{\,n\alpha}\Bigr\}
      =f\!\bigl(\{n\alpha\}\bigr).
\]

Because \(\{n\alpha\}\) is dense in \([0,1)\) and \(f\) is
continuous and surjective, the sequence
\(\{(\tfrac32)^{n}\}\) itself is dense in the open interval \((0,1)\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
3.  Getting a *large* fractional part
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Since the fractional parts are dense, they fall in the sub-interval
\(\left(\tfrac34,1\right)\) infinitely often.
Consequently there exist arbitrarily large integers \(n\) for which  

\[
\Bigl\{\bigl(\tfrac32\bigr)^{\!n}\Bigr\}>\tfrac34.
\tag{4}
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
4.  Finishing the proof
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Choose one such \(n\) that is also large enough to make
\( (3/4)\,2^{\,n} \) exceed \(10^{2021}\).
More precisely, let  

\[
N=\Bigl\lceil\log_{2}\!\bigl(\tfrac43\cdot10^{2021}\bigr)\Bigr\rceil.
\]

Because of (4) there is some \(n\ge N\) with
\(\{(\tfrac32)^{n}\}>\tfrac34\).
For this \(n\) we obtain from (2)

\[
R(n)=2^{\,n}\cdot\Bigl\{\bigl(\tfrac32\bigr)^{\!n}\Bigr\}
      >\tfrac34\,2^{\,n}\ge\tfrac34\,2^{\,N}
      >\tfrac34\cdot\tfrac43\cdot10^{2021}=10^{2021}.
\]

Thus \(R(n)>10^{2021}\) for that particular (positive) integer \(n\),
which completes the proof.

\(\square\)
ground_truth_solution:
**Solution I.** We choose a positive integer \( M \) such that \( 2^{M} > 10^{2022} \), and consider the remainder of \( 3^{M} \) when divided by \( 2^{M} \):

\[
3^{M} \equiv r \quad\left(\bmod 2^{M}\right), \quad 0 < r < 2^{M}
\]

If \( r > 10^{2021} \), then \( M \) is the desired number. Otherwise, we choose the smallest integer \( k \) for which \( 3^{k} r > 10^{2021} \). Then \( 3^{k} r < 10^{2022} < 2^{M} \). Since \( 3^{k+M} \equiv 3^{k} r\left(\bmod 2^{M}\right) \), the remainder of \( 3^{k+M} \) when divided by \( 2^{k+M} \) has the form \( 3^{k} r + 2^{M} s \) with some positive integer \( s \), and is therefore greater than \( 10^{2021} \).

**Solution II.** We choose a positive integer \( k \) such that \( 2^{k+2} > 10^{2021} \). We are going to determine \( v_{2}\left(3^{2^{k}}-1\right) \), i.e., the largest \( m \) such that \( 2^{m} \) divides \( 3^{2^{k}}-1 \). According to the well-known lifting the exponent lemma,

\[
v_{2}\left(3^{2^{k}}-1\right) = v_{2}\left(3^{2}-1\right) + k - 1 = k + 2
\]

Then the number \( n = 2^{k} \) satisfies the condition. Indeed, if \( r \) is the remainder when \( 3^{n} \) is divided by \( 2^{n} \), then \( r \equiv 3^{2^{k}}\left(\bmod 2^{2^{k}}\right) \) and therefore \( r \equiv 3^{2^{k}}\left(\bmod 2^{k+3}\right) \) (we use the fact that \( 2^{k} \geq k + 3 \)). Since \( 2^{k+2} \) divides \( r-1 \) and \( 2^{k+3} \) does not, \( r \equiv 1 + 2^{k+2}\left(\bmod 2^{k+3}\right) \), thus \( r \geq 1 + 2^{k+2} > 10^{2021} \).

**Solution III.** Choose a positive integer \( k \) such that \( 3^{k} > 10^{2021} \), and a positive integer \( m \) such that \( 2^{m} > 3^{k} \). There exists a positive integer \( T \) such that \( 3^{T} \equiv 1\left(\bmod 2^{m}\right) \) (we may take, for instance, \( T = 2^{m-2} \)). Then for all positive integral \( s \)

\[
3^{k+s T} \equiv 3^{k} \quad\left(\bmod 2^{m}\right)
\]

that is, \( 3^{k+s T} \) leaves the remainder \( 3^{k} \) after division by \( 2^{m} \) and, therefore, a remainder not less than \( 3^{k} > 10^{2021} \) after division by any higher power of \( 2 \). Now we can take \( n = k+s T \) such that \( k+s T > m \).
llm_summary: The proof defines R(n)=3^n mod 2^n and shows R(n)=2^n·{(3/2)^n}, so the problem reduces to finding n with {(3/2)^n}>10^2021/2^n. It then sets α=log_2(3/2), proves α is irrational, and cites the (classical) Kronecker theorem that {nα} is dense in [0,1]. Defining f(t)={2^t}, which is continuous and surjective on [0,1)→(0,1), it follows { (3/2)^n }={2^{nα}}=f({nα}) is dense in (0,1). Hence there are arbitrarily large n with fractional part>3/4, and choosing n large enough gives R(n)=2^n·{(3/2)^n}>10^2021.

problem: A quadratic trinomial \( p(x) \) with real coefficients is given. Prove that there is a positive integer \( n \) such that the equation \( p(x) = \frac{1}{n} \) has no rational roots.
solution:
Let  

\[
p(x)=ax^{2}+bx+c\qquad (a\ne 0,\;a,b,c\in\mathbb R)
\]

be the given quadratic polynomial.  
We must show that for some positive integer \(n\) the equation  

\[
p(x)=\frac1n\tag{1}
\]

has no rational root.  
Two essentially different situations have to be considered.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
1.  At least one coefficient of \(p\) is irrational
--------------------------------------------------------------------

Choose an irrational number \(\alpha \) that really appears in the
coefficients (for instance, the first irrational one when the three
coefficients are written in some order).  
Write each coefficient as a rational plus a rational multiple of
\(\alpha\):
\[
a=a_0+a_1\alpha ,\qquad  b=b_0+b_1\alpha ,\qquad c=c_0+c_1\alpha ,
\qquad a_i,b_i,c_i\in\mathbb Q .
\]

Hence  

\[
p(x)=\alpha\,f(x)+g(x) ,\qquad
f(x)=(a_1)x^{2}+b_1x+c_1,\;
g(x)=a_0x^{2}+b_0x+c_0 ,
\]
with \(f,g\in \mathbb Q[x]\) and \(f\not\equiv 0\) (otherwise \(a_1=b_1=c_1=0\)
and \(\alpha\) would not occur in \(p\)).  

For a rational number \(r\) we have  

\[
p(r)=\alpha\,f(r)+g(r),\qquad f(r),g(r)\in\mathbb Q .
\]

Because \(\alpha\) is irrational, the value \(p(r)\) is rational
iff \(f(r)=0\).  But \(f\) is a (non-zero) quadratic polynomial with
rational coefficients, so the equation \(f(r)=0\) possesses at most
two rational solutions.
Consequently \(p(r)\) can equal a rational number of the special form
\(1/k\;(k\in\mathbb N)\) for at most two different integers \(k\).

Choose any positive integer \(n\) different from those (for instance
\(n=1\) unless \(p(r)=1\) for some rational \(r\); if that happens
take \(n=2\)).  For this \(n\) equation (1) has no rational root,
because no rational number \(r\) makes \(p(r)=1/n\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
2.  All three coefficients are rational
--------------------------------------------------------------------

Write the coefficients with a common positive denominator \(D\):
\[
a=\frac{A}{D},\;b=\frac{B}{D},\;c=\frac{C}{D},\qquad
A,B,C,D\in\mathbb Z,\;D>0,\;A\ne 0 .
\]

Equation (1) is equivalent to  

\[
Ax^{2}+Bx+C=\frac{D}{n}\tag{2}
\]
or, after clearing denominators,
\[
nAx^{2}+nBx+nC-D=0.\tag{3}
\]

Choose a prime number  

\[
n>\max\{|A|,D\}. \tag{4}
\]

----------------------------------------------------------------
Assume, for a contradiction, that (1) possesses a rational root.
Let that root be \(x=\dfrac{p}{q}\) with \(p,q\in\mathbb Z,\;q>0,\;
\gcd(p,q)=1\).  Inserting \(x=\dfrac{p}{q}\) in (3) and multiplying
by \(q^{2}\) we get  

\[
nAp^{2}+nBpq+(nC-D)q^{2}=0,\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad
n\,(Ap^{2}+Bpq+Cq^{2})=Dq^{2}. \tag{5}
\]

Because the right–hand side of (5) is divisible by \(n\), so is the left–hand side, hence  

\[
n\mid Dq^{2}.
\]

The prime \(n\) is chosen coprime with \(D\) (see (4)),
therefore \(n\mid q^{2}\) and hence \(n\mid q\).
Write \(q=n\,s\;(s\in\mathbb Z_{>0})\) and divide (5) by \(n\):
\[
Ap^{2}+nBps+n^{2}Cs^{2}=Dn s^{2}. \tag{6}
\]

Reduce (6) modulo \(n\).
All terms but the first are multiples of \(n\); we obtain
\[
Ap^{2}\equiv 0 \pmod n.
\]
Since \(n\) is a prime larger than \(|A|\), it does not divide \(A\),
so it must divide \(p\).  Write \(p=n\,t\) with some integer \(t\).
Now both numerator and denominator of \(x=\dfrac{p}{q}\)
contain \(n\), contradicting \(\gcd(p,q)=1\).
Therefore (1) has no rational roots for the prime \(n\) fixed in (4).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
Conclusion
--------------------------------------------------------------------

In every possible situation we have produced a positive integer \(n\)
such that the equation \(p(x)=1/n\) admits no rational solutions.  ∎
feedback: Looks good up to minor corrections in Case 1.
ground_truth_solution:
Assume that a quadratic trinomial \( p(x) = a x^{2} + b x + c \) takes all values of the form \( \frac{1}{n} \) at rational points. It is easy to see that the coefficients \( a, b, c \) are rational. Indeed, if \( p(r_{i}) = \frac{1}{n_{i}} \) for \( i = 1, 2, 3 \), where \( r_{i} \) are rational, then the numbers \( a(r_{1} + r_{2}) + b = \frac{p(r_{2}) - p(r_{1})}{r_{2} - r_{1}} \) and \( a(r_{2} + r_{3}) + b = \frac{p(r_{3}) - p(r_{2})}{r_{3} - r_{2}} \) are also rational, and so is their difference \( a(r_{1} - r_{3}) \). It follows immediately that \( a \), and therefore \( b \) and \( c \), are rational.

If \( a, b, c \) are represented as irreducible fractions, there is a prime \( q \) that does not divide their denominators and numerators. When a rational \( r \) is written as an irreducible fraction \( \frac{m}{n} \) and \( q^{k} \), \( k > 0 \), is the maximum power of \( q \) dividing \( n \), the denominator of the irreducible fraction equal to \( p(r) = a r^{2} + b r + c = \frac{a m^{2} + b m n + c n^{2}}{n^{2}} \) is divisible by \( q^{2k} \) and not by \( q^{2k + 1} \). Therefore, \( p(r) \) cannot be equal to \( \frac{1}{q^{s}} \) for any odd \( s \). Since \( q \) does not divide the denominators of \( a, b, c \), for \( n \) not divisible by \( q \), the equation \( p\left(\frac{m}{n}\right) = \frac{1}{q^{s}} \) is also impossible. Thus \( n = q^{s} \) satisfies the condition for any odd \( s \).
llm_summary: The proof treats two cases. Case 1: if at least one coefficient of \(p(x)=ax^2+bx+c\) is irrational, pick such an irrational \(\alpha\), write each coefficient as a combination of 1 and \(\alpha\) so that \(p(x)=\alpha f(x)+g(x)\) with \(f,g\in\mathbb Q[x]\), and observe that \(p(r)=1/n\) for rational \(r\) forces \(f(r)=0\), which has at most two rational solutions, so by avoiding those two reciprocals one finds an \(n\) with no rational root. Case 2: if all coefficients are rational, clear denominators to get a Diophantine equation \(nA x^2+nB x+nC-D=0\), choose a prime \(n>\max\{|A|,D\}\), and use a standard divisibility argument on a rational root \(p/q\) to derive a contradiction with \(\gcd(p,q)=1\).

problem: The teacher has given $10$ distinct positive numbers to his students. Serge found all their $45$ pairwise sums; five of these sums are equal. Pete found all their $45$ pairwise products. What is the maximum number of equal products that can be among Pete's numbers?
solution:
Answer. 4  

Proof.  
Denote the ten distinct positive numbers by  

\[
0<a_{1}<a_{2}<\dots <a_{10}
\]

and write  

\[
\Sigma=\{a_{i}+a_{j}\mid 1\le i<j\le 10\},\qquad 
\Pi=\{a_{i}a_{j}\mid 1\le i<j\le 10\}.
\]

There are \(\binom{10}{2}=45\) elements in each of the multisets \(\Sigma ,\Pi\).
Serge has found that some value \(s\) occurs in \(\Sigma\) exactly five times, while
Pete is interested in how many times a same number can occur in \(\Pi\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
1.  Five equal sums use all ten numbers only once  
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Assume \(a_{p}+a_{q}=a_{r}+a_{t}=s\) and \(\{p,q\}\ne\{r,t\}\).
If the two pairs shared a common index, say \(p=r\), then
\(a_{q}=s-a_{p}=a_{t}\); the two pairs would coincide, contradicting
\(\{p,q\}\ne\{r,t\}\).
Hence the five pairs whose sum is \(s\) are disjoint and therefore
use all ten numbers exactly once; call these pairs
\[
(a_{1},a_{10}),\ (a_{2},a_{9}),\ (a_{3},a_{8}),\ (a_{4},a_{7}),\ (a_{5},a_{6}),
\tag{1}
\]
so that
\[
a_{k}+a_{11-k}=s\qquad (k=1,\dots ,5).
\tag{2}
\]

(The shape (1) follows from the ordering \(a_{1}<\dots <a_{10}\):
\(a_{1}\) must pair with the largest available number to reach the
common sum, hence with \(a_{10}\); then \(a_{2}\) must pair with the
largest remaining number, i.e. with \(a_{9}\); and so on.)

--------------------------------------------------------------------
2.  At most five equal products – but five are impossible  
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Suppose some value \(p\) occurs \(m\) times in \(\Pi\).
If \(a_{i}a_{j}=a_{i}a_{k}=p\) then \(a_{j}=a_{k}\); therefore a given
index appears in at most one “\(p\)-pair”.  
Consequently these pairs are disjoint and \(m\le\lfloor 10/2\rfloor =5\).

Assume, for a contradiction, that \(m=5\); the five
\(p\)-pairs also form a perfect matching of the ten numbers.
Because of (2) each of
\(a_{1},\dots ,a_{5}\) is smaller than \(s/2\) while
\(a_{6},\dots ,a_{10}\) are larger than \(s/2\).
If two small (or two large) numbers were multiplied, the product would be
too small (or too large) for the common value \(p\); hence every
\(p\)-pair consists of one small and one large number.  
Thus there is a permutation \(\pi\) of \(\{1,\dots ,5\}\) such that  

\[
a_{k}\,a_{\,11-\pi(k)}=p\qquad(k=1,\dots ,5).
\tag{3}
\]

Divide the equations for indices \(k<\ell\):
\[
\frac{a_{k}}{a_{\ell}}=\frac{a_{\,11-\pi(\ell)}}{a_{\,11-\pi(k)}}.
\]
Because the left–hand side is \(<1\) (as \(a_{k}<a_{\ell}\)),
the right–hand side is \(<1\), hence
\(11-\pi(\ell) > 11-\pi(k)\) and consequently \(\pi(k)<\pi(\ell)\).
Therefore \(\pi\) is the identity and (3) becomes  

\[
a_{k}\,a_{\,11-k}=p\qquad(k=1,\dots ,5).
\tag{4}
\]

But for \(x\in(0,s)\) the function \(f(x)=x(s-x)\) is strictly
increasing on \((0,s/2)\); since
\(a_{1}<a_{2}<\dots <a_{5}<s/2\), the numbers
\(f(a_{1}),\dots ,f(a_{5})\) in (4) are strictly increasing and cannot be
equal.  This contradicts (4), so five equal products are impossible.
Hence

\[
\boxed{\text{no number can appear more than four times in }\Pi}.
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
3.  Four equal products are attainable  
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Choose the ten numbers  

\[
\bigl\{\,2,\ 3,\tfrac12,\ \tfrac92,\ \tfrac13,\
\tfrac{14}{3},\ \tfrac{2}{9},\ \tfrac{43}{9},\ \tfrac{3}{14},\ \tfrac{67}{14}\bigr\}.
\]

(a)  Five equal sums.  
Group them as
\[
\begin{aligned}
2+3 &=5,\\
\frac12+\frac92 &=5,\\
\frac13+\frac{14}{3}&=5,\\
\frac{2}{9}+\frac{43}{9}&=5,\\
\frac{3}{14}+\frac{67}{14}&=5,
\end{aligned}
\]
so the sum \(5\) occurs exactly five times in \(\Sigma\).

(b)  Four equal products.  
The four pairs  

\[
\Bigl(2,\tfrac12\Bigr),\quad
\Bigl(3,\tfrac13\Bigr),\quad
\Bigl(\tfrac92,\tfrac29\Bigr),\quad
\Bigl(\tfrac{14}{3},\tfrac{3}{14}\Bigr)
\]
all have product \(1\).
No other unordered pair of the ten numbers gives product \(1\),
so the value \(1\) occurs exactly four times in \(\Pi\).

Thus the bound found in Section 2 is attainable.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
4.  Conclusion  
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Because five equal products are impossible while four equal products
can actually occur, the greatest possible number of equal products in
Pete’s list is  

\[
\boxed{4}.
\]
ground_truth_solution:
**Solution.** Let $2 s$ be the number that appears five times among the pairwise sums. One number obviously cannot appear in two of these sums (otherwise the other summands in these sums are also equal). Therefore the five sums equal to $2 s$ contain each of the ten numbers exactly once. In each of these sums one number is less than $s$ and another is greater than $s$. Let the terms less than $s$, in increasing order, be $a_{1}<a_{2}<a_{3}<a_{4}<a_{5}$. Writing $2 s=a_{1}+a_{10}=a_{2}+a_{9}=a_{3}+a_{8}=a_{4}+a_{7}=a_{5}+a_{6}$, we obtain the ordering of all the ten numbers: $a_{1}<a_{2}<a_{3}<a_{4}<a_{5}<a_{6}<a_{7}<a_{8}<a_{9}<a_{10}$.

If some product $t^{2}$, too, appears five times among the pairwise products, then, similarly, each of the ten numbers appears exactly once in those five products. If the smaller factors in these products are $b_{1}<b_{2}<b_{3}<b_{4}<b_{5}$ and $t^{2}=b_{1} b_{10}=b_{2} b_{9}=b_{3} b_{8}=b_{4} b_{7}=b_{5} b_{6}$, then $b_{1}<b_{2}<b_{3}<b_{4}<b_{5}<b_{6}<b_{7}<b_{8}<b_{9}<b_{10}$ is also an ordering of the original numbers. But then $a_{i}=b_{i}$ for all $i$, that is, $a_{1}+a_{10}=a_{2}+a_{9}$ and $a_{1} a_{10}=a_{2} a_{9}$. It follows that $a_{1}=a_{2}$ and $a_{9}=a_{10}$, a contradiction.

An example with four equal products can be constructed in the following way. Let $x_{1}=0,9, x_{2 k}=2-x_{2 k-1}$ for $1 \leq k \leq 5$ and $x_{2 k+1}=\frac{1}{2 k}$ for $1 \leq k \leq 4$. Then $x_{1}+x_{2}=x_{3}+x_{4}=x_{5}+x_{6}=x_{7}+x_{8}=x_{9}+x_{10}=2$ and $x_{2} x_{3}=x_{4} x_{5}=x_{6} x_{7}=x_{8} x_{9}=1$. Since obviously $x<\frac{1}{2-x}<1$ for $0<x<1$, we have $x_{1}<x_{3}<x_{5}<x_{7}<x_{9}<1<x_{10}<x_{8}<x_{6}<x_{4}<x_{2}$, and the $10$ numbers in this example are indeed distinct.
llm_summary: The proof shows that the five equal pairwise sums must form a perfect matching of the form (a₁,a₁₀),…,(a₅,a₆) by ordering arguments. It then proves any product value can appear at most five times since indices cannot repeat, and excludes the case of five equal products by demonstrating that a perfect matching a_k·a_{11−k}=p for k=1,…,5 contradicts the strict increase of f(x)=x(s−x) on (0,s/2). Finally, it gives an explicit example of ten rational numbers with exactly four equal products of 1, showing the bound 4 is sharp.

problem: A-3 The octagon $P_{1} P_{2} P_{3} P_{4} P_{5} P_{6} P_{7} P_{8}$ is inscribed in a circle, with the vertices around the circumference in the given order. Given that the polygon $P_{1} P_{3} P_{5} P_{7}$ is a square of area 5, and the polygon $P_{2} P_{4} P_{6} P_{8}$ is a rectangle of area $4$, find the maximum possible area of the octagon.
solution:
Let $C$ be the circle in which the octagon $P_1P_2\dots P_8$ is inscribed. Let $O$ be the center of $C$ and $R$ be its radius.

The polygon $P_1P_3P_5P_7$ is a square of area 5. Let $a$ be its side length. So $a^2=5$.
The vertices $P_1,P_3,P_5,P_7$ lie on the circle $C$. The diagonals of this square are diameters of $C$.
The length of a diagonal is $P_1P_5 = \sqrt{a^2+a^2} = \sqrt{2a^2} = \sqrt{2 \cdot 5} = \sqrt{10}$.
So, $2R = \sqrt{10}$, which implies $4R^2=10$, so $R^2 = 10/4 = 5/2$.

Since $P_1P_3P_5P_7$ is a square, the arcs $P_1P_3, P_3P_5, P_5P_7, P_7P_1$ must be equal.
The central angles subtended by the sides of this square are equal:
$\angle P_1OP_3 = \angle P_3OP_5 = \angle P_5OP_7 = \angle P_7OP_1 = \pi/2$.
The side length $a=P_1P_3$ satisfies $a^2 = R^2+R^2-2R^2\cos(\angle P_1OP_3) = 2R^2(1-\cos(\pi/2)) = 2R^2$.
So $5 = 2R^2 = 2(5/2)=5$. This is consistent.

The polygon $P_2P_4P_6P_8$ is a rectangle of area 4. Let its side lengths be $x$ and $y$. So $xy=4$.
Its vertices $P_2,P_4,P_6,P_8$ lie on $C$. Its diagonals $P_2P_6$ and $P_4P_8$ are diameters of $C$.
So $x^2+y^2 = (2R)^2 = 10$.
We have $xy=4$ and $x^2+y^2=10$.
$x^2+(4/x)^2=10 \implies x^4-10x^2+16=0$.
$(x^2-2)(x^2-8)=0$.
The side lengths are $x=\sqrt{2}$ and $y=\sqrt{8}=2\sqrt{2}$.
Let $P_2P_4 = \sqrt{2}$ and $P_4P_6 = 2\sqrt{2}$.
Let $\alpha = \angle P_2OP_4$ and $\beta = \angle P_4OP_6$.
Using the law of cosines for $P_2P_4$:
$x^2 = (\sqrt{2})^2 = 2 = R^2+R^2-2R^2\cos\alpha = 2R^2(1-\cos\alpha)$.
$2 = 2(5/2)(1-\cos\alpha) = 5(1-\cos\alpha)$.
$1-\cos\alpha = 2/5 \implies \cos\alpha = 3/5$.
Since $\alpha$ is an angle in a triangle $OP_2P_4$ and $P_2P_4$ is a chord, $0 < \alpha < \pi$. So $\sin\alpha = \sqrt{1-(3/5)^2} = 4/5$.
For $P_4P_6$: $y^2 = (2\sqrt{2})^2 = 8 = 2R^2(1-\cos\beta)$.
$8 = 5(1-\cos\beta)$.
$1-\cos\beta = 8/5 \implies \cos\beta = -3/5$.
So $\sin\beta = \sqrt{1-(-3/5)^2} = 4/5$.
Note that $\cos\beta = -\cos\alpha$ and $\sin\beta=\sin\alpha$. This means $\beta = \pi-\alpha$.
This is consistent, as $P_2P_6$ is a diameter, so $\angle P_2OP_6 = \pi$. Thus $\angle P_2OP_4 + \angle P_4OP_6 = \alpha+\beta=\pi$.
Similarly, $\angle P_6OP_8=\alpha$ and $\angle P_8OP_2=\beta$.

Let $\theta_k = \angle P_kOP_{k+1}$ for $k=1,\dots,7$ and $\theta_8 = \angle P_8OP_1$. These are the central angles subtended by the sides of the octagon. All $\theta_k>0$.
The sum of these angles is $\sum_{k=1}^8 \theta_k = 2\pi$.
The area of the octagon is $A = \sum_{k=1}^8 \text{Area}(\triangle OP_kP_{k+1}) = \sum_{k=1}^8 \frac{1}{2}R^2\sin\theta_k$.
Since $R^2=5/2$, $A = \frac{5}{4}\sum_{k=1}^8 \sin\theta_k$.

We have the following relations between the angles:
1.  $\theta_1+\theta_2 = \angle P_1OP_3 = \pi/2$.
2.  $\theta_2+\theta_3 = \angle P_2OP_4 = \alpha$.
3.  $\theta_3+\theta_4 = \angle P_3OP_5 = \pi/2$.
4.  $\theta_4+\theta_5 = \angle P_4OP_6 = \beta$.
5.  $\theta_5+\theta_6 = \angle P_5OP_7 = \pi/2$.
6.  $\theta_6+\theta_7 = \angle P_6OP_8 = \alpha$.
7.  $\theta_7+\theta_8 = \angle P_7OP_1 = \pi/2$.
8.  $\theta_8+\theta_1 = \angle P_8OP_2 = \beta$.

From (1), $\theta_2 = \pi/2-\theta_1$.
From (2), $\theta_3 = \alpha-\theta_2 = \alpha-(\pi/2-\theta_1) = \theta_1+\alpha-\pi/2$.
From (3), $\theta_4 = \pi/2-\theta_3 = \pi/2-(\theta_1+\alpha-\pi/2) = \pi-\theta_1-\alpha$.
From (4), $\theta_5 = \beta-\theta_4 = \beta-(\pi-\theta_1-\alpha)$. Since $\alpha+\beta=\pi$, $\beta-\pi=-\alpha$. So $\theta_5 = -\alpha+\theta_1+\alpha = \theta_1$.
Now we can deduce the pattern:
$\theta_5=\theta_1$.
$\theta_6 = \pi/2-\theta_5 = \pi/2-\theta_1 = \theta_2$.
$\theta_7 = \alpha-\theta_6 = \alpha-\theta_2 = \theta_3$.
$\theta_8 = \pi/2-\theta_7 = \pi/2-\theta_3 = \theta_4$.
We must check consistency with the last equation $\theta_8+\theta_1 = \beta$:
$\theta_4+\theta_1 = (\pi-\theta_1-\alpha)+\theta_1 = \pi-\alpha$. This is indeed $\beta$.
So the angles are in pairs: $\theta_1=\theta_5$, $\theta_2=\theta_6$, $\theta_3=\theta_7$, $\theta_4=\theta_8$.

The sum of sines becomes $\sum \sin\theta_k = 2(\sin\theta_1+\sin\theta_2+\sin\theta_3+\sin\theta_4)$.
Let $\gamma = \pi/2-\alpha$. Then $\cos\gamma = \cos(\pi/2-\alpha) = \sin\alpha = 4/5$ and $\sin\gamma = \sin(\pi/2-\alpha) = \cos\alpha = 3/5$.
The angles are:
$\theta_1$
$\theta_2 = \pi/2-\theta_1$
$\theta_3 = \theta_1+\alpha-\pi/2 = \theta_1-(\pi/2-\alpha) = \theta_1-\gamma$
$\theta_4 = \pi/2-\theta_3 = \pi/2-(\theta_1-\gamma) = \pi/2-\theta_1+\gamma$
The sum of sines is:
$\sin\theta_1$
$\sin\theta_2 = \sin(\pi/2-\theta_1) = \cos\theta_1$
$\sin\theta_3 = \sin(\theta_1-\gamma) = \sin\theta_1\cos\gamma - \cos\theta_1\sin\gamma = \frac{4}{5}\sin\theta_1 - \frac{3}{5}\cos\theta_1$
$\sin\theta_4 = \sin(\pi/2-(\theta_1-\gamma)) = \cos(\theta_1-\gamma) = \cos\theta_1\cos\gamma + \sin\theta_1\sin\gamma = \frac{4}{5}\cos\theta_1 + \frac{3}{5}\sin\theta_1$
So, $\sum \sin\theta_k = 2(\sin\theta_1 + \cos\theta_1 + \frac{4}{5}\sin\theta_1 - \frac{3}{5}\cos\theta_1 + \frac{4}{5}\cos\theta_1 + \frac{3}{5}\sin\theta_1)$.
$\sum \sin\theta_k = 2(\sin\theta_1(1+\frac{4}{5}+\frac{3}{5}) + \cos\theta_1(1-\frac{3}{5}+\frac{4}{5}))$.
$\sum \sin\theta_k = 2(\sin\theta_1(\frac{5+4+3}{5}) + \cos\theta_1(\frac{5-3+4}{5})) = 2(\frac{12}{5}\sin\theta_1 + \frac{6}{5}\cos\theta_1)$.
$\sum \sin\theta_k = \frac{24}{5}\sin\theta_1 + \frac{12}{5}\cos\theta_1$.
The area of the octagon is $A = \frac{5}{4}\left(\frac{24}{5}\sin\theta_1 + \frac{12}{5}\cos\theta_1\right) = 6\sin\theta_1 + 3\cos\theta_1$.

To maximize $A(\theta_1) = 6\sin\theta_1 + 3\cos\theta_1 = 3(2\sin\theta_1 + \cos\theta_1)$.
Let $f(\theta_1) = 2\sin\theta_1 + \cos\theta_1$. We can write this as $f(\theta_1) = K\sin(\theta_1+\delta)$ where $K=\sqrt{2^2+1^2}=\sqrt{5}$, and $\cos\delta = 2/\sqrt{5}$, $\sin\delta = 1/\sqrt{5}$.
So $f(\theta_1) = \sqrt{5}\sin(\theta_1+\delta)$. This function has a maximum value of $\sqrt{5}$.
The maximum area is $A = 3\sqrt{5}$.

This maximum occurs when $\theta_1+\delta = \pi/2$, so $\theta_1 = \pi/2-\delta$.
$\sin\theta_1 = \sin(\pi/2-\delta) = \cos\delta = 2/\sqrt{5}$.
$\cos\theta_1 = \cos(\pi/2-\delta) = \sin\delta = 1/\sqrt{5}$.
(Alternatively, $f'(\theta_1)=2\cos\theta_1-\sin\theta_1=0 \implies \tan\theta_1=2$. This gives $\sin\theta_1=2/\sqrt{5}$ and $\cos\theta_1=1/\sqrt{5}$.)

We must ensure that all angles $\theta_k$ are positive.
$\theta_1 > 0$: $\theta_1=\pi/2-\delta = \arctan(2) \approx 1.107$ rad. This is positive.
$\theta_2 = \pi/2-\theta_1 = \delta = \arctan(1/2) \approx 0.464$ rad. This is positive.
$\theta_3 = \theta_1-\gamma > 0 \implies \theta_1 > \gamma$.
$\gamma = \pi/2-\alpha$. Since $\cos\alpha=3/5, \sin\alpha=4/5$, $\alpha=\arctan(4/3)$.
So $\gamma = \pi/2-\arctan(4/3) = \arctan(3/4)$.
The condition is $\arctan(2) > \arctan(3/4)$. Since $\arctan$ is increasing, this is $2 > 3/4$, which is true.
$\theta_3 = \arctan(2) - \arctan(3/4)$.
$\tan\theta_3 = \tan(\arctan(2) - \arctan(3/4)) = \frac{2-3/4}{1+2(3/4)} = \frac{5/4}{1+6/4} = \frac{5/4}{10/4} = 1/2$. So $\theta_3=\arctan(1/2)$. This is positive.
$\theta_4 = \pi/2-\theta_1+\gamma = \pi/2-(\theta_1-\gamma) = \pi/2-\theta_3 = \pi/2-\arctan(1/2) = \arctan(2)$. This is positive.
All angles $\theta_1, \theta_2, \theta_3, \theta_4$ are positive, so $\theta_5, \theta_6, \theta_7, \theta_8$ are also positive.
The condition for $\theta_1$ for all angles to be positive is $\gamma < \theta_1 < \pi/2$.
$\theta_1 = \arctan(2)$. $\gamma = \arctan(3/4)$.
$\arctan(3/4) < \arctan(2) < \pi/2$. This is true because $3/4 < 2$ and $2>0$.
The value of $\theta_1$ that maximizes the area is within the allowed range.

Thus, the maximum possible area of the octagon is $3\sqrt{5}$.

To verify calculation of $A$:
$A = 6\sin\theta_1 + 3\cos\theta_1 = 6(2/\sqrt{5}) + 3(1/\sqrt{5}) = (12+3)/\sqrt{5} = 15/\sqrt{5} = 3\sqrt{5}$.

Final check of the problem setup:
1.  $P_1P_3P_5P_7$ is a square of area 5. This yields $R^2=5/2$. This means $\angle P_1OP_3=\pi/2$.
2.  $P_2P_4P_6P_8$ is a rectangle of area 4. Sides are $\sqrt{2}, 2\sqrt{2}$. $\angle P_2OP_4=\alpha$ with $\cos\alpha=3/5$.
3.  Vertices are in order $P_1, P_2, \dots, P_8$.
4.  Maximum area is $A = (5/4)\sum \sin\theta_k$.
All steps hold.

The final answer is $\boxed{3\sqrt{5}}$.
ground_truth_solution:
A-3 The maximum area is $3 \sqrt{5}$.
We deduce from the area of $P_{1} P_{3} P_{5} P_{7}$ that the radius of the circle is $\sqrt{5 / 2}$. An easy calculation using the

Pythagorean Theorem then shows that the rectangle $P_{2} P_{4} P_{6} P_{8}$ has sides $\sqrt{2}$ and $2 \sqrt{2}$. For notational ease, denote the area of a polygon by putting brackets around the name of the polygon.
By symmetry, the area of the octagon can be expressed as

$$
\left[P_{2} P_{4} P_{6} P_{8}\right]+2\left[P_{2} P_{3} P_{4}\right]+2\left[P_{4} P_{5} P_{6}\right]
$$

Note that $\left[P_{2} P_{3} P_{4}\right]$ is $\sqrt{2}$ times the distance from $P_{3}$ to $P_{2} P_{4}$, which is maximized when $P_{3}$ lies on the midpoint of $\operatorname{arc} P_{2} P_{4}$; similarly, $\left[P_{4} P_{5} P_{6}\right]$ is $\sqrt{2} / 2$ times the distance from $P_{5}$ to $P_{4} P_{6}$, which is maximized when $P_{5}$ lies on the midpoint of arc $P_{4} P_{6}$. Thus the area of the octagon is maximized when $P_{3}$ is the midpoint of $\operatorname{arc} P_{2} P_{4}$ and $P_{5}$ is the midpoint of arc $P_{4} P_{6}$. In this case, it is easy to calculate that $\left[P_{2} P_{3} P_{4}\right]=\sqrt{5}-1$ and $\left[P_{4} P_{5} P_{6}\right]=\sqrt{5} / 2-1$, and so the area of the octagon is $3 \sqrt{5}$.

problem:
B3 Determine all real numbers $a>0$ for which there exists a nonnegative continuous function $f(x)$ defined on $[0, a]$ with the property that the region

$$
R=\{(x, y) ; 0 \leq x \leq a, 0 \leq y \leq f(x)\}
$$
has perimeter $k$ units and area $k$ square units for some real number $k$.
solution:
Let  

\[
A=\int_{0}^{a}f(x)\,dx ,\qquad   
P=a+f(0)+f(a)+\int_{0}^{a}\sqrt{1+f'(x)^{2}}\;dx
\]

denote respectively the area and the perimeter of the region  

\[
R=\{(x,y)\; ;\; 0\le x\le a,\; 0\le y\le f(x)\}.
\]

(Here the four parts of the boundary of \(R\) are the bottom segment on the
\(x\)-axis, the two vertical sides and the graph \(y=f(x)\).)  
We have to decide for which positive numbers \(a\) there is a non–negative
continuous \(f\) with \(A=P\).  

--------------------------------------------------------------------
1.  A universal inequality between \(A\) and \(P\)
--------------------------------------------------------------------

Put  

\[
M=\max_{0\le x\le a}f(x)\;\;(\;M\ge 0\;).
\]

(i)  Since \(f(x)\le M\) on \([0,a]\),

\[
A\le Ma. \tag{1}
\]

(ii)  Fix a point \(x_{0}\in[0,a]\) with \(f(x_{0})=M\).
Moving anticlockwise around the boundary of \(R\) we first ascend
from height \(0\) to \(f(0)\), then climb along the graph up to height
\(M\), afterwards descend along the graph to height \(f(a)\), and finally
go down the right–hand vertical segment to height \(0\).
Hence the total vertical rise and fall along the three upper pieces of
the boundary equals \(2M\).  
Every boundary piece is at least as long as its vertical projection, so the
combined length of the two vertical sides and the
graph is at least \(2M\).
Adding the bottom side of length \(a\) gives  

\[
P\ge a+2M. \tag{2}
\]

(iii)  From (1) and (2) we obtain  

\[
A\le aM\le \frac{a}{2}(a+2M)\le\frac{a}{2}\,P. \tag{3}
\]

Consequently  

\[
\frac{A}{P}\le\frac{a}{2}\qquad\text{for \emph{every} admissible }f. \tag{4}
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
2.  Non–existence for \(a\le 2\)
--------------------------------------------------------------------

If \(a\le 2\) then \(a/2\le 1\).  Inequality (4) shows

\[
A\le\frac{a}{2}P\le P,
\]

and in fact strict inequality holds (because in (1) and (2) at least
one is strict unless \(f\equiv0\), which is impossible when \(A=P>0\)).
Thus \(A<P\) for every \(f\), so the equality \(A=P\) can
\emph{never} be achieved when \(a\le 2\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
3.  Construction for \(a>2\)
--------------------------------------------------------------------

Assume \(a>2\) and choose the constant function  

\[
f(x)\equiv c,\qquad c=\frac{2a}{a-2}>0 .
\]

Then  

\[
A=\int_{0}^{a}c\,dx=ac,
\]
while the boundary of the rectangle of width \(a\) and height \(c\) consists
of two horizontal sides of length \(a\) and two vertical sides of length
\(c\); hence  

\[
P=2a+2c=2(a+c)=2\!\left(a+\frac{2a}{a-2}\right)
          =\frac{2a^{2}}{a-2}=ac=A .
\]

Thus the equality \(A=P\) is attained when \(a>2\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
4.  Conclusion
--------------------------------------------------------------------

•  If \(a\le 2\) no suitable function exists.  
•  If \(a>2\) the constant function displayed above works.

Therefore the desired set is  

\[
\boxed{\;a>2\;}.
\]
ground_truth_solution: B-3 The answer is $\{a \mid a>2\}$. If $a>2$, then the function $f(x)=2 a /(a-2)$ has the desired property; both perimeter and area of $R$ in this case are $2 a^{2} /(a-2)$. Now suppose that $a \leq 2$, and let $f(x)$ be a nonnegative continuous function on $[0, a]$. Let $P=\left(x_{0}, y_{0}\right)$ be a point on the graph of $f(x)$ with maximal $y$-coordinate; then the area of $R$ is at most $a y_{0}$ since it lies below the line $y=y_{0}$. On the other hand, the points $(0,0),(a, 0)$, and $P$ divide the boundary of $R$ into three sections. The length of the section between $(0,0)$ and $P$ is at least the distance between $(0,0)$ and $P$, which is at least $y_{0}$; the length of the section between $P$ and $(a, 0)$ is similarly at least $y_{0}$; and the length of the section between $(0,0)$ and $(a, 0)$ is $a$. Since $a \leq 2$, we have $2 y_{0}+a>a y_{0}$ and hence the perimeter of $R$ is strictly greater than the area of $R$.

problem: A-2 Alice and Bob play a game in which they take turns removing stones from a heap that initially has $n$ stones. The number of stones removed at each turn must be one less than a prime number. The winner is the player who takes the last stone. Alice plays first. Prove that there are infinitely many $n$ such that Bob has a winning strategy. (For example, if $n=17$, then Alice might take $6$ leaving 11; then Bob might take $1$ leaving 10; then Alice can take the remaining stones to win.)
solution:
Here is a complete proof.  We think of the game as an impartial “subtraction” game with subtraction‐set  
\[
S \;=\;\{\,p-1: p\text{ is prime}\} \;=\;\{1,2,4,6,10,12,16,18,\dots\}.
\]
A position (heap of size) $n$ is called an  N–position if the next player to move can force a win, and a P–position if the previous player (i.e.\ the opponent of the player to move) can force a win.  In the usual theory one shows:

 1.  $0$ is a P–position.
 2.  A position $n>0$ is N exactly if it can move to some P (i.e.\ $\exists\,s\in S$, $s\le n$ with $n-s$ a P).
 3.  A position $n$ is P exactly if **every** move takes it to an N (i.e.\ for all $s\in S$, $s\le n$, the position $n-s$ is N).

We shall exhibit *infinitely many* P–positions.  We do so by the standard “greedy” construction of P–positions for a (possibly infinite) subtraction game.

Definition.  Let
\[
a_1 = 0,
\]
and having chosen
\[
a_1 < a_2 < \cdots < a_{k-1},
\]
define
\[
a_k
\;=\;
\min\Bigl\{\,n>a_{k-1}:\;n - a_j\not\in S\text{ for all }1\le j<k\Bigr\}.
\]
In words, we pick the next P–position to be the least integer bigger than the last one which is *not* at a subtraction‐distance in $S$ from *any* earlier P–position.  We will show:

(i) This process never gets stuck, so produces an *infinite* strictly increasing sequence
\[
0 = a_1 < a_2 < a_3 < \cdots.
\]

(ii) Exactly the set $\{a_k\}$ it produces is the set of P–positions of our game.

From (ii) it follows at once that there are infinitely many P–positions, i.e.\ infinitely many $n$ for which Bob (the *second* player) has a winning strategy.

——————————————

Proof of (i):  that the greedy process never stops.  

Let $k>1$ and suppose we already have $a_1<\cdots<a_{k-1}$.  We must show there is some $n>a_{k-1}$ with
\[
n-a_j\notin S
\quad\forall\,j<k.
\]
Equivalently, we must show the *union* of the finitely many “forbidden‐sets”
\[
F \;=\;\bigcup_{j=1}^{k-1}\bigl(S + a_j\bigr)
\;=\;\{\,s+a_j : s\in S,\;1\le j<k\}
\]
does *not* contain *all* sufficiently large integers.  Equivalently, the *complement* of $F$ in $\Bbb N$ is infinite, so we can pick 
\[
a_k \;=\;\min\bigl(\Bbb N\setminus F\cap (a_{k-1},\infty)\bigr).
\]
It suffices to see that $F$ has arbitrarily long gaps.  But $S=\{p-1\}$ has arbitrarily long gaps because prime‐gaps are unbounded:  indeed from elementary number theory one knows there are runs of composites
\[
(n+1)!,\,(n+1)!+2,\dots,(n+1)!+n
\]
of length $n-1$, none of which is of the form “prime − 1.”  Hence $S$ itself omits an interval of length $n-1$.  If $S$ omits $[x,x+L-1]$, then each translate $S+a_j$ omits 
\[
[x+a_j\,,\,x+a_j+L-1].
\]
Since only finitely many shifts $a_j$ appear, say $a_j\le D$ for $j<k$, the intersection of these $k-1$ “omitted‐intervals” is
\[
\bigcap_{j<k}[\,x+a_j\,,\,x+a_j+L-1\,]
\;=\;
[\,x+\max a_j\;,\;x+\min a_j+L-1\,]
\;=\;
[x + D\,,\,x + L-1].
\]
As soon as $L-1>D$, this is nonempty.  Thus there is some integer $>a_{k-1}=D$ missing from *every* translate $S+a_j$, i.e.\ not in the union $F$.  That becomes our $a_k$.  Hence we can continue forever, and the $a_k$ form an infinite strictly increasing sequence.

——————————————

Proof of (ii):  that exactly the $a_k$ are the P–positions.

Claim 1.  Each $a_k$ is a P–position.  
Proof by induction on $k$.  For $k=1$, $a_1=0$ is P by convention.  Now assume $a_1,\dots,a_{k-1}$ are all P.  We check that $n=a_k$ is P.  By construction, for *every* $s\in S$ with $s\le a_k$, the position
\[
a_k - s
\]
is *not* equal to any earlier $a_j$ (otherwise $a_k-s\in S$ with $a_k-s=a_j$ would contradict the defining condition of $a_k$).  Hence every move $s$ from $a_k$ lands in a position *not* in $\{a_j\}$; but by the inductive hypothesis every such position is N.  Therefore *all* moves from $a_k$ go to N–positions, so $a_k$ itself is P.

Claim 2.  Every $n\notin\{a_k\}$ is N.  
Indeed, if $n$ is not chosen as some $a_k$, then at the stage when the greedy algorithm had built $a_1<\cdots<a_{k-1}$ just below $n$, the condition “$n-a_j\notin S$ for all $j<k$” must have failed (otherwise $n$ *would* have been picked as $a_k$).  Thus there is some $j<k$ and some $s\in S$ with
\[
n - s \;=\; a_j.
\]
But $a_j$ is a P–position by Claim 1, so from $n$ the next player can move by taking $s$ stones directly to a P–position.  Hence *every* $n\notin\{a_k\}$ is an N–position.

Together Claim 1 and Claim 2 show that *exactly* the numbers $a_1,a_2,a_3,\dots$ are the P–positions of the game.  Since we showed there are infinitely many $a_k$, the set of P–positions is infinite.  In particular there are infinitely many starting‐heap‐sizes $n$ for which the first player (Alice) is on a P–position and so Bob, playing second, has a winning strategy.

This completes the proof that there are infinitely many $n$ for which Bob wins.  QED.
